column17: On September 19, 2016, the City of Atlanta hosted an Agenda Setting Workshop at The Carter Center. It was well attended by a diverse cross section of Atlanta stakeholders and was the initial kick-off of the Resilient Atlanta effort. In November 2016, the City of Atlanta hired its first Chief Resilience Officer (CRO) and expanded, restructured, and renamed the Mayor's Office of Sustainability to become the Mayor's Office of Resilience. The CRO is an innovative position in city government that serves on the Mayor's Cabinet and coordinates resilience efforts across the City. From November 2016 to October 2017, Atlanta's CRO and her team worked with over 7,000 Metro Atlantans to develop a clear actionable set of initiatives that articulate their aspirations for the city's future. Diversity is a cornerstone of Atlanta's rich history and culture, so the process was designed to ensure a broad range of participants representing Metro Atlanta's communities, neighborhoods, and perspectives.

column17: City of Atlanta's OSR and Department of City Planning helped create and fund AgLanta which represents a combination of agriculture and Atlanta to help tackle issues like food insecurity that is widespread in Atlanta. It's goal is to create a more equitable access to fresh, healthy food in low-income, food desert areas of Atlanta and make sure 85% of Atlanta residents are within a 1/2 mile of fresh food. Some of AgLanta's programs include Urban Food Forest at Browns Mill, AgLanta grown, AgLanta \'Grows-A-Lot\', and Food Matters. The Urban Food Forest is the city's first managed food forest and the seven acre city owned land is located in Lakewood. The area is identified as a food desert so residents who have difficulty with transportation or financial issues can have a local source to buy locally grown produce. Carbon emissions can be greatly lowered by reducing the distance residents travel for a necessity like food and also cutting down transportation emissions from trucks supplying the food to grocery stores from farms. AgLanta \'Grows-A-Lot\' helps entrepreneurs, non-profits, and residents to create food forests of their own by adopting an empty public property to help create a new urban garden or urban farm. Excluding the food forest at Browns Mill, 7 other food forests have been adopted in places like Mechanicsville, Carver Hills, Venetian Hills, Downtown, Fairburn Heights, Vine City, and Oakland City. The Food Matters program is focused on saving the percentage of produce wasted which is up to 40% of all produce. Reducing food waste has environmental, societal, and economic benefits as less food is in landfill producing methane and carbon emissions and more disadvantaged communities can have access to the food that's not being used. Preventing food waste is reducing the quantity of food wasted, recovery is utilizing the excess food, and composting is using food scraps for soil nutrition which help grow healthier crops and sequester carbon.https://www.aglanta.org/

column17: In 2020, the City of Austin approved a five-year interlocal agreement (ILA) between the City and The University of Texas at Austin that streamlines and coordinate research efforts between the two organizations. This has allowed us to save time, money, and allowing staff to meet the needs of City residents more easily. Prior to the adoption of the ILA, the process to identify research partners and secure funding was time-consuming and decentralized. Now, the ILA streamlines city research projects by establishing pre-negotiated terms and conditions, removing administrative barriers, and pre-approving $7.5 million for research, consulting and technical assistance from UT faculty and researchers. To date, multiple projects have used the ILA to advance research and projects to address challenging civic issues. Some of those projects include updating climate projections, a projections of Green Job opportunities in Austin, support tool for promoting equitable Transit-Oriented Development, mapping ambient heat in low-income communities and improving housing conditions and stability for residents experiencing gentrification, and advancing a localized air quality monitoring network. Recently, staff from the Office of Sustainability have worked with UT Austin faculty, community organizers and community members to map heat in low-income communities and For the Resilience Hub Network initiative, City of Austin staff continue their collaboration with Austin Independent School District (AISD) and Travis County staff to explore what it would take to deliver on the Resilience Hub resolution's intent. This initiative represents a robust collaborative among key Central Texas agencies, which yield a strong long-term program aimed at better preparing our community to respond to and bounce back from extreme events. Organizations participating in the initiative include local hospitals, community organizers, food pantries, disaster relief organizations, and other groups representing low-income, communities of color.The Office of Sustainability partnered with the UT School of Public Health and Dell Medical School to assess community food needs during the COVID-19 pandemic response utilizing call data from United Way's 211 hotline. Additionally, the Office of Sustainability contracted the Division of Community Engagement and Healthy Equity at Dell Medical School at UT Austin to identify community needs related to food access during the heigh of the COVID-19 pandemic by gathering data from local organizations. The research contributed to the strategy for emergency food access implemented by the City of Austin's Emergency Operations Center.The Austin Climate Equity Plan was adopted in September 2021. The process to strategize and draft the plan was highly collaborative and involved partnerships and relationship-building with community-based organizations, academics, practitioners, and included the creation of a pilot Community Climate Ambassadors Program. Now that the plan has been passed, the City is in the process of creating an implementation framework that can continue to expand community engagement and move the City to a community ownership model of decision-making.

column17: The Energy Company Obligation (ECO) is a government energy efficiency scheme designed to tackle fuel poverty and help reduce carbon emissions, which is currently in its 4th iteration, ECO4, running from April 2022 to March 2026. Over the last year the council has identified several opportunities and made significant progress on drawing investment for Birmingham's homes through the ECO retrofit programme. Building on our previous experience with ECO and learning from best practice examples from other local authorities, including Greater Manchester Combined Authority and Liverpool City Council, Birmingham City Council took the bold decision to procure ECO installer partners to deliver home retrofit measures. The two partners have already commenced installations across the city and are working with the council, communities and other stakeholders, to drive the delivery of energy efficiency measures to Birmingham homes. The initiative aims to harness £45m per year of private investments, achieve estimated fuel bill savings of £1.2m, and reduce the carbon emissions from the city's homes by 4,500 tonnes per year.

column17: Heat networks are expected to provide significant emissions reductions, particularly in urban areas, through the decarbonisation of heating and cooling. The council has been working with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) on the Advanced Zoning Programme to identify locations in Birmingham where heat networks may present the most cost-effective method for decarbonising heat. Maps showing existing energy centres supplying heat via heat networks, and potential heat network zones across Birmingham have been published by DESNZ. These maps are an output of the National Heat Network tool, which will be used to refine the boundaries of potential zones once the legislation commences. The Energy Act 2023 enables government to implement heat network zoning regulations in England and secondary legislation to formally commence heat network zoning is due to come into effect during 2025. The Council has a key enabling role to play in this energy transition and we are working with DESNZ and stakeholders from across the city to develop a heat network strategy and delivery plan for the city which identifies and realises these opportunities.

column17: Birmingham City Council is a partner, alongside Wolverhampton City Council, Aston University, Birmingham City University and the University of Birmingham, in the Digital Innovation Transformative Change (DIATOMIC) Accelerator project, which is designed to accelerate place-based innovation in the West Midlands, harnessing the region's existing international relationships through a series of targeted initiatives. Now in its third year, the programme led by Connected Places Catapult is designed to increase innovation capacity in the West Midlands, support economic growth, and strengthen the region's research and development ecosystem. At its core is the development of a Digital Twin platform, enabling SMEs to test and demonstrate new digital models in secure environments. These models are helping to unlock smart investment zones in Birmingham's Knowledge Quarter and Wolverhampton's Green Innovation Corridor. This digital infrastructure connects local authorities and academic partners with SMEs, allowing real-world challenges to be addressed through innovative solutions. It supports the translation of research into commercial applications, leading to more effective, data-led decision-making. DIATOMIC will support 10 more SMEs, deliver five new Digital Twin use cases, and generate an additional £10 million in co-investment. With a strong focus on the Black Country, the programme continues to create an innovation-led, resilient economy for the West Midlands.

column17: Birmingham City Council, in partnership with Solihull Metropolitan Borough Council, have secured £290k UK Shared Prosperity Funding to deliver our 'Sustainable Supply Chains for Birmingham & Solihull' (SSCBAS) project, which will work with our Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) and support them to decarbonise their operations. Since commencing this activity, and working across both councils, we have improved our understanding of the councils' procurement spend profile and GHG emissions, engaged with our suppliers about their net zero commitments, activities and performance, and delivered targeted support for our SME suppliers with the transition to net zero. Our ambition is for this activity to provide training and non-financial support to almost 60 SMEs, and work with a third of these to support them develop decarbonisation plans. We have maximised the reach and impact of these activities through collaborating with the UKSPF Circular Economy in Birmingham and Solihull (CEBAS) programme, which is being delivered by International Synergies. SSCBAS concluded in March 2025.

The Defra funded £1million LINC programme was part of the government's Green Finance Strategy and will build the capacity and capability of local leaders and partners to attract finance at scale to: Create a nature-positive future, restoring habitats and biodiversity, and connectivity for people and nature. Deliver nature-based solutions to climate risks; improve water quality; reduce flood risk; sequester carbon; improve air quality; and provide urban cooling. Address socio-economic related inequalities in health by improving the quality quantity, and access to green and blue space. Maximise the opportunities and benefits of ecosystem services and natural capital assets. Strengthen the region's green economy to provide environmental improvements and sustainable growth as part of the Levelling Up agenda, Climate Adaptation Plans, Local Nature Recovery Strategy, Net Zero, and Biodiversity Net Gain. The LINC programme has enabled the public sector (and their third sector partners) to become more market-facing with their projects and programmes, which will support the delivery of the West Midlands Natural Environment Plan. column17: Partnership working and collaboration across the heat network sector are critical for both the public and private sector to come together to support the delivery of heat networks that supply low carbon heat at a fair cost to consumers. With Heat Network Regulation and Zoning legislation introduced through the Energy Act 2023 and Secondary Legislation expected soon to deliver further detail on this. The GLA has an active collaboration with London Councils (collective of all London Boroughs and City of London) and the London Boroughs to work together to ensure a strategic approach to the development and delivery of multi-borough heat networks across London. The GLA have recently published some important reports on the opportunities represented by London's Waste Heat Sources and The River Thames (see link) to better understand the opportunity they represent and the scale of multi-borough heat networks that they could support, as an example seven strategic heat networks were identified requiring a combined investment iof around £2.4bn and that could deliver around 40 million tonnes of carbon savings over 40 years. Engagement with central Government is essential for helping to influence/shape what Regulation and Zoning ultimately looks like and that has continued over the last year as they continue to define what this will look like. Engagement with other stakeholders is also happening especially around important heat loads or heat sources, for example hospital and university sites for demand and Energy Recovery Facilities and Sewage Treatment Works for heat sources, that engagement will only get more extensive and detailed as the process of Regulation and Zoning continues through secondary legislation and then implementation. The GLA and London Councils are currently running workshops with boroughs to investigate how to deliver the Zone Coordinator role in London as an essential part of the new heat network delivery mechanism. The process is continuing across London Government and evolves as information and detail around the process becomes available from government. This is will involve collaboration with a wider group of stakeholders over the coming years The London Plan also sets clear policies in relation to heat networks, to ensure that developments support them or are built ready to connect to them in the future (where appropriate). The GLA is also working with London boroughs to deliver sub-regional Local Area Energy Plans (LAEPs), three of the four have been completed and the fourth will be completed by the end of 2025 (see link), these identify the amount and type of technology and retrofit required within different parts of the city to get to net zero and enable far more efficient energy planning and effective delivery of decarbonisation activity. The next phase of the sub-regional LAEP process is the borough-level LAEP where the detail and resolution is greater again so that portfolios of specific decarbonisation projects can be identified and then taken through development and into delivery and currently 17 of the 33 London Authorities have completed or are undertaking this final phase of the LAEP process.

column17: In March 2021 the Department for Transport published the National Bus Strategy, Bus Back Better which required Local Transport Authorities (LTAs) to produce a Bus Service Improvement Plan (BSIP.) In simple terms the BSIP sets out how Essex County Council (ECC) will increase the number of people travelling by bus and make buses more attractive than the car for more people. In June 2021 ECC agreed that the BSIP would be delivered through Enhanced Partnerships, a legal partnership between ECC and local bus operators. The partnership has published network reviews for each district; agreed distinct numbering for bus services within districts and common dates for network changes; undertaken 49 infrastructure schemes to improve the bus network at an ultra-local level and supported growth in bus patronage. (https://www.essexhighways.org/uploads/downloads/temp/enhanced%20plan%20and%20scheme.pdf) ECC has now commenced work on its first District level Enhanced Partnership for Tendring. It has also been successful, in partnership with First Essex, in securing 30m of investment including funding from the Department for Transport under their ZEBRA scheme to electrify the Basildon bus fleet and depot. This will bring 55 all-electric buses to Essex in 2025. Zebra https://news-easteng.firstbus.co.uk/news/work-starts-to-bring-electric-buses-to-basildon https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2024/new-electric-buses-basildon In addition ECC is investing 9.8m of BSIP funding in a range of projects including DigiGo, its demand responsive minibus service, and a range of projects aimed at securing growth in market town services. DigiGo will run until at least 2026, and has been expanded to cover more of Essex (https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2023/digigo-service-extended-march-2026) (https://www.essex.gov.uk/news/2024/digigo-service-expands). \nECC has also received some £17,802,280 in funding for capital and revenue support for bus services for 2025 to 20-27 and is currently in the process of delivering this. \n

- deliver the necessary action to reverse the current path of decline in our biodiversity

-farmers and landowners 
-environmental and community groups 
-parish and town councils 
-supporting authorities

- To create networks of bigger, better, more connected habitats
- To have green and blue habitats covering 25% of the county 
by 2030, with an ambition to achieve 30%, compared to 14% 
coverage today

column17: The Low Carbon Across the South and East (LoCASE) programme was supported by the European Regional Development Fund to provide a free business support programme in the South and East of England. Its aim was to help businesses become more competitive and profitable while protecting the environment and encouraging low carbon solutions. To do this, LoCASE provided grants for businesses of up to 10,000, as well as training workshops and fully funded events. Targeted business support was on offer for companies which offer “green” or low carbon goods and services The programme started in 2016 and ended in mid-2023. Since its beginning 2.6m has been awarded to 397 businesses with an estimated 2,902 tonnes CO2 equivalent emissions reduction and 992,534 cost savings per annum within Greater Essex (including Southend and Thurrock). Further funding was secured for the partnership to extend the delivery of support to SMEs until June 2023, with an expected 2.7m of grants available to Greater Essex businesses. In Essex alone it has delivered support to over 460 businesses, annual savings of close to 1,400,000, and saved over 3,000 tonnes CO2e. Over 50 jobs have also been created as a result of this programme. We've already helped part fund the development and marketing of 87 new products and services.

The Community Energy Team within Essex County Council's Energy and Low Carbon Team has made significant strides in supporting and growing the community energy movement across the county.

Through our flagship Pathways programme, we continue to mentor and empower a growing network of community energy groups. What began with just four incorporated groups in 2024 has now doubled to eight, with a further 20 groups actively developing new community-led energy projects. This growth reflects the increasing appetite across Essex for local, sustainable energy solutions.

In July 2025, we are proud to launch the wider rollout of our pioneering Community-Led Energy Planning initiative. Following a successful pilot, this place-based approach is now being introduced in towns and villages across Essex. It enables residents to shape how their local energy systems should evolve, helping communities to co-create tailored strategies for a more sustainable and resilient energy future.

We are also holding renewable energy developers to account, ensuring they contribute meaningfully to the communities they operate in—whether through community benefit funds, shared ownership models, or both. This will ensure that the transition to low-carbon energy is not only green but fair. We are in discussions with over 6 developers with a potential community benefit fund yield of £1.5 million/year for communities across the county. 

Our monthly Essex Community Energy Network meetings bring together groups from across the county to share knowledge, collaborate, and build a strong community of practice. These sessions foster peer learning and keep the momentum going.

We are also working to strengthen the relationship between schools and community energy groups. By staying on top of policy developments and raising awareness among headteachers and estate managers, we're helping schools become active participants in the local energy transition.

Internally, we continue to raise the profile of community energy within Essex County Council, ensuring it is embedded in wider strategic thinking and delivery.

column17: ECC is a partner on the Ofgem Strategic Innovation Funded (SIF) SHIELD project. SHIELD stands for Smart Heat and Intelligent Energy in Low Income Districts and was designed to address the issue of a just transition for all in the journey toward net zero. SHIELD offers an innovative low carbon, affordable heat and energy solution for low income households. SHIELD seeks to combine various technologies, some established (PV and battery) and some novel (the Thermify HeatHub) (How it works - thermify, which captures waste heat from data processing activities and makes it available for affordable space and water heating within homes) to address the issue of fuel poverty. It will also explore the technological and financial possibilities of trading energy locally, creating new markets with both a social and a commercial focus. Funding to date has allowed for extensive modelling of proposed solutions, two instances of pilot technology installations and most recently a scale up of those trials over a four year period. SHIELD is delivered by a large partnership of organisations including UKPower Networks, ECC, UK Community Works CIC, Power Circle Projects Ltd and UK Power Networks, Citizens' Advice Essex, Thermify, Urban Chain and a number of social landlords.\n

column17: The new National Energy System Operator (NESO), has been commissioned by the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to provide independent advice on the pathways towards the 2030 Clean Power ambition. NESO will also produce a Regional Energy Strategic Plan (RESP) to bring together local and regional stakeholders to create joined-up energy plans (including electricity, gas, and hydrogen) for each region of Great Britain. There will be a RESP for the Eastern region covering Essex, Suffolk and Norfolk. The RESP aims to support local strategic priorities as well as national goals related to clean power. It does this by informing Ofgem's 5-yearly Electricity Price Control (ED) determination with the network operator (which in Essex is UK Power Networks). The next ED period is ED3 which covers 2028-2033. ED3 will be determined in early 2026 and NESO will provide a 'Transitional Regional Energy Strategic Plan' (tRESP) to support the outcome. This is in advance of NESO developing a more “enduring RESP” in late-2027 to a pathway to 2050. The tRESP serves as an opportunity for ECC to feed in its priorities for growth and identify areas of strategic network investment need. ECC are currently inputting data on strategically important projects to inform the tRESP. ECC have convened a working group that covers multiple internal and external partners to input projects from across Essex. ECC will be engaging fully with the RESP process and have already attended multiple forum meetings and responded to consultations and will continue to do so as the work progresses.

Essex County Council Travel Planning Programme: Essex County Council's Sustainable Travel Planning Officers support the development and implementation of Travel Plans for residential, workplace, and schools, aiming to reduce single-occupancy car use and promote sustainable travel - key actions in lowering transport-related carbon emissions.

Residential Travel Plans are Required for developments with 80+ dwellings and should include:
•	Targets to reduce car use, based on census data
•	Measures to support behavioural change
•	Annual Monitoring Reports to track progress
•	Monitoring Fees secured via Section 106 agreements, covering a minimum five-year period

New and enhanced guidance is currently being developed for large developments (1,000 dwellings+) and Garden Community sites providing a more robust process with greater links to Transport Assessments, with the aim of supporting ECC objectives in achieving better net zero carbon outcomes. 

Residential Travel Information Packs are distributed to new residents, these district-specific packs promote sustainable travel through:
•	highlighting the benefits of walking/cycling 
•	Local cycling routes
•	Bus timetables
•	Electric Vehicle grants and ownership, plus car sharing info

Workplace Travel Plans are required for developments with 50+ employees or those impacting local transport networks. Plans aim to reduce car commuting and include:
•	Targets and measures as stated above 
•	Access to our Smarter Travel for Essex Network (STEN), offering free, tailored support for sustainable travel, congestion, air quality, and staff retention - we have increased participation in this group by 25% over the past few years

School Travel Plans are mandatory for new/expanding schools and encouraged for all. Plans focus on pupil travel, engaging staff and parents to improve safety, health, and sustainability. ECC supports schools in creating and monitoring plans. There are currently 41 schools holding national accreditation for their Travel Plans. 

Case Study: Saffron Walden Clean Air Project All local schools achieved full accreditation by integrating active travel and anti-idling measures into their Travel Plans. The project led to measurable reductions in CO₂ and air pollutants, with pupils actively engaged in observing improvements.

In Our Nature is a collaborative programme designed to place the needs of Manchester's communities at the forefront of climate action. This initiative is a partnership involving Manchester Climate Change Agency, Hubbub, Groundwork Greater Manchester, Amity, the Tyndall Centre for Climate Research, and Manchester City Council.

The Net Zero New Build City Challenge ran throughout 2023 and into early 2024. Working across four sub-groups, and with Manchester City Council's planning department, this City Challenge developed recommendations for reducing the operational and embodied carbon in new buildings to be considered for inclusion within the city's next Local Plan. 
The group reviewed other building standards, examined the challenges around financial viability, analysed environmental performance data from 112 new buildings, and explored planning policy approaches taken by other local authorities.
From this research, they proposed a suite of stretching net zero standards for various building types that increase over time and recommended that Manchester establish a local carbon off set fund, create an independent body to assess environmental information in planning applications, and form an open learning forum to accelerate the adoption of effective net zero designs and construction processes. Their work will be published by the Partnership in summer 2024 and has fed into the evidence-base for Manchester's next Local Plan due out for consultation in 2024

The Commercial Building Retrofit City Challenge ran throughout 2023 and into early 2024, working across four sub-groups and feeding into Greater Manchester's Retrofit Taskforce.
This City Challenge explored the barriers to retrofit including an unambitious regulatory landscape, a lack of fiscal incentives and an underdeveloped retrofit supply chain; and identified that less than 10% of commercial buildings in Manchester are responsible for over 60% of the direct emissions from this sector.
The group developed a clear decarbonisation pathway with targets for different sizes of commercial building escalating over time and recommended that the city-region explore how local fiscal instruments, planning policies and skills/supply chain development can accelerate change. The group's recommendations have been tested 
with wider stakeholders and are due to be published in summer 2024. https://www.manchesterclimate.com/impact-reports

Recycle Dat, a citywide Mardi Gras recycling initiative launched in 2023 and now expanding annually. Recycle Dat brings together a diverse coalition of partners from government, business, and civil society to address the longstanding environmental challenges of Carnival season while preserving its cultural and economic vitality.

The City of New Orleans, through the Office of Resilience & Sustainability, coordinates this effort in partnership with New Orleans & Company and local nonprofits and businesses such as Grounds Krewe, Glass Half Full, Osprey Initiative and the Green Project, as well as corporate sponsors. Philanthropic support and dedicated city general funds have also been secured to help scale the program.

The results demonstrate steady growth and impact:
2023: approximately 10 tons diverted in the pilot year.
2024: more than 20,000 lbs of glass, aluminum, and parade throws collected.
2025: a record 73,858 lbs diverted from landfills, including glass recycled into sand for coastal restoration.

Beyond the diversion numbers, Recycle Dat has built strong community engagement, with thousands of volunteers and parade-goers participating, and created seasonal jobs that connect local workers to the growing recycling and circular economy sector.

By turning Mardi Gras into a platform for public education, innovation, and civic pride, Recycle Dat demonstrates how New Orleans can align cultural traditions with sustainability goals. The initiative exemplifies the City's collaborative approach—leveraging grassroots organizations, municipal resources, and private sector participation—to advance climate and environmental action in ways that are visible, inclusive, and uniquely local.

Since its formation in 1992, the Nottingham Green Partnership (NGP) has united sustainability work across the city and coordinated efforts to build a greener future for Nottingham. It has continually sought to bring together partners from diverse sectors and fields of expertise to advance sustainable development, recognising that the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.

In 2019, the City's Carbon Neutral Charter and subsequent action plan in 2020 placed robust and sustainable city wide partnership working, collaboration and multiple organisational contributions as critical to Nottingham ever hoping to achieve the ambition to become the first city in the UK to be carbon neutral in 2028.

In order to make the NGP as effective as possible, the way it is governed, communicates and operates has been revised to ensure it is fit for purpose. The following are the areas that have been developed:

1. Each partner provides a brief high level highlight report to the NGP each quarter to ensure there is clear visibility of the work being undertaken by all partner organisations. The report will focus on the work towards climate change that has been undertaken by their organisation. These reports will be provided on a quarterly basis and compiled as a summary for discussion at each NGP meeting. Individual partners will not be expected to present their reports. The information provided can be used to promote good news stories on a regular basis from across the city. A common report template was created for this purpose.

2. NGP chair attends meetings of the City Council's CN28 Strategy Board and routinely reports progress of the partnership.

3. 3 vice-chairs have been appointed for the NGP. These were appointed from the existing NGP membership through a process in which any application would be considered along with recommendations from two other NGP members. The vice-chairs will provide cover for the NGP chair in their absence, particularly at the CN28 Strategy Board.

4. NCC has developed a website on behalf of the NGP. The content of the website is something the partnership actively contribute to and own.

5. A new Terms of Reference for the NGP has been developed and adopted.

Through this collaboration, implementation of climate measures can be adapted to business needs, and the city can identify necessary solutions such as grants to remove barriers to climate action in the corporate sector. column17: The City of Seattle has shaped policies to reduce waste and climate impacts at the state and regional level. Sustained advocacy led to the state's passage of “Right to Repair” legislation for digital electronic products and mobility devices and the 2025 Recycling Reform Act, a state-mandated product stewardship policy (also known as “extended producer responsibility” or EPR) for consumer packaging and paper products. Extended producer responsibility means companies are responsible for their products' waste, not local government. The adoption of these two nation-leading policies capstone over a decade of effort by a broad coalition of advocates. Right to Repair reduces waste by extending the life of digital and mobility products and reducing the need for new devices. The Recycling Reform Act will help reduce emissions by keeping materials away from landfills, increasing reuse and recycling, and encouraging manufacturers to design less wasteful products with greater potential for reuse and recycling.\nSPU also helped secure the adoption of additional state-mandated product stewardship programs. These include LightRecycle (2015), Safe Medication Return (2020), and PaintCare (2021), with programs for batteries (2027), packaging and paper products (2030), and solar panels (2031) now in development. Additionally, SPR significantly reduces natural organic materials, such as grass clippings and woody debris, through mulch mowing nearly all grass in parks and chipping branches and logs for use as mulch in shrub beds. \n

• Initial exploration and subsequent development, subject to feasibility study completion, of Project Genesis, a project to explore supply and 
demand of low cost, affordable heat at scale, recognising the opportunities presented by heat network expansion, heat zoning, energy storage 
and fleet decarbonisation.
• Development and implementation of a pipeline of innovation projects exploring new technologies and proof of concepts. Trials will include 
product development and piloting of residential and micro business solutions and propositions.

column17: One example of how the District is ensuring equitable climate action is in implementing its Climate Ready DC plan. The plan identified neighborhoods and communities most impacted by climate change and has been working with residents living in one of the most climate-vulnerable parts of the District since 2017 to determine how best to implement the climate adaptation plan in their community. As part of the project, DOEE launched the Equity Advisory Group (EAG), a community body made up of 13 residents chosen to be demographically representative of this Ward 7 community, to lead this effort. One of the EAG's key recommendations was to develop a community resilience hub to support residents, coordinate communication, distribute resources, and reduce carbon pollution. In 2020, the EAG produced a report on the components and services they felt most important in a resilience hub for their community, and launched the Resilience Hub Community Committee to continue development of that concept. They have since selected the FH Faunteroy Community Enrichment Center as a pilot hub site, secured funding to provide solar and a battery system to provide resilient power in the event of an outage, and are pursuing funding to support key programming and ongoing community engagement. While work on this project continues, this group of residents has continued to guide engagement with their community on other resources, including recent work to identify flooding education and resources needed to help the disproportionate number of residents living in the floodplain in this community as compared with other District neighborhoods. The Center now hosts a monthly resilience series, including on flooding in this community, as a way to continue to connect communities with different government agencies, including DOEE and the Homeland Security and Emergency Management Agency (HSEMA) around priority community concerns and interests. (https://doee.dc.gov/service/watts-branch-neighborhoods-flood-risk-management). DOEE has also convened a new community of practice around resilience hubs, which meets quarterly to connect community organizations who are interested in becoming resilience hubs with information, technical assistance, and potential resources. Finally, DOEE has led the development of two neighborhood-scale resilience strategies (Southwest/Buzzard Point, Ivy City) rooted in collaboration with residents of those communities, to design a network of projects to reduce vulnerabilities to heat and flooding, while also providing other benefits to the community such as improved park space, more shade and greenery, and improved air quality. These collaborations underpin the the Climate Ready DC plan and the approach of to both engage with and prioritize implementation in climate-vulnerable communities based both on exposure and sensitivity to climate impacts.

Major Initiative 32 Lead the Food Organics Green Organics rollout: This is a pilot program rolling out industrial food dehydrators to high-rise buildings across City of Melbourne as an alternative to kerbside FOGO collection for high density residential properties. The first stage of the pilot saw dehydrator units installed in 6 high-rise buildings, 5 residential apartment buildings in Docklands CBD and West Melbourne, and a 6th unit at a high-density student accommodation in Carlton. By processing FOGO on site were able to divert 37 tonnes of FOGO from landfill without significantly increasing trucks on our roads. The units also work to eliminate odours pests and rodents which can be attracted to large collections of FOGO. In February 2023 the pilot was reported on by the national broadcaster ABC news. The second stage of the pilot program expanded the dehydrator service to another 4 buildings located in Docklands, Kensington and the Melbourne CBD. This phase explores the dehydrator service in mixed use buildings, therefore includes businesses in its scope whilst maintaining a strong residential focus. The dehydrator machines were installed between September and November 2024. By December 2024 a total of 39 tonnes of food waste was diverted from landfill from all pilot sites.

CoM launched the pilot in 2022 in conjunction with City of Boroondara and Stonnington and iterated the program in October 2023 and November 2024 with 24 businesses successfully completing the program to date. CoM is collaborating with business to support the transition of the municipality's buildings and business operations to net zero, and to drive the growth of our green economy. For example, addressing the climate impacts of new buildings is at the heart of Melbourne's Planning Scheme Amendment C376, which targets reductions in energy use, carbon emissions, waste, and water consumption while boosting climate resilience and urban greening. Planning Scheme Amendment C376 was unanimously adopted by the City of Melbourne Council on 29 July 2025 and has been forwarded to the Minister for Planning for approval and gazettal. The City developed this planning policy and supporting technical evidence by engaging widely with industry, including the Property Council of Australia, as well as the State Government to ensure feasibility and alignment with benchmarks, while seeking statutory endorsement from the Victorian Government. 

Our management of the National Cityswitch program helps office-based tenancies to develop business decarbonisation action plans and report on net zero progress. Businesses representing a total of 3 million sqm of Net Lettable Area are currently participating in the program. 

Existing buildings contribute 60% of our municipal emissions. To address this challenge, we developed the Retrofit Melbourne Plan, endorsed by Council in 2023. Retrofit Melbourne sets out our framework for accelerating decarbonisation of existing buildings, with a goal for all buildings to be zero carbon ready by 2040. Since 2023, we have progressed implementation of the Retrofit Melbourne Plan initiatives, with a core focus on advocacy, evidence based-research, deep collaboration with industry, and development of targeted policy interventions. 

The City of Melbourne, the Facilities Management Association of Australia, and leading industry partners are establishing a Sustainable Buildings Operations Forum, to improve the environmental performance of existing buildings and support the transition to net zero. The Forum will create best practice ESG guidance for the built environment sector, generating green jobs and upskilling the facilities management workforce through pilots, tools, training, and events.

column17: Resilient Sydney is a local government led program hosted by the City of Sydney on behalf of all the councils of metropolitan Sydney. The Resilient Sydney Strategy (2018) is the first resilience strategy for metropolitan Sydney which calls for business, government, academia, communities and individuals to lead and work as one city. The Resilient Sydney strategy was developed with an unprecedented level of voluntary cooperation and collaboration across Sydney. The process involved all 33 metropolitan councils in consultation with over 1,000 residents and 100 businesses, government and community organisations over three years of effort. The Strategy lays out a set of five directions and 35 tangible actions Sydney can take to build resilience and strengthen the city's ability to survive, adapt and thrive in the face of global uncertainty and local shocks and chronic stresses. Resilient Sydney's vision for Sydney is a metropolis that is connected, inclusive and resilient. The program is a true collaboration with a metropolitan Steering Committee of leaders governing the program from the metropolitan councils of Sydney, the New South Wales state government (including a representative of the Greater Sydney Commission), business and community partners. The Resilient Sydney Office is a small team led by the Chief Resilience Officer providing secretariat, research, strategy development and facilitation of actions and collaboration. Resilient Sydney is hosted by the City of Sydney on behalf of Sydney. The program is funded by the local governments of Sydney.

Johannesburg partnered with fellow C40 cities including Cape Town, eThekwini, Tshwane, and eKurhuleni to contribute to the development and refinement of South Africa's Climate Change Bill, enacted in 2024. This collaboration emphasized the critical role of municipalities in climate governance and secured clear mandates for local governments. In partnership with the Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment (DFFE) and the South African Local Government Association (SALGA), the City participated in capacity-building sessions to disseminate municipal responsibilities under the new Act. Additionally, consultations with the Presidential Climate Commission (PCC) helped shape the draft Just Transition Framework, ensuring local perspectives are integrated into national climate policy.
At the City level, Johannesburg also collaborates through regional multi-jurisdictional forums and task teams addressing energy security, transport, and water resilience, fostering alignment and resource-sharing among metropolitan municipalities in Gauteng Province.
Significantly, Johannesburg hosted the Urban 20 (U20) Summit, providing a global platform for cities to engage in dialogue on urban climate action, share best practices, and amplify the voice of urban areas in international climate governance. Hosting the U20 strengthened Johannesburg's leadership and expanded collaboration opportunities with international cities, governments, civil society, and business sectors.

In partnership with students from Wits University, the City participated in the Reinventing Cities competition, proposing a transit-oriented development at Marlboro Train Station and surrounding informal settlements. The project focused on creating a high-density, mixed-use development integrating green spaces and leveraging the Jukskei River for food security, agricultural trade, and renewable energy generation. This initiative brought attention to social inequities in informal settlements such as Alexandra and fostered community engagement through direct dialogues with residents. It exemplifies the City's commitment to innovative, intersectional design approaches that address resilience, equity, and sustainable infrastructure development.
Additionally, Johannesburg collaborates with local universities and research institutions through climate data sharing, joint research projects, and capacity building workshops, strengthening evidence-based policymaking and implementation.

The social inequities that still exist in South Africa's informal settlements, especially in Alexandra, where Marlboro train Station is, have been brought to light by this initiative. The students got an opportunity to visit the location and engage in conversation with the residents of Alexandra regarding their living circumstances. After reviewing the site's history, it was concluded that, given the attention that has been paid to the effects housing projects have on the environment and the social welfare of the land's residents, there is a greater need than ever for housing projects. It was also discovered that by collaborating across diverse design philosophies and methods, intersectional designs are possible in such settings. 

The city collaborates with Wits University on what is called Community of Practice (CoP), where academics and city officials collaborate on finding solutions for current and future water problems in the city. This CoP is part of a broader project which involves the University of Cape Town (twinned with City of Cape Town officials) and the University of KwaZulu Natal (twinned with eThekwini). Toronto's Environment, Climate & Forestry Division (ECF) is currently undertaking a project to build a suite of modelling tools that can support policy and program development towards meeting our interim and long-term GHG emissions reduction targets. As part of the project, ECF is convening a Technical Advisory Group (TAG), which will include representatives from federal and provincial agencies. The role of the TAG will be to ensure that the modelling tools' development is aligned with current best practices to model and track short-term and long-term GHG reduction targets, and to identify an optimal scenario pathway to reach net zero emissions across various sectors in Toronto (buildings, transportation, and waste). Importantly, including provincial and federal government staff in the project's TAG will help align various modelling activities and climate action programs being developed across different levels of government.

The “15-Minute Pocket Parks throughout Bangkok” project is a pioneering initiative to transform Bangkok's landscape, with a clear goal of creating at least 500 new parks by 2026. This project aims to increase the city's green spaces by converting neglected urban voids into functional and beautiful public havens. Each park is a unique and vibrant space, with designs that adapt to its specific location. We prioritize the use of diverse, low-maintenance plant species to create shaded and pleasant environments for all ages and abilities.

At the heart of this initiative is community. By encouraging residents to actively participate in the design and upkeep of their neighborhood parks, we foster a sense of ownership and belonging. These green spaces are intended to be more than just parks; they are new centers for relaxation, physical activity, and shared community events that promote both physical and mental well-being.

Ultimately, the project contributes to a healthier city by reducing pollution and restoring vital balance between urban development and environmental conservation. This collaborative effort is a cornerstone of our vision to make Bangkok a truly livable city for all.

De manera general, la PPAC se alinea con el Compromiso 3 de la citada Declaración, que establece que cada jurisdicción de la RAPE debe contar con un plan detallado que defina la ruta para lograr los objetivos deseados a 2030.En materia de mitigación, está alineado con el Compromiso 1 de la citada Declaración, que señala que se deben establecer medidas, políticas y normativas que garanticen la reducción de gases efecto invernadero en un 50% para el 2030, el Distrito ha establecido como objetivo específico Reducir las emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero de Bogotá D.C. para alcanzar la carbono neutralidad a 2050. En cuanto al componente de adaptación se alinea con los compromisos 2, 4 y 5 de la Declaratoria de Emergencia Climática de la RAPE; toda vez que el Distrito se quiere Reducir la vulnerabilidad de la ciudad ante las amenazas climáticas y hacerla resiliente al cambio climático. La Secretaría de Ambiente, en representación de la Alcaldía de Bogotá participa en el Nodo Regional de Cambio Climático Centro Oriente Andino el cual tiene como finalidad lograr la coordinación interinstitucional entre el nivel central y territorial de su jurisdicción, para promover las políticas, estrategias, planes, programas, proyectos y acciones de mitigación de emisiones de gases efecto invernadero y adaptación en materia de variabilidad y cambio climático, articulados con los procesos de planificación territorial a través del ordenamiento ambiental territorial, ordenamiento territorial y gestión del riesgo de desastres.

column17: Desde el año 2019, el Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires ha realizado distintos encuentros con el sector privado con el objetivo de incorporar su visión en la planificación de la acción climática de largo plazo de la Ciudad. De acuerdo a los resultados de dichos encuentros, en el año 2022 se trabajó en la formalización de un grupo de trabajo entre empresas y el GCBA sobre cambio climático. Para ello, en primer lugar se realizó un análisis de las principales actividades económicas de la Ciudad para decidir qué sectores debían ser representados en el grupo, en concordancia con los objetivos del PAC 2050. A partir de este análisis, y considerando a las empresas que venían participando en encuentros previos, se eligió un número reducido de empresas representantes de los distintos sectores claves de la Ciudad en relación al cambio climático para que conformen este grupo, y diseñen, lideren y coordinen iniciativas y estrategias conjuntas público-privadas. A partir un primer encuentro realizado en 2022, y con el apoyo de la red C40 y la iniciativa internacional City-Business Climate Alliance (CBCA), durante la Cumbre de Alcaldes de C40 se lanzó el Grupo Consultivo de Empresas y Cambio Climático, en el marco del Foro de Empresas y Ciudades. Las funciones de este Grupo son las de articular acciones público privadas tanto para la mitigación como la adaptación al cambio climático, trabajar en estrategias climáticas, compatibilizar indicadores climáticos, establecer metas conjuntas, y canalizar propuestas y oportunidades de articulación desde el sector privado hacia el GCBA. En el año 2024, se incluyeron nuevas empresas al grupo consultivo en base a su compromiso con la acción climática.

Entre os segmentos específicos haverá um representante de cada um dos seguintes grupos: comunidade LGBTQIA+, comunidade negra, pessoas com deficiência, pessoas idosas, mulheres, jovens, migrantes, representante do comércio, representante de trabalhadores da reciclagem e representante de projetos sociais. São elas que assumem a reorganização doméstica e dão conta da alteração na rotina familiar, vida escolar e saúde dos filhos. Entre outras ações, a Prefeitura de Curitiba vai entregar a documentação de posse das novas unidades habitacionais em nome da mulher da família.

CONFERÊNCIA DA MATA ATLÂNTICA - Realizada em Curitiba, em parceria com o Governo do Estado do Paraná, a conferência reuniu representantes de governos locais, estaduais, sociedade civil, setor privado, universidades e organizações internacionais em torno da agenda de preservação, restauração e governança do bioma.
O evento foi estruturado em blocos temáticos - preservação, mitigação de emissões de GEE, adaptação climática, financiamento, governança e transição justa - permitindo aprofundar o debate técnico e político sobre os principais desafios e oportunidades. A metodologia priorizou a integração de diferentes escalas de governo, além de assegurar ampla participação social, com destaque para grupos comunitários e acadêmicos.
A colaboração entre município e estado foi essencial para ampliar o alcance da conferência e consolidar resultados que orientam tanto políticas locais quanto regionais. Entre os desdobramentos, destacam-se a articulação de projetos de restauração ecológica, a formulação de propostas para mecanismos de financiamento climático e a criação de sinergias para desenvolvimento de mercados ambientais.
Esse exemplo demonstra como Curitiba atua como catalisadora de cooperação multiescalar e multissetorial, fortalecendo a governança climática e contribuindo para o avanço de políticas públicas de impacto regional, em linha com os compromissos internacionais de liderança climática, como os do grupo C40.

column17: City of Istanbul participated in WeLoveCities campaign last year for the first time. WeLoveCities is a friendly competition organised by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF). Since its begin in 2013, the event has reached over 200 million people in more than 150 cities world-wide and generated 100,000 improvement proposals which were shared with officials. WeLoveCities pursues the objective of building sustainable self-developing cities which respect ecological limits and where people live in harmony with nature. Istanbul reports its greenhouse gas emissions inventory every year to the CDP-ICLEI platform. This platform also offers the possibility to report the data to a number of other platforms or for competition purposes. One such competition is the WWF's One Planet City Challenge (OPCC). Istanbul has finished the competition as one of 75 global finalists. WWF recommends the OPCC finalists also to take part in the WeLoveCities contest. Istanbul did just that.Participants are requested to share their activities on issues such as the environment, climate and sustainability on their social media accounts using the logo or hashtag of #WeLoveCities. The city which receives most feedback wins the contest. In addition, on the main website a profile page has been inserted for every participating city which includes a “Citizen Wishes, Opinions, Suggestions and Requests” form. Between 19 September and 31 October 2022, on its social media accounts (Facebook, Twitter and Instagram) and with the #WeLoveIstanbul hashtag, the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality has shared its activities on a wide range of topics, including urban mobility, food systems, energy, infrastructure, nature, waste, the environment and climate. And with the aid of the form on its profile page, the municipality has gathered citizens' opinions and requests. The main topics addressed by citizens in their improvement suggestions can be summarised as follows: blue flag beaches, stricter controls during urban regeneration activities to prevent the felling of trees, more student hostels, more green areas, a wider choice of mass transport alternatives, rainwater collection systems, sea water purification plants, horizontal urbanisation, PET bottle collection machines, sports incentives. It is being planned to participate in WeLoveCities campaign this year too.

column17: Several hundred enterprises are already part of the Network \'Sustainable mangement in Small and Medium sized Enterprises\'. The aim of the network, which has been coordinated by the Office of Environmental Protection, Trade Supervision and Energy since 2001, is to support small and medium-sized enterprieses with 5 to 250 employees in implementing an environmental management system. This includes the investigation of internal processes and optimization potentials, in particular with regard to resource consumption and disposal as well as occupational safety for the protection of employees and the environment. Questions of social sustainability, such as new forms of personnel management or corporate social responsibitily are also adressed.With about 200 involved companies and around 15.000 employees this network is one of the largest sustainability networks of companies in Germany. In the 2023/24 project phase, the companies drew up a greenhouse gas balance sheet for their company for the first time. The most recent data collection revealed an annual CO2 saving of more than 2,400 tonnes. Operating costs have been reduced by a total of 1.3 million euros per year. A network of committed entrepreneurs has emerged, who exchange ideas with each other in working group meetings and with representatives of the administration. These include craft businesses, service companies and social and municipal organisations.

With the funding support from the ECF, the ECC has rolled out the two-year Carbon Neutrality Publicity Campaign (CNPC) 1.0 to enhance public awareness on the imminence of the climate crisis, and instil a sense of urgency to start adopting a low-carbon lifestyle since late 2022. The CNPC adopts the overarching theme of carbon neutrality, with three sub-themes, viz. energy saving, green transport, and waste reduction and recycling. To sustain the momentum of the awareness built under the CNPC1.0, CNPC2.0 was launched from Q3 2024 to encourage the public to transform carbon reduction awareness into action, change their daily habits, practise low-carbon living together, aiming at achieving carbon reduction by 2050. Around 150 strategic and collaboration partners including public and business corporations, industry groups, non-governmental organisations and schools sponsoring bodies have been engaged to jointly promote low-carbon living to their stakeholders and/or publicize the campaign on their premises, social media and website.


To strengthen the publicity and education on waste reduction and recycling in the community and at school level, the Environmental Protection Department (EPD) launched the “We-recycle@School” Activity on 1 March 2024, to encourage students to actively practise resource separation and recycling together with their family members to cultivate habits of waste reduction and recycling in their daily lives. As at June 2025, around 550 primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong have participated in the programme, covering about 350 000 students.
Regarding the Regulation on Disposable Plastic Tableware and Other Plastic Products (the Regulation), in order to reduce the use of disposable plastic tableware and other plastic products with a view to reducing the impact of plastic pollution on marine ecology and human health and mitigating climate change, the EPD and the former Council for Sustainable Development launched a public consultation on the Scheme on Regulation of Disposable Plastic Tableware (Regulation Scheme) in July 2021 and a public engagement on control of single-use plastics in September 2021, respectively. During these periods, more than 30 briefings, public forums, focus group meetings etc. were held to collect opinions on the proposed Regulation Scheme from the public, the trade and various stakeholders, including the catering industry, catering suppliers, green groups, medical sector, retail sector, wholesale sector, chambers of commerce, recycling sector and other professional bodies. Thereafter, we continued to keep close communication with the major stakeholders.

To assist the trade in understanding which alternatives comply with the Regulation with a view to facilitating the trade in the early adoption of more environmental-friendly non-plastic tableware (such as paper and plant fibre), in lieu of the disposable plastic ones, we established a “Green Tableware Platform” (www.greentableware.hk) in January 2022. To ensure that the products meet the plastic-free requirement of the Regulation, the platform secretariat reviews the tableware to be placed on the platform in each application, through assessing information such as material testing reports, certifications and product samples, etc.

Following the announcement in the 2023 and 2024 Policy Address by the Chief Executive of the HKSAR Government to develop Hong Kong into a green maritime centre, the HKSAR Government has commissioned a feasibility study on the provision of green maritime fuel bunkering to vessels, and promulgated in November 2024 the Action Plan on Green Maritime Fuel Bunkering upon consultation with the industry. The Action Plan was well-received by both local and international stakeholders, many of which expressed an interest in starting green maritime fuel bunkering and other green shipping-related businesses in Hong Kong. The HKSAR Government is working closely with relevant companies, partners and organisations to implement the Action Plan in an orderly manner. The first collaborative platform event which aimed to bring together suppliers and users of green maritime fuels was held in late June, where the Transport and Logistics Bureau of the HKSAR Government signed four memoranda of understanding with green maritime-related entities. With support from relevant energy, bunkering and shipping companies, Hong Kong's first LNG bunkering operation was conducted in February 2025. Besides, to encourage the green transformation of the maritime industry, the HKSAR Government introduced the Green Incentive Scheme in June 2024 for eligible Hong Kong-registered ships attaining rating A or B in the Carbon Intensity Indicator formulated by the International Maritime Organization.
 
The Airport Authority (AA) administers the HKIA Carbon Reduction Programme which is a platform for engaging airport business partners (i.e. franchisees and licensees operating at HKIA) to measure, reduce and report their carbon emissions and share best practices. Over the past ten years, the AA and its airport business partners have made two short-term pledges to reduce HKIA's airport-wide carbon emissions. Since 2021, the AA and 29 key aviation-related business partners have committed to achieve Net Zero Carbon by 2050, with a midpoint target of 55% absolute emissions reduction by 2035 from a 2018 baseline, which aligns with the HKSAR Government's commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050, and the global long-term carbon goal for airports set by Airports Council International (ACI) World. 

The AA is one of the initial signatories of the Business Environment Council (BEC)'s Low Carbon Charter (now rebranded as Net-zero Carbon Charter). With the support of business leaders and the Environment Bureau, the BEC Low Carbon Charter was launched in March 2019 to mobilise companies to collectively support Hong Kong's long-term decarbonisation through their pledge to set and achieve carbon reduction targets. Regular events are organized to support signatories and businesses in setting, operationalising, and achieving their emission reduction targets. The AA is also a member of the Steering Committees of Climate Change Business Forum Advisory Group, Circular Economy Advisory Group and Sustainable Living Environment Advisory Group under BEC. Additionally, AA is a partner of the HK Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition organised by BEC.

At the wider aviation industry level, the AA participates in the global dialogue, supporting the sustainable development of aviation and airports through our industry body, Airports Council International (ACI). Under ACI, AA is a Regional Representativeof the World Environment Standing Committee and the Chair of the Asia-Pacific and Middle East Regional Environment Committee. The AA is also currently the chair of the ACI Asia Pacific and Middle East Climate Adaptation Working Group, the regional representative for the ACI Airport Carbon Accreditation Programme and the co-lead of the ACI World Environment Standing Committee (WEnSC) Long-Term Carbon Goal (LTCG) Implementation Task Force. Through these roles, we endeavor to positively contribute to industry transformation and best practice sharing.

AA was also a member of the Infrastructure Rating System Committee under HK Green Building Council (HKGBC) and a supporting organisation in the development of the HKGBC Climate Change Framework for Built Environment.

The Action Plan was well-received by both local and international stakeholders, many of which expressed an interest in starting green maritime fuel bunkering and other green shipping-related businesses in Hong Kong. The HKSAR Government is working closely with relevant companies, partners and organisations to implement the Action Plan in an orderly manner. The first collaborative platform event which aimed to bring together suppliers and users of green maritime fuels was held in late June, where the Transport and Logistics Bureau of the HKSAR Government signed four memoranda of understanding with green maritime-related entities. With support from relevant energy, bunkering and shipping companies, Hong Kong's first LNG bunkering operation was conducted in February 2025. Besides, to encourage the green transformation of the maritime industry, the HKSAR Government introduced the Green Incentive Scheme in June 2024 for eligible Hong Kong-registered ships attaining rating A or B in the Carbon Intensity Indicator formulated by the International Maritime Organization.
 
The Airport Authority (AA) administers the HKIA Carbon Reduction Programme which is a platform for engaging airport business partners (i.e. franchisees and licensees operating at HKIA) to measure, reduce and report their carbon emissions and share best practices. Over the past ten years, the AA and its airport business partners have made two short-term pledges to reduce HKIA's airport-wide carbon emissions. Since 2021, the AA and 29 key aviation-related business partners have committed to achieve Net Zero Carbon by 2050, with a midpoint target of 55% absolute emissions reduction by 2035 from a 2018 baseline, which aligns with the HKSAR Government's commitment to carbon neutrality by 2050, and the global long-term carbon goal for airports set by Airports Council International (ACI) World. 

The AA is one of the initial signatories of the Business Environment Council (BEC)'s Low Carbon Charter (now rebranded as Net-zero Carbon Charter). With the support of business leaders and the Environment Bureau, the BEC Low Carbon Charter was launched in March 2019 to mobilise companies to collectively support Hong Kong's long-term decarbonisation through their pledge to set and achieve carbon reduction targets. Regular events are organized to support signatories and businesses in setting, operationalising, and achieving their emission reduction targets. The AA is also a member of the Steering Committees of Climate Change Business Forum Advisory Group, Circular Economy Advisory Group and Sustainable Living Environment Advisory Group under BEC. Additionally, AA is a partner of the HK Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition organised by BEC.

At the wider aviation industry level, the AA participates in the global dialogue, supporting the sustainable development of aviation and airports through our industry body, Airports Council International (ACI). Under ACI, AA is a Regional Representativeof the World Environment Standing Committee and the Chair of the Asia-Pacific and Middle East Regional Environment Committee. The AA is also currently the chair of the ACI Asia Pacific and Middle East Climate Adaptation Working Group, the regional representative for the ACI Airport Carbon Accreditation Programme and the co-lead of the ACI World Environment Standing Committee (WEnSC) Long-Term Carbon Goal (LTCG) Implementation Task Force. Through these roles, we endeavor to positively contribute to industry transformation and best practice sharing.

AA was also a member of the Infrastructure Rating System Committee under HK Green Building Council (HKGBC) and a supporting organisation in the development of the HKGBC Climate Change Framework for Built Environment.

Develop Carbon-Neutral Communities
To explore measures, such as wider use of renewable energy, energy efficient design and technologies, green transport, higher greening ratio, more advanced recycling and waste management measures, to progress towards the vision of carbon-neutral community. Also, adopt smart, green and resilient measures.

Adoption of Ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) Concrete Cement is one of the main elements for concrete production. However, cement production is one of the main contributor of carbon dioxide. GGBS may be added to replace up to 75% of the cement in concrete. Hence, GGBS concrete could significantly reduce carbon footprint as compared to cement and PFA concrete. Apart from lower carbon footprint, the use of GGBS also has other advantages, such as improved durability, dimensional stability and aesthetic appearance.

Mobility / Transportation to Reduce Energy Demand
There are various ways to reduce energy demand from transportation's perspective. One of the ways is to adopt Transit-oriented Development (TOD) mode in town planning in which railways would serve as the backbone of transport mode. TOD could bring many benefits, such as providing easy access to transit without a car, to avoid traffic congestion, hence better utilize land resources etc. Integrated transport hubs could be considered at the close vicinity of station to provide feeder service so people could reach other destinations conveniently. Besides, the active use of non-motorized transport mode, including walking and cycling, should be encouraged. To promote the use of non-motorized transport mode, pedestrian-friendly environment would be created, such as car free zone, covered walkway etc. so as to increase walkability and to achieve a better connection and linkage between the communities and the railway station. 

Greening Master Plan
Recognising the public's aspirations for a greener, lusher environment, the Civil Engineering and Development Department (CEDD) started to develop and implement Greening Master Plans (GMPs) for urban areas since 2004. A GMP seeks to define the overall greening framework of a district, and serves as a guide for all parties involved in planning, design and implementation of greening works. In addition to identifying planting locations, the GMP establishes the greening themes and proposes suitable planting species.

column17: The “Hong Kong 2030+: Towards a Planning Vision and Strategy Transcending 2030 (Hong Kong 2030+)” is a vision-driven, pragmatic and action-oriented strategic plan. Its vision is for Hong Kong to become a liveable, competitive and sustainable “Asia's World City”. The overarching planning goal is to champion sustainable development with a view to meeting our present and future social, environmental and economic needs and aspirations. Hong Kong 2030+ advocates a vision-driven and capacity creating approach for strategic planning in a holistic manner. The finalised territorial spatial development strategy is underscored by three building blocks: enhancing liveability, embracing economic opportunities and challenges, and creating capacity for sustainable growth and one conceptual spatial framework that translates these building blocks in spatial planning terms. To uphold environmental stewardship, we need to mainstream climate change, biodiversity and other environmental considerations in the planning and development process and proactively manage selected areas of high ecological value, thereby contributing to environmental sustainability and achieving carbon neutrality before 2050.During the formulation of the final recommendations of the Hong Kong 2030+, multiple public engagement events (such as public forums, briefings to stakeholders, knowledge-sharing seminars and topical discussions) have been organised for engaging the general public and relevant stakeholders including District Councils, professional institutes, green groups etc., for their views and comments on how to achieve the overarching planning goals. An Expert Advisory Panel has also been set up for Hong Kong 2030+ to provide professional third-party input to the study. It comprises mainly academics, professionals and experts/ representatives from various sectors such as economics, architecture, engineering, planning, surveying, social and environment. The final recommendations of the Hong Kong 2030+ was promulgated in October 2021.

Cooperation frameworks 

The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), set up in May 2020, aims to co-ordinate the management of climate and environmental risks to the financial sector, accelerate the growth of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong and support the Government's climate strategies. It is co-chaired by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), with the Environment and Ecology Bureau, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) of the Hong Kong SAR Government, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX), the Insurance Authority (IA), the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority (MPFA) and the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council as Members.

The Green Technology and Finance Development Committee (Committee) was established in June 2023 under the chairmanship of the Financial Secretary of the HKSAR Government with membership comprising representatives from relevant policy bureaux, departments and financial regulators, as well as non-official members from industries concerned. The Committee aims to assist in the formation of an action agenda for promoting the development of Hong Kong into an international green technology and financial centre. 

Policy and regulation development/ implementation

In March 2024, the FSTB published a vision statement, setting out the vision and approach of the Government and financial regulators in developing a comprehensive ecosystem for sustainability disclosure in Hong Kong. In April 2024, HKEX issued its consultation conclusions on enhancing climate-related disclosure requirements for Hong Kong-listed companies. The new climate-related disclosures Listing Rule requirements are developed based on International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) S2 Climate-related Disclosures and came into effect in phases from 1 January 2025, preparing companies to start climate reporting early in accordance with provisions of the ISSB Standards. HKEX also published an implementation guidance to assist issuers in preparing disclosures that makes reference to ISSB Standards S1 General Requirements.

As the sustainability reporting standard setter in Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants published in December 2024 the Hong Kong Sustainability Disclosure Standards (Hong Kong Standards) which is fully aligned with the ISSB Standards. The Hong Kong Standards have become effective since 1 August 2025. The FSTB launched in December 2024 the Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure in Hong Kong. The roadmap sets out Hong Kong's approach to require publicly accountable entities (PAEs) to adopt the ISSB Standards. It provides a well-defined pathway for large PAEs to fully adopt the ISSB Standards no later than 2028. In June 2025, the IFRS Foundation published the jurisdictional profiles on adoption of the ISSB Standards, which confirms Hong Kong as among the initial set of jurisdictions having set a target of fully adopting the ISSB Standards. This demonstrates Hong Kong's commitment to enhancing the transparency of information on sustainable development in the capital markets, facilitating investors to make investment decisions and promoting global capital flows.

The HKMA launched the Sustainable Finance Action Agenda (Action Agenda) last year, setting out 8 goals in 4 areas, namely banking for net zero, investing in a sustainable future, financing net zero, and making sustainability more inclusive. Regarding banking for net zero, all banks should, in accordance with science-based pathways, strive to achieve net zero in their own operations by 2030 and in their financed emissions by 2050 with a view to supporting their clients and wider economy in the net zero transition. In addition, tentatively from 2030, banks should start making available their transition plans to the HKMA regularly on a “comply or explain” basis. The transition plans should consist of decarbonisation and financing targets, and clear action plans for achieving 2050 net zero ambition, including a plan for managed phase-out of financing for carbon-intensive assets. The transition plans should be Paris-aligned, robust, actionable and up-to-date.

With a view to promoting Hong Kong as a transition finance hub, the Steering Group convened an industry working group to develop guidance for practicing transition finance under a sectoral approach.
