Water Conservation

Water Supplies Department (WSD) of Hong Kong SAR Government has established collaborative endeavours with green groups, non-government organisations and various other stakeholders in promoting water conservation. We have co-organised or supported various events such as Race for Water, Walk for Water , Water for Living Water,Hong Kong Green Day, Green Run, Green Carnival, Eco-Expo Asia 2024, Kowloon Chamber of Commerce Youth Festival 2024 and etc. 

Water Loss Management

WSD pledges to reduce the leakage rate from the current 13.4% to below 10% on or before 2030. To achieve the target, one of the approaches is to provide systematic training to the professional and leak detection frontline officers, which directly contributes to the 5% water-saving. WSD collaborates with the Hong Kong Polytechnic University to design and construct a training ground of about 2,000 square metres. Purpose of the training ground is to simulate various types of leakage patterns that are common in the water supply networks. Various leakage detection methods, for example, step test, noise logging, leak noise correlator, ground microphone, hydrophone, and inline inspection methods, electromagnetic/pipe cable locating, ground penetrating radar, etc. are all feasible to be carried out in the site. Also, a show room and classroom at the training ground could conduct seminars, training courses and demonstrations. The training ground is utilized primarily for training and qualifying professional and frontline officers for leakage detection and diagnosis. The second purpose is research and development of new leakage detection technologies. The training ground would also be a hub for public engagement/education and experience sharing locally and internationally. The training ground was commissioned on 26 July 2021 and various training, research and collaboration activities were on-going since then.

Biodiversity

In collaboration with several green groups, WSD conducted a baseline ecology study of irrigation reservoirs by an academia of the University of Hong Kong to understand their current ecological status and ways to enhance their ecological value. WSD also completed a trial on ecological enhancement of Hung Shui Hang Irrigation Reservoir through ecological floating platforms. Furthermore, WSD applied for Lantau Conservation Fund (LCF) for another project which is to establish artificial ecological floating platforms in Shap Long Irrigation Reservoir on Lantau Island. The project is currently under planning stage.

With the funding support from the ECF, the ECC has rolled out the two-year Carbon Neutrality Publicity Campaign (CNPC) 1.0 to enhance public awareness on the imminence of the climate crisis, and instil a sense of urgency to start adopting a low-carbon lifestyle since late 2022. The CNPC adopts the overarching theme of carbon neutrality, with three sub-themes, viz. energy saving, green transport, and waste reduction and recycling. To sustain the momentum of the awareness built under the CNPC1.0, CNPC2.0 was launched from Q3 2024 to encourage the public to transform carbon reduction awareness into action, change their daily habits, practise low-carbon living together, aiming at achieving carbon reduction by 2050. Around 150 strategic and collaboration partners including public and business corporations, industry groups, non-governmental organisations and schools sponsoring bodies have been engaged to jointly promote low-carbon living to their stakeholders and/or publicize the campaign on their premises, social media and website.


To strengthen the publicity and education on waste reduction and recycling in the community and at school level, the Environmental Protection Department (EPD) launched the “We-recycle@School” Activity on 1 March 2024, to encourage students to actively practise resource separation and recycling together with their family members to cultivate habits of waste reduction and recycling in their daily lives. As at June 2025, around 550 primary and secondary schools in Hong Kong have participated in the programme, covering about 350 000 students.
Regarding the Regulation on Disposable Plastic Tableware and Other Plastic Products (the Regulation), in order to reduce the use of disposable plastic tableware and other plastic products with a view to reducing the impact of plastic pollution on marine ecology and human health and mitigating climate change, the EPD and the former Council for Sustainable Development launched a public consultation on the Scheme on Regulation of Disposable Plastic Tableware (Regulation Scheme) in July 2021 and a public engagement on control of single-use plastics in September 2021, respectively. During these periods, more than 30 briefings, public forums, focus group meetings etc. were held to collect opinions on the proposed Regulation Scheme from the public, the trade and various stakeholders, including the catering industry, catering suppliers, green groups, medical sector, retail sector, wholesale sector, chambers of commerce, recycling sector and other professional bodies. Thereafter, we continued to keep close communication with the major stakeholders.

To assist the trade in understanding which alternatives comply with the Regulation with a view to facilitating the trade in the early adoption of more environmental-friendly non-plastic tableware (such as paper and plant fibre), in lieu of the disposable plastic ones, we established a “Green Tableware Platform” (www.greentableware.hk) in January 2022. To ensure that the products meet the plastic-free requirement of the Regulation, the platform secretariat reviews the tableware to be placed on the platform in each application, through assessing information such as material testing reports, certifications and product samples, etc.

Develop Carbon-Neutral Communities
To explore measures, such as wider use of renewable energy, energy efficient design and technologies, green transport, higher greening ratio, more advanced recycling and waste management measures, to progress towards the vision of carbon-neutral community. Also, adopt smart, green and resilient measures.

Adoption of Ground granulated blast-furnace slag (GGBS) Concrete Cement is one of the main elements for concrete production. However, cement production is one of the main contributor of carbon dioxide. GGBS may be added to replace up to 75% of the cement in concrete. Hence, GGBS concrete could significantly reduce carbon footprint as compared to cement and PFA concrete. Apart from lower carbon footprint, the use of GGBS also has other advantages, such as improved durability, dimensional stability and aesthetic appearance.

Mobility / Transportation to Reduce Energy Demand
There are various ways to reduce energy demand from transportation's perspective. One of the ways is to adopt Transit-oriented Development (TOD) mode in town planning in which railways would serve as the backbone of transport mode. TOD could bring many benefits, such as providing easy access to transit without a car, to avoid traffic congestion, hence better utilize land resources etc. Integrated transport hubs could be considered at the close vicinity of station to provide feeder service so people could reach other destinations conveniently. Besides, the active use of non-motorized transport mode, including walking and cycling, should be encouraged. To promote the use of non-motorized transport mode, pedestrian-friendly environment would be created, such as car free zone, covered walkway etc. so as to increase walkability and to achieve a better connection and linkage between the communities and the railway station. 

Greening Master Plan
Recognising the public's aspirations for a greener, lusher environment, the Civil Engineering and Development Department (CEDD) started to develop and implement Greening Master Plans (GMPs) for urban areas since 2004. A GMP seeks to define the overall greening framework of a district, and serves as a guide for all parties involved in planning, design and implementation of greening works. In addition to identifying planting locations, the GMP establishes the greening themes and proposes suitable planting species.

Cooperation frameworks 

The Green and Sustainable Finance Cross-Agency Steering Group (Steering Group), set up in May 2020, aims to co-ordinate the management of climate and environmental risks to the financial sector, accelerate the growth of green and sustainable finance in Hong Kong and support the Government's climate strategies. It is co-chaired by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) and the Securities and Futures Commission (SFC), with the Environment and Ecology Bureau, the Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau (FSTB) of the Hong Kong SAR Government, Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX), the Insurance Authority (IA), the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority (MPFA) and the Accounting and Financial Reporting Council as Members.

The Green Technology and Finance Development Committee (Committee) was established in June 2023 under the chairmanship of the Financial Secretary of the HKSAR Government with membership comprising representatives from relevant policy bureaux, departments and financial regulators, as well as non-official members from industries concerned. The Committee aims to assist in the formation of an action agenda for promoting the development of Hong Kong into an international green technology and financial centre. 

Policy and regulation development/ implementation

In March 2024, the FSTB published a vision statement, setting out the vision and approach of the Government and financial regulators in developing a comprehensive ecosystem for sustainability disclosure in Hong Kong. In April 2024, HKEX issued its consultation conclusions on enhancing climate-related disclosure requirements for Hong Kong-listed companies. The new climate-related disclosures Listing Rule requirements are developed based on International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) S2 Climate-related Disclosures and came into effect in phases from 1 January 2025, preparing companies to start climate reporting early in accordance with provisions of the ISSB Standards. HKEX also published an implementation guidance to assist issuers in preparing disclosures that makes reference to ISSB Standards S1 General Requirements.

As the sustainability reporting standard setter in Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants published in December 2024 the Hong Kong Sustainability Disclosure Standards (Hong Kong Standards) which is fully aligned with the ISSB Standards. The Hong Kong Standards have become effective since 1 August 2025. The FSTB launched in December 2024 the Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure in Hong Kong. The roadmap sets out Hong Kong's approach to require publicly accountable entities (PAEs) to adopt the ISSB Standards. It provides a well-defined pathway for large PAEs to fully adopt the ISSB Standards no later than 2028. In June 2025, the IFRS Foundation published the jurisdictional profiles on adoption of the ISSB Standards, which confirms Hong Kong as among the initial set of jurisdictions having set a target of fully adopting the ISSB Standards. This demonstrates Hong Kong's commitment to enhancing the transparency of information on sustainable development in the capital markets, facilitating investors to make investment decisions and promoting global capital flows.

The HKMA launched the Sustainable Finance Action Agenda (Action Agenda) last year, setting out 8 goals in 4 areas, namely banking for net zero, investing in a sustainable future, financing net zero, and making sustainability more inclusive. Regarding banking for net zero, all banks should, in accordance with science-based pathways, strive to achieve net zero in their own operations by 2030 and in their financed emissions by 2050 with a view to supporting their clients and wider economy in the net zero transition. In addition, tentatively from 2030, banks should start making available their transition plans to the HKMA regularly on a “comply or explain” basis. The transition plans should consist of decarbonisation and financing targets, and clear action plans for achieving 2050 net zero ambition, including a plan for managed phase-out of financing for carbon-intensive assets. The transition plans should be Paris-aligned, robust, actionable and up-to-date.

With a view to promoting Hong Kong as a transition finance hub, the Steering Group convened an industry working group to develop guidance for practicing transition finance under a sectoral approach.

The HKMA published the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Hong Kong Taxonomy) in early May 2024. It serves as a pivotal tool to scale up the flow of green and sustainable finance and address greenwashing concerns. Phase 1 operationalises the Common Ground Taxonomy (CGT) to achieve alignment with the two mainstream taxonomies of Mainland China and the European Union (EU), and encompasses 12 economic activities under four sectors, namely power generation, transportation, construction, and water and waste management. To make the Taxonomy more usable and support the transition of the region, the HKMA has embarked on Phase 2 development, under which the scope of sectors and economic activities will be expanded to introduce transition elements and add new green activities. Examples of new activities include other forms of energy production, clean transportation, and manufacturing of basic chemicals and materials, etc. The expanded taxonomy will also cover a new environmental objective, namely climate change adaptation, as well as new components like “Do No Significant Harm”. The HKMA plans to consult the public on the next phase taxonomy prototype in September 2025. The HKMA has been engaging with a broad set of stakeholders (including banks, corporates and investors), with a view to launching a taxonomy that can further facilitate the flow of green and sustainable finance.

Financial support

The Government launched the Green and Sustainable Finance Grant Scheme in 2021 to provide subsidy for eligible bond issuers and loan borrowers to cover part of their expenses on bond issuance and external review services. The Scheme has been extended by three years from 2024 to 2027, with an expanded scope of subsidies to cover transition bonds and loans. These measures encourage relevant industries in the region to make use of Hong Kong's transition financing platform towards decarbonisation. As of early August 2025, we have granted around HK$360 million to over 590 green and sustainable debt instruments issued in Hong Kong, involving a total underlying debt issuance of around HK$1.3 trillion (or over US$160 billion).

The Government launched the brand new “Green and Sustainable Fintech Proof-of-Concept Funding Support Scheme” in June 2024 to provide early-stage funding to support technology companies or research institutes conducting green fintech activities to collaborate with local enterprises to co-develop new projects in the market that can address the industry pain points. The Scheme facilitates the commercialisation of the solutions and the completion of the proof-of-concept stage, enabling wider adoption of green and sustainable fintech solutions with potential in the business landscape of Hong Kong. 60 projects were approved, with grant of HK$150,000 for each project.
 
Capacity development & Knowledge or data sharing
In October 2022, the Steering Group launched the Sustainable Finance Internship Initiative to create more sustainable finance internship opportunities in Hong Kong for students, facilitating them to gain relevant hands-on experience and supporting the development of the GSF talent pool in Hong Kong.

To nurture talent for further promoting the development of green and sustainable finance, the Government launched in 2022 the Pilot Green and Sustainable Finance Capacity Building Support Scheme (Pilot Scheme) for application by local eligible market practitioners and related professionals (including legal practitioners with responsibilities involving green and sustainable finance considerations) as well as students and graduates of relevant disciplines. Upon completing eligible programmes or accomplishing relevant qualifications, applicants can apply for reimbursement of up to $10,000. As of end-July 2025, there were 95 eligible programmes and qualifications, which are provided by the professional and continuing education schools of local universities, professional institutions, international training providers, etc., and the list will continue to be updated. Over 7 600 reimbursement applications were approved under the Pilot Scheme, involving a total reimbursement amount of over HK$42 million. As announced in the 2025-26 Budget, to continuously support local green-finance talent training, the Scheme will be extended to 2028. The Scheme is administered by the Steering Group.

The Steering Group announced in December 2022 that it entered into a collaboration arrangement with CDP and developed a Climate and Environmental Risk Questionnaire for Non-listed companies/small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Hong Kong. The Questionnaire is intended to provide an easy-to use template to assist the sustainability reporting by corporates without sufficient know-how or resources. This helps them understand their sustainability performance and raise their sustainability profile to lenders, investors and supply chain clients, which in turn facilitates financial institutions' collection and assessment of company-level data for climate related risk assessment and business decisions. In 2024, the Questionnaire was digitalised to facilitate online reporting. The Steering Group has continued to enhance the Questionnaire to make it more robust and user friendly. 

In February 2024, the Steering Group, in collaboration with the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, launched greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions calculation and estimation tools. These tools are available for free public access on the website of the Steering Group, facilitating sustainability reporting by corporates and financial institutions in Hong Kong. These tools equip SMEs with the means to manage their environmental footprint and encourage market participants to improve sustainable business practices. In April 2025, the Steering Group introduced new features to enhance the GHG emissions calculation tool. These new features, which were developed based on industry feedback, include incorporating emission factors from various years to enable more accurate GHG emissions calculation and allow the generation of comprehensive reports that outline the calculation process to facilitate GHG emissions reporting and third-party assurance.

In April 2025, HKEX and the SFC co-hosted the first-ever International Carbon Markets Summit, which welcomed over 200 distinguished guests from around the world, to discuss the opportunities and challenges in developing global voluntary carbon markets, as well as ways to promote market connectivity and collaboration for cross-border carbon asset trading.

Collaborative initiative

The HKMA published the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Hong Kong Taxonomy) in early May 2024. It serves as a pivotal tool to raise awareness about green finance, promote common understanding on green activities, facilitate green finance flows, and provide a foundation for further applications. It aligns with the two mainstream taxonomies of the Mainland and the European Union (EU), and currently encompasses 12 economic activities under four sectors namely power generation, transportation, construction, and water and waste management. For the next step, the HKMA will seek to expand the coverage of the taxonomy to include more sectors and activities, including transition activities.

HKEX signed the following Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with Exchanges in the Mainland to enhance collaboration in carbon market development -
―	August 2021: with the Guangzhou Futures Exchange (GFEX) with a view to driving a green and low-carbon market in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) and supporting sustainable development;
―	March 2022: with the Guangzhou-based China Emissions Exchange to explore cooperation opportunities in carbon finance;
―	October 2023: with the Shenzhen Green Exchange (formerly known as China Emissions Exchange Shenzhen) to cooperate in accelerating the carbon market ecosystem development in Hong Kong and across the GBA; and
―	November 2023: with the China Beijing Green Exchange (CBGEX) to explore cooperation in a number of areas, including building an ESG ecosystem, promoting green and sustainable finance and contributing to the green development of the Belt and Road Initiative.

This helps them understand their sustainability performance and raise their sustainability profile to lenders, investors and supply chain clients, which in turn facilitates financial institutions' collection and assessment of company-level data for climate related risk assessment and business decisions. In 2024, the Questionnaire was digitalised to facilitate online reporting. The Steering Group has continued to enhance the Questionnaire to make it more robust and user friendly. 

In February 2024, the Steering Group, in collaboration with the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, launched greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions calculation and estimation tools. These tools are available for free public access on the website of the Steering Group, facilitating sustainability reporting by corporates and financial institutions in Hong Kong. These tools equip SMEs with the means to manage their environmental footprint and encourage market participants to improve sustainable business practices. In April 2025, the Steering Group introduced new features to enhance the GHG emissions calculation tool. These new features, which were developed based on industry feedback, include incorporating emission factors from various years to enable more accurate GHG emissions calculation and allow the generation of comprehensive reports that outline the calculation process to facilitate GHG emissions reporting and third-party assurance.

In April 2025, HKEX and the SFC co-hosted the first-ever International Carbon Markets Summit, which welcomed over 200 distinguished guests from around the world, to discuss the opportunities and challenges in developing global voluntary carbon markets, as well as ways to promote market connectivity and collaboration for cross-border carbon asset trading.

Collaborative initiative

The HKMA published the Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Hong Kong Taxonomy) in early May 2024. It serves as a pivotal tool to raise awareness about green finance, promote common understanding on green activities, facilitate green finance flows, and provide a foundation for further applications. It aligns with the two mainstream taxonomies of the Mainland and the European Union (EU), and currently encompasses 12 economic activities under four sectors namely power generation, transportation, construction, and water and waste management. For the next step, the HKMA will seek to expand the coverage of the taxonomy to include more sectors and activities, including transition activities.

HKEX signed the following Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with Exchanges in the Mainland to enhance collaboration in carbon market development -
―	August 2021: with the Guangzhou Futures Exchange (GFEX) with a view to driving a green and low-carbon market in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) and supporting sustainable development;
―	March 2022: with the Guangzhou-based China Emissions Exchange to explore cooperation opportunities in carbon finance;
―	October 2023: with the Shenzhen Green Exchange (formerly known as China Emissions Exchange Shenzhen) to cooperate in accelerating the carbon market ecosystem development in Hong Kong and across the GBA; and
―	November 2023: with the China Beijing Green Exchange (CBGEX) to explore cooperation in a number of areas, including building an ESG ecosystem, promoting green and sustainable finance and contributing to the green development of the Belt and Road Initiative.

column17: Reporte del Gobierno de la Ciudad de México en el Registro Nacional de Emisiones (RENE)\n\nEl RENE es un instrumento de política pública que permite compilar la información de las emisiones de los diferentes sectores productivos del país, que generan más de 25,000 toneladas de bióxido de carbono equivalente al año (tCO2e). Instrumento que es coordinado por la Federación a través de la Secretaría de Medio Ambiente y Recursos Naturales (SEMARNAT), de acuerdo con los lineamientos del reglamento de la Ley General de Cambio Climático en Materia del Registro Nacional de Emisiones. El Gobierno de la Ciudad de México al emitir más de 25,000 tCO2e al año, es un sujeto obligado a reportar sus emisiones de GEI; actividad que viene realizando de manera anual desde el año 2015. Para lograrlo, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente (SEDEMA) capacita y coordina alrededor de 80 instituciones que conforman el Gobierno de la Ciudad de México, con la finalidad de recopilar su información de consumos energéticos en: sus instalaciones y flota vehicular, así como por el tratamiento del agua residual de las instalaciones a su cargo; para posteriormente estimar las emisiones derivadas, e integrar el Reporte a nombre del Gobierno de la Ciudad de México. También la SEDEMA contrata cada tres años a un Organismo Verificador de Emisiones de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (debidamente acreditado por la Ley Federal sobre Metrología y Normalización y su Reglamento), para verificar el reporte de emisiones del año aplicable; dando así transparencia y trazabilidad de las emisiones del propio Gobierno de la Ciudad de México.

El desarrollo de la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática (ELAC) 2021-2050 y el Programa de Acción Climática (PACCM) 2021-2030 consideró el uso de metodologías y marco de referencia para la planificación en materia de cambio climático con el Acuerdo de París. A través de asistencia técnica y mediante el uso de metodologías comparables a nivel internacional, se apoyó el desarrollo de contenidos de mitigación y adaptación del documento integrado, y se mantuvo una revisión e intercambio permanente de información para asegurar la ambición de los compromisos climáticos de la Ciudad de México. En septiembre de 2021 se confirmó la total compatibilidad de la ELAC y el PACCM con el Marco de Planificación de Acción Climática de C40, destacando como uno de los instrumentos líderes en el mundo en reflejar ambición frente a la emergencia climática. Actualmente, se trabaja con C40 en la actualización del Programa de Acción Climática, con el fin de asegurar su alineación con el Marco de Transición Climática de las Ciudades (CCTF, por sus siglas en inglés) y los Estándares de Liderazgo de C40. También, la Ciudad participa en diversos Aceleradores de la red, a través de los cuales se participa en el intercambio de experiencias y divulgación de datos climáticos, como Aire Limpio, Construcción Limpia, Calles verdes y saludables y Edificios de cero emisiones netas de carbono.

En julio de 2024 se firmó una colaboración por un periodo de seis meses entre la persona moral denominada VO.BO. Asesores Integrales, S.C. (VO.BO.); y, por la otra parte, la persona moral denominada “Conservación Biológica y Desarrollo Social, A.C. (CONBIODES) para la ejecución del Proyecto “Contribución de las áreas de valor ambiental en la Ciudad de México a la conectividad ecológica y la conservación de la biodiversidad”. 
El objetivo de esta colaboración fue evaluar la contribución de las Áreas de Valor Ambiental (AVA) a la conservación de la biodiversidad y a la conectividad ecológica en la Ciudad de México, y con ello, al manejo integrado del paisaje.
El proyecto generó una línea base de conocimiento en torno a las AVA con categoría de barrancas y la ejecución de un piloto que permitiera evaluar la conectividad estructural y funcional a través de la identificación con especies indicadoras de la calidad y conectividad ambiental; el desarrollo de una guía metodológica para el monitoreo de las especies indicadoras y de la conectividad biológica que pudiera ser replicable en otras áreas protegidas; un informe del análisis de conectividad estructural y funcional en las barrancas y recomendaciones para mejorar la gestión y la conectividad de las AVA.
El desarrollo de este proyecto contribuye a fortalecer la conservación de la biodiversidad y la conectividad ecológica en las Áreas de Valor Ambiental (AVA) de la Ciudad de México. Por un lado, la generación de una línea base de conocimiento y la aplicación de metodologías para evaluar la conectividad estructural y funcional permiten identificar espacios clave para mantener y restaurar los servicios ecosistémicos, tales como la captura de carbono, la regulación microclimática y la provisión de hábitat para especies que favorecen la resiliencia de los ecosistemas urbanos. Por otro lado, las recomendaciones derivadas del análisis de las barrancas y el diseño de herramientas replicables para el monitoreo de especies indicadoras aportan elementos estratégicos para una gestión del territorio más sostenible, capaz de reducir la vulnerabilidad de la ciudad frente a los impactos climáticos.

Como parte de sus esfuerzos por acelerar las transiciones urbanas sostenibles y con el propósito de escalar la implementación de Soluciones Basadas en la Naturaleza (SbN) en entornos urbanos, el Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Medio Ambiente (PNUMA) lanzó el proyecto Generación Restauración (2023-2025), cuyo objetivo es implementar un conjunto de medidas para enfrentar desafíos políticos, técnicos y financieros en torno a la restauración ecológica, particularmente en zonas urbanas, en el marco del Decenio de las Naciones Unidas sobre la Restauración de los Ecosistemas y del Marco Mundial de la Biodiversidad.
En mayo de 2023, la Dirección General de Coordinación de Políticas y Cultura Ambiental (DGCPCA) a través de la Coordinación de Estrategias para la Biodiversidad, aplicó a la convocatoria para participar en el proyecto, y tras un proceso de evaluación técnica, en septiembre de 2023, la Ciudad de México fue seleccionada como ciudad piloto con la propuesta de proyecto “Tequios por la Restauración”, centrada en fortalecer la participación ciudadana para impulsar acciones de restauración ecológica como parte de los esfuerzos del Gobierno capitalino para reincorporar la naturaleza en el entorno urbano.
Reforestamos México A.C. fue seleccionada como organización ejecutora del proyecto gracias a su sólida trayectoria, experiencia técnica, redes locales y resultados comprobables en materia de restauración de ecosistemas. Por su parte, la Coordinación de Estrategias para la Biodiversidad funge como el área responsable del seguimiento técnico y operativo, en estrecha coordinación con Reforestamos México A.C.
La Ciudad de México destaca por su activa participación ciudadana en iniciativas como jardines polinizadores, huertos urbanos y recuperación de espacios verdes. Sin embargo, muchos de estos esfuerzos se desarrollan al margen de las instituciones y carecen de coordinación con las autoridades. El proyecto “Tequios por la Restauración” busca atender este reto mediante el fortalecimiento del trabajo conjunto entre ciudadanía y gobierno, impulsando acciones de restauración ecológica y la aplicación de Soluciones Basadas en la Naturaleza, con el fin de dar continuidad y respaldo institucional a estas iniciativas y potenciar la reintegración de la naturaleza en la ciudad.
A partir del proyecto se conformó la Red de Tequios por la Restauración, un espacio colaborativo que articula los esfuerzos de la ciudadanía y promueve la restauración ambiental comunitaria. Aunque el piloto concluye en agosto de 2025, se busca fortalecer la Red para asegurar su continuidad más allá de los cambios administrativos, manteniendo el impulso ciudadano en la recuperación de espacios verdes y azules, la conservación de la biodiversidad y la mitigación del cambio climático.

El Sistema de Huertos Urbanos de la Ciudad de México, también conocido como Rizoma, es una red colaborativa que impulsa la creación, fortalecimiento y conexión de huertos urbanos, brindando apoyo y acompañamiento. Su propósito es maximizar los beneficios compartidos de los huertos, fomentar la sostenibilidad, la seguridad alimentaria y la cohesión comunitaria, así como promover el intercambio de saberes, experiencias y productos. Su organización es horizontal, sin jerarquías entre sus nodos o unidades básicas, siguiendo la analogía de un rizoma: dinámico, que se expande, se conecta, se construye y se enriquece continuamente. 
En cumplimiento con lo establecido en el artículo 12 de la Ley de Huertos Urbanos de la Ciudad de México, y como parte de una estrategia para consolidar proyectos ciudadanos de agricultura urbana y garantizar la permanencia de sus beneficios, desde 2022, la Secretaría del Medio Ambiente de la Ciudad de México (SEDEMA) ha impulsado la conformación y operación del Sistema de Huertos Urbanos de la Ciudad de México (SHU-Rizoma).
El SHU-Rizoma es una iniciativa participativa que surge del trabajo colectivo de la ciudadanía interesada en la agricultura urbana. La SEDEMA es uno de los actores que lidera su organización y coordinación, articulándose con otras dependencias del gobierno local y con las alcaldías para atender las demandas de las y los huerteros, facilitar procedimientos administrativos y consolidar acciones que fortalezcan el desarrollo, la permanencia y la sostenibilidad de los huertos urbanos en la Ciudad de México. 
El SHU-Rizoma se sustenta en la participación activa y colaborativa de la comunidad, reconociendo el papel fundamental de las y los huerteros como agentes de cambio para la construcción de una ciudad más verde, resiliente y equitativa. Asimismo, promueve la consolidación de huertos urbanos sostenibles que no solo fortalecen la seguridad alimentaria local, sino que también brindan servicios ambientales esenciales, como la conservación de la biodiversidad (agrobiodiversidad), la captura de carbono, la infiltración de agua de lluvia y la generación de espacios verdes para el disfrute y el bienestar colectivo.
Entre 2024 y agosto de 2025, las asambleas generales permitieron avanzar en una planeación estratégica para fortalecer al SHU-Rizoma, con el objetivo de incrementar el número de huertos urbanos en la Ciudad de México y garantizar que al menos el 20% cuenten con insumos, tecnología y capacitación. Las prioridades definidas incluyen: implementar sistemas de recolección de agua de lluvia y manejo de aguas grises; desarrollar un sistema integral de manejo de residuos; incorporar al menos nueve investigaciones aplicadas por año en los proyectos estratégicos; y consolidarse como una organización representativa de los huertos urbanos que articule y dé voz a las necesidades del sector.
En resumen, el SHU-Rizoma es una estrategia de infraestructura verde y de gobernanza comunitaria que convierte a la agricultura urbana en un mecanismo clave para que la Ciudad de México avance hacia la sostenibilidad, la resiliencia y la acción climática integral.

column17: La Coordinación de Estrategias para la Biodiversidad de la Dirección General de Coordinación de Políticas y Cultura Ambiental de la SEDEMA, se apoyó de diversas áreas e instituciones de gobierno, la academia y, en especial, llevó una colaboración cercana con la Comisión Nacional para el Conocimiento y Uso de la Biodiversidad (CONABIO), el Instituto de Ecología y la Facultad de Ciencias de la Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México (UNAM) para desarrollar el Índice de BIodiversidad Urbana de la Ciudad de México (IBU). Esta evaluación tuvo como principal objetivo generar una línea base en el periodo 2019-2020, lo que permitió conocer el estado de la biodiversidad en sus diferentes componentes, identificar prioridades y proponer recomendaciones para fortalecer las áreas de oportunidad detectadas; así como potenciar los esfuerzos que ya se realizan en la ciudad para la conservación y uso sostenible de la biodiversidad. En el 2024 se publicó esta obra terminada.\nLa generación de una línea base sobre el estado de la biodiversidad en la Ciudad de México permite identificar los ecosistemas y especies más vulnerables a los impactos climáticos, así como reconocer aquellos que brindan servicios ambientales fundamentales, como la captura de carbono, la regulación hídrica y la moderación de la temperatura local. Al establecer prioridades y formular recomendaciones para fortalecer la conservación y el uso sostenible de la biodiversidad, esta obra contribuye a diseñar estrategias de gestión territorial más resilientes, capaces de reducir la vulnerabilidad de la ciudad frente a fenómenos climáticos extremos y, al mismo tiempo, de potenciar los beneficios de los ecosistemas como aliados en la mitigación del cambio climático.

The Citizens' Permanent Assembly on Climate is a civic participation body aiming to give citizens a voice on municipal activities related to the fight against climate change, air quality and the ecological transition. It is one of the actions of Milan's Air and Climate Plan dedicated to citizen engagement and awareness-raising. 
The Assembly is composed of 90 people above 16 years old and residing in the city. To ensure the greatest plurality, they are chosen randomly so that the final group is representative of the entire population of Milan and as inclusive as possible of the voices of all minorities. Every year, the Statistics Office of the Municipality draws a sample of 10,000 citizens, whose composition proportionally reflects the characteristics of the city population, with reference to the residence district, gender and age (data from the Registry Office). These citizens are sent an invitation to participate in the works of the Assembly for one year. To make the composition of the Assembly more representative and inclusive, a final selection of the invited people is undertaken through a questionnaire on their personal profile, to which they can respond voluntarily.
The Permanent Assembly meets in plenary once a month. Between plenary sessions, participants are invited to work in small groups to discuss and express suggestions on the various actions of the Air and Climate Plan. The Municipality is committed to respond promptly to the recommendations of the Assembly.
Participants are also required to attend a training on climate change and the Air and Climate Plan. Associations working in the fields of environmental issues or civic participation can support the Permanent Citizens' Assembly on Climate.

The Milan Air and Climate Alliance is a structured collaboration between local institutions and the private sector to achieve the objectives of the Air Quality and Climate Plan (ACP) more quickly and effectively.
It is a common and shared path to:
- involve companies that already have advanced sustainability strategies;
- stimulate companies that have not yet started developing sustainability strategies;
- facilitate collaborative processes to support the green transition.
To create this framework, a participatory process in three phases was designed:
1. First Phase (completed): Different municipal departments and representatives of business associations discussed and agreed the Alliance's fundamentals.
2. Second Phase (in progress): The aim of the co-design phase is to develop the Air and Climate Alliance Guidelines, defining the structure and operating methods of the Alliance. Through a Call for Proposals, the Municipality selected 21 companies, which have started to draft the guidelines in collaboration with relevant municipal departments. They are: Biotitan Nanotechnology - Capgemini Italia - Carbotermo - Carrefour Italia - Cariplo Factory - Deloitte Italy - Edison - Havas - InVento Innovation Lab - Legacoop Lombardia - Liquigas - L'Oreal Italia - Maire - OpenDot - Re-Solution Hub - Sky Italia - SOS-LOGistica - SYNLAB Italia Srl - Taua Srl Società Benefit - TEKNE SpA - Up2You. After conclusion of the co-design phase (expected in 2024), the draft guidelines will be submitted to public consultation to allow the entire city business community to contribute to their finalization and then possibly join the actual Alliance.
3. Third Phase (end 2024): The launch of the Alliance is expected to take place at the end of 2024. Through an Expression of Interest, all local companies interested in contributing to the city's transition process and meeting the requirements will join the Air and Climate Alliance.

The Municipality of Milan participated in the EuComMeet project, an experimental project funded by the European Union through the Horizon 2020 Programme, with the goal of supporting citizens' active participation in public life and fostering exchanges and connections between EU citizens at local, national and European level. The project aimed to explore how deliberation and participation can help reduce opinion polarization, strengthening the European identity, promoting inclusiveness in deliberative processes, narrow the representative gap between politicians and citizens. 100 citizens for each of the 10 participating city were involved. They had the opportunity to get informed and work in small groups on existing challenges and good practices on three themes: sustainable and local food consumption, plastic pollution, and sustainable mobility. After an information and training session on these three themes, the citizens involved had about a month and a half to discuss and deliberate through an interactive online platform developed by the project itself. The results of their discussions at three levels was gathered in a summary document available here: https://www.eucommeet.eu/
https://www.comune.milano.it/web/milano-cambia-aria/progetti/eucomeet.
The project is concluded, but it has left us with a series of insights and reflections to use, some of which are accessible here: https://www.eucommeet.eu/resources/.
For the City of Milan, this represents the methodological reflection on digital participation carried forward with this project, which will complement the other four types of citizen participation currently underway.

column17: The Municipality of Milan stipulates Collaboration Agreements with active citizens for the regeneration and shared management of urban common goods, i.e. open or closed spaces in the city belonging to the Municipality or to private subjects, that citizens can choose to take care of, if the owner gives his/her consent. Today in Milan green areas are treated as common goods, including flower beds, gardens, streets, squares, transit areas, sports facilities, assets confiscated to the mafia, hospitals, and abandoned areas later recovered. In this way, with their commitment, citizens redevelop these places, restore their original functions and often redesign them with new functions. Intangible objects can also become common goods, such as the information data that the municipal administration produces and publishes in an open format, or the investigation and knowledge activities that are useful for localized monitoring of the environment (citizen science).The cornerstones of every project that leads to a Collaboration Agreement are the commitment and responsibility of the parties involved in carrying out the agreed and planned activities.One of the most recent practical examples is a Collaboration Agreement for the observation and monitoring of the biodiversity of the green area that arose in the old gas-works plant of Bovisa (northern area of Milan), which is one of the most significant examples of spontaneous nature that takes back its space in the urban context. Two other Collaboration Agreements were signed between the Municipality of Milan and two primary schools to promote the autonomy of movement in the home/school path and outdoor education as a common good for boys and girls in the neighbourhood of Lambrate. The essential requirements are the presence and the possibility of exploring nature, the city, the world outside classrooms and school spaces, to be realized through the installation of furniture (chairs and blackboards) and recognition items. https://www.comune.milano.it/web/patti-di-collaborazione

The project actions also extend to Slovenia with the aim of evaluating and reducing the transport of pollutants even beyond the Adriatic Sea.The 18 project partners include:- 6 Regions (Emilia Romagna, Veneto, Lombardy, Piedmont, Friuli Venezia Giulia, and the Autnomous Province of Trento);- 7 environmental protection agencies (ARPAE Emilia Romagna, ARPA Veneto, ARPA Piemonte, ARPA Lombardia, ARPA Valle d'Aosta, ARPA Friuli Venezia Giulia, Slovenia Environment Agency );- 3 municipalities (Bologna, Milan, Turin);- 1 regional development agency (ART-ER);- 1 foundation (FLA).In addition to partners collaboration for the implementation of actions, each local and regional administration involved as project partner has set up a Stakeholder Board involving the local authorities (municipalities or associations of municipalities) as well as the environmental and socio-economic associations relevant to the project activities and interested in following up . The Stakeholder Boards were convened at the start of the project and periodically during its implementation (at least once for each project phase). Milan's Climate City Contract: 
In the context of the EU Mission “100 Climate-Neutral and Smart Cities”, on 15 March 2024 Milan presented its Climate City Contract, an agreement promoted by the Municipality and supported by various local stakeholders, with the ambitious goal of achieving climate neutrality by 2030, contributing to the anticipation of the Air and Climate Plan target set for 2050. 
Together with 25 stakeholders, including companies owned by the Municipality of Milan, universities, urban regeneration operators, building cooperatives and civil society organizations, the Mayor of Milan signed a series of commitments that translate into a portfolio of 157 concrete and measurable actions that will contribute in various ways to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Of these, 51 actions will be implemented by the Municipality and 106 by stakeholders, to be completed in the next six years: 'carbon neutral' urban regeneration projects, interventions on energy networks, new infrastructures for cycle-pedestrian mobility, forestation actions and awareness-raising initiatives on sustainable energy behaviors and sustainable mobility. The total cost of the actions is estimated at around 6 billion euros. The Municipality will invest 2.6 billion thanks also to the extraordinary funds of the PNRR and React EU, while the remaining 3.3 billion will be covered by the other stakeholders.

Power Up! involves young people aged 15 to 23 from three different European cities: Milan (Italy), Pernik and Kuystendil (Bulgaria), and Ljubljana (Slovenia).

A co-design process has been activated to develop the YCA, involving experts in key areas: civic participation, youth policies, deliberative processes, education, communication, and sustainability;
- The International Forum in Milan (2026), a moment of discussion between young people, policymakers, experts, and activists.

column17: A new resource center the Climate Academy The Academy opened its doors on September, 15, 2021. Created following the Climate Marches it is a space for raising awareness training and mobilization around environmental issues. This inclusive institution provides a space for collective intelligence and action to allow all audiences particularly young people aged 9 to 25 to imagine and build a more desirable future. This project follows a pedagogical and innovative approach addressing the climate issue in all its facets. The Academy has numerous partners including the Paris Rectorate, Eau de Paris, the Paris Climate Agency, the Forum des Images, the Interdisciplinary Research Center and many active and recognized associations such as, La fresque de la Renaissance, École comestible, the LPO, the REPAR, and more. The Climate Academy offers training programs for young people adults city employees and all Parisians. It has already hosted numerous events including the first four editions of a new series of monthly climate conferences organized by the City of Paris: Climate Conversations. Each evening brings together more than a hundred people and addresses a specific theme such as COPs, Climate and Digital, Climate Change, etc. During weekdays, workshops are offered to schoolchildren middle schoolers and high school students focusing on the challenges of the transition. The Academy features a teaching kitchen a bicycle repair and DIY workshop, a green courtyard with an educational garden, a sewing space, an ecoconstruction lab and a nursery. In the evenings and on weekends, many free and open events are organized including conferences exhibitions workshops coworking and more. https://www.academieduclimat.paris https://www.paris.fr/dossiers/l-academie-du-climat-44 Over 600 cities applied for the 2021 Global Mayors Challenge initiated by Bloomberg Philanthropies which aimed to support cities in developing innovative projects in various areas postCOVID19. Paris made it to the top 50 cities with its Climate Academy project a one-of-a-kind institution set to open in the City.

column17: The tourism development plan represents a significant milestone for the city of Paris as it outlines an ambitious strategy aimed at positioning the capital as not only the most visited city in the world, but also as a leading destination for high-quality sustainable tourism that generates employment opportunities. With this plan Paris seeks to enhance its tourism sector by focusing on delivering exceptional experiences and fostering sustainable practices. The objective is to create an environment where visitors can enjoy the best that the city has to offer while ensuring the preservation of its cultural heritage natural resources and local communities. To achieve these goals the tourism development plan emphasizes the importance of maintaining and enhancing the quality of visitor services accommodations attractions and amenities. It promotes a holistic approach that considers the environmental social and economic impacts of tourism activities. By prioritizing sustainability, Paris aims to minimize the ecological footprint of tourism and actively contribute to the global effort to combat climate change and preserve the environment. The plan encourages the adoption of ecofriendly practices the promotion of responsible tourism and the development of partnerships with local communities and businesses. Additionally, the tourism development plan recognizes the potential of the tourism sector to generate employment and stimulate economic growth. By attracting visitors from around the world, Paris aims to create job opportunities support local businesses and contribute to the overall prosperity of the city and its residents. Overall the tourism development plan represents a comprehensive and forward-thinking approach to position Paris as a global leader in tourism known for its outstanding visitor experiences commitment to sustainability and positive impact on the local economy and community https://www.paris.fr/pages/un-plan-en-59-mesures-pour-le-tourisme-parisien-4196 The Sustainable Tourism Conference of March 2021 brought together 150 stakeholders to explore a more local green and resilient tourism approach. First unveiled for the 2024 Olympics, the City of Paris has implemented a 'bathing plan' ever since 2015, in cooperation with neighboring local authority and state services. Targeting environmental quality, in conjunction with heatwaves getting more intense and longer, the program aims to improve the Seine water quality enough to make it consequentially fit for public bathing. Thereby increasing the public supply of affordable refreshing activities during summer for Parisians, the program provides a form of inclusive nature based solution (taking into account that lower income families are more likely to stay in Paris during the hotter months). In the summer of 2025, the City officially opened 3 protected public bathing areas (equipped with piers and cabins).
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/se-baigner-dans-la-seine-en-2024-et-au-dela-6935)

This program was dependent on a decade long local cooperation in order to succeed, given the sources of Seine pollution and the measures that were needed to restore and control water quality. Collectively, the French State, the City of Paris ans local authorities invested more than 1,4 billions euros spread over 10 years to accomplish the results observable today. 

One of these building blocks was improving the regional water treatment plants. Two disinfection units were achieved by 2023. 

Another was runoff infrastructures, in order to avoid the spill of sewers into the river during heavy rainfalls. One of these infrastructures is the Austerlitz Basin, opened by May 2024, which acts as an emergency rainfall stocking system that can contain 50 000 m3, the equivalent capacity of 20 Olympic swimming pools. 
(https://www.paris.fr/pages/assainissement-de-la-seine-les-travaux-du-tunnelier-d-austerlitz-vont-bientot-demarrer-21535)

Other comparable equipment were put in service upstream since 2024 : the Saint-Baudile basin, the 10km VL8 great capacity collector in-between the Essone and Val-de-Marne areas, and the de-polluting station in Val-de-Marne. All these infrastructures share the same objective, collect and treat rainfall and runoff waters before their release in the natural habitat. 

At the eve of the Olympics, the bathing plan was reinforced on regarding quality testing and monitoring, in order to prevent peaks of pollution, to identify potential remaining sources and to ensure immediate corrective measures. This implied increased involvement of the City, the State, the upstream departments (Essone and Val-de-Marne), the regional water treatment operator (SIAAP), and other port and river navigation authorities (Haropa Port, Voies Navigables de France). The increased monitoring concerned the water treatment networks, as well as the boating activity and wastewater connections, for which a dedicated intervention team was created.

National cooperation too also shape through the 2018 law obligating wastewater sewage connection to all stationary boat and floating devices, resulting in the connection of 260 boats for Paris alone. Additionally, 23 000 connection issues were identified and treated upstream, housing whereby wastewater was previously released untreated in the natural habitat. 

Last but not least, regionally, an increased focus on re-naturalization of water banks was implemented, as a natural solution to improve water quality in the filtering of rainfalls and runoffs. 

The three protected bathing area opened in 2025 are actively monitored, the water quality tested daily in order to ensure quality within the recommendations of the Regional Health Agency. Notably, relying on the ColiMinder technology, used upstream, the City can detect E.coli within 15-20 minutes (as opposed to 24 to 48 hours in lab) and close bathing before contamination reaches the areas. (https://www.paris.fr/pages/baignade-dans-la-seine-comment-sera-mesuree-la-qualite-de-l-eau-31118)

O projeto visa desenvolver uma aliança educacional para treinar a próxima geração de profissionais urbanos do clima a navegar na complexidade dos domínios de conhecimento interconectados ligados à ação climática urbana nas cidades. O programa inclui uma série de atividades de educação e trocas de conhecimento. O evento é organizado pelos parceiros locais da UCCRN_edu: Departamento de Arquitetura e Urbanismo da PUC-Rio, FIOCRUZ, COPPE-UFRJ e UCCRN Latin American Hub, e será a oportunidade de testar o potencial de replicação dos métodos e ferramentas da UCCRN_edu no Rio de Janeiro e no Brasil.

Ao longo de duas semanas de atividades, foi realizada uma série de eventos de divulgação, oficinas técnicas e estúdio de desenho urbano. O UDCW envolveu especialistas internacionais da UCCRN, partes interessadas locais e estudantes da PUC-Rio, UNINA e NYIT, convocados para desenvolver cenários de projeto urbano resilientes ao clima para a área de São Cristóvão. 
O UDCW explorou estratégias de design integrado para o bairro de São Cristóvão, trazendo exemplos de boas práticas que ajudam a moldar comunidades sustentáveis e resilientes que podem se adaptar e prosperar nas condições globais em constante mudança, atender às metas de redução de carbono, fornecer novos espaços e instalações públicas em relação às prioridades das partes interessadas, configurando ou reformando distritos ecológicos compactos e de uso misto, com atenção para as possibilidades de contribuição que o projeto e o planejamento urbano podem dar para expandir a justiça e a equidade socioterritoriais.

BMC works collaboratively with NGOs and climate expert organisations and networks such as C40 Cities, WRI, Waatavaran and so on, on the implementation of Climate actions in the city. City has collaborated with WRI on greening measures in the city for heat resilience and also in developing climate resilient streets through nature-based solutions. Several measures on air quality improvement and mobility are also being worked with WRI. BMC has been associated with C40 Cities since 2020 and has successfully launched the Paris agreement-aligned CAP in 2022 with the support of WRI as a Knowledge Partner. The first round of consultations for CAP was held with experts from NGOs, research organizations, citizens' forums, international development agencies and municipal service providers such as BEST and private companies. Six consultations were held in the first round, one for each sector. In each consultation, 5-7 subject experts shared specific recommendations, which formed the basis of the initial approach, goals and actions for each sectoral priority. These consultations were widely attended by climate enthusiasts, subject experts, students and citizens, with an average participation of 80-100 people. These consultations highlighted the key priorities and impact groups for each sector, with a focus on ensuring inclusivity in the planning process and representation of the needs of vulnerable citizens. The second round of consultations was hosted with various departments within BMC, external agencies such as Brinhanmumbai Electric Supply & Transport (BEST), Mumbai Port Trust (MbPT), Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority (MMRDA), Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB) and DISCOMS such as TATA Power and Adani Electricity Mumbai Ltd. In this round, the overarching goals and actions were discussed and the participants shared their feedback and recommendations on priority actions proposed in the MCAP. This process helped assess the relevance and feasibility of actions, the status of projects underway and the key barriers to timely implementation. The third round of consultations was held at the ward level for seven administrative zones across three divisions - City, Western Suburbs and Eastern Suburbs. During these consultations, Assistant Commissioners (ACs) and zonal DMCs of the divisions were familiarized with the MCAP and the proposed actions. The officials shared their perspectives with respect to the challenges and priorities at the grassroots and offered their support and commitment for the implementation of MCAP at the ward level. The ACs' recommendations for increased capacities to monitor progress, track projects and ensure timely collaboration is reflected in the form of the recently set up Environment and Climate Change Department. BMC also released its Climate Budget this year which was also a result of support from expert organisations and from different departments in the city.

Networks like C40 helps the Environment and Climate Change department to further the climate actions in the city and the ULB by providing exposure to climate accelerators and network which serves as a platform for peer-to-peer knowledge exchange and also leading amongst the cities across the world to set an example of climate leadership. C40 also provides technical assistance to the city and is actively engaged in initiatives relevant to heat resilience in building sector and structuring implementation support for decarbonisation efforts in public buildings.
There are many other such support that the city receives through climate initiatives and networks.

창원시는 정부·기업·시민사회와 다층적 협력 구조를 통해 기후변화 대응을 체계적으로 추진하고 있다.
특히, 공공기관과의 정책 연계, 기업과의 기술·투자 파트너십, 시민사회와의 참여 기반 확산을 통해 배출 감축-적응-회복력 강화-시민 교육의 전 영역에서 성과를 도출하고 있으며, 이는 창원시 기후행동의 공평성과 포용성을 강화하는 핵심적 기반이 되고 있다.

1. 정부와의 협력
1)환경부 협력: 기후변화 대응 시범도시 선정
창원시는 환경부와 협력하여 기후변화 대응 시범도시로 선정되었으며, 녹색교통 중심 도시 건설(대중교통·전기차·수소차 확대), 도시 침수 대응을 위한 하수도 정비 계획 강화 등을 공동 추진하고 있음.
2)경상남도·공공기관과의 협력: 광역정부 및 공공기관(한국전력, 한국에너지공단 등)과 협력해 온실가스 인벤토리 작성, 재생에너지 보급사업, 공공건물 에너지 효율화를 진행.

2. 기업과의 협력
1)환경 보호 활동 및 기술 투자: 지역 기업(현대차, 두산에너빌리티, 산업단지 기업 등)과 협력하여 친환경 교통수단(전기버스, 수소충전소) 확대, 산업단지 내 스마트에너지 플랫폼 및 폐열 회수 시스템 도입, 임직원 환경 자원봉사 활동 전개를 실현하고 있음.
2)환경의 날 행사 참여: 기업들은 창원시가 주최하는 환경의 날 행사에 적극 참여하여, 친환경 기술·제품 전시, 시민 참여 체험 프로그램 후원, 환경보호 캠페인 활동을 공동 추진.

3. 시민 사회와의 협력
1)환경 교육·참여 프로그램 운영: 시민 단체와 함께「우리에게 남은 탄소시간」캠페인, 자전거 출퇴근 챌린지, 공유텀블러 프로그램 등을 운영, 시민들의 인식을 높이고 공동체적 기후행동을 강화.
2)환경의 날 행사 - 시민 주도 참여
NGO·학계·주민 커뮤니티가 함께 참여하여, 기후행동 체험·교육 부스를 운영하고 환경보호 메시지를 확산.

4. 대표 협력 사례 - 환경의 날 행사
창원시가 주최하는 환경의 날 행사는 정부·기업·시민사회가 모두 참여하는 대표적 기후행동 협력 사례이다. 
정부 기관은 정책과 지원을 제공, 기업은 친환경 기술과 활동을 전개, 시민사회는 교육·참여 프로그램을 운영. 이 행사를 통해 창원시는 기후변화 대응의 중요성을 알리고, 지속 가능한 도시로 발전하기 위한 공동의 노력을 공유하며, 협력 기반의 성과를 가시화하고 있다.

창원시는 환경의 날 행사를 포함한 다양한 협력 프로젝트를 통해 정부·기업·시민사회의 역량을 결집하고 있다. 이러한 협력은 ▲배출 감축 ▲적응력 강화 ▲시민 인식 제고라는 세 축을 아우르며, 창원시가 지속 가능한 도시로 나아가는 핵심 기반으로 작동하고 있다.

The CoA formed a partnership with the Government of South Australia to work towards a shared aspiration of carbon neutrality, formalised through two mechanisms:

- The joint signing of the Compact of Mayors by Council and the Compact of States and Regions by the Premier, the first such pairing in Australia of these two important international networks.

This action plan was concluded in 2021 and new ways of working together are under development.

In 2023 the City of Adelaide contributed to a report of the CNCA on best practice Scope 3 emissions calculations and reporting for city communities, following extensive collaboration. column17: The Metropolitan Mayors Coalition is a group of cities and towns in the urban core of Metro Boston whose leaders gather to exchange information and create solutions for common problems. The municipal officials in this group represent more than 1.4 million residents in the cities and towns of Arlington, Boston, Braintree, Brookline, Cambridge, Chelsea, Everett, Malden, Medford, Melrose, Newton, Quincy, Revere, Somerville, and Winthrop. In May 2015, the Metro Mayors Coalition convened to sign a historic Climate Preparedness Commitment. The mayors and managers pledged to work together to prepare the region for climate change and to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. As part of the summit, the Coalition also launched an ongoing task force to guide collaborative efforts that address vulnerabilities in the region's communities and shared infrastructure. In 2016, the Taskforce communities signed a second agreement, this time focused on Climate Mitigation. Inspired by the Paris Climate Accord, the mayors and managers agreed that by 2050, the region would be net zero, and outlined a menu of mitigation options each municipality could undertake in order to advance toward this goal. The Metro Mayors Climate Taskforce coordinates a regional and cross-governmental effort to protect critical infrastructure and other vital resources and systems. The Taskforce makes policy recommendations and sets regional priorities based on the goals outlined in the Climate Preparedness and Mitigation Commitments. As part of the City of Boston's Climate Ready Boston program, the City regularly engages with other cities, State government, and Federal government in support of the City's adaptation and resilience goals. For example, the City participates in the Metropolitan Area Planning Council's Metro Mayors Task Force, which is a group of cities in the Greater Boston region focused on coordination and knowledge sharing around climate resilience priorities. The City participates in the Resilient Mystic Collaborative, a group created by the Mystic River Watershed Association to coordinate among cities along the Mystic River around climate resilience priorities. The City participates in the Charles River Climate Compact, a group created by the Charles River Watershed Association to coordinate among cities along the Charles River around climate resilience priorities. And the City participates with the Neponset River Watershed Association on proposals for regional coordination among cities along the Neponset River around climate resilience priorities. Boston also serves on the steering committee of the Greater Boston Regional Advisory Group (GBRAG), which develops updated regional climate risk assessments for the Greater Boston region.

column17: The City of Boston has identified vulnerable population groups as part of the Climate Ready Boston initiative. We work to center frontline communities in the development and implementation of climate-related initiatives. For example, we have convened Community Advisory Boards to inform specific processes, such as coastal resilience solutions planning for East Boston and Charlestown, heat resilience planning in environmental justice communities, or the development of regulations for the Wetlands Protection Ordinance. We also work with community-based organizations on engagement strategies, for example as part of the Resident Advisory Group convened to co-design the Building Emissions Reduction and Disclosure Ordinance, Boston's building emissions performance standard, in a process that focused on frontline community members who live in large buildings that would be affected by the policy, with integration of language justice as a core part of the initiative. We also design programs that focus on environmental justice communities, with dedicated and multilingual outreach as part of programs like Community Choice Electricity or for the deployment of solar and battery storage as part of Solarize East Boston.

Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (AMM) places civil society and academia at the center of its climate governance framework, recognizing that inclusive and evidence-based approaches are essential for effective climate action. Collaboration with universities, research institutions, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), residents, and vulnerable groups has been systematically integrated into both planning and implementation stages of climate-related policies.

Through informational and engagement mechanisms, AMM organizes public consultations, participatory workshops, and awareness campaigns on key climate issues such as water conservation, zero-waste practices, sustainable mobility, and air quality. These engagements ensure that residents and community groups are well-informed and actively involved in shaping municipal decisions. For example, the water-saving campaign developed in cooperation with the General Directorate of Water and Sewerage Administration (GDWSA) and NGOs reached thousands of households, raising awareness about drought risks and encouraging behavioral changes in daily water use. Similarly, city-wide zero-waste training sessions and outreach campaigns have significantly increased recycling rates and community participation.

Through collaborative initiatives, AMM works closely with NGOs, grassroots organizations, and academia to co-design and implement climate actions. Universities in Ankara have provided technical expertise and modeling support for the preparation of the Ankara Climate Change Action Plan (ACCAP) and the Green City Action Plan (GCAP). Academic institutions have also contributed to vulnerability assessments, social inclusion studies, and gender equality analyses, ensuring that scientific rigor and equity considerations are embedded into climate strategies. Partnerships with NGOs such as environmental associations and local resident groups help pilot innovative solutions, including green roof projects, community gardens, and neighborhood-level adaptation initiatives.

Knowledge and data sharing is another cornerstone of collaboration. Universities and research centers share climate modeling results, greenhouse gas (GHG) inventory data, and socio-economic impact assessments with the municipality, which then integrates these findings into planning documents and performance monitoring systems. Joint research projects have produced data on heat island effects, air quality trends, and water stress, enabling AMM to take preventive action. NGOs and residents' groups also provide valuable local knowledge, reporting environmental challenges observed in their neighborhoods and co-developing solutions with municipal departments.

Finally, capacity development efforts ensure that municipal staff, community leaders, and citizens are empowered with the skills and knowledge needed to respond to climate change. Training sessions, workshops, and university-led courses provide expertise on renewable energy, energy efficiency, disaster preparedness, and social resilience. AMM has collaborated with universities to develop internship and training programs for students in environmental engineering and urban planning, creating opportunities for the next generation of professionals to contribute to the city's climate goals. NGOs also contribute by organizing educational campaigns in schools and community centers, fostering a culture of sustainability among children and young people.

Special emphasis is placed on equity and inclusivity. Vulnerable populations, including low-income households, women, the elderly, and residents of flood-prone areas, are actively engaged in climate planning processes. AMM ensures that their perspectives are included in adaptation projects such as flood protection infrastructure, urban cooling measures, and affordable public transport services. These participatory approaches not only increase social acceptance but also strengthen resilience by addressing the needs of those most affected by climate change.

Overall, collaboration with civil society and academia has enabled AMM to implement climate action that is socially inclusive, scientifically credible, and widely supported. This approach enhances transparency, builds trust between citizens and government, and ensures that climate strategies deliver co-benefits such as improved public health, enhanced quality of life, and greater social equity. By leveraging engagement, collaboration, knowledge sharing, and capacity development, AMM has created a strong model of participatory governance that integrates climate resilience into the fabric of urban life.

개인, 가정, 학교, 기업, 지역사회가 함께 탄소중립 실천 생활화를 문화로 정착시켜야 한다. 오랫동안 굳어진 편리한 생활습관에서 탄소중립 생활이 일반화되기 위해서는 개인의 의지와 노력만으로 어려울 수 있으므로 직장, 학교, 마을, 사회 곳곳에서 지속적인 교육과 홍보, 캠페인을 통해 탄소중립 생활화에 대한 공감대가 형성되어야 하고, 구성원들이 실천하기 쉽게 시스템 개선과 함께 그 시스템에 적응 하도록 유도하여야 한다. 이를 위해 부산시에서는 아래와 같은 사업들을 지역 주민, 단체 등과 협업하여 추진해오고 있다.
 
2050년까지 탄소중립 사회로 이행하기 위해서는 시민이 주도하여 마을단위의 생활습관 개선 등을 통한 효율적인 온실가스 감축 도모는 필수적이다. 
이에 2016년부터 매년 탄소중립마을을 10여개 선정하여 마을주민들의 인식증진 교육 추진, 미니 태양광 설치 사업으로 각 가정의 에너지 효율개선, 생활전반에 탄소중립 실천을 유도하는 1~3단계 사업을 추진해 오고 있다.
기후변화 교육부터 탄소중립 생활실천 정착을 위해 탄소중립마을 별로 사업 추진예산을 지원하고 원할한 추진이 될 수 있도록 마을 활동가를 지원해 오고 있다.
마을이나 단체 주민들이 함께 학습하여 기후변화의 심각성을 깨닫고 이를 해소하기 위해 에너지, 자원 절약의 생활실천을 지속적으로 추진하고 있다.

매년 부산형 탄소중립 그린아파트 인증 사업을 추진하여 전년도 대비 전기, 도시가스. 물 사용량, 생활 폐기물, 음식물쓰레기 절감률이 높은 공동주택에는 일정액의 상금과 상장을 수여해 격려하고 공동주택 각 가정에서 탄소중립을 실천을 유도하는 사업을 2017년부터 해마다 추진해 오고 있다.

2022년부터는 탄소중립 그린액션 소문내기 경진대회를 개최해오고 있다.
그린액션이란 생활 속에서 대중교통 이용하기, 1회용품 사용 안 하기, 전기 아껴쓰기, 지역 농산물 이용하기, 폐자원 재활용하기 등의 에너지와 자원 절약으로 기후 위기에 대응하고자 하는 행동들을 말하는데, 이런 활동을 생활 속에서 실천해 오고 있는 단체나, 마을, 기업, 공공기관 등이 참여하는 경진대회를 개최하여 우수 사례를 자랑함으로써 지역 사회로 확산시키고자 매년 추진해 오고 있다.
2024년에는 어린이옷과 장난감 등을 수거해서, 세탁, 수선한 옷이나, 장난감 등을 필요로 하는 다른 어린이 가정에 대여하거나 판매하는 단체가 최우수상을 받았다.
경진대회는 매년 10월경에 개최하여 상장 수여 대상을 선정하고 12월초에 경진대회 시상식을 개최하면서 우수한 사례를 다시 발표하게 함으로써 우수 사례 확산을 도모하고 있다.

column17: Climate Safe Neighborhoods is an effort to educate residents and other stakeholders in underinvested neighborhoods about how extreme heat and flooding affect their neighborhood. It also discusses historical inequities that led to this increased vulnerability, reviews the challenges facing the community related to extreme weather, and identifies pathways to address these challenges. The final product is a climate resilience plan specific to and designed by the neighborhoods. The Climate Equity Indicators Report is an effort to identify the links between changing climate conditions and individual and neighborhood level characteristics brought about by historical processes of segregation, red-lining, infrastructural (dis)investment, and economic prosperity. This report compiles a wide range of demographic, environmental, health outcome, economic, and planning indicators, aggregated at the neighborhood level. This report serves as the foundation of a broad range of decision-making and action to provide redress to the inequities it details.

column17: The City's Green Cincinnati Plan (\'GCP\') serves as the climate action plan for the entire city. The 2023 GCP focused on buildings and energy, mobility, city operations, natural environment, community activation, resilience, and climate adaptation, food, and zero waste. The City worked to ensure that community-based engagement, data-driven decisions, and collaborative efforts with partners were central components of the GCP process. The City held community engagement sessions in underserved neighborhoods to collect feedback from residents that was used to shape the plan. In addition, groups focused on specific subject areas were formed to engage stakeholders through a series of public meetings to assist with the development of goals, strategies, and actions that are included in the plan. The City recognizes that community input is central to the success of the GCP, Without the support of its residents and partners, the City will not be able to achieve its goals.

column17: The City of Cincinnati is a member of the PJM Cities and Communities Coalition (PJMCCC), the first formal coalition of local governments with ambitious clean energy goals organized to drive decarbonization at the wholesale electricity market level. The members of the PJMCCC are dedicated to pursuing solutions to climate change, reducing carbon emissions and removing barriers to decarbonization in their regional wholesale electricity market — the PJM Interconnection. PJMCCC recognizes that significant barriers have historically limited the ability of cities and communities to engage in the wholesale market, including the high level of market expertise required to participate, inadequate educational resources and limited staff capacity. Members work together to: 1) Support and preserve policies that open markets to zero-emission energy sources and storage; 2) Ensure organizational and governance reforms so that cities and other end users can equitably weigh in on key decisions affecting their constituencies; 3) Focus on maintaining access, transparency, and accountability in PJM governance and operations; and 4) Align PJM's long-term planning to be consistent with global climate science, consumer demand for clean energy, and city climate goals.

Collaboration with C40: 

The City of Cape Town joined the C40 Cities Climate Leadership group in 2014 and remains an active member through the participation in several of its thematic networks, programmes and accelerators/declarations. Many of these include close collaboration between respective City departments and C40 technical teams. 

A few examples include: 
•	Participation in the C40 Deadline 2020 Climate Action Programme between 2018 and 2021, which included Cape Town together with 10 other African cities collaborating with C40 to develop climate action plans aligned with the Paris Agreement ambition, and included an embedded staff member and technical support for 3 years.
•	Participation in the C40 SA Buildings Programme between 2018 and 2021, which included Cape Town together with together with SA metros of Johannesburg, eThekwini and Tshwane working to accelerate the development and implementation of transformational energy efficiency policies and programmes in the built environment, towards zero carbon performance for new buildings in South African cities. The programme included an embedded staff member and technical support, including from partners organisation Sustainable Energy Africa, over three years. 
•	Participating in the 'Supporting South African Cities to deliver An Energy Secure Future programme' (2024, extended to Phase 2 in 2025), which seeks to support five South African C40 member cities (Cape Town, Johannesburg, Durban, Ekurhuleni, Tshwane) to transform electricity systems, by increasing renewable energy capacity through peer-to-peer learning, capacity building and technical assistance by C40.
•	Participation in the C40 Cities Finance Facility (CFF): The City secured technical assistance through this programme for two projects over two years (2022-2024, with extended 6 month support that ended in 2025) focusing on Renewable Energy and Energy Efficiency implementation for Net Zero Carbon Municipal Buildings and Green infrastructure options for flood resilience and improved catchment management in Cape Town.
•	In an effort to support the City of Cape Town's MyCiti Phase 2a plans to deploy battery-electric buses, C40 and the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) will, as part of the Zero Emission Bus Rapid-deployment Accelerator (ZEBRA) Partnership, are providing technical assistance to the City from 2025 in a number of activities, including E-bus infrastructure design support, City-2-City knowledge exchange, Engaging on areas requiring further analysis, such as the development of alternative procurement and Innovative Business Models, for the next phase of e-bus procurement etc.
•	Participation and knowledge sharing in a number of events (online and in person): Since the last round of CDP reporting (July 2024), this included: C40 Land Use Planning Mini-Workshop in Accra, Ghana (September 2024); Transforming Cities Waste Management Programme: Peer Support & Capacity Building Workshop in eThekwini, SA (October 2024); C40 city communication directors network engagement in Phoenix, USA (April 2025); C40 Electric Bus Workshop (Africa) in Durban, SA (February 2025); Green and Resilient UrbanShift Africa Forum 2025 in Nairobi, Kenya (February 2025); C40 Food Systems Network Worship in Nairobi, Kenya (June 2025); C40 Sustainable Mobility in African workshop in Dakar Senegal (July 2025) etc.
