Liveable Urban Waterways Programme:

The City of Cape Town's Liveable Urban Waterway (LUW) Programme focusses on rehabilitating waterways across the city, through water-sensitive design, nature-based solutions and green infrastructure. The programme consists of work in two adjacent catchments, the Diep/Sand River and Zeekoe catchments and outputs includes multiple socioeconomic and environmental benefits. The main partners of the programme include, catchment forums, civil society groups and academia such as the University of Cape Town Future Water unit, Zandvlei Catchment Forum, Friends of Constantia Valley Green Belts, Zandvlei Protected Areas Advisory Committee, Friends of Kirstenhof Wetland, Kirstenhof and Environs Residents Association and Young Urbanists NPC.

For more on the Liveable Urban Waterways programme please see here: https://www.capetown.gov.za/Family%20and%20home/residential-utility-services/residential-water-and-sanitation-services/liveable-urban-waterways and the case study serieshttps://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/CCT_Liveable_urban_waterways_Case_Studies.pdf

Climate Change Platform with Civil Society Organisations:

The City of Cape Town recognises that communication and collaboration within and between the different social and economic actors are a critical pillar in responding to climate change and ensuring all stakeholders are part of the journey to strengthen Cape Town's climate change response. Many of the actions in the City's Climate Change Action Plan (2021) are therefore enabling activities that requires the City to work closely in partnership with Cape Town's residents, businesses, organisations such as non-governmental organisations (NGOs), Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) and faith-based organisations, academia, other spheres of government and international partners. 

The City's Resilience and Climate Change Team, within the Risk and Resilience Department, has over the past few years been collaborating with the Western Cape Economic Development Partnership (EDP) on various stakeholder engagement processes to support this partnership approach to climate change response. The EDP is an independent, not‑for‑profit company that operates as a collaborative intermediary. Its primary role is to convene and support public, private, civil society, academia and philanthropic partners across the Western Cape to work collectively on complex socio‑economic challenges, foster inclusive job‑creating growth and strengthen local systems (such as metropolitan and regional economies).

The EDP has therefore played an important supporting role to the City over the past 4 years as independent/neutral “intermediary” for stakeholder engagement processes around climate change response in Cape Town. 

Most recently (2023-2025) this has included a project to explore ways of enabling the City and CSOs to engage meaningfully around mutually beneficial areas of implementation of the City's Climate Change Action Plan and to co-create an enabling environment for CSO and community action agency and voice. In 2024, this work led to the establishment of a Climate Change Platform for CSOs. The platform meets quarterly and focuses on supporting engagements between the City, Western Cape Government and CSOs, mapping relevant initiatives, maintaining ongoing communication and fostering collaboration between key stakeholders. The work is ongoing and will continue to build on the collaboration areas of action collectively identified to date, including heat response, disaster risk response, communication and awareness raising and will explore additional required inclusive climate action focus areas, as these emerge, for future engagement. For more on EDP programmes see here: https://wcedp.co.za/edp-programmes-energy-and-climate/

City global reporting to networks and partners: 

The City annually reports its climate change and environmental data to CDP. This also forms part of its ongoing partnership with C40 and associated membership criteria. The data reported to CDP subsequently feeds into the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM), Race to Zero and Race to Resilience and One Planet City Challenge (WWF) reporting platforms. The City also participates in the webinars, events and campaigns related to these platforms. 

Voluntary Local Review - A review of the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals in Cape Town: Cities, local and regional governments worldwide are increasingly using Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs) to track and report on SDG progress. Cape Town was the first city in South Africa to develop a VLR report in 2021. This report served as a focused and brief analysis of a set of priority SDGs for the City as derived through internal analysis. The information presented in the SDG analysis focuses on key indicators where there are available data and established a baseline for City SDG performance and achievement monitoring. Several efforts are in progress globally to strengthen the SDGs, but more importantly, to ensure that the 2030 Agenda goals and aims are reached. However, significant challenges - both global and local - persist to hamper progress to 'leave no one behind'. The City's Voluntary Local Review was updated in 2024 is an attempt to not only showcase the City's sustainability performance and achievements but also to reflect on how the City can build on the past to progress to a better future.
The VLR provides a platform for the alignment and inclusion of the SDGs into strategic documents, notably the City's overall master plan (the Integrated Development Plan). This may allow for deeper goal and target alignment and increased localisations around monitoring and evaluation. 

See the reports here: 
2021: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/CCT_Voluntary_Local_Review_2021.pdf

Ongoing periodic collaboration with Universities/Academia: 

University of Cape Town: 
The City of Cape Town has a long-standing and ongoing research and collaboration relationship with the University of Cape Town (UCT). Major collaborations to date have included technical and scientific input and support related to water management interventions during the drought, collaboration on adaptation and resilience project implementation including the City's Liveable Urban Waterways Programme, input into the development of the City's climate change strategy and water strategy, and staff capacity building. The City is currently working towards finalising Memorandums of Understanding with two UCT institutions - African Climate and Development Initiative (ACDI) and the Climate System Analysis Group (CSAG) to improve and formalise working relationships on climate change related work areas with the City for example work related to the Cascading Climate and Health Risks in African Cities (CASCADE) project and the Heat Adaptation Benefits for Vulnerable groups In Africa (HABVIA) project.

Academia including Stellenbosch University, the University of Cape Town, and the University of the Western Cape are also part of the City's Food Systems Working Group and conducts various research related to food and urban agriculture in Cape Town.

Special purpose vehicle partnerships: GreenCape 

GreenCape was initially established as a Special Purpose Vehicle to unlock the manufacturing and employment potential in the green economy (initially in the Western Cape, now operating at a broader scale). GreenCape's work is at the interface between business, government and academia in order to identify and remove barriers to economically viable green economy infrastructure solutions in developing countries, thereby catalysing their replicable and large-scale uptake.

Through GreenCape, Cape Town has harnessed substantial investments, provided crucial support to businesses offering waste management solutions, and generated invaluable market intelligence reports, industry briefs, and case studies that empower green economy businesses and potential investors with informed decision-making tools.

The City is a key partner of GreenCape and provides financial support to the organisation on an annual basis to assist the City on a number of programmes - ranging from the circular economy, energy and water resilience (website: http://greencape.co.za/)

City and business climate advocacy partnerships: 

Alliances for Climate Action is a global network of domestic multi-sector coalitions committed to supporting the delivery and enhancement of their countries' climate goals. The South African Alliance is connecting the private sector, cities, provinces, investors, research institutions, and others to form “surprising alliances” to collectively achieve a net carbon neutral economy by 2050. As of 2019, the City of Cape Town is a member of the Alliance for Climate Action South Africa, a grouping of cities and businesses convened by WWF-SA and the National Business Initiative (NBI). Alliance for Climate Action coalition members work together in a wide variety of ways — in-person and virtually, in small-group encounters and large public forums. The City of Cape Town regularly participates and presents in the quarterly member meetings. 

See the link: http://www.alliancesforclimateaction.co.za/ for more.

Food Systems Working Group: 

The City facilitates and leads a Food System Working Group (since 2020), which comprises of representatives from local and provincial government and academia. The Working Group contributes to the implementation of the City's Food Systems Programme that aims to increase food security and the resilience of the City's food system against the impacts of shocks such as climate change, droughts and flooding. The Food Systems Programme established a wide-ranging mandate across City functions under six themes, which were developed into an eighteen month Implementation Programme in 2022. The programme is further included in the IDP, illustrating its growing maturity. Even though the programme emphasises that the food system is loosely governed, it nevertheless provides a central convening space via the Food Systems Working Group, Food Indaba and Food Systems Research Community of Practice. These platforms continue to meet regularly. The Food Systems Programme was one of 15 shortlisted submissions to the prestigious Guangzhou International Award for Urban Innovation (the Guangzhou Award) in 2023 and was awarded a Medal of Honour, in addition to a Scholarship Certificate for International Design Education (IDE) Programme. 

The Food Systems Working (FSWG) group is recognised as a valuable space for identifying challenges and opportunities in the food system. Its greatest successes lie in building networks, increasing awareness, and fostering systems thinking among stakeholders. Participants, particularly City officials, have indicated a growing understanding of how their work intersects with food systems, though the deeper impact of this awareness will become evident only through long-term application in their respective roles.

Other collaboration components of the Food Systems Programme include: 
•Collaboration with ICLEI Africa and a number of other partners in AfriFOODLinks, a pan African food consortium, sees Cape Town partnering with Lusaka, Arusha and Lisbon (our European partner) to explore ways to improve markets and thereby, aiming to enhance up to 70% of Capetonian's access to fresh food. The partnership includes a research, innovation and experimentation programme and was launched in June 2023 in Kisumu, Kenya. Under this partnership a “State of Cape Town's Food System Report” was developed and published in May 2024 - see here: https://www.africancentreforcities.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/State-of-City-Food-System-Report_Cape-Town__.pdf 
•Using the FSWG influence in the initiation of a Black Soldier Fly waste management pilot. Following a presentation by partners organisation GreenCape at one of the FSWG meetings, the City's Urban Waste Department commissioned a study, which has since evolved into pilot projects under AfriFOODLinks. 
•Supporting research includes investigating food gardens' potential for cooling, particularly on the Cape Flats, whilst a market study will assist in improving the City's knowledge of the 'food shed's' exposure to climate shocks and stresses. Markets included in the study are the Epping Fresh Produce Market, Harvest of Hope and the Oranjezicht Farm Market. 
•The City partners with the annual Food Dialogues - last year included a focus on the 'poly crisis' and teen nutrition. City representatives participated in a number of workshops and events including teens, activists and practitioners. 
•The City of Cape Town and the Consumer Goods Council of South Africa (CGCSA) has recently signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to partner and collaborate on efforts to plan and implement risk response measures with the intent of food system strengthening in times of shock.
•The City has also signed MOUs with five NGOs to improve response capacity during disasters, recognising the vital role these organisations play in supporting vulnerable households.

Collaborative approach towards implementing the Cape Town Water Strategy: 

The City's Water Strategy identifies collaboration as a key component to implement the goals of the strategy towards sustainable water management for the City and surrounding areas and users and is implemented on a continual basis. The City of Cape Town receives a significant portion of its water supply from the Western Cape Water Supply System (WCWSS) which is managed by the National Department of Water and Sanitation. The WCWSS is shared with the agriculture sector (provincial government) and surrounding local municipalities and thus comprises of a range of stakeholders involved in planning, managing, and conducting research to ensure water security and implement sustainable water management practices. In addition, the ongoing Alien Clearing Programme of the City forms an important part of the New Water Programme as outlined in the Cape Town Water Strategy. The Alien Clearing Programme consists of various partnerships that are central to implementation and funding and include, the Nature Conservancy, CapeNature, WWF-South Africa and Working on Fire.

Water Star Rating Certification system: 

The City has in place a programme to certify businesses and institutions that make wise use of water, through the City's voluntary Water Star Rating Certification system. The system promotes best practices in water management, conservation and pollution control in the business sector; government departments; education and health institutions; and residential estates. Those who achieve five stars are certified as champion innovators that have found unique or extraordinary ways in which to conserve water and limit water pollution. The certification underscores the continuation of the strong partnerships that were forged between the City and the private sector in Cape Town get through the severe drought that occurred between 2015 and 2018. These partnerships are ongoing as the City looks towards ensuring the wise use of water in the long term in a water-scarce region. The awards also create awareness amongst other businesses to implement water wise management techniques. 

See here for more: https://www.capetown.gov.za/City-Connect/Apply/Municipal-services/Water-and-sanitation/apply-for-water-star-rating-certification 

During the 2024/25 financial year, the City of Cape Town's Water and Sanitation Directorate recognised 18 businesses and organisations with six organisations receiving five star ratings for implementing innovative water-saving measures, such as recycling water multiple times, installing water-efficient fixtures, and engaging stakeholders in sustainable practices., 

More information on the recent awards ceremony is available here:

Cape Town's Energy Water Waste Forum: 

An Energy Efficiency Forum for the commercial sector in Cape Town was established by the City of Cape Town, energy utility Eskom & South African Property Owners' Association (SAPOA) as a pioneering public-private initiative in 2009. Now known as the Energy Water Waste (EWW) Forum, it aims to promote resource efficiency in commercial buildings and operations for economic, environmental and energy security reasons. This Forum shares practical knowledge and support for taking action. Its members are the owners and managers of commercial buildings, resource and energy efficiency-related service providers, policy-makers and other relevant stakeholders. There are usually three main meetings a year, which offer case studies, expert views, panel discussions and updates on financing options, innovation, policy and training and advisory opportunities. Participation is free of charge, and the meetings normally attract between 100-200 participants. The forum played a key role in promoting and enabling knowledge sharing on water efficiency for businesses during the drought in 2017/18. Over the past 3 years the focus has been on disruptive technologies in the energy sector, waste sector opportunities and economic recovery through net zero carbon buildings and transport systems. 

Since the previous reporting, the following Energy Water Waste Forum meetings took place: 
•28 November 2024: Building Resilience through Desalination 
•15 April 2025: Re-imagining Waste: The impact of AI - Innovative Solutions for the City of Hope
•12 June 2025: The Changing Business of Green Energy

Information on the Forum can be found here: https://www.capetown.gov.za/Work%20and%20business/Greener-business/energy-water-waste-forum/about-the-energy-water-waste-forum

National Energy Efficiency Demand-Side Management Programme: 

The City of Cape Town is a participant in the National Department of Electricity and Energy 'Energy Efficiency Demand Side Management' (EEDSM) programme. The EEDSM program is a grant fund disbursed to municipalities to implement energy efficient retrofits within the municipal infrastructure. The City of Cape Town has implemented interventions in street lighting, traffic lighting and municipal buildings as part of its participation in this programme. The City actively participates in EEDSM engagements, committees and information exchange with municipalities from around the country. 

The City has historically been allocated an annual EEDSM grant of between R 9-15 million via the Division of Revenue Act tabled at the national budget to use for energy efficiency projects in buildings and municipal infrastructure (the most recent financial year allocation is R7 million). The City allocates funds from its own budget towards the programme on an annual basis as well.

Cape Town Water Exchange: 

In 2021, the Mayor of Cape Town prioritized the rapid improvement in sewer network management, sewer pump station management, wastewater treatment upgrades and improvements in recreational water body and river water quality as one of four Mayoral Priority Programmes over his term of office. Effective implementation of the Mayoral Priority Programme and the Cape Town Water Strategy is dependent on the transformation of the City's Water and Sanitation Department into a modern, customer-oriented utility. 

In response, the City's Water and Sanitation Department in partnership with Leading Utilities of the World, host the Cape Town Water Exchange, which is a series of webinars centred on key transitions that the City is undertaking on its journey to water resilience and becoming a modern water utility. The purpose of the Cape Town Water Exchange is to expose Cape Town staff to leading thinking and practices in utility management around the world and to reflect on the opportunity and challenges in implementing these in the Cape Town context. 

To date, the City has engaged: 
•PUB Singapore on sewer network management
•DC Water on financial sustainability
•Water Corporation (Perth, Australia) on desalination and water resilience
•Orange County Water District (USA) on Water Reuse
•Sydney Water (Australia) on Transition to Water Sensitive City
•Watercare (Auckland, Australia) on organisational transformation
•Paris, on Swimming in the Seine
•John Ringham - The Chair of the Leading Utilities of the World and ex CEO of SA Water, on organisational culture change
•Nice on Future Pathways for wastewater treatment and reuse;
•Medellin which was on informal upgrading through co-creation.

Heat response collaboration work: 

1) The City collaborated with World Resource Institute (WRI) to develop the Cool Cities Lab, a new platform designed to help cities plan smarter, cooler, and more heat-resilient spaces using city views from Monterrey, Rio de Janeiro, and Cape Town as examples of the practical implementation of the tool. This initiative forms part of the City's Heat Action Plan and Climate Change Action Plan. The platform is currently in beta phase and included guided input from City officials to ensure that the platform is specific to Cape Town's context. 

2) The Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative is a flagship program of the Bloomberg Center for Cities and coordinates the Bloomberg Harvard Summer Fellowship programme. The programme offers graduate students from Harvard University an opportunity to spend their summer embedded in local government in “Bloomberg Harvard Mayors Offices” around the world including the City of Cape Town. The City hosted a student during May - July 2024 (who worked on the risk assessment related to the City's Heat Action Plan) and is currently working towards finalising a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Bloomberg Harvard City Leadership Initiative, to serve as an umbrella MOU for all future partnerships including fellowship programmes. 

3) The City of Cape Town joined the City Champions for Heat Action (CCHA) initiative during 2024. The CCHA is a corner stone initiative of the Extreme Heat Resilience Alliance (EHRA) formed by the Atlantic Council's Adrienne Arsht-Rockefeller Foundation Resilience Center in 2020The CCHA membership consist of a network of chief heat officers and 8 global cities at the forefront of heat response that share best practices, develop metrics, mobilize partners to tackle extreme heat in cities and advance the international conversations and development around heat. As part of the partnership, the City will announce a chief heat officer later in 2025.

Dassenberg Coastal Catchment Partnership, DCCP: Atlantis Land Bank 

The DCCP began as a partnership initiative between the City of Cape Town, Cape Nature, TMF and the Wilderness Trust to create a viable ecological link between the Dassenberg Hills and the coast. The partnership aims to protect critical ecological infrastructure, unlock socio-economic opportunities, promote climate change adaptation and mitigation and promote the natural and cultural heritage of the area. It currently is an ongoing initiative between the City and various stakeholders including provincial government, research institutes, NGO's and national organisation,(CapeNature, the Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF), the Wilderness Foundation, the Cape West Coast Biosphere, SANParks, Province's Department of Environmental Affairs and Development Planning, and the South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI)). This landscape-scale conservation initiative was identified as a critical Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation Corridor in the 2010 WWF-Table Mountain Fund study and is also included in the City's BioNet. For more see here: https://www.capetown.gov.za/City-Connect/Get-involved/Partner/dassenberg-coastal-catchment-partnership and https://gef5pa.org/2021/04/22/conservation-collaboration-under-the-dccp/ 

The City of Cape Town has proactively acquired and is managing and retaining important biodiversity land outside the urban edge within the DCCP as a mechanism to facilitate development in Atlantis while mitigating the loss of critically endangered and endangered vegetation in the area. Key work undertaken as part of the Atlantis Land Bank programme include the exclusion of the “removal of indigenous vegetation” trigger from the listed activities that require Environmental Authorisation within the Atlantis Urban Edge. During the 2023/24 financial year, the City's Biodiversity Management branch continued to undertake valuations to increase the land bank and assisted the Human Settlements Department in ground-truthing wetland patches within the Atlantis Residential Urban Edge that could potentially pose significant constraints to their proposed social housing projects. 

See pg 17: https://resource.capetown.gov.za/documentcentre/Documents/City%20research%20reports%20and%20review/BiodiversityManagementProgressReport_Jul2023-Jun2024.pdf

The Comprehensive Urban Agriculture Plan (CUAP) stems from the directives of the 2020 Comprehensive Environmental and Climate Action Plan (CECAP) and reflects a commitment to acknowledge and address past, present, and future inequities, risks, and challenges related to agriculture and food security in Dallas. As outlined in CECAP, this initiative aligns with global climate frameworks, such as the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, recognizing the need to adapt our systems and societies to live within planetary limits while supporting our social foundations.
In Dallas, various social, political, economic, and environmental factors make strengthening urban agriculture essential to achieving greater equity, resilience, and sustainability.
The CUAP focuses on five key recommendations, each encompassing several solutions and actionable items:
•	Reduce Regulatory Barriers
•	Support Land Access
•	Provide Urban Agriculture Education, Resources, and Support to Dallas Residents
•	Facilitate Collaboration and Partnerships Among Urban Agriculture Stakeholders
•	Build Market Opportunities
These recommendations, along with their action items, are described in more detail below, with a suggested timeline for implementation. Some actions have already been initiated by the Office of Environmental Quality & Sustainability (OEQS), other City of Dallas departments, and local stakeholders. Others will begin after the plan's adoption by the Dallas City Council. The successful implementation of these recommendations will enhance the growth and organizational capacity of urban agriculture in Dallas.

column17: The City of Ekurhuleni finalised an 'Urban Heat Assessment' study with support from the World Bank through National Treasury's City Support Programme. The Urban heat assessment was undertaken in both Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni metropolitan area. The purpose of the urban heat assessment was to understand which part of the city and surrounding areas are highly vulnerable to excessive heat due to the urban heat island phenomena. Since both metros are highly urbanised, exposure to extreme heat is exacerbated by the urban heat island phenomenon, i.e., the fact that city centres tend to be warmer than nearby rural areas. The assessment made use of in-situ participatory collection of heat stress data and climate modelling to create maps that indicate areas in the city that are highly vulnerable to excessive heat. The in-situ participatory work was done by a group of community members who recorded temperatures through data loggers at various times of the day in selected locations. These measurements were then used to validate the climate modelling results. Some of the key findings from this session include:•Johannesburg and Ekurhuleni experience a strong urban heat island effect, urban neighbourhoods being warmer than nearby rural areas by 3-4°C at night, in some areas rising to 6°C. •Within neighbourhoods, large disparities in heat exposure also exist in green residential areas, on a heatwave day, daytime heat stress levels range from 'limited' in the shade of trees to 'strong' at open and unshaded locations; densely built settlements that are devoid of green vegetation experience heat stress levels ranging from 'moderate' in the shade of buildings to 'very strong' at open locations -The community-based heat monitoring campaign demonstrates that low-cost dwellings may face extreme temperatures. Light-weight constructions built around a wooden frame and involving corrugated iron sheets are particularly prone to overheating, indoor temperatures in such dwellings being higher by up to 15°C compared to more robust buildings constructed with bricks and concrete. •Currently most of Johannesburg sees less than 20 hot nights per year (nights with temperatures greater than 20 degrees), under medium or high climate scenarios poorer neighbourhoods will see 80 - 120 of such nights. The health impacts of these are severe and include increased mortality. •The indoor heat assessment campaign that was carried out confirmed the impact of building material and structures on heat exposure. These campaigns showed that temperatures in poorer communities (shacks and townships) can vary by up to 8 degrees when comparing to more affluent communities (under a moderate hot spell in Feb 2022). The final report and heat maps give a clear indication of areas at risk (including settlement type) while providing various measures that should be implemented by the metros to reduce the impacts of excessive heat. Some of the recommended mitigation options include: 1. Integrating heat responses into core city strategies is vital: ensure that heat is included in city climate strategies. Both City of Johannesburg and City of Ekurhuleni have climate change action plans and strategies. However, in the adaptation plans of both cities the impact of heat are not stressed enough, in comparison to drought and flooding impact. It is important that these action plans address adaptation measures for extreme heat.2. Understanding heat as a cross-departmental/ sectoral risk and ensuring that heat mitigation action strategies are mainstreamed across the city. 3.Urban greening efforts need to be strategically directed to neighbourhoods that currently do not have green infrastructure. 4.Cooling strategies for low-quality dwellings: Low-cost dwellings are prone to overheating; therefore, measures need to be put in place to tackle high indoor temperatures5.Priority needs to be given to the refurbishment of public spaces such as clinics and schools to include active cooling strategies using solar power sources. 6.The need for both cities to foster partnerships with public health authorities and South African Weather services to establish a heat-health early warning system.7.Protecting workers and ensure labour productivity: Engaging with employers to ensure that existing heat-related occupational health regulations are complied with constitutes a priority measure. The project commenced in 2021 and the report was finalised in early October 2022, and later presented to internal and external stakeholders in December 2022. The work was also presented at the Understanding Risk conference in Brazil 2022; in early 2023 National Treasury hosted a workshop that was attended by other metros, where the city was able to share the outcomes from this work with other cities, provincial government, Health Department and Academia. The city is currently drafting its first Heat Action Plan.

column17: In 2022, the City of Ekurhuleni received technical assistance from the World Bank through the National Treasury's City Support Programme to develop a portfolio analysis and resilience-rating system. The portfolio analysis and resilience-rating system sought to provide an evaluation of how resilient City's capital investment projects are and whether climate risk had been considered in these projects or not. A resilient project is not a project that cannot fail, but a project for which the risk of failure considered climate and disaster risks in its business case or economic or financial analysis (e.g., the risk that a road is washed out by a flood is included in the benefit-cost analysis of the road). The pilot project evaluated three City projects. The portfolio analysis and resilience-rating system provided outcomes that strengthen city systems and tools to plan and prioritize capital investment in resilience building projects; and through follow up training workshops with project managers, the city is beginning to strengthen its capability to package and prepare capital investments projects/ projects and portfolios and mobilise private investments. The resilience-rating tool requires that the projects to be evaluated to have undergone an economic evaluation (cost-benefit analysis). For the purpose of this pilot the City selected 4 projects for the assessment. The pilot project is near conclusion and final reports should be received by the end of October. This work will will inform the City's project selection, conceptualization and implementation. This pilot will also help in mainstreaming the importance of considering climate change and disaster risk in big capital investment City projects.

Fortaleza tem consolidado parcerias estratégicas com diferentes setores para fortalecer sua ação climática, destacando-se a colaboração com a academia, empresas e sociedade civil organizada.

No campo acadêmico, a Universidade Federal do Ceará (UFC) tem sido parceira fundamental. Foram firmados termos de cooperação técnico-científica, como o Nº 04/2022, com o Departamento de Geografia, para suporte ao Projeto TropiCool - Infraestrutura Verde em Cidades Tropicais para Redução do Stress Térmico e Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, liderado pelo Instituto Meteorológico e Hidrológico Sueco (SMHI), no âmbito do Memorando de Entendimento Brasil-Suécia (2013). Também o Nº 01/2022, com o Instituto de Ciências do Mar (Labomar) e o Departamento de Engenharia de Transportes, voltado ao monitoramento e avaliação da qualidade do ar em Fortaleza. Esse projeto evoluiu para uma parceria com a Vital Strategies, no desenvolvimento de monitores de baixo custo e na elaboração do 5º Inventário de Emissões de GEE da cidade. Em 2025, a Fundação da UFC também passou a integrar a equipe técnica de elaboração do inventário referente aos anos-base 2020 e 2021, reforçando a robustez metodológica do processo.

Além disso, a academia tem desempenhado papel ativo nos processos de planejamento e participação social. Professores e pesquisadores integram grupos de trabalho da revisão do Plano Diretor Participativo e Sustentável de Fortaleza, especialmente no eixo de riscos climáticos, e vêm apoiando diretamente a condução de momentos participativos por meio de moderação de debates e palestras em conferências e no FORCLIMA. Essa colaboração garante maior qualificação técnica às discussões e fortalece a legitimidade das propostas junto à população.

No setor empresarial, destaca-se o termo de cooperação com a Federação das Empresas de Transportes de Passageiros do Ceará, Piauí e Maranhão (FETRANS), que permite o compartilhamento de dados sobre as condições das frotas a diesel das empresas associadas, viabilizando estudos estatísticos e aprimorando os diagnósticos de emissões. Essa parceria é complementada pela realização do Prêmio Melhoria da Qualidade do Ar, que reconhece boas práticas empresariais alinhadas aos Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS).

Essas colaborações demonstram que a ação climática em Fortaleza é construída de forma integrada, com a academia oferecendo suporte técnico e científico, o setor privado contribuindo com dados e boas práticas, e a sociedade civil participando ativamente dos processos deliberativos. Esse arranjo garante maior qualidade técnica, legitimidade social e capacidade de transformar os compromissos climáticos em políticas e projetos efetivos para a cidade.

Fortaleza reforça continuamente seus compromissos públicos com a agenda de enfrentamento da crise climática, participando ativamente de redes internacionais e firmando acordos que ampliam sua capacidade de planejamento e execução de políticas climáticas. Esses compromissos consolidam a integração da cidade às metas do Acordo de Paris, favorecendo o acesso a assistência técnica, oportunidades de financiamento e troca de experiências globais.
Em 2025, a cidade avançou ao assinar o Memorando de Entendimento com a Rede Global C40, que reúne quase 100 prefeitos das principais cidades do mundo comprometidos com a agenda climática. O memorando consolida Fortaleza como integrante ativo da rede, fortalecendo a cooperação internacional e estabelecendo requisitos de reporte e engajamento organizados em cinco eixos: Planejamento, Execução, Promoção, Inovação e Liderança. Essa adesão também representa a institucionalização de processos que já vinham sendo apoiados pela rede, como auditorias técnicas nos inventários de GEE e apoio metodológico à atualização do Plano de Ação Climática (PAC).
Além disso, Fortaleza é signatária do Pacto Global de Prefeitos pelo Clima e a Energia (GCoM), que reúne cidades comprometidas com a redução de emissões, adaptação climática e acesso à energia sustentável. Essa aliança global facilita o acesso a metodologias padronizadas e mecanismos de financiamento, reforçando a credibilidade do município.
Outro compromisso é a Race to Zero, campanha global da ONU que visa zerar as emissões líquidas até 2050. Ao aderir, Fortaleza assumiu metas que incluem a criação de ruas verdes, redução da poluição do ar, estímulo a edifícios de carbono zero e avanços em sistemas energéticos resilientes e sustentáveis.
A cidade também participa do movimento Construindo Cidades Resilientes (MCR 2030), que busca garantir que os centros urbanos sejam inclusivos, seguros, resilientes e sustentáveis até 2030, alinhando-se à Agenda 2030 da ONU.
Ainda em 2021, Fortaleza aderiu ao Fórum de Ação Climática Inclusiva (ICA) da Rede C40, espaço que conecta cidades engajadas na promoção de uma transição justa. O fórum integra as dimensões de justiça social e climática às ações urbanas, promovendo negócios verdes, inovação inclusiva e estratégias de retomada econômica sustentável.
Esses compromissos evidenciam que Fortaleza estrutura sua ação climática em colaboração direta com redes internacionais, garantindo alinhamento às metas globais e fortalecendo sua governança climática local.

Após essa fase, o projeto será submetido ao BID para avaliação, financiamento e posterior implementação em escala.

Esses exemplos demonstram como a parceria com o BID tem possibilitado a Fortaleza avançar na agenda climática, tanto pela experimentação de projetos-piloto inovadores quanto pelo acesso a recursos e cooperação técnica internacional, transformando compromissos em ações concretas de mitigação, adaptação e melhoria da qualidade de vida urbana.

Fortaleza tem se destacado internacionalmente por meio da Parceria para Cidades Saudáveis, iniciativa global apoiada pela Organização Mundial da Saúde (OMS), pela Bloomberg Philanthropies e pela Vital Strategies. Essa colaboração vem permitindo que a cidade integre de forma inovadora as agendas de saúde pública e ação climática, por meio de políticas baseadas em dados, projetos-piloto inovadores e cooperação técnica.

Em 2023, Fortaleza se tornou a primeira cidade do Brasil a instituir uma estrutura legal para vigilância da qualidade do ar, por meio de decreto municipal que garante o monitoramento contínuo dos poluentes atmosféricos. A medida foi reconhecida em 2025, quando Fortaleza foi uma das vencedoras do Prêmio Parceria para Cidades Saudáveis, ao lado de Córdoba (Argentina) e Manchester (Reino Unido), pelo pioneirismo na integração entre monitoramento ambiental e saúde. O projeto contou com o apoio técnico da Vital Strategies e marcou a instalação de sensores de baixo custo, desenvolvidos em parceria com a Universidade Federal do Ceará, ampliando a coleta de dados e subsidiando a criação de políticas municipais para redução da poluição do ar.

Na sequência, Fortaleza anunciou a expansão da Rede de Monitoramento da Qualidade do Ar, que passou de 30 para 60 sensores distribuídos em todas as 12 regionais da cidade, com prioridade para áreas periféricas. A iniciativa fortalece a vigilância ambiental, permitindo diagnósticos precisos sobre a dispersão de poluentes e seus efeitos sobre doenças respiratórias, cardiovasculares e outros agravos. Os dados coletados orientam políticas intersetoriais de saúde, mobilidade, meio ambiente e planejamento urbano, e estão sendo organizados em plataformas abertas para uso da gestão pública e da sociedade civil.

A parceria com a Vital Strategies também impulsionou projetos voltados ao enfrentamento do calor extremo, em especial o programa Fortaleza Resiliente ao Calor, desenvolvido pelo Instituto de Pesquisa e Planejamento (Ipplan) com o apoio da rede. A iniciativa integra monitoramento climático, participação cidadã e políticas de saúde pública, incluindo um mapa colaborativo para registrar os impactos do calor na vida cotidiana. A partir desses dados, será possível subsidiar a criação da primeira Política Pública de Calor e Saúde de Fortaleza, conectando defesa civil, saúde, urbanismo e mobilidade para proteger comunidades mais vulneráveis.

Outro desdobramento foi a captação de novos recursos internacionais: a cidade já recebeu US$ 250 mil para expansão da rede de qualidade do ar e dois novos aportes de US$ 50 mil cada para o desenvolvimento de projetos-piloto em calor urbano e em saúde e doenças crônicas. Essas iniciativas envolvem órgãos como Seuma, SMS, Segov, Seinf, SCSP, Urbfor, Defesa Civil e Citinova, garantindo uma abordagem multissetorial.

Além disso, a cooperação internacional tem proporcionado troca de experiências bilaterais com cidades como Córdoba, Cali, Barcelona, Tóquio e Istambul, fortalecendo a inserção de Fortaleza em redes globais de inovação climática e de saúde. A participação da cidade em encontros internacionais da Parceria tem ampliado as possibilidades de financiamento e replicação de soluções em larga escala.

Essa colaboração com a Vital Strategies demonstra como a ação climática pode ser integrada ao campo da saúde pública, trazendo benefícios diretos para a qualidade de vida da população, reduzindo desigualdades e fortalecendo a resiliência urbana. Ao articular ciência, tecnologia, participação social e cooperação internacional, Fortaleza avança para se consolidar como referência mundial em políticas urbanas que integram sustentabilidade, saúde e justiça climática.

column17: The City of Miami is collaborating with Florida Power and Light, Miami-Dade County, and the owners/managers of the City's largest real estate properties to implement the City of Miami's Building Efficiency 305 (BE305) Energy and Water Benchmarking program. Under this program, building owners of multi-family and commercial buildings with 20,000 square feet or greater of floor space and 5 or more units are required to benchmark their energy and water use annually. In 2023 the City of Miami's Building Efficiency Program (BE305) kicked off its initial year of compliance. Buildings over 200,000 sq. ft. were required to comply by June 30, 2023 and buildings between 100,000 - 199,999 sq. ft. were required to comply by October 1, 2023. On October 1, 2024, buildings between 50,000 - 99,999 sq. ft. were required to comply. At the end of the 2024 reporting period, buildings over 200,000 sq. ft. had a total of 223 buildings or 57.5% in compliance. Buildings between 100,000 - 199,999 sq. ft. saw a total 86 buildings or 37% in compliance. Buildings between 50,000 - 99,999 sq. ft. saw a total of 56 buildings or 17% in compliance. Initial compliance rates for municipalities in their first year of benchmarking tend to see compliance rates between 15% - 25%. Buildings 100,000 sq. ft. and above were required to benchmark by June 30, 2024, for their second year of reporting. The City has been leading on this initiative by benchmarking over 80 of its City-owned buildings, regardless of size. Through the BE305 program, the City was able to identify Miami City Hall as a high performing building and applied for the Energy Star Certification. In November 2024, the City earned EPA's Energy Star Certification for Miami City Hall, earning a score of 80, proving it is more energy efficient than 80% of similar properties nationwide.

column17: The challenges in the immediate response period after Hurricane Irma brought the concept of Resilience Hubs to local governments, spearheaded locally by Catalyst Miami, a community-based non-profit organization. Subsequently, Resilience Hubs were included in the Resilient305 strategy as “Action 38: Support Resilience Hubs” under “Objective 8: Strengthen Community Response.” In 2018, the City hosted a workshop at Hadley Park with many government, non-profit, and resident stakeholders to discuss Resilience Hub components and the site's feasibility of serving as a hub. In spring 2019, a representative from ORS (Alissa Farina) and a representative from the Parks Department (Zhaoming Guan) participated in a USDN-run peer learning exchange workshop with other cities such as Washington, DC; Minneapolis, MN; and Ann Arbor, MI to advance the City's Resilience Hub plan and concept. At this workshop, the idea of the Resilience Hub network was developed, and proposed sites selected based on their use/popularity within neighborhoods (i.e., are they already trusted community sites), as well as their physical capacity to support the programming and operations necessary to be a Resilience Hub. In early 2022, the Adrienne Arsht Rockefeller Center for Resilience was awarded $1.1 million as part of the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity's (DEO) Rebuild Florida General Planning Support Program to scale a strategy to design and network Resilience Hubs to create an interconnected system of community-serving facilities designed to support residents, educate the public, distribute resources, coordinate communications, and stage government services. The grant dollars will go towards creation of a guidance document with basic specifications for the development of resilience hubs as well as buildout of three hub prototypes. As this project was designed in partnership with Resilient305, it has been discussed that one prototype will be launched in each of the three jurisdictions that make up Resilient Greater Miami and the Beaches. In addition, the City applied for and received a $779,000 Community Development Block Grant Mitigation (CDBG-MIT) for the development of a Resilience Hub at Charles Hadley Park in Liberty City, a historic black neighborhood. The City will be installing Category 5 impact windows and doors, enhanced wifi, charging stations, and an on-site diesel generator. As of summer 2025, the project has a complete design package and the City is in the process of procuring a contractor to construct the project. The project will be complete in 2026. As an initial way to activate the Resilience Hubs network, City of Miami soft launched 3 Cooling Centers to round out the 2024 Heat Season from October 7, 2024 - November 3, 2024. These Cooling Centers provided residents with a safe and cool environment during extreme heat events, further enhancing the community's resilience. Each facility was equipped with outdoor signage to help residents identify the Cooling Center as well as a dedicated area with chairs, access to restrooms, PSA flyers about heat safety, and paper cups/reusable water bottles for ice and water. The pilot helped inform future locations and identify lessons learned as well as gather feedback from residents to understand what resources should be included at each Center. During the 2025 Extreme Heat Season beginning May 1, 2025 the City launched a network of 10 Cooling Centers at City park facilities. The 10 City-operated Cooling Centers complement the greater network of cooling sites offered by Miami-Dade County at local libraries and government facilities, 11 of which are within City of Miami limits. All City-run Cooling Centers will operate through the end of the Extreme Heat Season (October 31, 2025). The City developed a suite of marketing materials to inform residents of the new Cooling Centers including flyers, videos, social media posts, and digital display board ads.

column17: The City of Miami passed a Fertilizer Ordinance (Ordinance No. 14006) in April 2020 that sets restrictions on what kind of fertilizers can be applied on public and private grounds within the City limits as well as when and where fertilizers can be applied. This policy was enacted due to the fact that many fertilizers contain nitrogen and phosphorus that, in large quantities, can pollute our waterways, harm marine wildlife, and cause harmful algal blooms. All businesses of any category that apply fertilizer must ensure that at least one (1) employee has an appropriate “Florida-Friendly Best Management Practices for Protection of Water Resources by the Green Industries” certificate a.k.a. state fertilizer license from Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS) prior to obtaining a Business Tax Receipt (BTR). The City is collaborating with Miami-Dade County and local water-focused NGOs to educate the public on this policy and its beneficial impacts to Biscayne Bay and other waterways. In 2025, the City developed new flyers and social media posts to inform residents of the fertilizer application restrictions.

column17: The U.S. Economic Development Administration (EDA) Tech Hubs program was established under the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 and aims to strengthen U.S. economic and national security by making investments in regions across the country that are poised to become globally competitive in the technologies and industries of the future. In October 2023, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Economic Development Administration (EDA) announced that the South Florida Climate Resilience Tech Hub (now the Risk and Resilience Tech Hub/“RRTH”), led by Miami-Dade County, was designated as one of 31 Tech Hubs in the country, selected from a competitive pool of nearly 200 applicants across the United States and its territories. The initial goals of the RRTH were to meet climate urgency by developing, commercializing, and scaling Sustainable Resilient Infrastructure (SRI) technologies focused on climate adaptation and mitigation, including: coastal resilience and marine infrastructure; clean cement; energy-efficient building operations; and clean energy generation, transmission, and storage. Each Tech Hub is built around a consortium of business, government, higher education, workforce, labor and community organizations. South Florida's consortium includes 60 members and partners - including the City of Miami - that participated in developing the application. In July 2024, EDA awarded RRTH grant funding of approximately $19 million to implement three projects, including: (1) Scaling advanced concrete technologies made with reduced emissions that protect environments in low-lying areas, specifically focusing on communities most affected by extreme weather events; (2) Establishing workforce development programs that offer career pathways for small businesses and workforce development through certifications, training, and apprenticeships, supplemented with wraparound services; and (3) Cutting red tape to foster collaboration among government, startups, corporations, capital partners, community advocates, and academia to rapidly affect change by deploying new risk and resilience technology where it is most needed. RRTH consortium members join monthly hub-wide zoom calls to share success, identify opportunities, and coordinate action.

column17: Recognizing its acute vulnerability to the effects of sea level rise (SLR), in 2015 the City of Miami established its Sea Level Rise Committee to study the effects of SLR on the City and recommend changes to City policy to help better combat the deleterious effects of SLR. In 2019, the City of Miami consolidated the Sea Level Rise Committee and Waterfront Advisory Board into the Climate Resilience Committee. The purpose, powers, and duties of the Climate Resilience Committee are; (1) Shall recommend changes to the City Code and any City policy necessary to help the City, its residents, businesses, institutions, and natural systems adapt to, prepare for, and thrive in the various stresses related to climate change, including but not limited to emissions of greenhouse gases, increasing flood risks, increasing groundwater levels, more intense storms resulting in high tides and storm surges, increasing high heat days, salt water intrusion, drought, extreme weather events, and water and vector-borne illnesses. (2) Have the responsibility to review and evaluate issues related to the use, disposition, and/or development of City-owned waterfront property and shall provide advice to the City Commission concerning those issues and only such other matters as are referred to it by the City Commission in regard to City or public land abutting water. (3) Expected to be aware of City policies concerning development and coordinate its endeavors with other City committees and boards which will be affected by the Committee's recommendations. The Climate Resilience Committee consists of nine (9) voting members who shall be city residents, work in the city, own a business in the city, or own real property in the city. All voting members shall be invested in the city and serve without compensation. In addition: (1) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in civil engineering or architecture with a focus on infrastructure; (2) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in community and real estate development; (3) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in one (1) or more of the following areas: climatology, geophysics, coastal management, oceanography, or coastal ocean science; (4) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in emergency management; (5) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in economics; and (6) At least one (1) member shall possess an expertise in advocating for vulnerable low-income communities. At least two (2) members shall be eighteen to twenty-five (18 - 25) years of age and possess a strong interest in and background or education in climate resilience including but not limited to impacts on infrastructure, water supply and quality, ecosystem health, housing, socioeconomics, or advocacy for vulnerable low-income communities. The Committee meets monthly.

column17: Food Systems Programs Impact through implementation of the 2025 Food Action Plan (https://www.phoenix.gov/content/dam/phoenix/oepsite/documents/food/2025%20Phoenix%20Food%20Action%20Plan%20Jan%202020.pdf) serves as guidance on activities to provide healthy food for all in Phoenix through a resilient, sustainable, thriving, and equitable local food system. The City's Food Systems Program achieved over 90% of the 2025 Food Action Plan goals. From 2020 through 2025, the actions identified in the 2025 plan were achieved through the Phoenix Resilient Food Systems (RFSI) Initiative using municipal funds and American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funds. The City innovatively and creatively used the funds available for food assistance by creating 14 programs. Through the collective efforts of our community partners, grantees, and Phoenix residents, Phoenix made significant progress toward the goals outlined in the 2025 Phoenix Food Action Plan. The following summarizes the most notable outcomes of the RFSI initiative: Meals Distributed: 5,546,605 meals were distributed to residents during and post-pandemic. Pounds of Food Produced Overall: 51,264 pounds of food were produced across 12 grant projects and the Backyard Garden Program. Grant Funds Distributed: $1,808,694 and 31 projects were supported between 2022 and 2024, which supported local farmers and non-profit organizations to increase food access and implement innovative practices, such as agrivoltaics, indoor vertical farming, portable cold storage containers, irrigation, and shade improvements. Food Waste Diverted: 94,840 pounds of food waste were diverted from landfills. Local Businesses Supported: 58 local food businesses were supported through technical assistance, business training, and seed funding, helping to build capacity within the local food economy. Residents Trained: 818 residents received hands-on education and training on topics related to local food systems like gardening, composting, and starting a food business. Partnerships Developed: 152 direct partnerships were developed with non-profit organizations, cooperatives, benefit corporations, and community groups, and 116 indirect partnerships were developed through entities managing city-funded programs. In Fall 2024, the TruLocal Container Solar Vertical Farm Project was initiated through a partnership between the City (Office of Environmental Programs, Fire Department, Human Services Department), the Salt River Project, Arizona State University, and Homer Farms. The farm, located within a food desert, will be operational in mid-2025, using photovoltaics for energy efficiency, combined with the innate water efficiency of vertical farming, will be an example of a resilient, sustainable project. The community will also benefit from workshops available on vertical farming and twenty percent of the produce will be donated directly to the community. The Arizona Fresh Agri-food Innovation Center, located on a former landfill site adjacent to the Rio Salado/Salt River within the South Phoenix area, will begin construction in 2025 on the first of four phases of the project. The project will promote capital investment, job creation, and planning for entrepreneurial spaces for food innovation. A community park and green space along the Rio Salado will also be developed on the site. This project will be the largest Brownfields to Healthfields project in Arizona and provides increased access to healthy food and green space for the community along with research space for agri-food tech and urban agriculture innovation. The City established the Food Systems Program in the Office of Environmental Programs with general funds available for full-time staff and programmatic activities. Programs continuing from the RFSI, include the GardenPHX program (indoor and outdoor gardens for residents), Food System Transformation Grants, and Project REDUCE, focused on preventing and reducing food waste in restaurants. The City is developing the 2030 Food Action Plan with extensive community engagement, including visioning workshops with residents, food system businesses, and nonprofits. The final plan is expected to be completed by December 2025.

column17: Phoenix City Council selected the architectural firm for the C40 Cities Reinventing Cities Initiative to develop Phoenix's Resource Innovation Campus in December 2024 with a net positive carbon footprint design (https://www.c40reinventingcities.org/en/professionals/winning-projects/resource-innovation-campus-1613.html). The City celebrated the grand reopening of the 27th Ave Materials Recovery Facility in May 2025 upgrading it with modern sorting technology for recycling (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/public-works-news/public-works-celebrates-reopening-of-27th-ave--materials-recover.html). Another advancement is the City of Phoenix Circular Plastics Microfactory that was recognized in 2024 with the Award of Distinction at the Arizona Forward Environmental Excellence Awards (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/public-works-news/environmental-excellence-awards--phoenix-circular-plastics-micro.html). Phoenix is a venue for major entertainment and sporting events and uses these opportunities to demonstrate its commitment to sustainability and environmental stewardship. The 2024 Final Four Fan Fest had a 94.2% waste diversion rate for City-held events, qualifying as a zero-waste event with 52,283 attendees. Zero waste is when more than ninety percent of waste is diverted from landfills. During the 2023 Super Bowl LVII, Phoenix reached its goal of diverting at least 92% of waste from Super Bowl LVII events away from the landfill (https://www.azfamily.com/2023/02/27/92-super-bowl-lvii-waste-diverted-landfills/). After final sorting and weighing, the 2023 Super Bowl LVII events hosted in downtown Phoenix surpassed a previous Super Bowl's diversion rate of 91% to become the greenest Super Bowl in history. The final diversion rate of city-collected trash from downtown Super Bowl events was 92.6%, qualifying it as a zero-waste event. With help from Downtown Phoenix, Inc., Keep Phoenix Beautiful, and Volunteer PHX, Phoenix had 51 volunteers serving as Zero Waste Ambassadors, who guided visitors to put trash, recyclables, and food waste into separate receptacles throughout the downtown area. When Phoenix hosted the Super Bowl in 2015, the city set a goal to divert 80% of waste from the landfill. Ultimately, the final diversion rate achieved in 2015 was 73%. Since then, however, the City of Phoenix has added more robust resources and technology at the Compost Facility, which has allowed for increased waste diversion. Public Works processed nearly 12 tons of food waste from the 2023 Super Bowl Experience - more than 11% of everything thrown away. In partnership with airport vendors, the City began collecting food waste organics for processing into compost at Sky Harbor International Airport in October 2023. The Phoenix Convention Center also reestablished a sustainable composting program in 2022. Composting removes organic material from the waste stream, creates less methane from decomposition than if it went to a landfill, and reduces transportation GHG emissions that would result if the material were taken to the landfill. Composting also saves landfill space and creates a functional product.

column17: The majority of Phoenix's greenhouse gas emissions are from the transportation sector. Public transit and alternative modes of transportation like micromobility can help reduce emissions. Since July 2024, the Shared Micromobility Program enabled users to complete over 505,000 miles using shared scooters in the City of Phoenix. Based on US EPA estimates, if just 35% of these trips displaced car use, this would avoid approximately 71 metric tons of CO2 emissions. Phoenix expanded the micromobility operations area in 2023 and expanded operation hours to 24/7 in 2024. Staff are working closely with the operators to ensure better transit integration to foster intermodality. More bicycle and pedestrian path connections are being made with the completion of the Grand Canalscape phase 3 project in March 2025 bringing more active paths to the community for walking, biking and other active transportation modes (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/street-transportation-department-news/grand-canalscape-phase-3-provides-more-active-paths-to-community.html). The City has been engaging younger residents 17-25 years old to help guide the Road Safety Action Plan through a student committee (https://www.phoenix.gov/administration/departments/streets/safety-improvements/road-safety-action-plan.html). The Phoenix City Council approved the plan to transition the city's bus fleet to 100% zero-emission buses by 2040, with the initial procurement contracts being approved for $230 million (https://kjzz.org/content/1837063/phoenix-approves-230m-buy-green-buses). The City has received 20 hybrid electric buses (HEBs), with another 25 HEBs are to be received in 2025. Phoenix was awarded a $16.3 million Federal Transit Administration (FTA) grant for greener (low and no-emission) buses and supporting infrastructure (https://www.kjzz.org/2022-08-23/content-1804434-phoenix-will-use-163-million-grant-greener-buses-workforce-program). The grant is made available through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law under the Low-No Emission and Buses and Bus Facilities highly competitive grant programs. The program's goal is to support the transition of the nation's fleet to more energy-efficient and cleaner transit vehicles. The use of zero-emission buses will also require training of the workforce and investments in infrastructure. In April 2024, the City was awarded a $1.2 million grant from the FTA for Transit Oriented Communities planning efforts with an emphasis on affordable housing and mixed-use development for the Phoenix Main Light Rail Line, the Northwest Extension Phase I that opened in 2016, and the 50th Street Station that opened in 2019. The Phoenix adopted the South Central Extension Transit Oriented Development (TOD) Community Plan in March 2022. This plan will serve to attract, guide, and prioritize strategic investments in infrastructure, housing, economic development, and other areas to realize a shared community vision—to make South Central a world-class destination in which current and future residents both share in the prosperity that a walkable and transit-oriented community brings. In November of 2022, the FTA announced the award of a $1 million grant for the City to enable implementation of the goals identified in the South Central TOD Community Plan. As of 2024, there are 18 miles of light rail in the City of Phoenix, with additional extensions in various planning, design, and construction stages. The first of these to be completed since the 2021 CAP is the 1.6-mile Northwest Extension Phase II that opened in January 2024. The project includes a bridge that crosses the I-17 highway, leading to an elevated end-of-line station and an adjacent four-story parking garage with solar panels. The light rail station is the top story of a multimodal transportation hub, the Thelda Williams Transit Center, which is serviced by local and express buses, with a possible future expansion to add Bus Rapid Transit (https://www.kjzz.org/2022-08-23/content-1804434-phoenix-will-use-163-million-grant-greener-buses-workforce-program). In June 2025 the South Central Extension and Downtown Hub light rail extension was completed. This 5.5 mile extension is expected to add more than 8,000 additional riders each day (https://www.phoenix.gov/newsroom/public-transit-news/south-central-downtown-hub-light-rail-extension-opens-june-7--.html).

In June 2022, a Regional Nature Covenant was signed by 12 mayors of municipalities neighboring Tel Aviv-Yafo. The covenant's goal is to foster collaborations for ecosystem preservation in their shared natural spaces, establish agreements on cross-border ecological corridors, and cultivate communities of nature stewards in the Greater Tel Aviv area. Recognizing that ecosystems are not bound by municipal limits, as cities share natural and ecological resources like coastlines, rivers, habitats, and corridors, the mayors understood the necessity of collaborative ecosystem management to ensure its resilience and continued function amidst climate change. In 2023, a municipal coordinator was appointed to advance the covenant's actions, and a kick-off meeting was held to develop a work plan, which is now taking shape. Looking ahead to 2025, this action plan is being updated in collaboration with the Regional Planning Committee and the National Parks and Nature Authority. The core of this regional initiative lies in connecting ecological corridors at both the regional and city levels. 
Ecological corridors are vital open spaces that link diverse natural habitats, facilitating the movement and dispersal of plant and animal species. They are essential for maintaining biodiversity, preventing population isolation, and supporting long-term ecosystem health. These corridors also provide crucial ecosystem services, including water regulation, air filtration, pollution reduction, and opportunities for recreation, effectively acting as 'arteries' within the landscape that sustain natural processes and mitigate the impacts of human development.
In Israel, national planning increasingly recognizes the strategic importance of ecological corridors. National Outline Plan 35 (TAMA 35) and its amendment (TAMA 35/1) have designated these corridors as mandatory planning components, establishing guidelines for their preservation. Within these plans, a national network of biogeographic ecological corridors has been defined, encompassing natural and open areas vital for biodiversity. The objective is to ensure the continuity and ecological functionality of these spaces despite developmental pressures. Local and district planning authorities are required to integrate these corridors into their master plans, maintaining their open and connective character while minimizing damage from infrastructure or construction. This reflects a comprehensive understanding of the human-nature connection and the necessity of holistic spatial planning for the future of natural systems and human well-being. The Tel Aviv-Yafo Master Plan specifically addresses ecological corridors within the Gush Dan (Greater Tel Aviv) area, defining them as a network of open spaces that connect partial or complete natural areas, such as groves, streams, and agricultural lands, within the urban environment. Their primary function is to enable the movement of animals and plants between these areas, thereby preserving biodiversity and the health of the entire ecosystem. In an era of climate change, the importance of ecological corridors significantly increases. They help reduce the 'urban heat island' effect by increasing vegetation and shade. Additionally, they contribute to regulating urban runoff during extreme rain events and assist in preventing floods. The corridors connect the city of Tel Aviv-Yafo, a metropolitan hub, to the surrounding ecological systems, such as the sea, the Yarkon and Ayalon rivers, and various open spaces in Gush Dan. This connection facilitates the transfer of vital ecological services into the city, improving air quality and the quality of life for residents.

Tel Aviv-Yafo's City-Business Climate Partnership operates under the guiding principles of materiality, moderation, and the commitment to leave no one behind. 
The initiative is designed to engage the private sector in climate action through tailored strategies divided into three key areas of focus:

1. Small Businesses: The City's Cultural Core
Small businesses are integral to Tel Aviv-Yafo's unique and vibrant character. These enterprises contribute to the city's dynamic atmosphere, and in turn, the municipality supports their efforts to become more climate-conscious. The city provides tools and guidance, such as:
Guidebooks offering best practices in sustainability.
Workshops and conferences aimed at educating business owners on environmental responsibility.
Furthermore, these businesses are encouraged to interact with their customers on climate issues. An example is the “Last Minute Challenge,” a platform for culinary businesses to offer last-minute deals on products close to expiration. This initiative helps reduce food waste while generating additional revenue for the companies. The city promotes these offers via its municipal communication platforms.

2. Commercial Zones: Reducing Carbon Footprints
The municipality supports commercial zones that are looking to minimize their environmental and carbon impacts. This involves:

Guidance and carbon mapping for businesses to assess their carbon footprint.
Development of goal-setting work plans to align with the city's Climate Action Plan (CAP).
Through this process, the municipality ensures that these commercial zones reduce their carbon emissions and set an example for other areas.

3. City-Business Climate Leadership Group: Leading by Example
In collaboration with the City Business Climate Alliance (CBCA), Tel Aviv-Yafo spearheads the City-Business Climate Leadership Table, a partnership between the city and leading businesses to address climate challenges. The focus is on creating innovative, impactful projects that generate environmental, social, and economic value.

The leadership group includes companies with significant activity in Tel Aviv-Yafo that have integrated sustainability into their core operations. These companies aim to lead and inspire both local and global transition through their environmental initiatives. The group includes high-profile companies such as:

Check Point
Google
Imperva
ironSource (Unity)
Meta
Monday

Senior representatives from these companies and the municipality meet in roundtable discussions to develop joint projects to address climate challenges, foster innovation, and promote green growth. The Sustainable Neighborhoods Plan implements the city's vision to encourage and make accessible a sustainable lifestyle in the city's neighborhoods, both on the part of the residents and community and in the diverting of municipal resources. The Sustainable Neighborhood Program promotes sustainability at the neighborhood level. Focusing on creating dense opportunities for sustainability at the neighborhood level while creating local cooperation between citizens, businesses, and the municipality, in order to increase and expand circles of influence, strengthen community solidarity and significantly improve the quality of life in the neighborhood. The principle of the program is to develop and assimilate the various areas of sustainability in day-to-day activities and in the community: agriculture and urban nature, environmental education, healthy and sustainable food, reducing consumption and landfilling waste, green businesses, and environmental innovation. Changing habits and local adaptation to climate change is built by promoting awareness, public participation, and developing partnerships. At the beginning of 2022, it was decided to expand the plan across the whole city, and 26 local sustainability coordinators were hired.

In 2023, sustainability coordinators were trained on the municipal climate program, and the areas of action in the neighborhoods were aligned with the maps of climate vulnerability and at-risk populations. As part of the activities of the Sustainability Unit and the Sustainable Neighborhoods Program in 2023, over 17,000 residents participated actively and regularly in activities related to strengthening urban nature, community gardens, reducing consumption, community composting, food initiatives, and more.

 One of the program's core projects is a collaboration with the Ministry of Environmental Protection, subsidizing residents' initiatives for sustainable lifestyles. In 2022, 22 initiatives across the city were funded. In 2023, the municipality supported 154,000 NIS for nine community initiatives led by residents that promote urban sustainability. These initiatives include establishing a community workshop, a community kitchen, a cargo bike network for collecting organic waste from businesses, and opening lending libraries and giving cabinets.
The new integrated Climate Plan emphasizes the neighborhood level as a core pathway for implementing change. This approach is realized through the 'Sustainable Neighborhoods' program, which strategically leverages existing community and physical infrastructure to tackle climate change locally. The program's objective is to develop a replicable model for neighborhood climate plans, drawing directly from the city's overarching climate strategy and the 'Sustainable Neighborhoods' framework itself. A key aspect involves realigning the activities of sustainability coordinators with the central missions of the city's climate plan.

This neighborhood-level initiative is structured into three main stages:

1. Building a Neighborhood Climate Profile: This initial phase involves comprehensively mapping both local physical vulnerabilities (e.g., shade deficits, flood frequency, proximity to green spaces) and social vulnerabilities (e.g., percentage of families receiving social services, single-parent households, home-bound residents, buildings predating 1980). Concurrently, the neighborhood's carbon footprint is measured using data such as per capita electricity consumption, vehicle density, and per capita waste generation.

2. Prioritizing Areas for Action: Following the climate profile analysis, specific local actions are prioritized to enhance climate resilience and promote sustainable living within each neighborhood. Examples include strategic tree planting in areas prone to heat, targeted waste reduction efforts in high-waste neighborhoods, and asphalt removal in flood-prone zones to increase permeable surfaces.

3. 
Developing a Neighborhood Work Plan: The identified neighborhood priorities are then translated into a collaborative action plan involving relevant municipal departments and active residents. This work plan harmonizes the climate priorities with the distinct needs and preferences of the neighborhood's residents. The program is fundamentally driven by a partnership-based, neighborhood-level system, which also serves as the foundation for all climate-related interventions.

As a leading member of the Israeli Coastal Authorities Forum, Tel Aviv-Yafo is actively developing guidelines and frameworks for local coastal adaptation. The Forum, in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and the UN PAPRAC, is working to address the challenges posed by climate change in the Mediterranean region.
Key Objectives and Approach:
•	Develop Guidelines: The program aims to create guidelines for incorporating climate change adaptation into coastal planning and management.
•	Scenario-Based Approach: These guidelines are based on contingency scenarios for Israel's coastal zone, focusing on sea level rise and extreme wave events.
•	Collaborative Workshops: Tel Aviv-Yafo participated in a series of webinars and a collaborative workshop, titled 'Coastal Adaptation in the Mediterranean: Challenges and Opportunities,' to identify key threats and adaptation measures for its coastline.
Key Findings and Recommendations:
•	Threats to the Coastline: The city identified specific threats to its coastline, including erosion, flooding, and saltwater intrusion.
•	Adaptation Measures: The city outlined a range of adaptation measures, which will form the basis for its coastal adaptation plan.
•	Municipal Authority Document: The plan should be a formal, binding document approved by the city council, with regular updates, a budget, and measurable success indicators.
•	Information Mapping: The city should conduct an initial mapping of existing data to identify challenges and inform its approach.
•	Integrated Planning and Management: Adaptation requires both planning and ongoing management, with clear collaboration between planning and management teams.
•	Government Support: The government should make data accessible and provide a list of potential actions for local authorities to choose from.
•	Performance Measurement: Success should be measured using benchmarks like the clean beach index, which can help prioritize climate action.
•	Continuous Improvement: The adaptation process should be ongoing, with regular feedback and updates to the plan.
•	Regional Collaboration: The coastal authorities forum can facilitate collaboration and knowledge sharing among cities.
•	Nationwide Planning: The government should consider the impact of construction in the south on the northern part of the coastline.
By implementing these recommendations, Tel Aviv-Yafo can effectively adapt to the challenges of climate change and protect its valuable coastline.
In December 2025, the Coastal Authorities Forum will celebrate 10 years of activity, and the Tel Aviv Municipality will host this focal event.
