Through this public consultation, we welcome views from all interested parties on how Singapore can work towards becoming a low-carbon country as we consider raising our long-term ambition to achieve net zero by 2050 and whether to raise our 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to support this ambition. 

NCCS also conducted a public consultation on the REACH website on Singapore's Decarbonisation Journey from 8 October to 5 November 2024, which built on the previous public consultation. These views were taken into consideration as Singapore developed out next bound of climate targets, measures and policies, including our 2035 NDC.

Resumen por mecanismo (colaboración con gobierno nacional) y avance aplicado a temas clave

1. Intercambio de datos (GIS, inventarios, mapas de riesgo, emisiones)
Cali ha integrado sus capas geoespaciales (IDESC/geoportal municipal) con insumos nacionales (IDEAM, IGAC, MinAmbiente) y comparte archivos GIS y mapas de riesgo para priorización de inversiones. Los Mapas de Riesgo del IDEAM (2023-2025) se usan operativamente en la selección de zonas para infraestructura verde y mitigación de inundaciones en Cali. Esto ha permitido armonizar inventarios (emisiones y riesgos) entre niveles municipal y nacional. 


2. Desarrollo de capacidades y asistencia técnica
Desde 2023 se han hecho talleres técnicos y apoyos metodológicos con IDEAM, MinAmbiente y CVC (censo arbóreo), fortaleciendo protocolos de monitoreo ambiental, generación de inventarios de GEI y elaboración de mapas de exposición. El DAGMA ha recibido asistencia técnica para mejorar la calidad de sus datos y metodologías de priorización territorial. Esto ha mejorado la calidad de las decisiones en energía, movilidad y arbolado. 


3. Colaboraciones regionales
La articulación con la Gobernación del Valle, la CVC y redes nacionales ha permitido proyectos conjuntos (manejo de cuencas, programas regionales de residuos y economía circular) y uso compartido de recursos técnicos (laboratorios y brigadas). Ejemplo: esquemas de gestión de residuos orgánicos piloto y coordinación para restauración de rondas hídricas. Esto ha reducido solapamientos y mejorado escalabilidad territorial. 


4. Economía circular y residuos
Cali ha participado en convocatorias y proyectos con MinAmbiente y programas regionales para implementar cadenas de valorización (pilotos de compostaje y recolección diferenciada), apoyados por asistencia técnica nacional y cofinanciación en algunos casos. El avance es incremental: protocolos y pilotos activos (2023-2025) y rutas de escalamiento identificadas en informes sectoriales. 
minambiente.gov.co


5. Implementación del Plan Integral de Gestión del Cambio Climático (PIGCCT / PAC)
El PAC de Cali está alineado con lineamientos nacionales; el DAGMA publica el Plan y rinde cuentas anualmente. El Gobierno nacional ha apoyado con guías metodológicas, seguimiento y cofinanciación técnica en ciertos proyectos (monitoreo, arbolado, adaptación urbana). El PAC se utiliza como marco para priorizar emisiones, movilidad, agua e infraestructura verde. 


6. Monitoreo y reporte de acciones ambientales
Cali reporta avances en audiencias públicas y documentos técnicos (Rendición de Cuentas DAGMA 2023-2025). Los inventarios de emisiones y datos de calidad del aire se actualizan con insumos nacionales y sirven para reportes locales y nacionales (alineamiento con MINAMBIENTE/IDEAM). Esto mejora trazabilidad de beneficiarios y focalización territorial. 


7. Sistemas de información aplicados a temáticas (emisiones, energía, movilidad, agua, residuos, educación, estructura ecológica, infraestructura)

Emisiones / Energía: Inventarios locales armonizados con lineamientos nacionales; diagnósticos sectoriales en transporte y consumo energético para priorizar medidas de mitigación.

Movilidad: Coordinación con MinTransporte y programas regionales para PEMS y promoción de flota limpia; empresas locales han suscrito compromisos con soporte técnico nacional. 
cali.gov.co

Residuos: Pilotos de economía circular y coordinación con UNGRD/MinAmbiente para manejo de residuos en emergencias y valorización.

Agua / Rondas hídricas: Uso de mapas hidrográficos y cooperación con autoridades nacionales para manejo de cuencas urbanas.

Educación: Programas y talleres con apoyo institucional para sensibilización, formación técnica y participación comunitaria en proyectos verdes.

column17: Durante el año 2023, la Empresa Pública Municipal de Acción Social y Educación (EP DASE) impulsó un trabajo articulado con diferentes instituciones municipales y prestadoras de servicios, cuyo objetivo principal fue fortalecer la cultura ciudadana en materia de cuidado ambiental, manejo responsable de los recursos naturales y promoción de hábitos sostenibles en comunidades y grupos vulnerables de Guayaquil. En coordinación con URVASEO, se llevaron a cabo campañas y talleres prácticos orientados a la clasificación y correcta disposición de los desechos sólidos generados en los hogares. Estas actividades no solo se enfocaron en sensibilizar a la ciudadanía sobre la importancia del reciclaje y la reducción de residuos, sino también en brindar herramientas sencillas y aplicables en la vida diaria para que las familias pudieran separar los materiales orgánicos e inorgánicos, identificar residuos aprovechables y disminuir la cantidad de basura enviada a los rellenos sanitarios. Gracias a esta colaboración, se logró que diversos sectores populares de la ciudad incorporaran nuevas prácticas ambientales, fomentando la participación comunitaria y el compromiso de los vecinos con la limpieza y el orden de sus entornos barriales. De igual manera, mediante la colaboración con EMAPAG EP, se ejecutaron acciones educativas orientadas al uso responsable y eficiente del agua potable, con énfasis en la concientización sobre su valor como recurso vital y limitado. A través de charlas comunitarias, dinámicas educativas y la entrega de material didáctico, se transmitió información clave sobre la importancia del ahorro de agua en las actividades cotidianas, la prevención de fugas y desperdicios, así como la necesidad de adoptar prácticas de consumo consciente que contribuyan a la sostenibilidad ambiental y al bienestar de las futuras generaciones. El impacto de estas acciones se refleja en un progreso tangible en la sensibilización ciudadana, evidenciado en la mejora de hábitos de las comunidades participantes y en la creación de una red de líderes barriales comprometidos con la réplica de los mensajes de educación ambiental. Estos esfuerzos conjuntos han permitido no solo reforzar el vínculo institucional con la ciudadanía, sino también sentar las bases para un cambio cultural en torno a la responsabilidad individual y colectiva frente al cuidado del medio ambiente. En resumen, la colaboración entre EP DASE, URVASEO y EMAPAG durante el año 2023 constituyó un proceso integral de formación, sensibilización y empoderamiento comunitario, cuyo progreso se traduce en la generación de entornos más limpios, la optimización del uso de los recursos y la consolidación de prácticas sostenibles que contribuyen al desarrollo social y ambiental de la ciudad.

column17: The City of Tallinn and OÜ Utilitas enter into a cooperation agreement to create a joint venture in the field of district heating, AS Utilitas Tallinna Soojus, which will be 33.34% owned by the City of Tallinn and 66.66% by the private limited company Utilitas. The business plan aims to complete the renewal of the district heating network in accordance with the Tallinn Unified District Heating Network Development Plan and to achieve carbon-neutral district heating and cooling supply by 2030 at the latest. At the same time, the objective of the accelerated investment plan is to reduce the share of natural gas in district heating to less than 10 percent by 2027 at the latest, which will reduce fossil fuels consumption by more than 500,000 MWh. The aim is also to expand the district heating and cooling network, enable convenient connection for new customers, and to bring the network to districts that today mainly use fossil sources for heating.\nIn addition, Utilitas has been a valuable consulting partner during designing and updating the renovation support measures for residential buildings to improve energy efficiency. Also, Utilitas, in collaboration with the City of Tallinn, is leading the development and implementation of the city's integrated heating and cooling plan through the joint venture AS Utilitas Tallinna Soojus.

column17: In 2014, with the “Manifesto digitale di Firenze” (Digital Florence Manifesto), the principle of assets sharing found its strategy and implementation. Its use is in providing the Municipality, as well as city's service providers, a reference point on digital values deemed fundamental for the city. , Region, Chamber of Commerce, University, Utilities and all the local stakeholders, joined their forces to provide direct advantages to citizens and city users, thanks also to an integrating offer of services and applications, based on those shared assets. The concept of the SCCR (smart city control room) as a unique platform combining dashboards on mobility, environment, resilience, social, energy and policy, making to manage the city, has been developed with the European project H2020-SCC1, 2016-2021. It is not only an IT tool enabling the sharing data system but it is also the physical sharing of spaces where manage the city.Every single service provider does not see many advantages in co-presence: the Municipality promote then the vision that all together we respond more quickly and efficiently: decide and manage public services in the same place and on shared system data based on information in real-time is the only way for a simpler daily life and the best service performance. The management of city services is a typical multi-operator activity: collaboration, synergies between bodies, utilities, promoted by the Municipality as a center of aggregation is like an orchestra. The orchestra conductor tunes the sounds but without the instruments or only with some of them would not have the right symphony. The strong point is that this is a federated model where data and digital assets of each subject are enhanced, without wanting to override the single.partner.

column17: In 2016, Orlando City Council unanimously passed the Building Energy and Water Efficiency Strategy (BEWES), a policy focused on tracking the energy and water output of our largest buildings. BEWES is a key strategy identified in the Green Works Orlando Community Action Plan. Since August 1, 2018, any city-owned building above 10,000 gross square feet and any commercial or multifamily building above 50,000 gross square feet is required to have whole-building energy use tracked and reported annually. This information must be provided to the city each year to be made transparent to the real estate market via an annual report and transparency map. Buildings that receive a score below 50 are required to perform an energy audit or a retro-commissioning service to better understand their building performance and cost saving opportunities, minimize our energy waste, and maximize cost savings. Free energy audits provided by OUC and Duke Energy will be eligible for compliance, meaning that there are no out-of-pocket expense to comply with the BEWES policy. The Office of Sustainability and Resilience website has clear instructions for buildings to adapt, report, and comply. To support with compliance, the city hosts multiple annual meetings to share updates, best practices, and field questions. The city has also offered our in-person benchmarking and ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager training courses, provided in partnership with USGBC Florida. https://www.orlando.gov/Initiatives/Building-Energy-Water-Efficiency-Strategy/Policy-Compliance-and-Impact-Report-2018-2019 https://www.orlando.gov/Initiatives/Building-Energy-Water-Efficiency-Strategy

column17: According to the U.S. EPA, heat islands are urbanized areas that experience higher temperatures than outlying areas. Columbus has one of the fastest-growing urban heat island effects in all major U.S. cities. This phenomenon impacts health, wildlife, and the economy. Extreme heat kills more Americans than any other weather event, and can lead to serious illnesses, such as heat stroke and exhaustion. But not everyone's risk is the same; a 2021 EPA report concluded that Black and African American individuals are 40-59% more likely than non-Black and non-African American individuals to currently live in high-impact heat mortality areas. Studies have also shown that hotter days are linked to worse test scores for Black and Hispanic children, widening the racial gap in schools.Source on urban heat island effect in Columbus: https://www.columbusufmp.org/the-facts.html#:~:text=Columbus%20has%20the%20fastest%2Dgrowing,and%20improve%20out%20tree%20canopy. US EPA report: https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-report-shows-disproportionate-impacts-climate-change-socially-vulnerable#:~:text=WASHINGTON%20(Sept.,%2C%20flooding%2C%20and%20other%20impacts. Through instruments provided by NOAA-funded CAPA Strategies, the City of Columbus, along with partners Franklin County Public Health, Green Columbus, the Ohio State University's Byrd Climate and Polar Research Center, Friends of the Lower Olentangy, MORPC, the Franklin County Soil and Water Conservation District, and nearly 80 volunteers helped map the hottest parts of the city and surrounding areas in Franklin County during a citizen-science afternoon of data collection in August 2022.Car- or bike-mounted heat sensors m captured data across 22 routes in the morning, afternoon, and evening time on one of the hottest days of the year. The sensors recorded temperature, humidity, time, and the volunteers' location every second. CAPA's end-to-end program, including sensor technology, analysis and modeling, and community engagement, allowed the City to record a hyper-local description of heat so that we could then strategize specific resilience-related programs in each of the most affected neighborhoods. Results found a nearly 18-degree difference throughout all three time slots in some of Columbus' more dense and center-city neighborhoods.Data gathered in Columbus will inform implementation of the community-wide Columbus Climate Action Plan, particularly around imparting environmental justice and building climate resiliency. It will shape actions such as creating a regional climate hazards alert system, establishing a network of resiliency hubs, and increasing equitable tree canopy.Columbus area heat map report: chrome-extension://efaidnbmnnnibpcajpcglclefindmkaj/https://www.columbus.gov/files/sharedassets/city/v/1/utilities/sustainability/summary-report_heat-watch-columbus_110722final.pdf

column17: The Canadian Urban Sustainability Practitioners (CUSP) network's mission is to pursue transformative impact for the equitable and lasting wellbeing of people and planet. Members work to mitigate climate change through deep GHG reductions and decarbonization, to build resilience among people and places to a changing climate, and with central commitment to restorative climate justice practiced with humility and tenacity. column17: The Renewable Energy & Efficiency Workforce (RENEW) Training Program is a skills-based short-term training program paired with industry certification that will educate and prepare participants for career opportunities in energy-efficient and sustainable technologies. Program graduates receive a paid work-based learning experience with a high potential for permanent job placement with program partners. The program is supported by the City of Charlotte in partnership currently with Good Will Industries and the Urban League to provide training and job placement and is currently focused on energy efficient HVAC training - the city financially supports the program as well as helps to monitor progress and support wraparound services. column17: In 2023, the City of Charlotte and Duke Energy Carolinas launched an income-qualified energy efficiency home rehabilitation pilot program. The High Energy Use Pilot Program will help income-qualified customers with high energy use receive much-needed home repairs and energy efficiency retrofits that will improve housing safety and reduce their electricity usage and overall costs. However, as many as 40% of households that could be eligible for this program would not be able to participate due to health and safety issues in the home, particularly housing repair issues such as damage to doors, windows or the roof that need to be addressed first. The funding provided by the city through this public-private partnership will ensure that customers who otherwise would not be able to engage in this pilot will now be able to take advantage of these retrofits. Duke Energy will invest approximately $4 million in the Charlotte region to support energy retrofits for approximately 500 high-electrical use, income-qualified customers. The city will provide up to $1 million in American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) funding to support home repairs necessary before energy efficiency retrofits can occur. Home repairs may include window, roof, chimney, plumbing, or water heater repairs or replacements, pressure relief valve installation, mechanical ventilation and lead-based paint hazard control. Energy retrofit measures may include the replacement of heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems as well as sealing air leaks, installing insulation, installing LED bulbs and exchanging older refrigerators with ENERGY STAR® models. Charlotte is one of three North Carolina municipalities, including Forsyth and Guilford counties, selected for the pilot program. The initial goal is to assist 1,000 participants over a two-year span from an estimated 22,000 income-qualified residents in all identified areas.

Graham/N. Tryon Corridor of Charlotte. column17: As a continuation of the City of Charlotte's 2022 partnership with the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, Duke Energy, and Centralina Regional Council, the second public PoleVolt charger was installed in the Belmont neighborhood adjacent to Seigle Point Apartments in Fall 2023. PoleVolt is an EV charger mounted onto pre-existing light poles with overhead power, making it cheaper and easier to install. While increasing access to electric power, PoleVolt also attempts to bridge the gap between inequity and sustainability by providing underrepresented communities with new innovative technologies. To inform and engage communities about technologies in public spaces that are being piloted, such as PoleVolt, the City of Charlotte is testing out Digital Trust for Places & Routines (DTPR) this summer and fall. DTPR is used as a way to promote transparency and accountability of public-facing technologies and the data it collects or uses. DTPR does three things 1) it provides an organized and standardized way of understanding public facing technologies, 2) it shares the information in an accessible way through both a sign and website, and 3) it provides a way for people to give feedback on the technology on the website.

column17: Since the buildings sector accounts for about 50% of carbon emissions in Charlotte, one core strategy to reduce emissions is to reduce energy consumption in existing buildings. Building energy performance benchmarking is an energy efficiency best practice that measures a building's energy use, tracks its performance over time and compares its performance to similar buildings. This information helps building owners identify opportunities to reduce or eliminate energy use. To encourage building owners to increase their buildings' energy efficiency and to highlight successful practices in that space, the City of Charlotte launched Power Down the Crown, a voluntary building energy performance benchmarking program that invites public and private organizations with buildings in Charlotte to share their building energy performance data and asks them to contribute to Power Down the Crown's goal of reducing the program-wide energy use intensity (energy use per ft2) by 10% by 2030. In return, the city will celebrate partner successes, offer opportunities to share and learn energy efficiency best practices, and provide benchmarking technical assistance. Additionally, to bring greater visibility to the program and celebrate broader sustainability successes, Power Down the Crown has partnered with the Charlotte Business Journal to sponsor a sustainability award in connection with the Best Places to Work award. The inaugural Sustainability Award will be presented in the 2025 Best Places to Work award cycle. Current Power Down the Crown partners include Caldwell Presbyterian Church, Central Piedmont Community College, Coca-Cola Consolidated Inc., Grubb Properties, Honeywell, Kimco Realty, IKEA Charlotte, Novant Health, Nucor, St. Peter's Episcopal Church, Trane Technologies, UNC Charlotte, and Unitarian Universalist Community of Charlotte.

That project is ongoing with the goal of having a GreenPrint for each of the six (6) corridors and to secure seed money to start implementation. column17: In October of 2022, planning began for the Charlotte deployment of AMP (The Affordable Mobility Platform). AMP provides access to electric vehicles at affordable housing in underserved communities to reduce barriers to transportation options and EV adoption. Charlotte is one of just 13 cities nationwide and the only city in the Southeast selected to receive grant funding through the national community carshare pilot. The program is a collaboration between the City of Charlotte, the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE), Centralina Clean Fuels Coalition, Ascent Housing, Envision Charlotte, and DreamKey Partners. It's part of the national AMP, a Community Car Share pilot developed by Forth to increase clean transportation options in underserved communities. Charlotte is the only city in the Southeast selected for the pilot and one of just 13 nationwide. The program will maintain, charge and manage vehicles to ensure long-term usability and affordability. Program planning and implementation included meetings with project partners and the electric utility; researching alternatives and travelling to host sites; coordinating and negotiating with lessees on City property to agree to being a carshare host; and reviewing and revising site host agreements. \nIn 2024, design and construction of EV charging infrastructure began. Construction of infrastructure was complete in October of 2024 at the first location, Peppertree Apartments, located in the Albemarle Road/Central Avenue Corridor of Opportunity. The affordable housing complex recently underwent $8 million in renovations to preserve affordability. This is the first of three activations for Carolina Carshare. column17: The Climate and Climate Change Scientific Council (CCSC) has been established. The council aims to support the achievement of goals and the effective implementation of sustainable energy and climate policies, as well as to reduce vulnerabilities and climate risks addressed in the \'Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan of Sofia Municipality 2021-2030\' (SECAP) and the \'Climate Change Adaptation Strategy of Sofia Municipality.\' Through an integrated approach, the CCSC brings together the efforts of universities, research institutions, and local authorities for research and action in the field of climate. Universities collaborate with the city to conduct research on renewable energy and public health impacts of climate change. Policies are informed by academic research. Sofia Municipality actively collaborates with research institutions to address climate change and improve environmental quality. Key projects include a study on the urban heat island effect conducted with researchers from Sofia University \'St. Kliment Ohridski\' in 2019, which led to increased greening efforts and improved air quality. In 2021, a study on solar energy potential analyzed the roofs of 880 municipal buildings, identifying 38 buildings suitable for photovoltaic installations. The \'Solar Cities\' project was also implemented, analyzing the solar potential of 5,784 buildings through photogrammetric surveys and an integrated GIS database. Additionally, a climate adaptation plan for the \'Lyulin\' district was developed using a digital twin and advanced geospatial technologies, providing simulations and modeling of climate risks up to 2050. A pilot project for remote ecological monitoring using drones is underway, offering rapid and precise information on air quality and pollutant concentrations.

The City of Ljubljana is actively involved and proactively contributes to important climate topics and issues, engaging in ongoing public dialogue and debate at the national level (e.g., preparation of new legislation) regarding climate-related matters such as the Energy Act, National Energy and Climate Plan, Climate Law of the Republic of Slovenia, Adaptation Strategy of the Republic of Slovenia (in preparation), which set requirements in regard to emission targets and emission inventories as well as climate action plans, etc. 

Given that Ljubljana is the capital city, with specificities that strongly impact national policies, such as transport, the city participated in bilateral meetings with the national government in 2023-2024 to address challenges and find solutions for transitional transport, with the aim of correctly highlighting it within the National Energy and Climate Plan (NEPN). Ljubljana is also involved in all significant projects, such as the construction of the main railway station or roads, forestry, etc. that fall under the state's domain but are located within the city, and are among other subject to assessment for compliance with the 'Do No Significant Harm' (DNSH) principle and climate screening.

As part of the preparation of the Climate City Contract (CCC), the city signed with the Ministry of Environment, Climate, and Energy of the Republic of Slovenia the Agreement on Co-financing needed studies (development of a Climate investment plan and a Study on identifying city vegetation and developing scenarios to mitigate the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect.

City Ljubljana is an active member of the largest community of municipalities, the Association of Urban Municipalities of Slovenia, which is an interest group at the national level, representing the interests of municipalities at the national and international level. An important program at the national level is an instrument for the implementation of integrated territorial investments (Integrated territorial investment - ITI), with which the MOL can apply for European Union funds within the objectives of the Operational Program for the Implementation of European Cohesion Policy. Energy consultancy 'ENSVET' - EKO SKLAD - Independent energy consultants of the ENSVET - EKO SKLAD network offer individual advice to interested citizens free of charge on energy rehabilitation of buildings or energy design of new constructions, thermal protection of the external thermal envelope of buildings, the possibility of obtaining grants and credits from the EKO Fund for EE and the use of RES.

Ljubljana tourism is included in the Green Scheme of Slovenian tourism. It is a national tool for introducing sustainable tourism into the operations of destinations and tourism companies operating under the Slovenia Green umbrella brand. The scheme is both a tool for assessing and improving sustainable performance.

The City of Ljubljana also actively applies green public procurement in compliance with the Public Procurement Act (ZJN-3) and Decree on Green Public Procurement of the Republic of Slovenia. These regulations ensure that environmental considerations are integrated into purchasing decisions, contributing to sustainable development goals and supporting the transition to a low-carbon economy. Green public procurement is a key tool to promote environmentally friendly products and services, align with national sustainability policies, and reduce overall environmental impact.

The City of Ljubljana is actively collaborating with the Regional Development Agency of Ljubljana Urban Region (RRA LUR) to address various climate-related and developmental challenges, particularly in the areas of sustainable urban mobility, energy, green infrastructure, and regional economic development.

column17: Auckland Council has led the development of climate actions across the region in collaboration with central government, business, public sector, communities and Aucklanders. Auckland Council leads the co-development of the Auckland Plan, a 30 year strategy to deliver on its vision to be a world class city. Auckland Council actively engages and collaborates with key business stakeholders to ensure the effective development and implementation of diverse sustainability issues and projects. It provides a platform on which Council can engage organisations, citizens and businesses toward achieving a liveable and low carbon future. In 2014 Auckland Council established a dedicated strategic partnerships programme to grow collaboration and investment for Auckland between council and business, Philanthropists, public funders and individuals to realise Auckland's potential. Our aim is to build long term values based relationships with a family of key partners to achieve Auckland's vision. Council also maintains strategic partnerships with the business sector via its memberships with the Sustainable Business Network and Sustainable Business Council. These organisations bring together the business community to create a sustainable future for business society and the environment. Council engages and collaborates with key business partners to co-design co-develop and co-fund targeted initiatives. During the development of Te Tārukeā-Tāwhiri: Auckland's Climate Plan, adopted in 2020, there has been extensive collaboration with stakeholders and partners to develop the key moves within the plan. Auckland council staff also contributed to national adaption plan.

Goyang City's 'Climate Crisis Emergency Action' (hereinafter referred to as the Goyang Emergency Action), in which 25 organizations - including civil society groups, religious groups, and educational groups - participate, was launched with a ceremony on November 11, 2020, to encourage interest and active participation among Goyang City citizens. The initiative aims to make Goyang City carbon-neutral by 2050. In a declaration, the participants said that in order to respond to the climate crisis, we must change the lifestyle of mass production, consumption, and disposal, stop development and resource destruction, and shift towards renewable energy. To do this, Goyang City is establishing and implementing fundamental and systematic GHG reduction policies, and the city council is actively cooperating in establishing an institutional foundation and climate-related budget based on this. Civil society also declared that it would expand action on the climate crisis to citizens through practical activities such as publicity and education, and take an active role in bringing about practical change.
We also launched a campaign and education program to change public perception about climate change and promote citizens' climate action. In 2020, we founded the Citizens' Action Coalition for Climate Neutrality to promote civic action. Initially, about 7,000 people joined in 2020, and now about 15,000 people have joined our coalition. As the coalition grew larger, we enacted an ordinance last year to support them financially. We also conducted educational work on climate change by age group. Over the past two years, about 5,400 people have participated in our program.

2. In September 2023, Goyang City established the Carbon Neutrality Support Center, a specialized institution responsible for promoting energy transition, developing and disseminating transition models, and supporting the formulation of basic plans for carbon neutrality. The center operates various educational programs in collaboration with civic groups and related organizations. 
Major programs conducted in 2024 include “Goyang Citizen Carbon Neutrality Forum', 'Upcycling Education for Discarded Toys', and 'Drawing a Heat Map in Our Village' etc.

In May 2023, Goyang City and SCG Lab signed a business agreement to convert carbon-neutral points into GasApp Cash so that users can pay for heating bills with carbon-neutral points. 

Carbon neutral point energy is a system that reduces electricity, water supply, and city gas consumption and grants carbon neutral points according to the reduction rate.

In particular, by converting the points earned through the carbon-neutral point energy system into gas app cash, you can receive a discount when paying your city gas bill or directly withdraw cash by combining it with the cache collected from the existing gas app.

In addition, CSG Lab has decided to provide specialized contents such as citizen welfare policies and systems customized for Goyang citizens using the Gas App personalized home screen, and eco-friendly and saving contents unique to Gas App in cooperation with Goyang City.

In addition, GasApp provides energy smart management solutions such as energy usage prediction to support Goyang citizens' convenient energy saving activities. Through this, Goyang citizens are expected to reduce energy usage effectively by accurately predicting and adjusting individual energy usage, while maximizing discounts on city gas bills through carbon neutrality points.

Under the vision of “Goyang—A Leading City in Overcoming the Climate Crisis Where Citizens Are Happy,” the plan sets out sector-specific strategies for the next ten years. Based on these strategies, in 2024 the City implemented a total of 34 action tasks across 15 strategies in seven sectors.

AMC has initiated 'Green Yellow Blue (GYB) Scheme' to promote urban greening, renewable energy, and rainwater conservation. AMC under 'Catch the Rain Campaign' is promoting implementation of rainwater harvesting/ groundwater recharge systems through public participation. Under the campaign, AMC is providing 80% of capital cost for implementing rainwater harvesting/ groundwater recharge systems while 20% of capital cost to be bear by local community.

AMC has also removed AMC's Vehicle Tax for procurement of electric vehicles by community (0% AMC Vehicle Tax for electric vehicles).

The city has held a variety of broad stakeholder engagement activities, many of which included mention of environmental, sustainability, and resilience concepts, but none of which were solely focused on climate change. 

This includes a residential compost collection pilot which has diverted more than 300,000 pounds of organics from the landfill as of July 2025, and a host of public events organized by the city to gather public input in various planning efforts, including the East Bank. 

The East Bank Development was born out of a two-year community visioning process led by the Nashville Planning Department called Imagine East Bank. The process included some of Metro's most robust community engagement efforts since NashvilleNext and resulted in a vision plan built off the ideas of Nashville's residents.

The Metro Nashville Planning Department expanded the Downtown Code (DTC) to include a new, 30-acre subdistrict for the East Bank. The East Bank will be a high density, multimodal, mixed use area that incorporates green space and respects its location in/ near the floodplain. Shifting a blighted industrial area into a vibrant community will have a number of salutary impacts. These include remediation of brownfields to beneficial uses, dense, mixed-use development providing affordable housing and the ability to move without a car, increased greenspace to assist with flood mitigation and resilience, and more.

Mayor O'Connell is committed to creating a modern transportation system that reduces Nashvillians' transportation costs and helps them get where they need to go. To support this work, Mayor O'Connell pursued and secured a dedicated funding source for transportation and mobility projects in November 2024. Metro activities supporting this initiative are collectively referred to as Choose How You Move - An All-Access Pass to Sidewalks, Signals, Service, and Safety in Nashville.

For the majority of February and March 2024, Mayor O'Connell sought public input, feedback from Metro Council Members, and worked with two advisory committees to craft a plan that works for Nashville. After that period of ongoing engagement, Mayor O'Connell unveiled a plan and continued the citywide conversation with Nashvillians about how we make our city easier to move around.

Mayor O'Connell is moving with urgency to addresses Nashville's transportation and mobility problems, but studying how to improve transit in Nashville is not new.

There are over 70 neighborhood, community, citywide, and regional plans created over the last 15 years that support expanded and enhanced transportation and mobility infrastructure. Choose How You Move draws on them all. 

This, combined with a robust public outreach effort throughout 2024, has laid a strong foundation for community involvement in establishing a transit system that works for everyone.

Since the transportation sector comprises the majority of Nashville/ Davidson county's greenhouse gas emissions, this effort is intimately connected to our climate mitigation goals.

In 2024, the City received $50,000 to administer a Youth Climate Action Fund that provided 8, $5,000 grants to youth (aged 15-24) and youth-serving organizations to fund youth-led projects: 

1.	Allentown School District: Building 21 High School Green Basketball Court
This project will create a lightly colored basketball court on the lower parking lot at Building 21 High School to reduce the Urban Heat Island effect. The initiative includes a community cleanup day, pavement repairs, court painting, and the installation of portable basketball hoops and educational signage.

2.	Allentown School District: Sheridan Garden Revamp: A Collaborative, Student-Led Community Transformation
This project aims to revitalize the Sheridan Elementary Garden with new flower beds, a mural, and a Zen space. It involves collaboration between high school students and local youth leaders to enhance the garden's functionality and beauty.

3.	Cohesion Network: Seeds of Change: Exploring Food Systems for Our Future
'Seeds of Change' tackles food insecurity by exploring sustainable food systems in a local food desert. The project includes research, community engagement, and a block party to distribute fresh produce. A documentary will be produced to raise awareness about food access and sustainability.

4.	Executive Education Academy Charter School: EEACS Community Garden
This project will create a sustainable community garden managed by high school students. The garden will provide fresh produce to a local soup kitchen and the school cafeteria, promoting environmental stewardship and healthy eating among students.

5.	Fine Feather Foundation: Later is Too Late: Climate Change Awareness Mural
A group of 15-25 students will design and paint a mural titled 'Later is Too Late - Climate Change Awareness' to highlight the urgency of addressing climate change and its interconnected impacts.

6.	Movement Moves Media: Planet Pulse: City Solutions
This project will produce social media content to raise awareness about urban sustainability solutions. Young participants will lead interviews, create and edit content, and manage sponsored ads to engage the community in environmental responsibility.

7.	Muhlenberg College: Tree Education and Stewardship Curriculum
Muhlenberg College students will develop a four-week climate curriculum focused on tree science for fifth-grade students at Muhlenberg Elementary. The program will culminate in a tree-planting festival, fostering environmental stewardship and climate action among young students.

8.	Valley Youth House: Silky Garden Space
This project will host garden workshops and storytelling events centered on environmental sustainability for youth and young adults. The events will feature plays, poems, and stories to raise awareness about climate change and offer a platform for youth to share their experiences.

Turku implements continuous open climate action where the Turku City Group is constantly planning, implementing and monitoring climate measures. Collective climate action is actively open to climate measures of businesses and communities, involvement by citizens, and development of new solutions in collaboration.

Turku has invited companies and other operators in the region to sign their own climate commitments as part of the Climate City Contract. By signing the commitment, Turku's climate partners declare that they are committed not only to realising the Carbon-neutral Turku 2029 goal and reducing emissions, but also to communicating about climate actions in their organisation, setting an example for climate work and participating in the activities of the Turku Climate Team. The implementing parties and signatories of the Turku Climate City Contract include local higher education institutions, local companies, such as Bayer Turku and Meyer Turku, and other partners, such as the Wellbeing Services County of Southwest Finland (Varha) and the Turku and Kaarina Parish Union.

Businesses and communities are encouraged to join collective climate action through their own climate measures. These are gathered and shared on a platform on the climate-themed Carbon Neutral Turku webpages. Turku Climate Team is a strong network that serves communities and businesses, implements and communicates climate, circular economy and nature measures and advances resource wisdom. More information and the member organizations can be found here: https://www.turku.fi/en/city-climate-and-nature/climate-work-companies.

Examples of climate-friendly new business can be found in Turku's top sectors: The maritime industry and the pharmaceutical industry. These include the concept of a carbon-neutral cruise ship and carbon-neutral pharmaceutical production facilities among others.

Collaboration with residents and NGOs is crucial. It is important to gain support and cooperation. The action of local governments, non-governmental organizations, entrepreneurs and residents of large metropolises in the area of reducing current emissions is a prerequisite for achieving climate goals that will limit the degradation of the natural environment. These goals are unequivocally supported by Krakow, which strives to achieve climate neutrality in the shortest possible time, under the conditions of a just transition.
The city consults its activities, including pro-climate ones, with residents and NGOs. In 2022, a total of 46 public consultations were carried out, of which 28 were attended by residents, and the remaining 18 consultation processes were conducted only among NGOs, in which 360 organizations participated.
In 2021, a citizens' assembly was held on climate protection, energy efficiency and the use of renewable energy. It resulted with 32 binding recommendations. The most important one concerns the preparation of the Krakow Climate Strategy by the end of 2022, presenting a plan to achieve climate neutrality, assuming at least a 30% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 compared to 2018, at least 80% emission reduction by 2040 and achieving climate neutrality no later than 2050.
In February 2023, at Wielopole 17a Street, in the building of the City of Krakow, the Krakow Center for Climate Education was opened. A place that was created to increase the climate awareness of Krakow residents of all ages. The center was established on the initiative of residents who participated in the first Krakow Climate Panel. They proposed its creation as part of one of the 32 recommendations developed during its work. The mission of the Center is to educate, inspire action and establish cooperation for Krakow in a good climate.
The center shows pro-climate solutions and supports residents in everyday activities for the climate. The space of the Center was created with the environment in mind. Decisions made during the preparation and adaptation of the rooms and their equipment were made taking into account their impact on the environment, hence the use of natural materials, filling the room with plants and applying solutions that reduce water and energy consumption.
The space of the Center is a shared space and is made available to organizations and institutions that want to carry out activities in its interiors aimed at increasing the knowledge and climate awareness of the inhabitants of our city. There are more and more institutions and NGOs that carry out their pro-climate activities in the city centre.

The “Pact for Climate' is a city initiative launched in 2022. Its goal is to increase the involvement of entrepreneurs, public institutions, social organizations and scientific communities operating in Krakow to achieve climate neutrality and counteract climate change. For years, Krakow has been consistently implementing actions aimed at achieving this goal, implementing sectoral programs in various areas, e.g. in terms of increasing the use of energy from renewable sources, energy efficiency or transport accessibility. In order to meet this challenge, Kraków also invites external partners to cooperate. In May 2023 the 'Pact for Climate' was signed by first 11 participants, than in 2024 and 2025 another 8 joined. Among those cooperating in Pact are: ASTOR, AstraZeneca Pharma Poland, BP, BWI Group, Columbus Energy, CH2M Polska Services (Jacobs), CRIF, HSBC, InPost, Intellias Poland, Leviathan Confederation, Krakow Technology Park, Regional Expert Center, Shell Business Operations Krakow, SIG, Krakow University of Economics, Krakow University of Agriculture, Krakow University of Phisical Culture.The partners declare to take action to limit global warming, develop a climate strategy and undertake to inform the city annually about the activities carried out in line with the ideas of the pact. The 'Pact for Climate' is also an exchange of experience between partners involved in climate action, the promotion of pro-climate solutions, and ultimately also the reduction of emissions. Signing the document is a strong declaration of support for the city's efforts to become climate neutral.
Other pro-climate activities realized together with business:
- Construction of a new tramway line to Mistrzejowice, big investments carried out in the public-private partnership formula. Cost is circa EUR 240 M) The new, approximately 4.5-kilometre-long line of the Krakow Fast Tram (KST stage IV) will shortening the travel time to the city center by approximately 12 minutes. It will also allow to change from private cars for electric public transportation. Passengers will use the connection in 2025. This is the first such large transport project in Poland implemented in the public-private partnership (PPP) formula. 
- Modernization of public lighting 
- Smart EPC project. Smart EPC is a project co-financed by the HORIZON 2020 program, which is implemented in cooperation with several European cities. Its coordinator is Croatia, and partners: Spain, France, Poland, Belgium. Krakow is a partner in the project and at the same time acts as a pilot, as a city that has committed itself to replacing street lighting with energy-saving one, based on the standards developed within the project. The main objective of the project is the possibility of replacing street lighting in the EPC standard - the ESCO company will be responsible for it, whose remuneration will be the generated electricity savings. The project plans to test the following activities:- execution of external light sensors for dynamic dimming/brightening of luminaires in relation to lighting from external sources, e.g. illuminated advertising, building displays,- implementation of additional services such as e-chargers,- communication with luminaires through the monitoring and control system,- implementation of a dynamic system for controlling and monitoring the operation of luminaires, enabling dynamic control of luminaires, collecting data on failures,- implementation of additional services in the form of data transmission infrastructure (considered).
- Continuous cooperation with business environment institutions and business associating organizations: Chamber of Industry and Commerce, ABSL, Lewiatan, Małopolska Chamber of Craft and Entrepreneurship, Małopolska Regional Development Agency

The EcoZonas project, conducted by the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the Wuppertal Institute in coordination with IMPLAN Hermosillo, focuses on implementing a pilot project in La Metalera, a neighborhood in Hermosillo highly vulnerable to climate and social challenges. The project aims to develop and strengthen participatory, inclusive, and replicable climate action methods at the community level, demonstrating the viability of resilient, low-carbon, low-cost, and easily replicable urban solutions.
EcoZonas addresses this vulnerability by identifying how local climate change impacts affect La Metalera residents. It empowers the community to propose mitigation and adaptation solutions through a bottom-up, participatory process.
The project in Hermosillo has three main components:

Developing a participatory planning process and implementing low-cost actions
Creating a diagnostic methodology and tool
Strengthening capacities and ensuring replicability

La Metalera is engaged in a participatory process to identify climate risks and potential short-, medium-, and long-term solutions. A digital community mapping tool is being developed to assess four key dimensions: 1) urban environment, 2) disaster risk, 3) environmental quality, and 4) socioeconomic well-being. This approach enables the community to identify and prioritize climate vulnerabilities, collaboratively implement low-cost interventions, and develop a long-term action plan to enhance the neighborhood's resilience.

Evidence: https://es.wri.org/proyectos/ecozonas

Biciclando, a winning project in the 2021 Global Mayors Challenge, was implemented over three years with funding and technical support from Bloomberg Philanthropies. Focused on gender-mainstreaming, recycling, and sustainable mobility, it aims to drive a paradigm shift addressing these challenges:

• Hermosillo recycles less than 2% of its waste.
• Pandemic-related job losses have impacted two women for every man.
• Motorized vehicles produce 35% of local GHG emissions.
• Only 15% of cyclists in Hermosillo are women.
• About 70% of women in Hermosillo perceive public spaces as unsafe.

The project comprises three initiatives:

• Circular Economy Centers (CECs): Social entrepreneurship hubs promoting gender-sensitive, circular-economy-based entrepreneurship, serving as operational centers for Biciclando.
• Biciclando Service: A waste-collection and recycling platform (app) connecting communities with women, known as “bicicladoras” (often in vulnerable socioeconomic conditions), who use electro-assisted cargo bikes to provide free services.
• Cycling Infrastructure: Developed to enhance connectivity between communities and CECs, promoting sustainable mobility, particularly for women.

Supported by a robust stakeholder ecosystem, including local and national companies like CINEMEX, DECSSON WELDING, and Parque LA RUINA, as well as social collectives focused on sustainable mobility, feminist causes, and public institutions addressing women's issues, sustainable development, and public security. It operates with the support of the local ONG 'Caminantes del Desierto A.C.'.

Biciclando will be implemented over three years with support from Bloomberg Philanthropies. Expected benefits include:

• Construction of up to three Circular Economy Centers (CECs).
• Development of the Biciclando app.
• A zero-carbon emission fleet with up to 18 professional waste collectors (bicicladoras, 6 per CEC).
• Up to 70,000 direct beneficiaries (users).
• Up to 200,000 kg of collected recyclable waste per year, including cardboard, paper, and aluminum.

The waste collection service operates via a mobile app: Users open the Biciclando app, register recyclable waste for pick-up, and place a request. A bicicladora is notified, schedules the collection, and collects the sorted waste. Users earn points exchangeable for goods from sponsors. The bicicladora delivers the waste to a CEC for value-added activities or a recycling center, receiving payment. All transactions are tracked through the app, and the service is free.

Goals: Achieve a paradigm shift by addressing:
• 97% of waste currently collected by public services, with less than 2% recycled.
• 35% of local GHG emissions from motorized vehicles.
• Only 15% of cyclists being women, with 70% of women perceiving public spaces as unsafe.

Evidence: Bloomberg Cities - Hermosillo, Mexico (https://bloombergcities.jhu.edu/mayors-challenge/2022/hermosillo-mexico)

The City Council of Hermosillo, through the System for the Integral Development of the Family of Hermosillo, invites private assistance organizations and non-profit civil society organizations to participate in a financing program for the acquisition and installation of solar panels. The program aims to strengthen the social sector's role in addressing social issues responsibly. It provides in-kind support to reduce energy costs for civil society organizations that promote social inclusion of vulnerable groups and significant community causes.

The City Hall of Hermosillo, through the System for the Integral Development of the Family of Hermosillo, seeks to significantly increase the share of renewable energy sources, aligning with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda promoted by the United Nations General Assembly. This initiative is consistent with:

• Agenda 2030
• SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy
• Declaration of Venice
• Paris Agreement
• General Law on Climate Change
• Law for the Use of Renewable Energies and the Financing of the Energy Transition
• Energy Transition Law
• Law for the Promotion of Renewable Energies
• Climate Change Law of the State of Sonora

The program includes two types of support:

• Support Component 1: Solar Panels 
 A co-investment scheme providing up to 50% of the total value of the solar panel installation project, or up to $100,000.00 (one hundred thousand pesos 00/100 M.N.).

• Support Component 2: Energy Efficiency 
 Support of up to $50,000.00 (fifty thousand pesos 00/100 M.N.) for projects aimed at improving energy efficiency in the CSO building. This support does not require co-investment.

Promoción de la Economía Circular en Córdoba

Córdoba ha consolidado una estrategia integral de economía circular mediante políticas públicas, institucionalidad específica y redes colaborativas. Entre sus pilares destacan:
1- Escuela Municipal de Economía Circular (EMEC): espacio educativo que combina procesos productivos reales con contenidos pedagógicos, capacitando a miles de personas en compostaje, separación en origen, ecodiseño y reutilización.
2- Clúster de Economía Circular de Córdoba: red multisectorial que articula empresas, cooperativas, universidades y organismos públicos para fomentar innovación, colaboración y desarrollo de modelos circulares.
3- Cumbre Mundial de Economia Circular: A nivel internacional, Córdoba ha organizado cinco ediciones consecutivas de la Cumbre Mundial de Economía Circular, un evento que reúne a líderes globales, expertos, emprendedores, gobiernos locales y organismos multilaterales en torno a la construcción de ciudades circulares e inclusivas. Estas cumbres han fortalecido el posicionamiento internacional de Córdoba y han contribuido a consolidar una comunidad global de práctica, basada en el intercambio de conocimientos, buenas prácticas y experiencias transformadoras. La quinta edición (2025) se desarrolló en el marco de la Conferencia Latinoamericana de Cambio Climático, reafirmando el compromiso local con la transición ecológica justa. Pasaron más de 6000 personas durante los 3 días. 
4- Centro de Excelencia e Innovación en Tecnología para la Economía Circular (CEITTEC) de la OEA. Es el único de Argentina y de Latinoamérica especializado en la materia. El de Córdoba trabajará junto a los otros cinco de la red, también enfocados en diversas áreas: Chile (Inteligencia Artificial); Perú (Materiales Avanzados y Nanotecnología); México (Blockchain); Colombia (Inteligencia Artificial y Robótica); Panamá (Biotecnología).

Colaboración entre la Municipalidad de Córdoba y la Universidad Nacional de Córdoba en cambio climático, sostenibilidad y economía circular
La Municipalidad de Córdoba mantiene una sólida agenda de cooperación con la Universidad Nacional de Córdoba (UNC), articulando proyectos académicos, de investigación, extensión y prácticas profesionales con impacto directo en la acción climática, la sostenibilidad urbana y la economía circular. Esta alianza estratégica combina la capacidad técnica y científica de la UNC con los programas y necesidades de gestión municipal, potenciando la formación de estudiantes y el fortalecimiento de las políticas públicas locales.
Uno de los hitos recientes es el Ejercicio de Simulación de Olas de Calor en Pueblo Alberdi (FCS, FCEFyN y FCM, septiembre 2025), declarado de Interés Municipal. La iniciativa busca entrenar a la comunidad en la identificación de riesgos para la salud, diseñar protocolos de acción y consolidar redes de apoyo comunitario frente a emergencias climáticas, al mismo tiempo que capacita a estudiantes de medicina en triage y atención de casos vinculados al calor extremo.
En el campo de la educación ambiental y la biodiversidad, se desarrollan prácticas con la Facultad de Ciencias Exactas, Físicas y Naturales y el Profesorado en Ciencias Biológicas, que realizan actividades de capacitación y extensión en el Parque de la Biodiversidad y en el Jardín Botánico. Estas experiencias acercan a estudiantes a la práctica docente y generan instancias de sensibilización ciudadana sobre la importancia de los ecosistemas urbanos.
La Facultad de Ciencias Agropecuarias participa activamente en proyectos de floricultura y jardinería sustentable, consolidando espacios de formación en el Jardín Botánico y promoviendo unidades productivas de plantas ornamentales con criterios sostenibles. Además, en conjunto con la Municipalidad, lleva adelante un relevamiento integral del arbolado público de Córdoba, fundamental para la planificación de la forestación y la mejora de la calidad ambiental urbana.
La cooperación también alcanza a otras áreas clave: la Facultad de Odontología incorporó mobiliario sustentable diseñado en la Escuela de Economía Circular para sus espacios académicos; la Facultad de Derecho y Ciencias Sociales facilita la inserción de estudiantes avanzados en dependencias municipales a través de prácticas jurídicas; y la Facultad de Filosofía y Humanidades desarrolla instancias de prácticas profesionales supervisadas y proyectos conjuntos en el campo educativo, científico y formativo.
En materia de economía circular y políticas ambientales, la UNC y la Municipalidad han firmado convenios que abarcan desde la recolección y gestión responsable de pilas y baterías, hasta el desarrollo de investigaciones sobre cadenas de valor, transferencia tecnológica, capacitación en sostenibilidad, proyectos con rumiantes menores y el impulso a iniciativas de innovación vinculadas al Clúster de Economía Circular.
La articulación se extiende además a posgrados y becas: el Acuerdo con la Facultad de Ciencias Sociales destina cupos de formación en la Maestría en Administración Pública para colaboradores del Ente Municipal BioCórdoba, fortaleciendo capacidades institucionales en clave de sostenibilidad.
En conjunto, estas acciones reflejan una alianza integral y de largo plazo entre la UNC y la Municipalidad de Córdoba, con vigencia en múltiples facultades, institutos y secretarías. Los proyectos abarcan desde la gestión de la biodiversidad y la educación ambiental, hasta la economía circular, la resiliencia urbana y la formación profesional.
De esta manera, Córdoba avanza hacia un modelo de ciudad sostenible y resiliente, donde la universidad y el Estado trabajan en conjunto para enfrentar el cambio climático, fortalecer la justicia socioambiental y promover una cultura ciudadana comprometida con el cuidado de la casa común.

La Provincia de Córdoba se posiciona como la cuarta mayor consumidora de electricidad del país, con 10.684 GWh en 2023, representando un 7,78 % del total nacional. El consumo se distribuye entre el sector residencial (43,2 %), no residencial menor a 300 kW (34,5 %), no residencial mayor a 300 kW (16,6 %) y grandes usuarios del Mercado Eléctrico Mayorista (5,8 %). En términos sectoriales, las viviendas consumen el 40 %, la industria, comercio y servicios el 53 % y el alumbrado público el 7 %. La matriz energética de la provincia se sustenta principalmente en combustibles fósiles (70 % gas natural, 30 % gasoil), con una participación menor de energía nuclear (8 %), importaciones (3 %) y energías renovables (34 %), que incluyen hidráulica, solar, eólica y biomasa.
En este contexto, la ciudad y la provincia han promovido una amplia colaboración intersectorial entre organismos públicos, empresas, instituciones académicas y la sociedad civil, para fomentar la eficiencia energética, la generación de energías limpias y la reducción de emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero.
Edificios públicos y energía renovable:
El Palacio Municipal “6 de Julio” fue equipado en 2019 con 400 paneles solares que abastecen la demanda diurna de las oficinas, mientras que el nuevo edificio del Concejo Deliberante se diseñó con criterios de eficiencia energética, ventilación cruzada, paneles solares y suelo permeable. La integración de la Plaza de la Palabra, con bosque nativo y luminarias LED, demuestra la coordinación entre planificación urbana, arquitectura sostenible y gestión ambiental municipal.
Instituto de Transformación Energética Córdoba (ITEC):
Impulsado por BioCórdoba y la Municipalidad, el ITEC articula actores públicos, privados, académicos y comunitarios para liderar la transición energética local. Sus acciones incluyen formación en eficiencia energética, instalación de energías renovables en espacios públicos y asesoramiento técnico a instituciones y comercios, promoviendo políticas públicas, generación distribuida y tecnologías limpias.
Producción de energía renovable a partir de residuos:
La planta de biogás en la EDAR Bajo Grande, inaugurada en 2023, convierte metano de efluentes cloacales en electricidad, abasteciendo trolebuses y cargadores de vehículos eléctricos. Este proyecto, desarrollado en conjunto por la provincia, la municipalidad, EPEC y TAMSE, representa una solución de economía circular que combina gestión de residuos, reducción de emisiones y electrificación del transporte urbano. De manera complementaria, en el Complejo Ambiental Piedras Blancas, Córdoba avanza en un proyecto de recuperación de biogás de residuos sólidos urbanos, en colaboración con CORMECOR y EPEC, para generar 3,2 MW de electricidad destinada a 20.000 personas, con potencial de expansión.
Alumbrado público y eficiencia energética:
La modernización del sistema de alumbrado incluye 82.830 luminarias LED y la implementación de telegestión, permitiendo control remoto, detección de fallas y optimización del consumo energético. Estas acciones se desarrollan en coordinación con TAMSE y forman parte del Plan 20.000 LED y del programa provincial Rutas Seguras, priorizando calles de mayor tránsito y espacios urbanos estratégicos.
Cambios en el consumo residencial:
En colaboración con EPEC, se instalan medidores inteligentes que permiten a los usuarios conocer su consumo por horario y acceder a tarifas diferenciadas. Para 2030 se proyecta que el 85 % de los kWh distribuidos sean facturados mediante medición inteligente, promoviendo autorregulación y hábitos de consumo eficientes.
Proyectos a futuro:
El Ente Metropolitano Córdoba impulsa un parque fotovoltaico de 50 MW que abastecerá alumbrado público de 25 municipios, en coordinación con EPEC y la CAF, generando ahorro de hasta 4 millones de dólares anuales y reduciendo entre un 20 % y 25 % los costos energéticos. Además, se promueven mejoras de eficiencia energética en viviendas, especialmente de bajos ingresos, mediante electrodomésticos eficientes, aislamiento térmico y calefones solares, apoyadas por microcréditos y capacitación comunitaria.
Gestión edilicia y etiquetado de sustentabilidad:
Se implementa el Programa Nacional de Etiquetado de Viviendas (PRONEV) y el protocolo de “Etiquetación de Sustentabilidad Edilicia” del Colegio de Arquitectos de Córdoba, evaluando eficiencia energética, consumo de agua, uso de materiales y confort ambiental. Las viviendas con mejor desempeño energético pueden recibir beneficios fiscales, incentivando la reducción de emisiones de CO2.
Generación distribuida y estaciones solares públicas:
La Municipalidad fomenta la generación distribuida mediante paneles fotovoltaicos, eólicos y de biomasa, con incentivos financieros y asistencia técnica. Se proyecta instalar 15 estaciones solares en plazas y parques, que ofrecerán agua caliente, recarga de celulares, wifi y potencial para vehículos eléctricos, combinando educación ambiental y energía limpia.

Córdoba ha desarrollado un modelo integral de gestión de residuos basado en la separación en origen y la recolección diferenciada, pilares de su estrategia de economía circular. Los hogares separan los residuos secos —papel y cartón, plásticos, metales, vidrios, telas y tetrabrik— que luego son recolectados en días específicos y enviados a los Centros Verdes. Estos centros, distribuidos estratégicamente en la ciudad (CV Sur, Norte, Centro, Ecofem, Este y Telas), clasifican y acondicionan los materiales para su comercialización y reinserción en circuitos productivos mediante cooperativas de reciclado. En 2019 recuperaron cerca de 4.000 toneladas de residuos, superando ampliamente las metas proyectadas para 2023. Además de su impacto ambiental, la formalización de los ecorrecolectores como cooperativistas con monotributo social, jornada regulada, obra social y aportes jubilatorios ha mejorado su calidad de vida.
Los Centros de Transferencia de Residuos (CTR), como Rancagua y Villa Unión, permiten el acopio y clasificación de residuos voluminosos, restos de obra, chatarras, neumáticos fuera de uso (NFU), residuos verdes y electrónicos. Estos materiales son derivados a plantas de reciclaje o tratamiento especializado, evitando su disposición en rellenos sanitarios y fortaleciendo la economía circular.
El Complejo Ambiental Piedras Blancas, gestionado por CORMECOR, concentra el tratamiento y disposición final de residuos de la ciudad y municipios cercanos. Combina disposición técnica de residuos no reciclables en celdas de seguridad con derivación de materiales reciclables o con valorización energética. Cuenta con monitoreo ambiental para controlar lixiviados, emisiones y calidad del aire, e incluye trituración de NFU, clasificación de residuos verdes y voluminosos y compostaje. Dentro del complejo funciona el Parque de Economía Circular, un modelo pionero que transforma residuos urbanos en recursos útiles, reduciendo el volumen destinado a disposición final.
El Parque alberga plantas y programas específicos: la Planta de Combustibles Derivados de Residuos - Geocycle convierte residuos no reciclables en combustibles alternativos para hornos cementeros, evitando emisiones equivalentes a 25 toneladas de GEI anuales y conservando aproximadamente 11.000 hectáreas de bosque. La Planta de Neumáticos Fuera de Uso - CONTRINI procesa NFU, previniendo enfermedades y reduciendo el uso de combustibles fósiles; los neumáticos se transforman en combustibles alternativos o se recuperan materiales como caucho, acero y textil para fabricar pisos amortiguados, bloques y asfaltos modificados. En 2024, se recuperaron cerca de 2.000 toneladas de NFU mediante rutas específicas y CTR.
El programa Sacate las Pilas, iniciado en 2021, ha recolectado más de 331.400 pilas y baterías, procesadas para reintegrar materiales al ciclo productivo. En 2022, Córdoba recuperó 50,13 toneladas de Residuos de Aparatos Eléctricos y Electrónicos (RAEE), reintegrando cobre, hierro, aluminio y plásticos y evitando impactos ambientales. La recuperación de aceite vegetal usado (AVU) se realiza a través de más de 400 puntos de acopio, produciendo biocombustibles y materiales sostenibles. La Planta de Restos Verdes procesó en 2023 unas 4.400 toneladas de restos de poda y desmalezamiento, generando leña social, chips de madera y mejoradores de suelo.
Para apoyar la gestión de residuos orgánicos, INTI elaboró en 2025 una guía técnica de compostaje urbano, dirigida a municipios, cooperativas y técnicos ambientales, con recomendaciones operativas y fichas de seguimiento.
El Instituto de Protección Ambiental y Animal (IPAA), creado en 2021, depende de la Secretaría de Gestión Ambiental y Sostenibilidad y se enfoca en fiscalización ambiental, bienestar animal y evaluación de impacto ambiental. Supervisa residuos sólidos y peligrosos, controla contaminación del agua, aire y suelo, y coordina acciones de cuidado animal, incluyendo castraciones, mediante la Patrulla Ambiental y plataformas digitales para trazabilidad y transparencia.
En 2019, la ciudad contaba con 100 macrobasurales y 400 microbasurales, generados por la falta de alternativas de disposición. Se implementan acciones de ordenamiento mediante relevamientos, creación de CTR y sanciones más severas, incluyendo denuncias penales y un Fondo de Recuperación Ambiental financiado por multas.
La ordenanza N° 12.648 establece la categoría de Grandes Generadores de RSU, quienes deben inscribirse, separar residuos en fracciones secas y húmedas, contratar servicios habilitados y elaborar planes de gestión. Actualmente Córdoba cuenta con 1.900 grandes generadores, responsables de 82.000 toneladas anuales de residuos. Se promueve además la inscripción de operadores y transportistas de la economía circular y la implementación de plantas de lombricompostaje para residuos orgánicos de comercios gastronómicos, consolidando un modelo integral de gestión, inclusión social y economía circular.

column17: El proyecto 100% Renovable (100% ER) es una iniciativa llevada adelante por el ICLEI y financiada por International Climate Initiative (IKI), del Ministerio Federal de Medio Ambiente, Protección de la Naturaleza y Seguridad Nuclear de Alemania (BMU), con el fin de apoyar a Rosario y a otras ciudades, para el desarrollo de una hoja de ruta para lograr el 100% de las energías renovables al 2050 en el territorio. Se trata de contribuir al cumplimiento de los objetivos climáticos y energéticos nacionales a través de las Contribuciones Nacionales Determinadas (NDC), mejorar la seguridad y eficiencia energética y la creación de empleo, teniendo en consideración a los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible (ODS). Esta iniciativa aborda la gobernanza multinivel y coloca esta colaboración en el centro de la transición energética sostenible y su implementación de forma efectiva en diferentes acciones climáticas. Este proceso se desarrolló desde 2019 hasta 2024, y se llevó a cabo de manera participativa en el marco de un grupo de trabajo local, del cual interactuaron diversas áreas municipales y organizaciones de los sectores privado y académico. La Hoja de Ruta se finalizó en 2024 y se encuentra publicada. Otra de las actuaciones se realiza a través del programa Cities Forward o Ciudades en Movimiento, que constituye una asociación de colaboración entre ICLEI, Resilient Cities Catalyst y el Instituto de las Américas, con el apoyo del Departamento de Estado de EE.UU. Dicho programa ofrece intercambio entre pares para el desarrollo de capacidades, implementación de proyectos que resuelvan desafíos urbanos críticos en torno a la sostenibilidad, la inclusión y la resiliencia, entre otros fines. Rosario es la única ciudad de Argentina elegida en este programa, y participa con el proyecto “Adaptación y Descarbonización en pequeñas y medianas empresas (pymes) de la ciudad de Rosario”, y busca fortalecer la capacidad de las mismas para adaptarse y ser resilientes frente a los riesgos climáticos y reducir sus emisiones de GEI. Para ello, trabaja con el horizonte 2035 para lograr que se sumen la mayor cantidad de empresas de distintos sectores y rubros, se integren al Programa Buenas Prácticas Ambientales. Se prevé que, a partir de un diagnóstico de riesgos, vulnerabilidades e impactos, así como de la medición de la huella de carbono, se elaboren planes de mitigación, adaptación y resiliencia climática, derivando en el reconocimiento y entrega de Sello Verde, haciéndolas más resilientes y promoviendo la descarbonización, en alineación con las metas del Plan Local de Acción Climática (PLAC) 2030. Otra de las intervenciones a mencionar, es el Proyecto de Edificios Municipales Energéticamente Sustentables, financiado por la Unión Europea y otros organismos internacionales de cooperación, conjuntamente con un consorcio conformado por la Universidad Nacional de La Plata, la Red Argentina de Municipios frente al Cambio Climático (RAMCC) y el Centro de Eficiencia Energética de Copenhague de la Universidad Técnica de Dinamarca. Esta iniciativa en 2024 comenzó con trabajos de aislamiento térmico en el edificio municipal de Distrito Centro para mejorar la eficiencia energética, reducir el consumo energético, mejorar el confort térmico y contribuir a las políticas locales de sustentabilidad. Dicho proyecto se enmarca en las acciones que se llevan adelante en el Plan de Gestión Energética en edificios municipales (Medida 40 del Sistema de Monitoreo del PLAC). Otra de las colaboraciones que se está realizando es el proyecto de Planta Solar Urbana Colaborativa, en el marco del GCom y la Comisión Europea, y otros organismos internacionales. Dicho proyecto busca introducir una fuente de energía renovable y limpia en un sector central de la ciudad, lo que permitirá reducir las emisiones GEI, promover la sostenibilidad energética y la resiliencia climática. Esta intervención proporciona un modelo replicable y escalable a otras áreas, ayuda a lograr los objetivos del PLAC, incluyendo el compromiso de carbono-neutralidad para el 2050.\n

column17: A través de espacios de gobernanza y acompañamiento para la sustentabilidad del proceso del PLAC, la conformación de una agenda climática que promueva el desarrollo climáticamente resiliente y la transición ecológica justa, se han fortalecido estos ámbitos: Gabinete Local de Cambio Climático y Transición Ecológica Justa, compuesto a su vez por dos instancias de actuación, un gabinete político y un gabinete técnico, y el Comité Asesor frente al Cambio Climático. Este último es un espacio de la gobernanza climática que tiene por objetivo asistir y asesorar al poder ejecutivo municipal para el cumplimiento de las metas del PLAC, así como en las políticas públicas locales de adaptación y mitigación al cambio climático. Dicho Comité está conformado por diversas instituciones, organismos ambientales, entidades académicas y empresariales y representación del Concejo Municipal, gobierno provincial y nacional. Este órgano consultivo contribuye al logro de los objetivos, las directrices estratégicas, las actuaciones prioritarias y a dar seguimiento y transparencia en la ejecución del PLAC. Asimismo, el PLAC está en consonancia con lo estipulado en la Ley de Presupuestos Mínimos de Cambio Climático No. 27.520 y la Ley Marco de Acción Climática Provincial No. 14.019. En el 2023, el Comité Asesor se reunió en plenario en seis oportunidades abordando diferentes temáticas, tales como, la coordinación de la agenda del propio comité y del Gabinete Político, la priorización de acciones de mitigación y adaptación, la revisión de las metas del PLAC, la elaboración del Sistema de Monitoreo, la planificación y establecimiento de grupos de trabajo, entre otros. Cabe señalar que en el 2023 se formaron varios espacios de colaboración y trabajo por temática para el seguimiento de algunas acciones específicas del PLAC. Estos grupos estuvieron conformado por miembros del Gabinete Técnico y del Comité Asesor sobre los siguientes temas: Biodiversidad y uso de suelo, Riesgo y resiliencia, Energía y Residuos, con diferentes cantidades de encuentros.

column17: La Comisión Interempresaria Municipal de Protección Ambiental de Rosario - CIMPAR- es un espacio de cooperación y articulación público y privada para la sustentabilidad ambiental. Está conformada por empresas, gobierno municipal y provincial, universidades públicas y privadas, asociaciones profesionales y otras instituciones. Desde el 2001 genera propuestas para mejorar la sustentabilidad en la región e impulsa acciones que acompañen el desarrollo productivo local de las pymes mediante procesos preventivos y estratégicos. Se les facilita a las empresas acceso a capacitación, información y herramientas para mejorar su gestión ambiental por medio de un trabajo conjunto y un fuerte acento en la articulación público-privada. En esta línea se han elaborado y publicado manuales de buenas prácticas ambientales (BPA) para distintas actividades productivas a fin de mejorar el desempeño de las empresas. A partir del diálogo y el intercambio entre actores involucrados y el Municipio, se pretende generar y mantener el compromiso de las empresas locales y de la región en la adopción de una gestión ambientalmente responsable. En 2024, prosiguieron las plenarias donde participa la Municipalidad de Rosario, así como de las diferentes jornadas de capacitación, en temas tales como estrategias ambientales en la gestión pública en planes de acción a nivel provincial y municipal, la medición de la huella de carbono para mejorar la gestión ambiental, entre otras temáticas ambientales y climáticas. La articulación de esfuerzos e intereses de los diferentes niveles de gobierno provincial y municipal, así como los diversos actores económicos, académicos e instituciones de la región metropolitana de Rosario, ha permitido en todos estos años la producción de contenidos técnicos, formación, divulgación e implementación de proyectos de impacto positivo en materia ambiental, mediante el trabajo participativo y la generación de alianzas para el desarrollo sustentable. https://www.cimpar.org.ar/\n
