Otro antecedente de colaboración y trabajo compartido público-privado es la conformación de espacio productivo los Parques huerta, en el marco de las políticas públicas locales de agricultura urbana desde el 2002 -Programa Agricultura Urbana-. El objetivo de esta política pública es promover un proceso de construcción de desarrollo endógeno, a partir de estrategias participativas y solidarias de producción, transformación, comercialización y consumo de alimentos sanos. Se busca favorecer el consumo proximidad, reduciendo las distancias entre producción y consumo, disminuyendo así el impacto en los costos, en la calidad de los productos y del ambiente (emisiones de gases de efecto invernadero por transporte, equipos de enfriamientos, etc.). Bajo el formato de convenios existen actualmente, 7 parques huertas y 6 huertas grupales dentro del Programa de Agricultura Urbana. Estas iniciativas municipales producen alimentos agroecológicos y generan empleo para más de 250 personas, utilizando 25 hectáreas de tierra y produciendo alrededor de 650 toneladas de hortalizas al año, las cuales se comercializan en puntos de venta municipales y ferias. Es importante señalar que, la agricultura urbana fue creciendo, consolidándose en el trabajo en conjunto entre el Municipio y diferentes actores de la sociedad civil. Los parques huertas, las huertas comunitarias, el vivero, el banco de semillas, las agroindustrias sociales y demás espacio del programa, representan un recorrido verde en la ciudad, mostrando cambios en el paisaje, mejorando el entorno de los barrios, recuperando lugares degradados o abandonados y convirtiéndolos en espacios verdes que contribuyen con el ambiente, el mejoramiento de la calidad de vida, la promoción de la participación comunitaria y la generación de vínculos entre productores y consumidores. \nhttps://datos.rosario.gob.ar/ciudadania-y-estado/desarrollo-humano/emprendimientos/agricultura-urbana

column17: El fortalecimiento del sistema de gobernanza climática local, y el acompañamiento para la sustentabilidad del PLAC, con sus estructuras, procesos y mecanismos de participación para la implementación de acciones que abordan el cambio climático, se ha visto en el avance de los diferentes ámbitos que lo componen: Gabinete Local de Cambio Climático y Transición Ecológica Justa, compuesto a su vez por dos instancias de actuación, un gabinete político y un gabinete técnico, y el Comité Asesor frente al Cambio Climático. Estos procesos favorecen la a la formulación, implementación de estrategias y monitoreo de políticas públicas para mitigar las emisiones de GEIs y adaptarse a los impactos del cambio climático, desde una mirada cooperativa y transversal de la interacción entre instituciones públicas y privadas, así como entre los múltiples actores y actrices involucrados e involucradas, en un contexto complejo y dinámico a nivel local, regional e internacional. En cuanto al Comité Asesor frente al Cambio Climático en 2023 renovó parte de su membresía, y continuó con su conformación de acuerdo a su reglamento interno, y se formaron varios espacios de colaboración y trabajo, tal como se ha mencionado anteriormente. Otra de las iniciativas de colaboración que está desarrollando la ciudad, es con el Fondo de jóvenes en Acción Climática, apoyado por la Filantropía Bloomberg e implementado en colaboración con Ciudades y Gobiernos Locales (CGLU), y otros organismos internacionales. A nivel global, la iniciativa comprende a 101 ciudades e involucra a jóvenes de entre 15 y 24 años en el diseño, la implementación y el monitoreo de soluciones climáticas urgentes, que abarcan desde la plantación de árboles hasta la formulación de políticas. La primera etapa se realizó en 2024, y dicho fondo proporcionó asistencia técnica y financiamiento a 17 proyectos de jóvenes, que desarrollaron las siguientes iniciativas: plantación de arbolado nativo, construcción de capacidades, eficiencia energética, energías renovables, separación de residuos e infraestructura resiliente, entre otras. Cabe señalar que Rosario ha sido seleccionada para una segunda etapa en 2025.\n

Cartagena de Indias ha consolidado un ecosistema de colaboración multiactor para fortalecer su acción climática, articulando esfuerzos con gobiernos, agencias de cooperación internacional, el sector privado, la academia y organizaciones sociales. Estas alianzas han permitido avanzar hacia una ciudad más resiliente, circular y baja en carbono, en coherencia con los compromisos del Acuerdo de París y los lineamientos del Plan de Acción Climática (Plan 4C).
Entre los casos más relevantes de cooperación internacional se destaca la alianza con el Gobierno de los Países Bajos, a través del proyecto Water as Leverage (WaL). Esta iniciativa busca fortalecer la resiliencia urbana frente a los impactos del cambio climático mediante el diseño de soluciones integrales de adaptación y gestión sostenible del agua. En este marco, se han identificado zonas críticas como Olaya Herrera, Marlinda, La María y sectores del centro histórico, priorizadas para intervenciones basadas en la naturaleza, drenajes sostenibles y soluciones que reduzcan la exposición a inundaciones y mejoren la calidad de vida de las comunidades. El proyecto ha favorecido la transferencia de conocimiento con ciudades como Rotterdam y la articulación técnica con entidades distritales para la planificación territorial con enfoque climático.
De igual manera, la cooperación con la GIZ (Agencia Alemana de Cooperación Internacional) a través del programa PREVEC (Prevención de Emergencias en el Caribe) ha fortalecido las capacidades institucionales y comunitarias para la gestión del riesgo y la transición hacia una economía circular. A través de esta iniciativa se han desarrollado procesos de formación de funcionarios, docentes, líderes comunitarios y recicladores, con el apoyo del SENA y el Establecimiento Público Ambiental (EPA), promoviendo empleos verdes, emprendimientos sostenibles y la formalización del reciclaje como estrategia de inclusión social y sostenibilidad.
En el ámbito de la cooperación técnica y multilateral, Cartagena mantiene una colaboración activa con la Unión Europea, C40 Cities, ICLEI - Gobiernos Locales por la Sustentabilidad y la Iniciativa Global de Alcaldes por el Clima y la Energía (GCoM), enfocada en fortalecer la gobernanza climática local. Gracias a este trabajo, la ciudad cuenta con una calculadora de Gases de Efecto Invernadero (GEI) que permite medir sus emisiones y orientar decisiones de mitigación. Este avance ha sido complementado con la capacitación de personal técnico en monitoreo, reporte y verificación (MRV), fortaleciendo la gestión climática basada en datos.
Asimismo, Cartagena promueve la colaboración con el sector empresarial a través de la Mesa Regional de Competitividad e Innovación de Bolívar, espacio en el que se fomenta la integración de criterios ambientales en las estrategias productivas de sectores como el turismo, la logística portuaria y la construcción. Estas acciones contribuyen a la descarbonización progresiva de la economía local, impulsando el crecimiento verde y la innovación sostenible.
La sociedad civil y la academia también juegan un papel esencial. Las mesas comunitarias de cambio climático y las iniciativas de educación ambiental impulsadas junto con universidades y organizaciones sociales permiten fortalecer la participación ciudadana y la apropiación del conocimiento climático en los barrios más vulnerables. Estas alianzas han facilitado la incorporación del enfoque de justicia climática, género y diversidad en la gestión distrital.
Los resultados de estas colaboraciones son tangibles: fortalecimiento de la capacidad institucional y comunitaria, implementación de herramientas técnicas de medición de emisiones, desarrollo de proyectos piloto de infraestructura resiliente y consolidación de un enfoque de economía circular que genera empleo y bienestar. Cartagena avanza así hacia un modelo de desarrollo urbano sostenible, con compromiso compartido entre el Estado, la empresa y la ciudadanía.
En conjunto, estas alianzas reflejan una visión de gobernanza climática colaborativa, donde la cooperación internacional y local convergen para reducir vulnerabilidades, mejorar la equidad y garantizar un futuro climático más seguro para todos los habitantes de la ciudad.

Por otro lado, se ha trabajado con asociaciones ambientalistas y empresas interesadas en contribuir al bienestar ambiental, en campañas de limpieza, de forestación y reforestación, en diversas áreas de la ciudad, tomando como prioridad las zonas de mayor degradación. column17: Durante el 2025 el Ayuntamiento de Mérida reforzó la vinculación con la GIZ al pactar el desarrollo de proyectos de adaptación dentro del municipio. El primero a ejecutar es el Biocorredor Mérida, el cual es busca transformar un espacio público en un corredor verde para incrementar su resiliencia como medida de adaptación al cambio climático. Este proyecto busca conectar el Parque Ecológico del Poniente con corredor verde de la AV.200 e involucra intervenciones en infraestructura verde como el equipamiento, calles, ciclovías, banquetas y la implementación de soluciones basadas en naturaleza. Los problemas a resolver son la permeabilidad de las superficies, la disminución de islas de calor y la accesibilidad a espacios verdes. Se implementarán jardineras infiltrantes, nuevos pavimentos en calle y banqueta, arborización y sembrado de vegetación nativa y un diseño accesible. Las actividades iniciaron en marzo en con la aplicación de encuestas a los ciudadanos de las dos colonias involucradas, así como a las y los jóvenes de la preparatoria más cercana al parque. Posteriormente se realizaron tres presentaciones, una a cada colonia y una a jóvenes preparatorianos, sobre la importancia de la recuperación de los humedales (característica principal del parque ecológico) como medida de resiliencia. Actualmente se encuentra en desarrollo la etapa de diseño en donde se incluirán los comentarios de las encuestas y las acciones propuestas. Se pretende concluir actividades de implementación para finales de octubre.\n\nEl segundo proyecto es la generación de un manual de identificación y recuperación de humedales, el cual busca identificar y establecer el potencial de los humedales dentro de la ciudad como puntos estratégicos para aumentar la resiliencia. Actualmente se encuentra en proceso de implementación.

column17: H2One is the City's initiative to conserve and sustain our water supply for Henderson. The initiative focuses on educating and encouraging residents and visitors to follow water compliance rules, reporting water waste and taking advantage of rebates to remove decorative grass and install water-smart landscaping. The City seeks to build a culture of water conservation and change behavior among all community members to actively engage with water conservation efforts. Water levels in Lake Mead have rose in 2023, reflecting positive impacts from the enforced water conservation tactics. Following the Nonfunctional Grass Law that prohibits the use of water delivered by SNWA for irrigation of nonfunctional grass, the H2One initiative encourages residents to remove or convert nonfunctional grass to receive a $3 rebate per square foot. The City has committed to achieving several water conservation goals through its 2024-2027 All-In Henderson Sustainability and Climate Action Plan. H2One builds upon previous insights and aligns with both regional and City goals to reduce water use and increase water conservation compliance.

This project aims to promote and provide energy efficiency, clean transportation and beneficial electrification for Arizona, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming. In 2014, the City adopted the 2012 International energy Conservation Code (IECC), which functions similarly to building codes, to implement and include the latest efficiency technologies in building development. Utilizing technology such as “smart” thermostats, high-quality insulation, and advanced systems for heating, cooling and ventilation, have helped the City reduce greenhouse gas emissions (GHG) by 30,000 metric tons saving residents and businesses about $2.3 million on utility bills from 2014 to 2018. Henderson is the second community to receive the Energy Codes Count SWEEP's award in 2018. The City participated in a statewide building performance standard (BPS) and benchmarking cohort facilitated by SWEEP. The Nevada Heat lab focuses on a social learning space for the community on the practice of extreme heat management and health while also bringing together public service providers such as social services, urban planners, and emergency responders. These resources and outreaches help implement new data and modeling options for designing potential solutions for the urban heat island effect. The goal of the heat resilience lab is to effectively deliver strategies for reducing the temperatures that residents experience daily and to develop it in a way that accommodates all socioeconomic backgrounds and diverse populations. Researchers at the heat resilience labs study and co-develop solutions, adaptations, and resilience to climate hazards. The City participates in the heat resilience lab meetings which are held ad-hoc throughout the summer after extreme heat events and in the spring ahead of the heat season.

column17: The City of London participates in several programs involving municipal governments in Ontario, Canada, and globally, working together to share information and resources on climate change mitigation and adaptation: Partners for Climate Protection - Administered by ICLEI—Local Governments for Sustainability (ICLEI Canada) and the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, this is a national network of over 400 municipalities with the shared goal of taking action against climate change and reducing local greenhouse gas emissions. The City of London has participated since 1994 and achieved the final milestone (Milestone 5 - Monitor progress and reporting results) for both corporate and community level actions. The Clean Air Partnership is the Ontario regional climate advisor for the FCM-ICLEI Partners for Climate Protection program. Clean Air Council - Administered by the Clean Air Partnership, the Clean Air Council is a network of 30+ municipalities and health units from across Ontario. Since 2000, Clean Air Council members have been working collaboratively on the development and implementation of clean air, climate change, sustainability, and resilience actions. Clean Air Council members work collaboratively on agreed upon priorities and bring together experts and practitioners to share experiences and lessons learned. QUEST Ontario Community Energy and Climate Working Group - Administered by QUEST Canada, this working group is a network of Ontario municipalities, electricity utilities, and natural gas utilities working together to encourage the development and implementation of community energy plans to use energy more efficiently to keep dollars circulating longer in its economy, generate opportunities for local energy projects and jobs, and help manage risks from increasing energy prices and a changing climate. Many municipal members are also members of the Clean Air Council and there is collaboration between the Clean Air Partnership and QUEST Canada on these activities. Regional Public Works Committee of Ontario (RPWCO) Climate Change Subcommittee - RPWCO, representing the public works commissioners (or the equivalent name) in Ontario's largest regional and single tier municipalities, collectively plan, design, build, operate and maintain over 75% of the province's public works and environmental services, including waste management services, roads and bridges, and water and wastewater services. The Climate Change Subcommittee is currently focused on producing, distributing, and promote training webinars guiding municipalities through implementation of A Climate Resilience Roadmap for Ontario Municipal Infrastructure and Systems. These training resources will support member municipalities through the process of climate vulnerability assessment, from scoping and stakeholder engagement, to monitoring and evaluation. ICLEI Canada - Building Sustainable Climate Ready Communities - The City of London has partnered with this non-profit organization on two recent initiatives related to climate change: Showcasing Cities (2019 - 2020) provided the opportunity for 20 Canadian small and medium sized municipalities to work together in addressing the goals for both mitigation and adaptation identified through the use of industry standard tools (e.g., Building Adaptative and Resilient Communities - BARC, Global Covenant of Mayors, CDP Cities). Advancing Adaptation (Sept / 2021 - ongoing) provided the opportunity for 25 Ontario municipalities (including several of London's peer municipalities) to work together to advance their efforts in all aspects of climate change adaptation including risk and vulnerability assessments, planning and implementation. This work is currently underway and is the topic of a separate workplan.

The City of London has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Western University for Action on Climate Change in 2022. This includes updating existing and upcoming projects, developing an Academic Research Agenda for Action on Climate Change that will assist with the implementation of the Climate Emergency Action Plan, and establishing objectives, metrics, and timelines. 

Conversations continue between Civic Administration and researchers from Western University's Environment and Geography, HEALab, Engineering, Ivey School, and other departments to match research needs of the City with student research projects. Recent projects include work relating to the creation of more circular economy opportunities in London, advancing active transportation use city-wide, and the development of GHG emissions mitigation projects through Western's Carbon Solutions Consortium.

Civic Administration continues to work with researchers from Western University on a federally funded project for improved multi-scale greenhouse gas emissions modelling from urban environments to enhance mitigation strategies. This work leverages the recently completed ScenaCommunity emissions reduction and financial model for climate actions in London (by SSG - Sustainability Solutions Consultants), including the use of this model to help London Hydro forecast future peak electricity demand associated with climate action.

Civic Administration supported researchers from Western University and the private sector (Comcor Environmental and GHGSat) on a federally funded project for testing the effectiveness of multi-scale measurement of methane emissions from London's W12A landfill. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with 28 times the global warming potential of carbon dioxide. This project compares the results from measurements take from ground sweeps, drones, and satellites to improve the ability to detect and measure methane emissions from the landfill.

column17: The City of Saskatoon and the University of Saskatchewan (U of S) have a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) that sets out terms for collaboratively addressing issues of mutual concern including environmental sustainability and reconciliation. In alignment with the MOU, a Sustainability Task Team was formed to share information on environmental sustainability initiatives currently underway or completed. The Team's current areas of focus are: (1) Climate Action Planning, (2) determining how to coordinate, and (3) determining how to support mutual goals and targets. In 2021, the City and U of S signed a Climate Commitment that acknowledges that they are working to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and to adapt infrastructure, services, and programs for the future impacts of a changing climate. Both organizations have committed to pursuing sustainable actions that achieve environmental, social, and economic benefits. This commitment recognizes the need to enhance sustainable and resilient practices and that action is needed to slow, and ultimately prevent, the rise in the global average temperature and to facilitate the equitable transition to a clean energy economy. It recognizes a human-centred approach and the importance of climate change effects on vulnerable populations. The City and U of S further collaborate on other initiatives that support climate action and environmental sustainability, such as: (1) Research Junction - an annual grant program that provides funding for collaborative research. Through this grant program, the U of S and the City collaborated on “Promising Practises in Food Reclamation”, a study that looked at opportunities to prevent and manage food waste effectively. The City and U of S are currently collaborating on a feasibility study of heat pump systems in Saskatoon's climate and Multi-unit Residential Energy Efficiency study. These studies can help reduce GHGs if findings are implemented; (2) Eco-hack - an annual event where students compete to solve local environmental challenges; and, (3) The Storm Water Collaboration Group - hosted by the City's Storm Water Utility, the group conducts water quality and best practice research in partnership with the U of S. Community stakeholders including Meewasin and the South Saskatchewan River Watershed Stewards also participate in the group.

column17: The Home Energy Loan Program (HELP) was launched in 2021 to offer loans for energy efficiency and renewable energy retrofits which are applied to the property tax of single-family homeowners. During the program design, the City collaborated with industry, business, residents, and internal stakeholders to develop a comprehensive program that would meet the community's needs. The program started with $2,500,000 of internal capital funding for participant loans. The Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM) Community Efficiency Financing program, which is funded by the Government of Canada, is providing $10,999,800 to the program. This total includes $7,333,200 for the City to loan to participants, and a grant of $3,666,600 for rebates ($1,276,700) and program enhancements ($2,389,900). The expanded program involved further collaboration with industry and residents and now includes a partnership with Canadian Home Builders' Association for net-zero training and to encourage retrofits, a partnership with the Saskatchewan Realtors Association to provide an education program for real estate agents, decision making tools to facilitate and encourage home retrofits, and further education/coaching programs delivered by third parties. At the end of 2024, there were 88 spots available in the program and 304 applicants had been approved to participate. Completed projects have resulted in an average energy reduction of 35 GJ per household and an average greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction of 2.2 tonnes CO2e, which results in a total of over 320 tonnes CO2e/yr (equivalent to removing 75 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles from the road for one year). By the end of the program, the total GHGs reduced are estimated to reach 688 tonnes CO2e/yr.

In the late 1970s, a partnership between the City, the University of Saskatchewan, and the Province of Saskatchewan culminated in the creation of the Meewasin Valley Authority. Since that time, Meewasin has coordinated long-term planning to support public access to the river valley, conservation activities to support ecological and cultural resources, and management of key natural sites. As Saskatoon grows, the City is working with partners like Meewasin to develop an integrated approach to support green spaces and natural areas. Coordinated efforts between the City and Meewasin lead to climate adaptation benefits (e.g. storm water management, flood mitigation, sequestration, heat reduction) and ecosystem services (e.g. biodiversity, water/air/soil quality, recreation, cultural activities).

The City is also collaborating with Meewasin, Parks Canada and other partners to explore the potential for a National Urban Park (NUP) in the Saskatoon area. A NUP would help provide high quality access to nature, as well as support conservation of natural areas.

The City of Saskatoon has received federal funding through the Natural Infrastructure Fund to advance over 20 activities that support improved access to nature for the community; green space enhancements and habitat restoration; climate mitigation and adaptation; and equity and reconciliation. 

Saskatoon has been working with the Natural Assets Initiative to establish a natural asset framework for the City. The City has received funding from Climate West to further this work and explore the economic valuation of ecosystem services for key natural assets in Saskatoon.

Saskatoon is also one of a select number of cities participating in David Suzuki Foundation and Habitat's Natural Infrastructure Platform, an online dashboard that will showcase data and mapping for the quantity, location, risks, and benefits related to key natural assets, such as the urban forest.

column17: The City has been partnering with about ten other cities in Minnesota, NGO's, and others in an effort to accelerate State of Minnesota commercial building energy codes toward net zero carbon. In Minnesota, State Law and case law require that cities utilize the State of Minnesota's Building and Energy codes and do not allow cities to add additional or more stringent requirements. Furthermore, the State Energy Code adoption cycle is slow and updated only every six years. The City has partnered with these other entities to persuade the Minnesota State Legislature to either expedite the state code adoption process or to give cities the ability to adopt an energy code that exceeds the State code. In 2023 the Minnesota Legislature adopted legislation that requires the state's commercial building energy code to achieve an 80% or greater reduction in annual net energy consumption by 2036 as compared to a 2004 model code baseline measure. The Department of Labor and Industry, which administers building codes, would also be expected to more rapidly implement the latest commercial building energy codes starting in 2024 (https://energynews.us/2023/05/24/minnesota-lawmakers-update-commercial-building-code-amid-flurry-of-energy-bills/)

column17: The EV Spot Network/Evie Carshare is a partnership between the Cities of Saint Paul and Minneapolis, electric utility Xcel Energy, and HourCar, a local nonprofit carsharing company. The project was funded by USDOT, USDOE, the Cities, and private philanthropy. In February 2022, the City, in partnership with the City of Minneapolis, Xcel Energy, and HourCar, launched Evie, the first city-owned and 100% renewably-powered electric carshare program in the United States, and the EV Spot Network, a network of curbside EV charging stations (https://eviecarshare.com/). This initial phase of the EV Spot Network and Evie Carshare program covers about 1/3 of the City's geography, and about 50% of the covered area is in the City's lowest-income communities, where a majority of the residents are Black, Indigenous, and (other) People of Color. Evie is designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while increasing clean mobility options for the City's under-resourced residents and neighborhoods. In the early stages of developing Evie, the City paid residents from these under-served neighborhoods to participate in focus groups to provide feedback on how residents might access the service, how much they could afford to pay, and how the service would ideally be designed to meet these residents' needs. The City partnered with our local nonprofit carsharing partner HourCar to work with 5 community-based organizations (NGOs) in these same neighborhoods to assist with community engagement and planning for the project. The City and HourCar are currently working on an expansion of the network to under-served areas and seeking funding to continue expansion.

O município de Évora é parceiro do projeto POCITYF - A Positive Energy CITY Transformation Framework, cujo objetivo é criar um conjunto de Positive Energy Blocks, isto é, áreas geograficamente delimitadas com uma produção de energia local renovável superior ao consumo energético total, em termos de média anual. Pretende assim, transformar o tecido urbano, em particular áreas cultural e historicamente protegidas, em locais mais sustentáveis, saudáveis e acessíveis para os cidadãos.
A estratégia do projeto desenvolve-se em quatro Linhas de Transição Energética, complementares e multidisciplinares, integrando sistemas energéticos inovadores.
O POCITYF dotará as infraestruturas, tecnologias e serviços (i.e., edifícios, rede e mobilidade elétrica) chave da cidade de camadas de inteligência, abrindo assim caminho para as tornar mais seguras, verdes e responsivas às necessidades atuais dos seus cidadãos, tecido empresarial e outras organizações.
Este projeto tem Évora e Alkmaar (Holanda), como cidades farol, e Granada (Espanha), Bari (Itália), Celje (Eslovénia), Ujpest (Hungria), Ioannina (Grécia) e Hvidovre (Dinamarca) como cidades seguidoras. A escolha de Évora e Alkmaar como cidades farol prendeu-se com o alargado potencial de replicação na Europa, devido à existência de inúmeras cidades com muralhas e centros históricos, em que os desafios para a integração de energias renováveis e implementação de medidas de eficiência energética são maiores, mas cuja competitividade é nivelada com outras cidades que não têm limitações ligadas à componente cultural e arquitetónica.
O POCITYF é liderado pela EDP Labelec e inclui 46 parceiros de 13 países. Em Évora, o consórcio, do qual o município faz parte, é constituído por uma equipa multidisciplinar de 13 entidades.

For shared activities—such as documentation and reporting—the fellow operates independently with oversight from staff in all three cities. These tasks are common across the cohort.

For city-specific activities, the fellow supports the execution of unique efforts in each city, collaborating closely with local staff and stakeholders. The cities coordinate a schedule that maximizes the fellow's exposure and brings fresh perspectives to each team. This schedule is shaped by each city's EECBG project timeline, available resources, and overall capacity.

Regular meetings with representatives from Phoenix, Tempe, and Mesa help determine the fellow's time allocation based on these factors.

Phoenix and Mesa, Arizona, aim to expand solar infrastructure by adding over ten new solar systems to public-facing facilities (i.e., libraries and parks) and using innovative financial models to have a broader impact on the community. Also, the City of Phoenix EECBG project will assess and repair existing solar installations and implement a dashboard for real-time monitoring. The initiatives of these two cities focus on community engagement and sustainability. They seek to enhance public spaces, increase renewable energy capacity, and raise awareness about solar benefits. The project aligns with the Phoenix and Mesa Climate Action Plan and their commitment to a greener, more resilient future.

Tempe, Arizona, has designed a mobile home retrofit pilot project to reduce community energy consumption, homeowners' electric bills, and energy burdens. EECBG funding will subsidize the expense of implementing structural energy audits and mitigation measures for energy efficiency improvements.

This is a strong example of cities working together because it demonstrates:

- Regional collaboration with local autonomy
- Resource sharing for efficiency
- Cross-jurisdictional learning
- Scalable model for regional partnerships

The City of Tempe Climate Justice Advisory Group (CJAG) was a resident group formed to ensure that equity and community voice were centered in the city's development of the Residential Energy Equity Roadmap.

The Sustainability and Resilience Office held a series of bilingual workshops community to provide feedback on energy and extreme heat challenges. Members of the advisory group:

- Learned about energy and resilience to extreme heat initiatives happening in Tempe and the country.
- Advised the city on the types of investments that should be made to address residential energy efficiency and neighborhood-level urban cooling needs.
- Co-created the city's first Energy Equity Roadmap that will be used to pursue funding for the community identified investments.
- Advised on the direction of programs, policies, and infrastructure recommendations for Tempe City Council.

The workshop series concluded with the development of the Residential Energy Equity Roadmap, which outlines the direction of programs, policies, and infrastructure recommendations aimed at helping residents meet their energy use and extreme heat challenges. City Council formally adopted the Residential Energy Equity Roadmap on March 6, 2025. 

Participants were primarily made up of residents from the Alegre, Escalante, and Victory Acres neighborhoods, an area of Tempe that is vulnerable to extreme heat and face high energy costs relative to household income.


A separate endeavor that highlights collaboration between the City and vulnerable groups is the Tree Stewards Program, which is a volunteer-based initiative designed to educate and empower community members to help care for and expand Tempe's urban forest.

The program aims to:

- Increase tree canopy coverage in Tempe, especially in neighborhoods that are vulnerable to extreme heat
- Build community capacity for long-term tree care and stewardship
- Support Tempe's climate and equity goals by greening underserved areas and involving residents in the process

Volunteers (Tree Stewards) receive hands-on training in tree planting, pruning, watering, and general care, typically through a series of workshops led by arborists and sustainability experts. Stewards participate in community planting events, neighborhood tree care days, and outreach activities to educate others about the benefits of trees. 

 The program supports Tempe's efforts to ensure all residents, especially in historically underserved areas, have access to the benefits of a healthy urban canopy.

The City of Tempe collaborates with faith-based organizations through the Resilience Hub Network. Since 2022, the Sustainability and Resilience Division has been working on establishing a Tempe Resilience Hub Network. Resilience hubs are versatile community facilities designed to assist residents in their daily lives, respond effectively during emergencies, and aid in recovery.

Tempe's Resilience Hub Network brings together hubs, partner organizations, and residents each month to coordinate community-led resilience efforts—from everyday services to emergency response. 

This grassroots model shifts power to local communities, using their knowledge and assets to respond quickly and effectively to disruptions. It complements first responders by extending support and ensuring more people can participate in and benefit from a coordinated response.

Each hub operates uniquely, offering essential programs and services year-round and stepping up during disruptions to support the community. 

Many hubs provide daily programs and services, which you can explore on their websites. As the network grows, so will the variety of programs offered. 

As a first step toward upgrading Resilience Hubs, the City of Tempe conducted a microgrid feasibility study with Tempe consultants to evaluate energy efficiency, solar, and battery storage options for Resilience Hubs. These upgrades aim to provide reliable power during disruptions, reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and support community resilience by ensuring essential services remain operational.

In 2023, active Resilience Hubs had the opportunity to apply for Resilience Hub Project Grants to enhance existing programs or launch new initiatives. Selected projects included CPR/AED and First Aid training, creating a community green space with a pollinator garden and native trees, developing a new community garden, establishing a Performing Arts Academy for children, and supporting their food banks.

This link shows a map of Tempe Resilience Hubs: https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/f8eae3dc29ce42b09ba5cba4ce573056/page/Resilience-Hub-Network?views=Share&org=tempegov

Learn more about Tempe's Resilience Hub Network here: https://www.tempe.gov/government/transportation-and-sustainability/sustainability-resilience/energy-team-clean-efficient-energy/resilience-hubs

These Resilience Hubs also participate in the Maricopa County's Heat Relief Network by acting as Cooling Centers during the heat season (May-October).

The City is also working with Arizona State University Community Energy Futures Hub to connect undergraduate students with the City through internships. In the Fall of 2025, the City will be hiring an ASU intern to support the development and implementation of a Community Asset Mapping and Engagement Program. This role will help advance local resilience by supporting neighborhood-based mapping workshops.

The intern will:

- Research best practices and design a community-driven ABCD program tailored to Tempe's neighborhoods and resilience hubs. 
- Create and deliver an engaging workshop series that introduces residents to the principles of ABCD and teaches them how to identify and map community assets. 
- Facilitate asset mapping sessions with residents through door-to-door outreach and small group activities to collect data on neighborhood resources, skills, talents, organizations, and physical assets. 
- Produce accessible, easy-to-update asset maps and inventories for each participating resilience hub to support both everyday community needs and emergency preparedness. 
- Coordinate asset map review events at each hub to gather feedback from residents and guide conversations around how mapped assets can be activated during disruptions and used to support ongoing neighborhood needs.

The City of Tempe partners with utilities like Arizona Public Service (APS) and Salt River Project (SRP) on various matters.

To begin with, SRP and City of Tempe have a Memorandum of Understanding first established in 2022. This MOU establishes a fundamental framework for an innovative collaboration to achieve ambitious goals for drought resilience and carbon-emission reductions. The collaboration seeks to align the efforts of the City of Tempe and SRP to create a resilient water supply and low carbon future that will benefit the City of Tempe, its residents, businesses and SRP's customers. 

Areas of Collaboration include:
a. Forest health: Tempe is part of the Biomass Power Partnership. This regional collaboration supports forest thinning projects in the Salt River, Verde River, and East Clear Creek watersheds, critical areas for long-term watershed resilience and wildfire risk reduction. Tempe purchases renewable energy from Novo BioPower, a biomass power plant in Snowflake, Arizona. Over the next 10.5 years, the partnership will help fund the use of biomass from forest restoration work on National Forest System lands, providing clean, renewable power for more than 3,000 SRP customers.

b. Electric vehicle partnerships: Tempe joined as a founding member of the Transportation Electrification (TE) Activator coalition in 202. The TE Activator is an SRP led initiative to advance EV adoption across the region with a large focus on commercial fleet electrification. The City hosted the Arizona EV Fleet Expo at Tempe Center for the Arts (March 2023) with the Mayor of Tempe participating as a key speaker.

c. Decarbonization: The City has partnered with SRP to install solar panels on seven municipal facilities through Power Purchase Agreements. In 2025, Tempe expanded its partnership with SRP through the Rec Select Program, purchasing 22,428,943 kWh of renewable energy. By 2027, 52 percent of Tempe's municipal energy will come from renewable sources through SRP's Rec Select Program, as well as the Solar Choice Select and Sustainable energy Offering programs, which are expected to launch by 2027.

d. Infrastructure: Tempe actively partners with APS and SRP to pursue utility rebates for energy efficiency upgrades at city facilities. Each year, the city conducts assessments of its buildings to identify opportunities to improve lighting, electrical systems, and overall energy performance. These annual evaluations also help pinpoint facilities that can benefit from retrocommissioning to further reduce energy use and improve demand response. Since 2017, Tempe has received $157,281.62 in utility rebates, reflecting its ongoing commitment to smart, cost-effective energy management.

e. Social justice and heat resilience: Tempe's partnership with SRP in this area focuses primarily on data sharing and community education. SRP has provided detailed customer data to support the city's energy equity work, including the number and percentage of households enrolled in utility discount programs, using prepaid plans, behind on payments, and average monthly bill costs. In addition, both SRP and APS have co-hosted educational workshops at Tempe's EnVision Center, also designated as a Resilience Hub, to help residents access utility bill assistance, discount programs, and available rebates.

column17: The “Northern Virginia Climate Resiliency Team” (NVCRT) was formed in November 2016 with funding from a FY16 grant from the Virginia Coastal Zone Management Program. The purpose of the grant and team was to develop a \'Roadmap for Resilient Critical Infrastructure\' by October of 2017. The Northern Virginia Regional Commission (NVRC) coordinated the existing regional, multi-stakeholder “Northern Virginia Climate Resilience Team” created under the first year of the grant. The collaboration between these entities focused on several key areas:
1. **Green Networks and Natural Infrastructure:** Fayetteville and its partners proposed projects to protect and restore natural areas, which are vital for carbon sequestration and reducing transportation emissions. These green networks also aim to enhance public access to natural spaces and promote active transportation options like biking and walking.

2. **Transportation Efficiency:** The coalition included plans to improve transportation infrastructure by converting public fleets to electric vehicles, installing EV charging stations, and upgrading streetlights to more energy-efficient LED technology. These initiatives are designed to reduce fossil fuel dependence and lower emissions from the transportation sector.

3. **Building Efficiency:** The coalition proposed innovative funding solutions to reduce energy consumption in buildings, particularly in low-income and disadvantaged communities. This includes establishing a revolving loan fund for energy efficiency projects and supporting small grants to help public buildings participate in energy savings programs.

Fayetteville's role in this collaboration involved providing data, planning expertise, and leadership in environmental sustainability, which helped align the goals of the NWARPC, Fort Smith, and Metroplan with state and federal objectives for climate action. The grant will fund impactful projects across the region, including in Northwest Arkansas, ensuring that the area remains competitive for future federal funding and continues to progress toward a more sustainable future.

This collaborative effort highlights Fayetteville's commitment to regional sustainability and its leadership in driving climate action through effective partnerships.

Fayetteville participates in regional climate and watershed planning through partnerships with the Northwest Arkansas Regional Planning Commission and state-level initiatives, aligning transportation, stormwater, and energy planning with climate targets.

In July 2024, a coalition comprising Metroplan, Northwest Arkansas Regional Planning Commission (NWARPC), City of Fort Smith, and City of Fayetteville secured nearly $100 million in EPA funding through the Climate Pollution Reduction Grant (CPRG) program .

Of this, $36.25 million was allocated to Northwest Arkansas, including approximately $11.89 million earmarked specifically for Fayetteville and its partners—the University of Arkansas, NWALT (Northwest Arkansas Land Trust), and WCRC (Watershed Conservation Resource Center) .

Fayetteville's Contributions & Projects

Fayetteville's 2024 Climate Action Plan (CAP) was instrumental in shaping the statewide CPRG application; its modeling and planning work were pivotal to securing the grant. 

Fayetteville developed the carbon sequestration modeling tool, serving as the analytical backbone of the CPRG application. River Commons Floodplain/Prairie/Riparian Restoration & Trail Construction—restoring 46 acres of wetlands, 109 acres of prairie, and reforesting streambanks on a 200-acre parcel along the West Fork of the White River. Includes 7,120 feet of multi-use trail connectivity .

Town Branch Corridor Riparian Restoration—protecting and restoring over 12,327 linear feet of streambank and 12 acres of riparian zone, enhancing trails and ecosystem resilience

In 2020, Mayor Kincannon convened the Mayor's Climate Council to identify and evaluate strategies to achieve the community-wide emission reduction goal established by City Council in 2019. The cross-sector group of over 65 members included clean energy experts, conservation activists, advocates for equity, neighborhood representatives, developers, business leaders, utility representatives, and more. Representatives from Knox County, University of Tennessee, Tennessee Valley Authority, and Oak Ridge National Lab actively participated.

Council members and working groups (transportation, buildings/energy, waste, and equity) evaluated dozens of proven high-impact strategies for their impact to climate, economy, and community. Specifically, strategies were ranked based not only on emission reduction but also impact on equity and other societal benefits (air quality, public health, mobility and access, housing affordability, human services, and civic engagement). The strategies ranked highest by the Council across transportation, buildings/energy, and waste formed the basis for the City's 2021 Energy & Sustainability Work Plan, which directs the Office of Sustainability's work and more.

Even after the Work Plan was adopted, the Office of Sustainability continues to engage external experts from state (TN Department of Environment and Conservation, TN Department of Transportation) and federal (TN Valley Authority, Oak Ridge National Lab) agencies on climate activities. The City regularly meets with state agencies to exchange information about program development, funding opportunities, opportunities to build capacity, and more. For example, the City collaborated with other MSAs in the state to the provide feedback on the state's proposed plan for expanding public EV charging infrastructure.

Details on the City's 2021 Energy & Sustainability Work Plan can be found at https://www.knoxvilletn.gov/cms/One.aspx?portalId=109562&pageId=190076.

The City of Knoxville collaborates with Knox County and the Town of Farragut to produce a Multi-Jurisdictional Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (HMP). The HMP identifies and profiles 12 natural hazards (dam failure, drought, earthquake, expansive soils, extreme temperatures, flood, land subsidence/sinkholes, landslide, severe storms, tornadoes, wildfire, and winter storms) across the County. The risk assessment also estimates the
exposure of lives, property, and infrastructure to these hazards.

The planning process followed a methodology prescribed by FEMA, which included a Hazard Mitigation Planning Committee that identified and profiled hazards that pose a risk to the planning area, assessed the vulnerability to these hazards, and examined the capabilities in place to mitigate them. The HMPC identified goals for reducing hazard risks, recommended mitigation actions to meet those goals, and developed an implementation plan for each action. The participating jurisdictions developed this
plan pursuant to the requirements of the Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 (Public Law 106-390) and the implementing regulations set forth by the Interim Final Rule published in the Federal Register in 2002 (44 CFR §201.6) and finalized in 2007 to achieve eligibility for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Assistance (HMA) programs.

The Plan was formally adopted by City and County Commissions in 2018 and was updated in 2025. Progress reports are also published periodically. Details can be found at https://www.knoxcounty.org/stormwater/fema_mitigation.php.

column17: The City founded the award-winning Sustainable Neighborhoods Program, which empowers residents to lead their own sustainability and climate related projects. The program gives residents the opportunity to become active partners in making Lakewood a vibrant and sustainable community. Neighborhoods participating in this unique certification program use guidance from city staff to organize workshops, projects and events that enhance the livability of their neighborhood and reduce residents' ecological footprint. The City of Sunnyvale has a strong partnership with Silicon Valley Clean Energy (SVCE), a Community Choice Aggregator (CCA), that supplies carbon-free electricity to residents and businesses across Santa Clara County and parts of San Benito County. Since 2017, 97% of Sunnyvale customers have received 100% carbon-free electricity through SVCE, making a major contribution to the City's greenhouse gas reduction goals by eliminating emissions from electricity generation. This collaboration not only supports Sunnyvale's local climate action targets but also aligns with California's broader clean energy and carbon neutrality policies.

In addition to clean electricity supply, Sunnyvale and SVCE work together on a range of initiatives, including climate education, building and transportation decarbonization programs, and opportunities for energy storage to better use local solar generation. These joint efforts provide residents and businesses with tools, incentives, and resources to reduce their carbon footprint while strengthening community resilience. Sunnyvale's collaboration with SVCE demonstrates how local governments can leverage regional partnerships to achieve meaningful and lasting progress on climate action.

Sunnyvale also works closely with Community Based Organizations in the region to reach our more vulnerable populations and connect them with services, incentives and programs that will support their health and wellbeing as well as provide home upgrades and energy efficient technologies to address extreme heat and high energy bills. Community Based Organizations connect the city to frontline communities and offer translation services; safe spaces provide education about programs that will directly benefit their lives and build trust within the community and the city.

The City of Sunnyvale collaborates extensively with Santa Clara County on climate planning, resilience, and emissions reduction. A key example is Sunnyvale's involvement in the Community Climate Roadmap 2035, a county-led framework that provides a shared vision and coordinated strategy for meeting regional climate goals. This Roadmap includes county-wide greenhouse gas inventories, adaptation priorities, and strategies for decarbonization, which are directly used by Sunnyvale to align its own policies and reporting. The partnership ensures that local climate actions are consistent with county and state targets, while also pooling resources for data collection, technical support, and community engagement.

Sunnyvale also participates with the County on adaptation and resilience initiatives such as climate risk mapping, extreme heat preparedness, and sea level rise planning through the County's Climate Collaborative group. This group discusses ways to address and mitigate the effects of climate change for residents in Santa Clara County. The collaborative focuses on equity, extreme heat, flooding and is developing a resilience fund to support infrastructure improvements and programs for frontline communities. By working jointly with county staff and neighboring jurisdictions, Sunnyvale can address climate challenges that cross city boundaries, such as transportation emissions, extreme heat and wildfire disaster relief, and flooding risks, etc.

Link to Community Climate Roadmap 2035: https://sustainability.santaclaracounty.gov/climate-change/climate-action-planning/community-climate-roadmap-2035

Creating a clean mobility system requires a collective effort. Boulder is fortunate to have many leaders and partners working together to achieve transformative change. The University of Colorado Boulder (CU) has an extensive program to significantly reduce the use of single occupancy vehicles and provide viable options in transit, biking and walking. The university provides transit EcoPasses to all of its students through student fees. 

Boulder County has invested in low-emissions transportation alternatives throughout the county and was a lead sponsor, along with the city and CU, in a countywide electric vehicle adoption assessment. In 2024, the county was awarded $4.9 million from the federal government to add more charging stations; the County will add stations in areas that need them the most, including rural places, mobile home communities, and neighborhoods with a density of apartments and condos.

Boulder Valley School District (BVSD) has initiated a wide range of programs to reduce emissions from its bus and administrative fleet, including initiatives to increase walking, biking, transit and carpooling as well as efforts to lower emissions through hybrid buses, alternative fuels and efficient routing schedules. 

University Corporation for Climate Research (UCAR) and its other federal lab partners in the Boulder area provide van pool and ride sharing support for employees, and free bicycle check outs, complementary bike share membership and EcoPasses for all employees. The labs were an active partner with the city, county, CU and BVSD in developing a community-wide EV adoption plan.

column17: The City of Boulder, and community partners University of Colorado Boulder (CU Boulder), Boulder County, Via Mobility Services (Via), Boulder Housing Partners (BHP), Colorado CarShare, Xcel Energy, and Fermata Energy, has completed the installation of several energy resilience projects that enable critical community and university services to maintain operations during unexpected events, such as a major grid outage. Components of this work include installations at Via to power their building and their incoming electric transportation fleet, and solar panels, back-up battery storage and a generator at BHP, the primary affordable housing provider in Boulder. In addition to maintaining power to critical systems in times of emergency or grid outage, the systems provide numerous economic benefits and add to the city's local renewable energy generation. Other components include the construction of a resilient public transit charging hub that jointly serves Via, BVSD and CU Boulder as they continue to electrify their transit buses. In 2024 the city, in collaboration with BHP, Colorado CarShare, Xcel Energy and Fermata Energy, launched an innovative program aimed at reducing building energy costs while providing affordable, sustainable transportation options for community members. This initiative features two car share electric vehicles paired with bi-directional charging stations, introducing two-way electricity flow and enabling energy exchange between a building and a car. Known as Vehicle-to-Everything technology, including Vehicle-to-Grid and Vehicle-to-Building, this pioneering approach holds immense potential to mitigate building peak demand, ultimately driving down energy costs and enhancing grid stability. The program builds on the success of the city's bi-directional EV charging pilot at North Boulder Recreation Center. Operated by the not-for-profit organization Colorado CarShare, shared Nissan Leaf EVs will be made available for the program, including subsidized use for those residing in affordable housing.

column17: In 2013, the City invested $70 million to upgrade the waste treatment plant to the Dubuque Water and Resource Recovery Center, which allowed the facility to capture methane and convert it into electricity. The facility uses anaerobic digestion to convert wastewater sludge to 12.5 tons of fertilizer per day. During the digestion process, methane gas is produced, which is captured, cleaned, and burned to power turbines that generate electricity for the facility. Through operational efficiencies and the conversion of waste to electricity and heat, the plant saved over $600,000 in operating costs in its first full year of operation. The plant also contributes significant environmental benefits, removing 10 tons of oxygen demand per day, which previously went into the Mississippi River, and using 400 kilowatts less per year, which results in 4,715 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent not going into out atmosphere. It also processes high strength waste from local businesses, saving companies around 60% on their disposal costs and generating revenue for the City. A later project, in 2016, a partnership with BioResource Development and Black Hills Energy, transforms excess methane gas generated at the facility into pipeline-quality natural gas.

column17: The new Active Transportation Plan (ATP) will be a consolidation of the City's existing Bicycle Master Plan (adopted in 2018) and the Pedestrian Master Plan (adopted in 2016), as well as incorporate the latest design practices, policies, and infrastructure planning for all active transportation modes (including bicycling, walking, and micromobility). The ATP project will also develop the next five-year strategic plan to encourage and promote active transportation use for all ages and abilities. The existing Pedestrian Master Plan and Bicycle Master Plan established a five-year action plan with recommendations centered on expanding safe, continuous, convenient, and comfortable pedestrian and bicyclist access for all ages and abilities who live, work and visit Fremont. Over the five years since the adoption of these plans, the City of Fremont has made significant progress in the implementation of the various identified action items, including installing over 20 new pedestrian crossing flashing beacons, 40 miles of separated bikeways, 13 new protected intersections, adopting the Trails Strategic Plan (2021), and completing School Safety Assessments and over 400 “quick build” improvements for all 40 public schools in the City. The ATP will continue the City's progress with comprehensive engagement with the Fremont community and establishing the next set of active transportation strategies and guidance for the next five years, ultimately continuing the City's overall mission of developing its infrastructure to be safe, convenient, connected, and comfortable for bicyclists and pedestrians of all ages and abilities who live, work, and visit Fremont.

一、建立气候投融资项目筛选培育机制。制定《气候投融资项目认定规范（试行）》，明确了新区气候投融资试点项目的认定标准、认定流程。印发《新区金融机构支持气候投融资项目的具体措施（试行）》，从机构建设、业务扩展、工具创新、能力建设等方面鼓励新区金融机构强化对气候投融资项目的支持。开展气候投融资项目收集并加强调度，51个项目纳入《青岛西海岸新区气候投融资项目库》，总投资达1000多亿元，其中7个项目将获得银行贷款32.42亿元。
二、督促创新开发气候投融资金融产品。融合金融监管部门的专业技术优势，组织召开气候投融资“政金企”对接会、“一对一”座谈交流会，为银行和企业搭建沟通渠道。公开征集气候投融资金融产品及项目案例，11家金融机构报送案例18个。引导驻区金融机构在低碳经济、循环经济和生态经济三大领域开展金融产品创新，省首单附带“绿色建筑性能责任保险”的绿色贷款在新区投放。
三、加强气候投融资能力建设。印发《青岛西海岸新区气候投融资试点工作方案》《青岛西海岸新区气候投融资试点实施方案》，确立试点的基本原则和工作目标，分解落实各项重点任务，对各年度工作做出了部署安排。制定《气候投融资加速平台研究成果应用工作方案》，参与了亚洲开发银行气候投融资加速平台建设。与北京绿交所达成《战略合作伙伴框架合作协议》，将在气候投融资、推进自愿减排等领域开展合作。制发了《气候投融资试点知识明白纸》，争取全国2023年第一期气候投融资专题培训班在新区举办，紧扣全国温室气体自愿减排交易专业知识举办了绿色低碳金融财税知识专题培训班，打造气候投融资领域专业化干部人才队伍。

column17: 青岛奥帆中心零碳社区项目\n青岛奥帆中心零碳园区项目位于青岛市福山湾畔，总占地面积45公顷，建筑面积22.7万平方米，包括海尔洲际酒店、国际会议中心、奥帆博物馆、媒体中心、海上宴会厅、航海学校、集团办公楼、燕岛宾馆、运动员中心等建筑，通过海水源热泵、太阳能光伏光热、风力发电、污水源热泵、工业余热和燃气等技术，实现了高效清洁供能。每年能够直接节约用电量303万度，节约燃气量5500标准立方米；直接减少碳排放8663吨，相当于在景区内种植了173.3万棵树木。最终园区将通过绿色供能，逐步实现能源消耗直接碳排放强度降低至零。\n2024年入选山东省能源绿色低碳转型典型案例（全省仅15个），入选中国投资协会能源投资专委会《零碳中国故事》画册，被授予“零碳园区”标准试点称号。

绿色出行“变现”成真 市民共享减碳红利 青碳行“低碳乘车抵扣”功能上线一周年

　　在“双碳”目标引领下，国内碳普惠创新实践再结硕果。“青碳行”碳普惠平台联合青岛地铁APP推出的“低碳乘车抵扣”功能迎来上线一周年，该创新模式将市民日常绿色出行的碳减排量转化为“真金白银”的乘车优惠，在激发公众参与低碳生活热情的同时，更以数字化手段为城市绿色转型注入新动能。

　　创新实践：绿色出行即时“变现”

　　作为全国首创推出的以数字人民币结算的碳普惠平台，“青碳行”平台遵循“人人有责、人人参与、人人受益”的理念，利用多样化手段激励公众日常出行、生活领域节能降碳，提升公众践行绿色低碳出行的参与感和获得感。

　　2024年，“青碳行”碳普惠平台联合青岛地铁APP推出“低碳乘车抵扣”功能，实现了全国地铁场景碳减排量直接抵扣乘车费用的首创应用。用户一键开启“低碳乘车抵扣”功能后，即可将个人在“青碳行”平台获得的低碳出行碳普惠减排量，按照每1250g碳减排量可抵0.01元乘车费的抵扣规则，用于后续地铁乘车费用抵扣，从而获得实实在在的出行优惠。



　　一年成绩单：50万用户、240万次、30万元

　　自上线以来，“低碳乘车抵扣”迅速成为不少岛城市民绿色出行的“新标配”。截至目前，已有近50万青岛地铁APP用户通过该功能完成地铁乘车费用抵扣，累计实现240余万次乘车费抵减，总计抵扣金额近30万元。这些数字背后，是青岛市民对绿色生活方式的高度认同和积极参与。

　　市民张女士告诉记者，她每日通勤选择地铁出行，一年间通过“青碳行”平台累计获得碳减排量超2500千克，折合抵扣乘车费20余元。“以前觉得环保是口号，现在发现每次刷码乘车都在为地球'减负'，还能通过'低碳抵扣'节省乘车费，这种'减碳即收益'的感觉太棒了！”张女士的体验折射出“低碳乘车抵扣”功能的深层价值——让绿色行为可量化、可激励、可持续。



　　技术赋能：“数字人民币+碳普惠+区块链”

　　“青碳行”平台创新性地将区块链技术、智能合约、数字人民币试点等金融科技前沿技术应用到碳普惠领域。除了抵扣乘车费用外，用户的个人碳普惠减排量还可在“青碳行”平台实时兑换为数字人民币，实现绿色低碳行为的价值转化。

　　用户在“青碳行”平台注册并授权后，根据公众通过地铁、公交、骑行、新能源车等绿色低碳出行方式对应产生的里程数、乘坐频次等信息，在保护公众隐私安全脱敏的前提下，按照青岛市发展和改革委员会、青岛市生态环境局联合印发的《青岛市低碳出行碳普惠方法学》科学核算绿色低碳出行的碳减排量，采用安全可信的分布式记账和区块链存证技术，对碳减排数据进行全生命周期监管和存证，并通过智能合约设定合规条件将碳减排量兑换为数字人民币，实现“数字金融+绿色金融+碳普惠机制”创新模式的有机结合。

　　多元运营：从“低碳出行”到“环保公益”

　　“青碳行”平台不断深化碳普惠场景覆盖，与多家低碳出行场景方、旧物回收服务商携手合作。目前，低碳出行场景已实现在青岛市地铁、公交、骑行、新能源车等场景全覆盖，并推出了旧机回收、旧衣回收等新场景，将碳普惠合作生态从低碳出行向循环经济领域逐步延伸，为公众提供更加丰富的绿色生活选择。

　　平台还先后开展“低碳出行日”“低碳挑战赛”“云上登山赛”“互联网+全民义务植树”等形式多样的主题活动，联合青岛市绿化委员会、洁之队等组织开展了100余场次义务植树、周末城市清洁等环保公益志愿行动，通过“线上+线下”多元运营模式和多样化激励措施，有效引导公众形成绿色低碳的生活方式。

　　青岛经验：碳普惠激活城市绿色基因

　　随着“低碳乘车抵扣”功能上线一周年，“青碳行”平台注册用户已突破750万，累计碳减排量超20万吨。这些数字不仅记录着青岛市民对绿色生活的选择，更勾勒出一座海滨城市绿色转型的轨迹。

　　“青碳行”凭借前瞻性的碳普惠商业模式、数字人民币的创新试点场景以及数字金融、绿色出行和智慧生活深度融合的新生态，为城市绿色低碳高质量发展铺设了一条坚实之路。

　　在地铁站内，乘客们习惯性地打开手机查看当日的碳减排量和乘车费用抵扣账单，“多乘一次地铁、多减一份碳排、多享一笔优惠”，这是金融科技与绿色低碳碰撞出的美好生活。未来，“青碳行”平台将持续优化用户体验，逐步拓展“衣、食、住、行、用”等多领域碳普惠场景生态，引领更多公众通过“绿色行动”参与城市减碳，共同绘制低碳生活新图景，让绿色基因融入城市绿色发展血脉。

Kota Medan telah menunjukkan kemajuan signifikan dalam kolaborasi dengan pemerintah pusat terkait pelaporan data iklim dan lingkungan, yaitu sebagai berikut :
1. Pelaporan Data Sampah melalui SIPSN (KLH/BPLH)
SIPSN (Sistem Informasi Pengelolaan Sampah Nasional) adalah platform milik Kementerian Lingkungan Hidup (KLH/BPLH).
DLH Kota Medan secara rutin melaporkan timbulan sampah harian, komposisi, dan capaian pengelolaan melalui SIPSN.
2. Implementasi Program ProKlim (Program Kampung Iklim)
Kota Medan aktif berkolaborasi dengan KLH/BPLH dalam Program Kampung Iklim (ProKlim).
Tujuan: meningkatkan kapasitas adaptasi dan mitigasi perubahan iklim berbasis masyarakat.
DLH Medan memfasilitasi pendataan lokasi ProKlim, kemudian melaporkannya ke sistem SIDIK (KLH/BPLH).
3. Pelaporan Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup (IKLH) Kota Medan setiap tahun melaporkan nilai IKLH ke KLH melalui Web IKLH (dulu) sekarang SITALA, mencakup:
a. Indeks Kualitas Air (IKA)
b. Indeks Kualitas Udara (IKU)
c. Indeks Kualitas Tutupan Lahan (IKTL)
Laporan ini digunakan pemerintah pusat untuk evaluasi kinerja daerah dalam pengelolaan lingkungan hidup.
4. Pelaporan Gas Rumah Kaca - SIGN SMART (KLH/BPLH)
SIGN SMART (Sistem Inventarisasi Gas Rumah Kaca Nasional - Strategic Monitoring, Assessment, and Reporting Tool) adalah sistem online dari KLH/BPLH untuk pencatatan emisi GRK.
Kota Medan menggunakan SIGN SMART untuk:
a. Melaporkan emisi GRK tahunan dari sektor energi, limbah, pertanian, dan IPPU.
b. Mengintegrasikan data lokal ke inventaris nasional, sesuai amanat Perpres No. 71 Tahun 2011.
c. Memantau capaian Rencana Aksi Daerah Penurunan Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (RAD-GRK).

Kota Medan telah membangun kolaborasi strategis dengan Kementerian Perhubungan (Kemenhub) dalam sektor transportasi, terutama dalam rangka mengurangi emisi, mengurangi kemacetan, dan mendukung target transisi menuju transportasi rendah karbon.
1. Pengembangan Transportasi Massal Ramah Lingkungan
a. LRT Medan - Binjai - Deli Serdang (Mebidang)
Proyek Light Rail Transit (LRT) Mebidang merupakan kerja sama Kota Medan, Kemenhub, dan Pemerintah Provinsi Sumut.
Tujuan:
- Mengurangi ketergantungan pada kendaraan pribadi.
- Menekan emisi GRK dari sektor transportasi.
- Mengintegrasikan kawasan perkotaan Medan, Binjai, dan Deli Serdang.
Status: Studi kelayakan diselesaikan oleh Kemenhub, dan proyek ini masuk dalam Proyek Strategis Nasional (PSN).
Kapasitas awal direncanakan mampu mengangkut 15.000-20.000 penumpang per jam.
b. Pengembangan Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Medan
- Kemenhub mendukung Kota Medan dalam proyek BRT Medan yang juga mencakup kawasan Mebidang.
- Proyek ini mendapatkan dukungan pendanaan dari Global Environment Facility (GEF) dan Asian Development Bank (ADB).
- Penerapan bus listrik menjadi fokus utama untuk mengurangi emisi transportasi perkotaan.
- Kota Medan telah memulai tahap awal berupa:
 1) Penyusunan rute koridor utama.
 2) Penataan halte dan terminal dengan konsep Transit Oriented Development (TOD).

2. Integrasi Data Transportasi
Dinas Perhubungan Medan bekerja sama dengan Kemenhub dalam pelaporan data transportasi, termasuk:
- Jumlah angkutan umum terdaftar (angkot, bus kota, taksi).
- Data emisi sektor transportasi untuk mendukung pelaporan SIGN SMART (KLHK).
- Pemantauan lalu lintas berbasis sistem digital untuk mendukung pengendalian kemacetan dan polusi udara.

3. Modernisasi Angkutan Umum dan Konversi BBM ke Listrik
a. Bersama Kemenhub, Kota Medan mendorong:
- Program peremajaan angkot (buy the service): armada lama berbasis BBM diganti dengan bus rendah emisi atau bus listrik.
- Insentif konversi kendaraan listrik, termasuk penyediaan stasiun pengisian kendaraan listrik umum (SPKLU).
b. Kolaborasi ini sejalan dengan Perpres No. 55 Tahun 2019 tentang Kendaraan Listrik.

4. Dukungan untuk Pengurangan Emisi Transportasi
Kolaborasi ini mendukung target Kota Medan dalam Rencana Aksi Daerah Penurunan Emisi Gas Rumah Kaca (RAD-GRK):
a. Sektor transportasi menyumbang >55% emisi GRK Kota Medan.
b. Kemenhub memberikan asistensi teknis dalam:
- Perhitungan baseline emisi transportasi.
- Perencanaan kebijakan konversi energi.
- Integrasi data transportasi ke Sistem Transportasi Nasional (Sistranas).

column17: Jordan's Economic Modernization Vision centers on the slogan of “A Better Future”, and is based on two strategic pillars: accelerated growth through unleashing Jordan's full economic potential; improved quality of life for all citizens, while sustainability is a cornerstone of this future vision. Through the first pillar, Jordan can achieve leaps in economic growth and create job opportunities in the next decade, with the continuous growth of citizens' per capita income. Through the second pillar, it can realize a significant improvement in the quality of life for Jordanians, standing at the forefront of countries in the region in this regard. The vision pillars:- Economic Growth Pillar (Unleashing our full potential)- Quality of Life Pillar (Improving the Living Standards for All Citizens)- Both Pillars Share a Characteristic of SustainabilityThe implementation roadmap was developed through an inclusive, multidisciplinary approach, taking into consideration the necessary steps in the short, medium, and long-term towards achieving the desired results and ultimately fulfilling the strategic objectives of the Vision. The proposed roadmap ensures the successful linkages among sectors and the proposed actions to maximize synergies while avoiding redundancy.The implementation roadmap includes comprehensive and various actionable initiatives, which have been identified throughout the sectoral economic workshops, with a particular focus on the period 2022-2025.At the heart of the roadmap are eight drivers that will lead the implementation. Each driver is broken down into specific sectors to action the implementation. In total, there are 35 sectors and sub-sectors and over 300 initiatives. Each initiative is mapped into an initiative card containing the initiative objectives, stakeholders subdivided into initiative owners and participants, a timeline with specific start and end points, initiative metrics to track the progress and delivery, and a detailed checklist of deliverables to be addressed through the implementation process, including an emphasis on unleashing women and youth's potential across all domains.The drivers were defined by combining logically connected sectors into cohesive groupings for the purposes of organizing concerted actions. The groupings were based on three factors:1- Linkages Among Sectors: logical linkages of a sector with other sectors to form value chains or growth clusters, e.g. mining with downstream chemical products manufacturing or agriculture with food processing, thus promoting the realization of synergies across the driver.2- Roles of Sectors: drivers of economic growth against enablers of economic growth.3- Common Sectors' Characteristics: shared attributes among sectors; for example, a common focus on knowledge and innovation as a source of competitive advantage.

column17: The updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) is a nationwide sectoral document aiming at (i) enhancing the Jordanian commitment to the international climate change governance system by raising its GHG emission reduction target from 14% to 31%; (ii) driving the post-COVID-19 recovery process into a lower carbon and more climate-resilient development pathway steered by national green growth priorities. Objectives and targets of this NDC document will be aligned with the Long Term Strategy (LTS) of the Government of Jordan to be developed through a new climate change policy for 2050. The document underlines the following strategies for a successful climate action (i) enhancing governance and institutional arrangements; (ii) mainstreaming NDCs in national and local planning; (iii) engaging the private sector; (iv) mainstreaming gender in NDC implementation; (v) targeting vulnerable groups in NDC implementation.The NDC considers both mitigation and adaptation actions. As for the mitigation actions they mainly deal with GHG emission reduction of 31% in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) sector (energy, industrial processes and product use, agriculture, forestry and land-use, and waste). Regarding the climate change adaptation, the following sectors are involved (i) Water Resource Management; (ii) Agriculture and Food security; (iii) Biodiversity and Ecosystems; (iv) Health; (v) Urban Resilience and Disaster Risk Reduction; (vi) Coastal Zone Management; (vii) Cultural Heritage and Tourism.As for Governance, it is necessary to integrate the sectoral actions included in the NDC Action Plan with the government's Executive Development Program (EDP) to improve the national-priority levels for allocating financial resources and readiness for implementation in the next years of the government plan including Greater Amman Municipality.

column17: “Long-Term Strategy” or “LTS” is the term used in this roadmap, particularly in referring to such a strategy for Jordan, encompassing low-emission 2050 pathways, climate resilience and national development goals. Beyond meeting the goals of the Paris Agreement, development of an LTS can also serve a number of valuable domestic purposes. The benefits of long-term planning are particularly relevant for Jordan, where most national plans and strategies are focussed on short and medium-term goals. Therefore, the development of Jordan's LTS represents an opportunity to shift decision-making and strategic thinking to the longer-term perspective. The LTS is not intended to be an “implementation plan” but a strategic document that guides other national climate and sectoral strategies. By providing the framework for the identification and prioritisation of the necessary actions to deliver the country's long-term climate change and development vision, short and medium-term climate change and sectoral plans can ensure actions are aligned to long term objectives. the LTS interact with the NDC and NAP processes, and also align with the government vision, national development plans and local government plans. The NDC and NAP processes, implementation plans, and local climate action plans can provide the vehicle by which implementation of climate action is driven, and thus reported under the national transparency framework. https://www.moenv.gov.jo/ebv4.0/root_storage/ar/eb_list_page/jordan_lts_roadmap.pdf

Davao City actively collaborates with the National Government through agencies such as the Climate Change Commission (CCC), Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Energy (DOE), Department of Health (DOH), and Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This collaboration is facilitated through technical assistance, capacity development, policy and regulation alignment, and reporting requirements under the Measurement, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system.

Key areas of progress include:

Emissions reduction: Development of the community-wide GHG inventory and alignment of emissions reduction targets with national requirements.

Adaptation and resilience: Integration of climate risks into the Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) and DRRM plans in line with the National Adaptation Plan.

Energy and transport: Pilot programs on renewable energy promotion and sustainable transport initiatives (e-jeepneys, eco-transport studies).

Waste management: Implementation of waste segregation, recycling, and DENR-backed solid waste programs.

Agriculture and food security: Introduction of climate-resilient crops and livelihood support to farmers under DA and LGU partnerships.

Forestry and ecosystem restoration: Mangrove rehabilitation, upland watershed management, and tree-growing initiatives in partnership with DENR.

Public health: Strengthened surveillance systems for climate-sensitive diseases and public health campaigns with DOH.

Education and inclusivity: Mainstreaming climate change in schools (DepEd and CHED) and prioritizing vulnerable groups in adaptation strategies.

This multi-sectoral collaboration ensures that Davao City's climate strategies are aligned with the Philippines' Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) and contribute directly to national adaptation and resilience-building targets.

Davao City works closely with the Regional Government of Region XI to strengthen climate action through joint planning, implementation, and monitoring of key initiatives. Collaboration is anchored on multi-sectoral coordination with agencies such as DENR-XI, DA-XI, DOE-XI, DOH-XI, DepEd-XI, and the Regional Development Council (RDC-XI), which ensures that city-level actions are aligned with regional development and climate priorities.

Key areas of collaboration include:

Disaster resilience and adaptation through joint risk assessments, early warning systems, and capacity development with the Regional Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council.

Climate-smart agriculture and food security, in partnership with DA-XI, to promote resilient farming practices and improve supply chain connectivity.

Energy and transport, where DOE-XI and regional planning bodies support the integration of renewable energy projects and sustainable mobility under the Metro Davao Urban Transport Integration Program.

Forestry, water, and ecosystem management, particularly in watershed rehabilitation, coastal protection, and biodiversity conservation programs with DENR-XI.

Public health and social services, with DOH-XI providing climate-sensitive health programs (e.g., dengue and heat-related illnesses) and DSWD-XI supporting vulnerable populations during climate-induced disasters.

Education and community empowerment, through DepEd-XI and local higher education institutions, integrating climate change modules into curricula and conducting community-based trainings.

Progress to date includes:

The adoption of a Davao Regional Climate Change Action Plan, which guides city and regional coordination.

Implementation of joint reforestation and watershed rehabilitation projects in priority areas.

Expansion of climate-resilient agriculture programs supporting smallholder farmers.

Ongoing infrastructure and transport planning under Metro Davao, designed with climate resilience standards.

Continuous capacity development and knowledge sharing across LGUs in the region, facilitated by RDC-XI and DENR-XI.

This collaboration has strengthened the city's ability to align local actions with regional and national climate commitments, particularly in supporting the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) and the Philippines' Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).

The City Government of Davao collaborates with Indigenous Peoples (IPs) with overlapping and neighboring territories through participatory consultations, joint planning, and the integration of traditional ecological knowledge into climate adaptation and resilience initiatives. Engagements are conducted in partnership with tribal councils and the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), ensuring that climate-related projects are culturally sensitive and aligned with the protection of ancestral domains.

Key areas of collaboration include watershed and forest protection in upland areas, sustainable agriculture and agroforestry, ecosystem restoration, and biodiversity conservation. IP communities also contribute to food security initiatives through the preservation of traditional farming systems and seed varieties. These efforts support resilience to climate impacts such as droughts, floods, and soil erosion.

Progress has been demonstrated through the inclusion of IP representatives in local climate and disaster risk reduction planning processes, implementation of reforestation and riverbank stabilization projects in ancestral lands, and livelihood support programs promoting sustainable and climate-smart practices. These collaborations strengthen the resilience of both indigenous communities and the wider Davao City population while promoting inclusive and equitable climate action.

Davao City's collaboration with other local governments has resulted in more coherent approaches to resilience, reduced duplication of efforts, and improved access to national funding for climate-related programs.

Progress includes increased community participation in solid waste management, expansion of green spaces through reforestation efforts, and stronger protection of critical ecosystems such as the Panigan-Tamugan watershed. These collaborations have enhanced resilience, promoted inclusive climate action, and ensured grassroots involvement in implementing the City's environmental and climate-related priorities.
