Due to changes in lifestyle and economic conditions in recent years, the volume and variety of surplus food and materials have continued to increase. To promote resource reuse and reduce waste, New Taipei City launched the Food Sharing Network in 2016. The initiative adopts a strategy grounded in public markets, cross-agency collaboration, and public-private partnerships to effectively redistribute surplus food to disadvantaged communities.

1.Building a Public Welfare-Oriented Resource Network
Through interdepartmental collaboration, the city has incorporated the concept of food conservation into its existing policies, promoting food-saving awareness in both industry and education. In cooperation with produce distributors, public and private markets, food companies, and local community sites, a supply-demand network for imperfect produce and surplus items has been established. These resources are repurposed to support community meal services for vulnerable populations, helping reduce food waste throughout the local supply chain.

2.Public-Private Collaboration
To ensure food safety and prevent spoilage during transport—thus avoiding secondary waste—the city partners with civil society organizations to provide three refrigerated trucks for distributing donated food to remote areas. This reduces urban-rural disparities in resource access and builds trust with donor enterprises regarding proper food handling and logistics. Since 2020, to enhance preservation and usability, donated ingredients have been processed into frozen meal packs by social welfare groups, extending shelf life and improving efficiency in community use.

New Taipei City has integrated central and local disaster response systems and monitoring data through the use of innovative disaster prevention technologies. The city has deployed a combination of the All-Hazards Smart Command and Monitoring Platform (EDP), the New Taipei Disaster Information E-point Access System, and the Disaster Prevention and Response Data Center. Among these, the “All-Hazards Smart Command and Monitoring Center—Typhoon and Flood Real-Time Early Warning System (EDP-DWS)” offers the following key functionalities:

1.Flood Warning Mode: This function integrates two-dimensional (2D) flood modeling with the city's known flood-prone areas to predict urban flooding hotspots in advance, enhancing early preparedness.
2.Localized Weather Integration Map: By combining meteorological data with the city's electronic map system, the platform provides time- and region-specific rainfall forecasts.
3.Dynamic Data Visualization: An intelligent decision-support module generates precipitation hotspot forecasts every 10 minutes and delivers hourly predictions for the next three hours with a spatial resolution of 20 meters for accumulated flood depths. Real-time disaster events are classified into four categories—general, severe, resolved, and ongoing—allowing incident commanders to quickly assess the severity and geographical spread of various disaster types. The system also enables side-by-side comparisons of current disaster site images with pre-disaster baselines to support situational awareness.

In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, New Taipei City applied the EDP system to support home care services. Through location-based spatial analysis, the system identified the distribution of home care recipients, aiding responsible agencies in delivering both health care and daily support. Furthermore, the New Taipei Disaster Information E-point Access System website provided timely information such as testing station capacity and service hours, frequently asked questions regarding home care, service hotlines, and direct links to the “New Taipei Home Care Network.” This ensured that residents could access essential pandemic-related information through multiple channels.

In 2023, New Taipei City established the nation's first New Taipei Net Zero Carbon Health Check Center, aimed at assisting enterprises in developing carbon inventory systems and carbon reduction strategies. The initiative is designed to enhance energy efficiency and green competitiveness among industries in New Taipei. Through seven core service functions, the center helps businesses implement cost-effective carbon reduction measures and achieve energy-saving improvements.

The center provides consultation and guidance through four main channels: a physical service counter, the “New Taipei LINE Low Carbon” account, the “New Taipei E-Low Carbon” email service, and the “New Taipei Net Zero Carbon Hotline.”

The seven core services include:
1.Industrial energy efficiency improvement
2.Subsidies for energy-saving equipment replacement and renewable energy adoption
3.Floor area ratio incentives for integrated energy management in industrial zones
4.Low-carbon transition consulting and project financing supported by the Industrial Development Bureau
5.Green finance action plans
6.Consultation on central government carbon reduction programs
7.Advisory services on domestic and international climate-related regulations

Starting in 2024, the center was upgraded to a Mobile Carbon Health Check Center, offering on-site services across New Taipei's industrial zones and parks. In 2024 alone, the mobile clinic has completed 20 sessions, providing professional consultation to support local enterprises in their energy-saving and carbon reduction efforts.

To support talent development across various industry sectors and assist enterprises in aligning with global trends and advancing digital transformation, the New Taipei City Government has launched annual professional training programs tailored to market trends, industry demands, and policy directions. These programs invite academic experts and industry leaders to deliver specialized courses for employees and managers recommended by local companies. Since the program's inception in 2011, a total of 3,509 industry professionals have been trained as of 2024. Participants span a wide range of sectors, including biotechnology, ICT, textiles, food processing, cultural and creative industries, and financial services.

Since 2007, the city has established the “Net-Zero Community Development Center” to actively promote carbon reduction efforts and engage directly with communities to implement greenhouse gas reduction initiatives.

To deepen community awareness of net-zero concepts and encourage energy-saving habits in daily home life, the city government launched the “New Taipei City Regional Net-Zero Promotion Center Development Program,” which consists of three main components:
1.Offering the “Building Net-Zero Communities” course, aiming to utilize educational functions to promote net-zero lifestyle concepts to the public and integrate them into everyday household practices.
2.Cultivating “Net-Zero Community Planners”, who, upon completing their training, will assist communities in planning and implementing net-zero transformation projects and help develop model net-zero communities in the city.
3.Establishing the “New Taipei City Regional Net-Zero Promotion Centers” within designated schools. These centers are responsible for conducting the “Building Net-Zero Communities” courses and serve as platforms for promoting the city's environmental protection policies and environmental education.

Since 2009, regional Net-Zero Promotion Centers have been successively established. Beginning in 2011, the “Building Net-Zero Communities” course has been offered, focusing on topics such as green transportation, electricity saving and energy conservation, resource reuse, and net-zero lifestyle.

Moving forward, the Net-Zero Promotion Centers will support the city's net-zero policies, including the promotion of low-pollution transportation options (e.g., public bike rental programs and electric scooter subsidies), net-zero tourism, intercity carpooling platforms for Taoyuan, Taipei, New Taipei, Yilan, and Keelung, as well as electricity-saving and energy-efficiency measures, with the goal of integrating carbon reduction practices into citizens' daily lives.

To accelerate the transition toward net-zero, the New Taipei City Government signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the University System of Taipei in October 2024 to officially establish the “New Taipei City Nudge-Based Net-Zero Impact Platform.” This platform is the first of its kind in Taiwan to adopt “nudging” as its core concept, emphasizing the use of soft governance approaches to guide enterprises and the public in participating in net-zero actions. The aim is to reduce perceived disruption during policy implementation while enhancing public and industrial support for and engagement in low-carbon transition.

The platform integrates resources from government, industry, academia, and research sectors. Through the operation of the Net-Zero Transformation Support Taskforce, it introduces innovative low-carbon business models such as “energy-saving insurance,” and provides diversified solutions covering technological, nature-based, and behavioral aspects to address the net-zero needs of different industries and social groups.

In the future, the platform will be linked with existing local policy tools in New Taipei City, such as the Energy-Saving Clinics, Carbon Health Check Centers, Industry and Economy University, and the “Energy-Saving E-Housing” program. It will also leverage the academic strengths of the University System of Taipei in areas including energy engineering, resource recycling, healthcare, maritime affairs, and water resources to jointly build a comprehensive local support system.

In addition, the platform will launch three major training programs: the “Corporate Net-Zero ESG Program,” the “Net-Zero Lifestyle Empowerment Program,” and the “Government Net-Zero Practice Program.” These programs aim to cultivate professionals with practical skills and strategic thinking in net-zero, while also responding to the growing international emphasis on consumer participation. The platform will promote both community and individual carbon asset initiatives, realizing an inclusive and participatory vision for sustainable transformation.

column17: 鑑於過去在私人土地上建立綠色能源經驗，在自由市場機制下發展。導致土地開發商與行業運營商勾結。參與者不裝設太陽能板，卻哄抬土地和饋線的價值，或者土地所有者出租土地後得不到權利和義務的保護，出現了種種亂象。為了有效整合和解決各種問題，我們通過經濟激勵，選擇合格、有能力的投資者參與本項目，以行政合約的形式在投資者和地主之間建立溝通平台，確保地主和太陽能業者雙方的權利和義務。地主可以從太陽能業者那裡獲得土地租金，而太陽能業者可以通過出售電力獲得收入。此外，太陽能業者還將售電收入的2%作為綠色基金，用於縣政府發展綠色能源。 這使得地主和太陽能業者在追求私人利益的同時，也可以配合推動屏東綠色能源政策，追求綜合的社會利益。本方案採用公開招標程序，加強太陽能裝設的流程和規模，防止劣質投資者不擇手段地簽訂行政契約，嚴重損害地主的權益。契約製訂自治規則：在規範項目輔導參與方變更土地類別設置太陽能時，雖然免除土地公告現值50%的費用（返還費用），但必須按照行政契約的內容，分期向綠地支付能源基金。對投資者的申請程序，我們會同有關部門進行同步審核。過去需要12個多月的土地類別變更流程縮短至不到半年，大大降低了投資者申請的時間成本。 由於土地所有者對背景知識了解不完整，因此我們收集了相關問題。透過網站搭建，公開相關資訊。然而，大多數地主都是長者。因此，我們到各鄉鎮辦說明會，進行現場溝通。通過行政契約，土地租金價格可以保持在合理範圍內。 此外，在與地主簽訂土地契約前，業者必須先向地主說明土地的使用方式， 在20年躉售契約到期後，地主可以繼續出租，或者復原。We carefully executed overall planning in consideration of the fact that the plan is a project for collective private land development. This was in view of the past promotional experience of “Aqua Solar Farm” project to set up green energy on private lands, where a lack of relevant specification limits resulted in land and PV industry participants developing under a free market mechanism. This in turn led land development participants to collude with industry operators to falsely occupy feeder lines. All sorts of chaos occurred as participants did not install PV capacity yet were driving up the value of land and of feeders, or landholders would not obtain the protection of rights and obligations after leasing their properties. In order to effectively integrate and solve various problems, we selected qualified and competent investors to participate in this project, established a communication platform between investors and landholders with administrative contracts to ensure the rights and obligations of both landholders and PV investors. The landholders can receive land rent from PV investors, while PV investors can have income by selling electricity. Furthermore, PV investors also provide 2% income of selling electricity as green funds for the County Government to develop green energy. This enabled landholders and PV investors to pursue private interests while also cooperating with the promotion of Pingtung's green energy policy and pursuing comprehensive social interests.This plan adopts an open tendering procedure in order to strengthen the process and scale of solar PV capacity in SSA, and to prevent inferior investors from unscrupulously attempting to sign an administrative contract and seriously damaging the rights and interests of the landholders. The contract formulates autonomous rules: in regulating project counseling participants when changing category of land for setting up solar energy, although 50% of the current value of the land announcement fee is waived (rebate fee), it must be paid in installments to the green energy fund in accordance with the commitment to the administrative contract. With regard to the application procedures of investors, we will conduct simultaneous examinations in conjunction with relevant departments. The land category change process, which took more than 12 months in the past, has been shortened to less than half a year, and this has greatly reduced the time cost of investors' applications.Private land shall be given priority for promotion in this SSA. Due to the large number of landowners in the SSA, they do not have a complete understanding of the background knowledge of PV installations on leased land and we have collected the relevant problems of PV installations on farmland in practice (including land category change procedures, taxation, agricultural insurance qualifications, and solar PV recycling). By building a digital platform, we have disclosed relevant information on the Internet. However, most local residents fall under the classification of digitally challenged senior citizens. Therefore, while in the early stages of plan implementation, we go to township offices to handle SSA project briefings with on-site explanations and answer to resolve public doubts. In addition, we also use administrative contracts to require investors to set up special accounts for performance management trusts for landholders in order to protect their rights.Through the constraints of our “administrative contract,” the land leasing price can be maintained within a reasonable range. Moreover, before signing a land contract with the landholders, the investor must first explain to the landholders the method of land use, such as whether the land needs to be backfilled, and the source of the backfilled earth, so as to avoid illegal dumping and backfilling of the land without the government's permit. After the investor's acquisition of the land is completed, it can only be used to build PV facilities. In addition, after the 20-year feed-in tariff contract with Tai-power Company has expired, the landholder can also choose whether to continue to rent out the solar PV system according to the current setup or ask the investor to remove the solar PV facility and restore it to agricultural land.

Pingtung County Government as a matchmaker, actively encourages pig farmers to provide animal manure and urine to farmland as fertilizer, building a circular economy. On the other hand, Pingtung County Government also persuades farmers to use biogas slurry and residue as fertilizer. Farmer Mr. Kuo experimented by dividing the farmland into an \'treatment group\' and a \'control group\' and treatment group was irrigated with biogas slurry and residue as fertilizer. After two to three years, farmer Mr. Kuo sent the soil for testing. The results proved that Farmlands using biogas slurry and residue will not produce problems such as odor, heavy metal or chemical pollution, and the crops will grow well, successfully attracting many farmers to use biogas slurry and residue as fertilizer. According to the statistics of the Environmental Protection Agency, Pingtung County can provide about 856,000 metric tons of biogas slurry and residue every year, and irrigate about 413 hectares of Farmlands, which can save about 10 million New Taiwan dollars in purchasing chemical fertilizer every year. Irrigation with biogas slurry and residue as fertilizer can prevent rivers from waste water pollution, reduce chemical fertilizer consumption and reduce green house gas emission.

Pingtung County Government plans to build a centralized processing plant near the Sanguan Livestock Farm in Neipu Township. The biogas power plan will be able to generate 7,200 kWh every day, supplying about 480 households for daily needs. The local people hope that the government can assist in solving the problem of odor and pollution of pig farms. The pig farmers are also willing to cooperate with County government and biogas investors to have more revenue.

column17: We are working with the New Bedford Community Economic Development Center to develop a Resilience Hub which will enable the CEDC to expand social services and to maintain operations even in the event of weather emergencies. Resilience Hubs have become a key community of practice of the Urban Sustainability Directors' Network (USDN), of which New Bedford is an active member. Resilience is the ability of people and communities to anticipate and adapt to or thrive amidst changing climate conditions and other hazard events. Resilience Hubs operate through three very different conditions: everyday; disruption; and recovery. At its core, the Resilience Hub serves as a central point to design and implement a strategy to address everyday stressors that are the root causes of vulnerability, and to help the community thrive. In addition, the Resilience Hub can deliver preparedness messaging to the communities that the Hub serves, and trusted community leaders can disseminate information and facilitate community cohesion before a disruption. Ideally, residents, businesses, and organizations will collectively manage the Hub including both internal and external communications. During a severe weather event or other disruptions, a Resilience Hub can be the central point for gathering, assessing impact, assembling information, accessing resources, and spearheading non-governmental response. Resilience Hubs can play a critical role in post-disruption recovery and ongoing communications needs. For resilient communications, the site can remain a central point for gathering, sharing information, and accessing resources. Hubs can also provide space for additional experts, aid organizations, volunteers, and support networks to gather and better understand and help meet community needs.

The Climate Action Fund was a municipal initiative aimed at supporting community-led projects that directly contributed to climate action. It was part of the broader Green Leaf 2024 program, and focused on promoting sustainable practices within local communities. The fund, sourced from Green Leaf's budget, had a total of DKK 500,000 for 2024, distributed over two application rounds, providing grants of up to DKK 20,000 per project.

The concept of climate action in this initiative went beyond discussions and encouraged practical interventions. Eligible projects included initiatives that repaired and reused materials, promoted resource sharing, encouraged climate-friendly food practices, or enhanced local biodiversity through activities like transforming gardens or building greenhouses from recycled materials. The focus was on hands-on, community-based solutions to environmental challenges.

In total, DKK 405,000 was distributed across 25 different projects, all aiming to foster sustainable, community-driven climate action. The fund, as part of Green Leaf 2024, played a crucial role in empowering communities to take meaningful steps in addressing climate change through collaboration and innovation.

This collaboration aims to promote sustainable commuting by providing free bike rentals to Helsingør Municipality employees until March 2025.

As part of the initiative, 50 bikes are available at Snekkersten Station and 20 on at Elsinor Station, encouraging employees to combine cycling with train travel for greener commuting. The program supports Helsingør's goal to reduce carbon emissions and improve its environmental footprint.

As a part of the newly started collaboration, it is free to use for Elsinor municipality's employees until march 2025, while other citizens can rent them through Donkey Republic's app at standard rates or with a membership. The bikes can be rented for short trips or multiple days, making sustainable travel more accessible to everyone in the area.

La Municipalidad de Independencia mantiene una relación de colaboración con ReSimple, en el marco de la Ley REP (Ley 20.920 de Responsabilidad Extendida del Productor), que establece la obligación de los productores de asumir la gestión de ciertos residuos prioritarios, incluyendo envases y embalajes.

Desde 2023, ambas instituciones cuentan con un convenio de colaboración que permite la recolección y valorización de envases y embalajes a nivel domiciliario, cubriendo aproximadamente el 70% de la comuna, y la operación de dos puntos limpios, donde las labores son ejecutadas en su totalidad por recicladores de base.

Para el año 2024, se recolectaron 1.200 toneladas de envases y embalajes, cifra que se proyecta aumentar durante el año 2025.

El convenio considera la contratación de los recicladores de base para todas las labores realizadas, tanto en las rutas de recolección domiciliaria como en los puntos limpios, asegurando que las operaciones se realicen de manera eficiente y sostenible, en línea con los objetivos ambientales de la municipalidad.

Cabe destacar que, de acuerdo con la Ley REP, todas las empresas productoras de envases y embalajes deben aportar con financiamiento para que los sistemas de gestión como ReSimple puedan financiar la recolección, valorización y reciclaje de estos residuos, garantizando su correcta disposición y fortaleciendo la economía circular en la comuna.

Esta colaboración asegura que los residuos sean gestionados adecuadamente, evitando su disposición inadecuada en la vía pública o en vertederos no autorizados.

La Municipalidad ha coordinado la vinculación con talleres de vehículos locales, de manera que Valoramas genere rutas de recolección eficientes, además de acopiar los neumáticos que se encuentran en la vía pública o en terrenos municipales, asegurando su disposición correcta y segura.

Al igual que ocurre con los envases y embalajes, las empresas productoras de neumáticos tienen la obligación de financiar a Valoramas para garantizar la valorización de este residuo, promoviendo la economía circular y el cumplimiento de la normativa ambiental vigente.

column17: Saanich has been an active committee member supporting the Greater Victoria Extreme Weather Response Plan (EWP). This strategy coordinates the region's overnight shelters in the event of extreme/dangerous weather conditions. In 2024, the Salvation Army Housing and Support Services Division is continued to fill the role of EWP Coordinator in collaboration with BC Housing, local governments and non-governmental organizations including shelter providers. Saanich Emergency Program and Police receive correspondence from the EWP Coordinator any time criteria is met to activate seasonal shelters. Saanich Police conduct proactive check-ins with vulnerable persons and enhance park patrols during extreme weather events. Police have access to shelter information and connect those who are in need with appropriate services including medical and transportation services. The District has collaborated with the Capital Regional District and researchers at the School of Public Administration at the University of Victoria to survey populations who are vulnerable to extreme heat about their experiences with the 2021 heat dome and accessing government information and supports.

column17: The District of Saanich partnered with researchers at the UBC Research on Active Transportation (REACT) Lab, a group dedicated to finding ways to make transportation systems more effective, sustainable, equitable, and healthy and who were interested in accessing data from a local e-bike incentive program. A research project on the pilot incentive program was established with funding from Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council (NSERC) and support letters and funding from Saanich, the Capital Regional District (CRD), the Community Social Planning Council (CSPC), and non-profit One Earth. Results indicated a 30-40% reduction in car travel and an average decrease of 16 kilograms of CO2 emissions per week among participants. Notably, lower-income households reduced their GHG emissions the most, with many indicating they wouldn't have purchased an e-bike without the incentive. This program demonstrated cost-effectiveness, finding that the e-bike incentives surpassed cost-effectiveness of electric car incentives in reducing emissions while offering additional benefits like increased physical activity and reduced travel costs. About the REACT Lab: https://reactlab.civil.ubc.ca/ Full study: https://reactlab.civil.ubc.ca/saanich-ebike-incentives

The City Government of Batangas fully complies with the Government Energy Management Program (GEMP) as mandated under the Energy Efficiency and Conservation Act (RA 11285) and related administrative orders. In line with this, all city-owned and operated offices have adopted energy efficiency and conservation measures, including the retrofitting of government facilities with LED lighting and energy-efficient cooling systems, the conduct of regular energy audits, and the installation of renewable energy technologies such as solar panels in select buildings.

Furthermore, the City has institutionalized its commitment through the enactment of the Local Energy Code (Ordinance No. 22-19, Series of 2023) and the earlier E-Code of 2010, which mandate energy conservation practices across all government buildings and operations. These policies reinforce the city's adherence to the 10% annual reduction target in electricity and fuel consumption set under the GEMP.

By complying with the GEMP, Batangas City not only strengthens operational efficiency and reduces costs, but also contributes significantly to the Philippines' national energy efficiency goals and climate change mitigation strategies.

Other program also includes the following: crafting and implementing the Local Energy Efficiency and Conservation Plan, including energy audits of public buildings and training on energy management for LGU staff.

column17: The Batangas City Mangrove Conservation Ecopark delivers environmental, social, and economic gains that extend beyond carbon sequestration. By restoring and protecting vital mangrove habitats, it safeguards coastal communities from storm surges and erosion while preserving biodiversity. The Ecopark also serves as a living laboratory for academic institutions, enabling scientific research, environmental education, and citizen science programs. Its scenic boardwalks and interpretive trails attract eco-tourists, generating livelihood opportunities for local residents. By linking conservation with tourism, education, and community participation, the Ecopark strengthens climate resilience, fosters inclusive economic growth, and promotes Batangas City as a model for nature-based solutions.

column17: The Annual Environmental Summit for Batangas City business establishments is envisioned as a collaborative platform that brings together Environmental Compliance Officers (ECOs), local industries, and government partners to strengthen collective action on sustainability and climate-related issues. By serving as a business refresher on environmental compliance, the summit reinforces each establishment's responsibilities under national and local regulations while opening opportunities for dialogue on emerging challenges such as waste management, water use efficiency, air quality, and carbon reduction. Beyond compliance, the gathering promotes public-private collaboration in climate adaptation and mitigation, encouraging companies to share best practices, align with citywide environmental targets, and co-create innovative solutions that balance economic growth with ecological protection. In doing so, the summit fosters a culture of shared accountability and positions Batangas City's business sector as an active partner in achieving climate resilience and sustainable urban development.

Batangas City Katuwang ng Barangay: Responsable, Aktibo, Disiplinado (KaBRAD) is a collaborative community-driven program championed by the Batangas City government. It's spearheaded by the City Solid Waste Management Board (BCSWMB), with active support from the Office of the City Environment and Natural Resources Office (OCENRO) and the Office of the City General Services Officer (OCGSO).

It encourages barangays to take an active role in maintaining cleanliness, practicing proper waste management, and instilling responsibility, activeness, and discipline among residents.

The program demonstrates how local action can drive big change. By empowering communities at the grassroots level, Batangas City has built a culture of environmental responsibility that contributes to cleaner surroundings, better waste diversion, and a stronger sense of community ownership in environmental protection.

Cagayan de Oro City, through its partnership with the National Resilience Council (NRC) and academic partner Xavier University (XU), has advanced evidence-based resilience initiatives that bridge local governance, science, and community engagement. Since 2018, XU has worked closely with the city and NRC under the Resilient LGU Program, developing tools such as the Web-based Geospatial Risk Dashboard (Web-GRiD) to provide real-time spatial analysis for disaster risk reduction and crisis response—an innovation that gained national recognition in 2021. The collaboration was further strengthened through the NRC's “Adopt-A-City” Program, where XU was formally recognized as the primary academic partner for Cagayan de Oro, contributing technical expertise, training, and research support. High-level engagements, such as the April 2023 courtesy visit of NRC leaders to XU and the LGU, reaffirmed a shared commitment to applying science and technology for resilience planning, ensuring that the city's strategies for risk reduction, climate adaptation, and sustainable urban development are grounded in data, collaboration, and long-term capacity building.

In October 2019, Cagayan de Oro City took part in a landmark renewable energy initiative when the European Union, in partnership with the Department of Energy, launched the ASEP-CELL (Access to Sustainable Energy Programme - Clean Energy Living Laboratories). The project was implemented by ICLEI-SEAS and Xavier University, which aimed to bolster energy policy-making and capacity-building by linking academic institutions from Mindanao in support of the Department of Energy's rural electrification and clean energy goals. Anchored on three pillars—knowledge management, capacity development, and advocacy—the ASEP-CELL initiative sought to advance public awareness, cultivate institutional skills, and shape low-carbon energy pathways to benefit underserved communities.

Recently, in July 2025, the City Government of Cagayan de Oro and Xavier University formally entered into a collaborative partnership through the Smart Waste-to-Energy Empowerment for Cagayan de Oro City (SWEEP CDOC) project. Signed on July 25, 2025, the agreement involves Xavier University leading research and implementation while the LGU provides crucial support—such as data, logistical assistance, technical resources, and project funding—underscoring a shared commitment to adopting waste-to-energy (WtE) technology as part of the city's urban sustainability efforts. This initiative builds on foundational groundwork laid in 2024, when the Department of Science and Technology (DOST), through its research arm PCIEERD, established the Green Bio-H₂E Research and Development Laboratory at Xavier University's College of Engineering. Supported by a combined investment of approximately ₱6 million, the lab explores innovative methods of converting municipal and industrial waste—especially wastewater—into viable clean energy sources like bio-hydrogen, aiming to lower energy costs and strengthen the regional renewable energy landscape. The 2025 SWEEP CDOC agreement represents the latest and most tangible expression of this evolving partnership, transforming academic research into actionable, city-level programs that support the transition toward renewable energy and sustainable urban systems.

For resilient building and infrastructure, since the formal signing of the MOA in November 2021, Cagayan de Oro City and Xavier University have partnered to localize the Philippine Green Building Code to better reflect the city's specific environmental realities and development priorities. Xavier University led technical analysis and recommendation efforts, focusing on sustainability dimensions, enforcement mechanisms, and incentivization strategies. Their recommendations were formally presented to city officials in mid-2022. Building on that groundwork, a multi-sectoral Technical Working Group—led by the OBO with XU participation—has been refining a local green building ordinance since 2023. The goal is to embed green building standards into municipal regulation in a manner that promotes resource efficiency, healthy indoor environments, and climate resilience across all housing sectors.

Moreover, several academic institutions in Cagayan de Oro City have partnered with the local government in advancing climate change mitigation and adaptation initiatives. In May 2024, the youth-led coalition Youth for Climate Justice (Y4CJ)—with members from Golden Heritage Polytechnic State College, Pilgrim Christian College, Southern Philippines College, University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines (USTP), Capitol University, Xavier University, and the Archdiocese of Cagayan de Oro—submitted over 3,000 signatures to city officials, urging the declaration of a climate emergency and the adoption of stronger climate-responsive policies.

column17: “Calder and Colne Landscape Links” (CCaLL), is set to rejuvenate the natural environment across Kirklees and Calderdale, enhancing wildlife habitats, cutting carbon emissions, boosting flood resilience, and reducing wildfire risks. With Kirklees and Calderdale Council working in partnership, the initiative has secured substantial grant funding to embark on this transformative venture. The project has received £750,000 from the Government's Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) Landscape Recovery programme and £100,000 from the Yorkshire Regional Flood and Coastal Committee. The CCaLL project aims to restore moorlands, plant trees, and create wildlife-rich habitats that better connect valley towns with moorland tops along the rivers Calder and Colne. Collaborators include the Calder and Colne Rivers Trust, Environmental Projects in Kirklees (EPIKs), Moors for the Future Partnership, and the Environment Agency. This initiative aligns with Kirklees and Calderdale's commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2038. The project will contribute to this goal by planting trees, hedges, woodlands, and wildflower meadows, restoring peat moorlands, and creating wetlands. These natural “sponges” will absorb carbon dioxide, enhance wildlife habitats, and mitigate climate change impacts.

The partnership covers the full local authority areas of Angus, Dundee, and Perth & Kinross and is supported by Adaptation Scotland, a programme funded by the Scottish Government. Dundee City Council plays an active role in its governance and delivery, contributing time, staff expertise, and resources to help build the partnership's foundations, including its vision, priorities, governance structure, and branding.

The CRT Vision and Priorities were co-developed through workshops and consultations with over 60 representatives from local organisations and community groups. This inclusive process has built shared ownership of eight regional priorities, spanning themes such as nature-based solutions, health and community resilience, and communication and engagement.

Concrete outcomes to date include securing funding for a two-year secretariat role, establishing working groups to drive delivery, and beginning development of a pipeline of priority projects for investment. CRT has also committed in the next two year to host knowledge-sharing events and provide free climate resilience training to local organisations and communities, supporting capacity-building across sectors.

By engaging local authorities, national government programmes, businesses, and civil society in a single coordinated structure, Climate Ready Tayside represents a transformative model of regional collaboration that strengthens local resilience while aligning with the Scottish Government's national adaptation objectives.

Another example of collaboration is Dundee's active engagement in the Scottish Climate Intelligence Service (SCIS), a national initiative funded by the Scottish Government and all 32 Scottish local authorities through COSLA. SCIS is delivered through the Edinburgh Climate Change Institute (ECCI), the Improvement Service, and the Sustainable Scotland Network, with the ClimateOS platform (developed by ClimateView) providing the national data and modelling capability.

Through SCIS, Dundee has worked closely with national and local government partners to share knowledge, build capacity, and co-develop consistent approaches to climate planning. This has included participation in national workshops, peer-to-peer learning sessions, and joint development of data methodologies. The service provides a platform for local authorities to learn from one another, strengthen the evidence base for decision-making, and align local climate action with national policy objectives.

Dundee has also played a leadership role within this collaboration, having been the first local authority in Scotland to use the ClimateView (ClimateOS) platform in 2021, prior to SCIS being established. This early experience allowed Dundee to provide feedback on the platform's functionality and share practical insights with peers once the tool was rolled out nationally.

By contributing to and benefiting from SCIS, Dundee is helping to build a stronger, collective capacity for climate action across Scotland's local authorities, ensuring a more coordinated and evidence-led pathway to net zero.

El objetivo del plan era combatir el cambio climático a lo largo del país mediante la disminución de residuos orgánicos dispuestos en rellenos sanitarios; para lograrlo se propusieron diferentes acciones, siendo una de ellas el tratamiento domiciliario de la materia orgánica a través del compostaje, lo que resulta en la conversión de los desechos orgánicos en un fertilizante natural.
El beneficio incluyó capacitaciones para el equipo municipal y la entrega de 300 kits de compostaje que beneficiaron a 14 jardines Infantiles y 286 Familias de la comuna. Por su parte, la entrega de dichos kits fue el puntapié para que el municipio impulsará el 'Programa de Compostaje Domiciliario' que a la fecha alcanza una cobertura de cerca de 1.500 hogares y establecimientos educacionales en Peñalolén.

column17: El programa \'Aires Nuevos para la Primera Infancia\' es una iniciativa dirigida a promover el bienestar y el desarrollo integral de los niños y niñas en sus primeros años de vida. El programa busca brindar un ambiente saludable y estimulante para los niños, centrándose en aspectos como la calidad del aire, la seguridad, la alimentación y la estimulación temprana. El programa se enfoca en la importancia de garantizar espacios físicos adecuados, libres de contaminantes y con una buena calidad del aire, ya que esto puede tener un impacto significativo en la salud y el desarrollo de los niños pequeños. Además, se hace hincapié en la seguridad de los entornos donde los niños pasan su tiempo, asegurándose de que estén libres de peligros y riesgos. La colaboración entre el programa y el municipio se basa en un convenio que conlleva la instalación por parte del programa de monitores (instrumentos electrónicos) en colegios y jardines infantiles , como también por parte del municipio el rol de fiscalización con inspectores municipales situaciones que atenten contra la calidad del aire(consumo de Leña, vehículos motorizados no autorizados y potenciales contaminantes a la calidad del aire)En resumen, el programa \'Aires Nuevos para la Primera Infancia\' se centra en proporcionar un entorno saludable, seguro y estimulante para los niños en sus primeros años de vida, abordando aspectos como la calidad del aire, la seguridad, la alimentación y la estimulación temprana.

A través de un trabajo colaborativo con los Centros de Formación Técnica Escolares de la comuna, se implementa el proyecto “Huertas Urbanas”, en el que jóvenes estudiantes de la carrera “Construcción con mención en Edificaciones y Terminaciones” diseñan y construyen 154 huertos de cama alta, destinados a ser instalados en 66 espacios comunitarios de la comuna dentro del marco del programa municipal “Infraestructuras Verdes”.
Esta iniciativa cumple múltiples objetivos estratégicos:
- Fortalecimiento del tejido comunitario, al promover la colaboración entre el municipio, vecinos y estudiantes.
- Seguridad alimentaria, generando espacios productivos que contribuyen a la disponibilidad de alimentos frescos en la comuna.
- Transferencia de conocimientos y formación técnica, al integrar a jóvenes en experiencias prácticas que combinan educación, sostenibilidad y acción comunitaria.
- Impacto ambiental, mediante la implementación de infraestructuras verdes que mejora la calidad ambiental y la resiliencia urbana frente al cambio climático.
El proyecto constituye un modelo replicable de educación ambiental y desarrollo comunitario, que integra aprendizaje técnico, participación ciudadana y sostenibilidad urbana.

En el marco del programa del Gobierno Regional Metropolitano “Bosque de Bolsillo”, en alianza con la Fundación Cultiva, la Municipalidad de Peñalolén implementó la plantación de un bosque urbano en un terreno municipal de 400 m2, con más de 1.000 árboles nativos de bajo consumo hídrico.
Esta iniciativa responde a los impactos de las olas de calor extremo, promoviendo la creación de refugios climáticos en entornos urbanos mediante la naturalización de espacios públicos. Los bosques de bolsillo generan múltiples beneficios:
- Reducción de la temperatura urbana y adaptación al cambio climático.
- Incremento de áreas verdes accesibles, favoreciendo la equidad territorial en el acceso a infraestructura verde.
- Conservación de biodiversidad nativa y fortalecimiento de servicios ecosistémicos urbanos.
- Espacios de encuentro comunitario, orientados a la contemplación, la recreación y la educación ambiental.
De esta manera, la comuna contribuye a la resiliencia urbana frente al cambio climático, integrando soluciones basadas en la naturaleza dentro de su estrategia local de acción climática.

Proyecto automatización de composteras El municipio de Peñalolén desarrolla desde hace varios años un programa de compostaje domiciliario que ha beneficiado a más de 1.400 familias, cuyo principal sello diferenciador es el monitoreo, seguimiento y acompañamiento técnico realizado por un equipo municipal especializado. Este enfoque busca garantizar que la inversión pública destinada al programa se traduzca efectivamente en los retornos ambientales esperados, tales como la reducción de residuos orgánicos enviados a disposición final y la disminución de los gases de efecto invernadero. 
No obstante, se reconoce que el recurso humano disponible es limitado, lo que dificulta la escalabilidad del programa. En este contexto, se está implementando un proyecto piloto de innovación tecnológica, financiado a través de un fondo adjudicado en la Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, mediante el cual un equipo del área de diseño desarrollan un prototipo de mecanismo de automatización que permitirá obtener datos en tiempo real sobre el uso y funcionamiento de las composteras domiciliarias.
La incorporación de esta tecnología permitirá:
- Optimizar el monitoreo y control del proceso de compostaje.
- Escalar el programa a un mayor número de hogares sin incrementar proporcionalmente los recursos humanos requeridos.

column17: McGill University's Dr. Mylene Riva, in collaboration with the Town of Bridgewater, conducted an energy poverty study in 2022. The aim of the study was to document the extent of energy poverty in the Town of Bridgewater before the implementation of the Energy Poverty Reduction Program (EPRP). To do so, a survey covering energy costs, household incomes, housing conditions, and wellbeing was distributed to a representative sample of the population. This information was gathered and analysed. Among its key findings was a confirmation that the community's energy poverty rate is 38%. This research has allowed the TOB and the research team to draw a more complete picture of energy poverty in the community. The research initiative was the first of its kind in Canada. Results are now hosted on the www.energizebridgewater.ca website and will be published in academic journals and distributed to government and community partners. Follow-up research between the Town and McGill University is being planned.

column17: La Convention Citoyenne des Transitions de la Métropole Rouen Normandie a été créée en juin 2023 pour réfléchir et proposer des solutions pour un avenir durable et résilient face aux enjeux climatiques et environnementaux à l'échelle de la métropole Rouen Normandie et dans la perspective de la révision de documents de planification à l'horizon 2050. La Convention Citoyenne se compose de 80 membres représentatifs de la diversité des communes de la Métropole, qui se sont réunis pendant 9 mois pour travailler sur trois grandes familles de dilemmes : l'aménagement du territoire, les risques et la nature, et l'attractivité, la sobriété et la production d'énergie. Les membres de la Convention ont été informés et sensibilisés aux enjeux de la transition écologique et ont auditionné des experts de l'ensemble des questions liées à l'aménagement du territoire, à la lutte contre le changement climatique et à l'adaptation à une société bas carbone. Ils ont également échangé et débattu entre eux pour proposer des positions sur les questions difficiles qui leur étaient posées, les actions prioritaires à mettre en œuvre pour y parvenir et les conditions de réussite de ces actions. Le rapport final de la Convention a été adopté par 96% des membres et a été rédigé par les membres de la Convention. A l'occasion du grand oral organisé au Pavillon des Transitions à Rouen, les membres de la convention ont exposé leur vision du territoire à une centaine d'élus, techniciens et citoyens. Ce travail a été salué par la Métropole pour sa pertinence et son exhaustivité. Les élus ont exprimé leur gratitude envers les membres de la Convention pour leur travail et ont souligné l'importance de cette vision citoyenne pour la construction des politiques publiques de demain.

L'ensemble de la démarche menée avec le CETE entre 2020 et 2021 est reprise en annexe, avec leur contribution qui a fait l'objet d'une restitution aux élus métropolitains le 16 juin 2021. À partir de septembre 2021, le CETE a intégré le Conseil de Développement Durable, comme un des trois comités du CDD (les deux autres sont le comité des partenaires mobilité et le comité changement climatique et aménagement du territoire).En 2022, le comité des partenaires mobilités de ce CDD a contribué au futur Plan des Mobilités (PDM) de la Métropole. Après une séance dédiée à la présentation du PDM et de ses enjeux et un atelier de travail spécifique, les membres de ce comité ont décidé de bâtir leur contribution autour de 2 axes :- La mobilité inclusive et solidaire- Le stationnement comme outil pour diminuer la part modale de la voiture en centre-ville.Deux groupes de travail thématiques ont ainsi été organisés, ils se sont réunis 6 fois sur le thème de la mobilité inclusive et 3 fois sur celui du stationnement. Il est à noter que le thème de la démobillité (ou mobilité maîtrisée) n'a pu être traité faute de temps, mais qu'il pourrait faire l'objet de travaux ultérieurs au sein du comité et en lien avec les services de la Métropole. Le document est joint en annexe.En 2023, le comité Changement Climatique et Aménagement du Territoire du CDD a rendu sa contribution au projet du quartier Flaubert. column17: Plusieurs outils d'accompagnement des habitants aux changements liés à la transition écologique sont déployés depuis 2020. 1/ Mon P'tit Atelier : dans le dispositif Mon P'tit Atelier de la COP21, la Métropole cherche à sensibiliser le grand public en favorisant l'organisation d'expositions, ateliers participatifs, sorties pédagogiques, manifestations en lien avec la transition écologique sur le territoire des communes. Elle s'appuie ce faisant sur la logistique des communes et leur propose un catalogue d'animations qu'elle subventionne. Depuis 2020, 435 animations ont été réalisées et 12 453 participants ont été sensibilisés. 2/ Le club COP21 : le club de la Cop21 de la Métropole Rouen Normandie est une communauté de citoyens engagés - ou qui veulent s'engager - en faveur du climat. Au 31 décembre 2022, le Club comptait 1 853 membres sur Facebook. 3/ Accompagnement de structures sociales : dans l'objectif de sensibiliser et accompagner les publics plus précaires, la Métropole travaille depuis plusieurs années avec des structures sociales (entreprises d'insertion, Centre Communal d'Action Social, Centres médico-sociaux, centres socio-culturels, centres d'hébergement et d'insertion, bailleurs sociaux, structures d'accompagnement des jeunes...). Elle propose des formations pour les travailleurs sociaux portant notamment sur l'énergie, la mobilité, l'initiation au vélo et l'alimentation durable. Ces formations sont gratuites, et permettent aux travailleurs sociaux d'appréhender les enjeux et de connaître les moyens de mettre en pratique pour accompagner les personnes. Ces travailleurs sociaux deviennent ainsi des relais pour accompagner les citoyens dans la transition écologique. 4/ Accompagnement des scolaires : depuis 2018, une convention de partenariat a été signée entre la Métropole et l'Éducation Nationale (Direction des Services Départementaux de l'Éducation Nationale) pour l'accompagnement des établissements du premier degré. Les actions pédagogiques visent prioritairement les élèves des écoles primaires (maternelles et élémentaires). Les enseignants des collèges et lycées sont accompagnés au cas par cas, en fonction de leurs demandes, et notamment dans le cadre des labellisations « établissements du développement durable ». 3 types d'offre sont proposés aux enseignants : les appels à projets (accompagnement à l'année des enseignants), les parcours pédagogiques (composés d'une animation, d'une visite et d'un engagement de la classe) et l'animation ponctuelle (qui a pour but de sensibiliser les élèves en amont d'un programme plus complet). En complément, de nombreuses fiches pédagogiques sont disponibles sur le site internet de la Métropole. 5/ Accompagnement de clubs sportifs : les associations sportives font l'objet d'accompagnement pour réduire leur empreinte carbone. 6/ Club de jardiniers : le Club des jardiniers de la Métropole propose, à tous les habitants du territoire de la Métropole qui souhaitent y adhérer, tout au long de l'année, des ateliers, des visites, des rencontres conviviales, pour des jardins toujours plus durables, respectueux de l'environnement et de la santé. La grainothèque mobile du club est à disposition lors de chaque rencontre pour les échanges de graines entre jardiniers. L'adhésion est gratuite et donne accès à l'espace réservé en ligne et au groupe Facebook. Le club comptait 1 426 membres en 2022. 7/ Le Pavillon des Transitions : Lieu dédié à tous les publics et gratuit, le Pavillon des Transitions propose de faire comprendre les enjeux écologiques afin d'avoir les moyens d'agir au quotidien : « connaître pour agir ». Biodiversité, protection des ressources, réemploi, réduction des déchets... le Pavillon des transitions aborde tous les sujets de la protection de l'environnement et de l'adaptation de notre territoire à ces enjeux, à travers des expositions thématiques, des cycles de conférences, un centre de ressources, des animations de sensibilisation et des ateliers « Faire soi‐même ». Le Pavillon des transitions se positionne également comme un « laboratoire » des transitions, en mêlant les approches pluridisciplinaires et les acteurs : scientifiques, artistes, associations de protection de l'environnement, etc... Depuis son ouverture le 7 juin 2022, le Pavillon des Transitions a accueilli plus de 20 000 visiteurs (à la date du 8 juin 2023).

column17: Dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre de son Plan Climat Air Énergie Territorial (PCAET), la Métropole a souhaité constituer et animer un groupe d'experts locaux et indépendants sur les questions d'adaptation au changement climatique : le « Groupe d'experts interdisciplinaire sur l'évolution du climat local » de la Métropole de Rouen (« GIEC LOCAL »). Des experts membres de l'Université de Rouen Normandie, du Centre Hospitalier Universitaire de Rouen, de l'Agence Normande de la Biodiversité et le Développement Durable, d'ATMO Normandie, du Centre d'Etudes et d'Expertise sur les Risques, l'Environnement, la Mobilité et l'Aménagement, l'Institut Polytechnique Unilasalle, l'Institut National des Sciences Appliquées Rouen Normandie ainsi que l'Ecole Nationale d'Architecture de Normandie ont donc été sollicités pour le composer. Les relations entre les différents membres du GIEC local sont nombreuses dans des secteurs aussi divers que l'innovation et le développement économique, le rayonnement international, le financement de la pédagogie et de la recherche, le transport, l'urbanisme, l'accès à la culture, la médiation scientifique, le logement (notamment étudiant), la qualité de la vie étudiante et l'attractivité.Créé en 2018, l'ambition du GIEC LOCAL est de fournir une expertise approfondie des impacts du changement climatique et de ses conséquences à l'échelle locale autour de plusieurs thématiques : climat, psychologie sociale, ressources en eau, agriculture, biodiversité, qualité de l'air, santé publique, urbanisme, architecture, mobilités, énergie, économie. Cette expertise prend la forme de synthèses regroupant et confrontant les principales conclusions de la littérature scientifique complétées par la vision d'autres experts locaux provenant de structures spécialistes du sujet. Le GIEC LOCAL a produit neuf expertises et l'état des lieux des connaissances des impacts locaux du changement climatique sera terminé à la fin de l'année 2023. Ces premiers travaux ont mis en évidence la nécessité de renforcer les connaissances à l'échelle locale sur le changement climatique. L'objectif final est d'aboutir, avec la Métropole, à une stratégie et à un plan d'actions pour l'adaptation du territoire au changement climatique, qui viendront s'intégrer dans le PCAET. Les publications du GIEC Local peuvent être consultées sur le site de la COP 21 locale Rouen Normandie : https://www.notrecop21.fr/comite-scientifique-sur-le-climat-giec-local

column17: Par délibération du conseil métropolitain du 16 décembre 2019, la Métropole a engagé l'élaboration de son PACTE (Plan d'Accompagnement des Changements de la Transition Ecologique). À partir des engagements pris par les communes dans le cadre de l'Accord de Rouen pour le Climat (novembre 2018) pour la sensibilisation du public, elle propose un accompagnement aux communes via le renforcement de dispositifs existants et le développement de nouveaux outils. Le projet de PACTE développe un réseau de lieux communaux \'relais COP21\' accueillant des animations et des expositions, et diffusant de la ressource pour l'action citoyenne quotidienne en faveur du climat.Au 31 décembre 2022, 24 communes sont signataires de la convention PACTE : Malaunay, Elbeuf-sur-seine, La Londe, Roncherolles-sur-le-Vivier, Sotteville-lès-Rouen, Duclair, Quévreville-la-Poterie, Sainte-Marguerite-sur-Duclair, Bois-Guillaume, Saint-Paër, Grand-Quevilly, Mont-Saint-Aignan, Darnétal, Saint-Pierre-lès-Elbeuf, Cléon, Saint-Aubin-lès-Elbeuf, Saint-Martin-de-Boscherville, Rouen, Petit-Couronne, Grand Couronne, Canteleu, La Bouille, Maromme et Jumièges. L'accompagnement de la Métropole consiste en la prise en charge financière d'animations de sensibilisation à l'environnement et de mise à disposition de matériels pédagogiques, ainsi que la de la mise en œuvre de dispositifs d'accompagnement par le biais notamment de \'Mon P'tit Atelier de la COP21\'. Les thématiques concernées par ces dispositifs sont :- la réduction des déchets- l'alimentation saine, durable et locale- la réduction des consommations d'énergie- la préservation de la biodiversité et de la nature- l'éco-consommation- la mobilité durable- le jardinage durable...

column17: La Métropole Rouen Normandie s'est engagée en 2019 dans le réseau européen « Urbenpact - towards net-zero cities », qui a été constitué dans le cadre d'un appel à projet Urbact. Il rassemble 8 villes ou régions européennes qui travaillent sur l'objectif « net zero energy » ou « 100% énergie renouvelable » à l'horizon 2050 :-Tampere (Finlande)-Bialystok (Pologne)-Galati (Roumanie)-Elefsina (Grèce)-Palma di Montechiaro (Italie)-Alto Minho (Portugal)-Clermont-Ferrand Auvergne Métropole (France)-Métropole Rouen Normandie.Clermont-Ferrand Auvergne Métropole est le leader du partenariat.Après une première phase de mise en place du réseau et de définition des modalités de travail entre juin 2019 et juin 2020, les partenaires ont travaillé entre juillet 2020 et juillet 2022 selon la méthodologie définie pour les projets Urbact.La Métropole a ainsi rédigé un plan d'action intégré visant l'atteinte de l'objectif 100% énergie renouvelable et de récupération et la neutralité carbone à l'horizon 2050. Basé sur la stratégie et le plan d'actions approuvés en 2019 dans le cadre du PCAET, il les précise en opérant sur les principaux facteurs d'émissions de gaz à effet de serre : énergie et bâtiment, mais aussi transport et industrie que le PCAET approuvé en 2019 n'avait pas traités. Il intègre notamment les études en cours afférentes à la révision de Plan de Mobilité. Il constituera une base pour l'élaboration du futur SCOT valant PCAET.La stratégie repose ainsi sur 4 priorités et 13 challenges qui sont déclinés en fiches actions.La co-construction a été réalisée dans le cadre du Groupe Local Urbact, constitué d'une vingtaine de membres représentant les principales thématiques du plan d'action (Industrie, énergies renouvelables, rénovation thermique des bâtiments, mobilité et vision transversale). Ce groupe s'est réuni à 9 reprises depuis 2019 (4 réunions en 2022). Un groupe thématique dédié à l'industrie a été constitué, auquel a été adjoint la participation de 10 industriels et de représentants des filières économiques. Ce groupe continuera à se réunir au cours des prochains mois pour suivre l'étude de « définition d'une stratégie et d'un plan d'actions pour l'atteinte des objectifs 100% énergie renouvelable et neutralité carbone dans le secteur industriel » encore en cours.La Métropole a également participé aux 12 meetings transnationaux (3 en 2022) qui ont permis des échanges méthodologiques et de bonnes pratiques entre les membres du réseau. Le soutien des experts a été notamment donné dans le cadre de ces meetings, ainsi que pour l'élaboration de du plan d'action intégré.Dans le cadre de l'élaboration du plan d'action, la Métropole a expérimenté plusieurs actions de petite échelle, dont le bilan a alimenté l'écriture des fiches actions et qui ont été subventionnées dans le cadre du projet :-Salon des solutions durables-Comité citoyen sur la mobilité-Ambassadeurs de la mobilité-CollaborathonsL'ensemble des activités effectuées dans le cadre d'Urbenpact fait l'objet d'une subvention du FEDER à hauteur de 47 971,62€.

column17: 1/ Salon des solutions durables :Le jeudi 6 octobre 2022 s'est déroulé au Parc Expo de Rouen une nouvelle édition du salon des solutions durables dans le cadre de de l'édition 3 de l'événement « Rouen Métropole Capitale du Monde d'après ». Un rendez-vous dédié aux acteurs économiques et aux collectivités pour trouver des solutions concrètes et prendre des contacts entre entreprises. Composé de 50 stands d'offreurs de solutions, le salon a attiré près de 400 personnes autour des nouvelles solutions durables, avec un focus cette année sur la rénovation énergétique. Tout au long de la journée, des ateliers ont permis de sensibiliser les professionnels et collectivités sur la rénovation énergétique, la décarbonation, le numérique responsable ou encore l'écologie industrielle et territoriale ... Les entreprises engagées étaient également à l'honneur tout au long de cette journée. 5 entreprises ou administrations ont renouvelé leur engagement COP21 et 7 ont signé la charte de l'Institut du Numérique Responsable. Enfin, le salon s'est conclu par la cérémonie de remise du label éco-défis à 14 artisans et commerçants, dans le cadre du partenariat entre la Chambre des Métiers et de l'Artisanat et la Métropole. 2/ Eco-défis des artisans et commerçantsLe dispositif « écodéfis » est porté par la Chambre de Commerce et d'artisanat, dans le cadre d'une convention avec la Métropole. La Chambre de Métiers et de l'Artisanat de Normandie a souhaité prendre part à la démarche de COP21 locale par le déploiement de l'action Eco-Défis sur le territoire métropolitain, visant à mobiliser collectivement les artisans sur des engagements en faveur du climat, et de les valoriser au moyen du label national. Chaque artisan doit choisir et relever au moins 3 défis engendrant un impact positif et significatif sur le climat, la qualité de l'air, la biodiversité, l'eau, l'environnement, ... Les 3 défis choisis doivent appartenir à au moins 2 familles de défis distinctes. L'entreprise peut choisir 2 défis déjà relevés durant les 2 dernières années (au maximum), à condition qu'ils aient été significatifs, et s'engage à réaliser un défi supplémentaire au minimum.En 2022, 14 dossiers ont été labellisés.En guise de preuve, voici un lien vers le site notreCOP21.fr détaillant le bilan des évènements : https://www.notrecop21.fr/index.php/retour-sur-capitale-du-monde-dapres

column17: Préfiguration de l'assemblée des partenaires (STERN) avec pour objectifs de :- Rassembler l'ensemble des partenaires intervenant dans la rénovation énergétique- Faire émerger un écosystème et des filières professionnelles- Faciliter la rénovation énergétique massive sur le territoireL'Assemblée des partenaires est constituée de représentants de collectivités territoriales (Région, Département, Métropole), des agences nationales ou régionales ( CCI, CMA, CAUE, ADIL, ADEME, ANAH), des têtes de réseaux professionnels sur secteur du bâtiment et de l'énergie (FFB, CAPEB, Enedis, GRDF) quelques associations telles que UFC-Que-Choisir.Elle devra faciliter les conditions d'une accélération des rénovations énergétiques sur le territoire.Un fonctionnement par coalitions d'acteurs sera mis en place et auront pour mission de travailler sur :- La mobilisation des professionnels de la rénovation du bâtiment- Les filières biosourcées- Les parties prenantes du parcours d'accompagnement- Financement des projets de transition énergétique- Autres thématiques (ouverture de coalition d'acteur en fonction des freins identifiés collectivement)La première assemblée des partenaires qui s'est réunie mardi 1er février 2022 à l'initiative de la Métropole Rouen Normandie. Plus de 80 acteurs majeurs du territoire œuvrant pour la transition énergétique ont répondu présents : collectivités locales, ingénieries publiques et parapubliques, financeurs, gestionnaires de réseaux, associations, fédérations, représentants des réseaux et filières professionnelles ainsi que des représentants des porteurs de projets. Épicentre d'une nouvelle dynamique collective nommée «Énergies Métropole Rouen Normandie», cette assemblée a permis de dresser un diagnostic réaliste et concret des enjeux et opportunités de notre territoire en la matière. La Métropole souhaite un dispositif co-construit qui couvrira tous les domaines de l'efficacité et de la performance énergétique, le déploiement de la sobriété énergétique, et le développement des énergies renouvelables et de récupération. La Métropole se veut aussi exemplaire et s'applique ces principes à elle-même dans le cadre de la mise en place de son Système de management de l'énergie (norme NF EN ISO 50 001). Une 2e assemblée des partenaires s'est tenue le 6 octobre 2022 et une 3e assemblée le mercredi 28 juin 2023.

The Greater Sydney Heat Taskforce is an initiative aimed at coordinating efforts to manage and mitigate the impacts of extreme heat in the Greater Sydney region. Heatwaves pose a growing threat to Sydney's infrastructure, economy, and environment. The Taskforce is composed of senior leaders and decision-makers from local and state government agencies, industry, and the community sector. 
The Greater Sydney Heat Taskforce is led by 'Western Sydney Regional Organisation of Councils', 'Resilient Sydney' and chaired by Blacktown's CEO Kerry Robinson OAM.   

The Focus:
-Establishing clear roles and responsibilities for heat management across different sectors.   
-Integrating heat considerations into urban planning and design to create cooler and more resilient communities.   
-Improving preparedness and response to heatwave events.

Goals include:
-Develop a comprehensive Heat Smart City Plan to improve long-term resilience to heat.   
-Design and implement heat smart strategies within government, industry, and the community sector. 
-Raise awareness of heat risks and promote our strategies for staying safe during heatwaves.

column17: Blacktown City Council's Cool Centres program provides air-conditioned facilities and drinking water during heatwaves that are serviced by Climate and Sustainability Officers. These spaces are also supervised by NGO volunteers such as Red Cross and The Salvation Army. \nThe program is activated when a heatwave warning exceeding 'Low Intensity' for the area is predicted. Libraries, community centres, and churches are temporarily converted to a 'Cool Centre' for vulnerable individuals to escape the heat and reduce the risk of heat-related illness. \nOur 'Cool Centres' offer comfortable seating, drinking water, cool packs, restrooms, and some locations may also provide activities, Wi-Fi access and snacks. This initiative is part of Blacktown City's broader strategy to combat the growing threat of extreme heat events and protect the health and wellbeing of its residents.

Blacktown Council engaged Professor Sebastian Pfautsch from Western Sydney University to undertake the study 'Benchmarking summer heat across Blacktown's diverse urban landscapes.' Based on the findings of this study, recommendations to improve microclimates across Blacktown were identified. This study was used to implement changes to our Development Control Plan's (DCP) and Local Environmental Plan's (LEP) and advocate for relevant cooling strategies to be adopted through the State Environmental Planning Policy (Precincts - Central River City) 2021 and the State Environmental Planning Policy (Sustainable Buildings) 202.

Data collected in eight case studies revealed a tight correlation between high temperatures and low tree canopy cover. Where green infrastructure and open space was limited but the cover of grey infrastructure was high. 
The increasing heat is being driven by two key factors - the warming global climate, and increased urbanisation creates an Urban Heat Island Effect (UHIE). The population of Blacktown City has grown markedly. Between 2018 and 2023 alone, the population of Blacktown City increased by 56,800 to 426,200 people. Blacktown spans an area of 247 km2 resulting in a population density of 1,726 people km2, making it the most heavily populated local government area (LGA) in Sydney.
The Urban Heat Island Effect describes a phenomenon where land surface and air temperatures in cities become warmer than nearby vegetated areas. Long-term, chronic effects of rising air temperatures due to climate change are a growing health concern.

Blacktown held a creative 'Big Idea's' design competition in collaborating with Future Anything. In attendance were six schools from within the LGA that had the task of designing a resilient city in the face of urban heat challenges. The Environmental Services team at Blacktown assisted students in refining their creative outcomes with a focus on building collaboration amongst young change makers. These learning spaces provide a competitive, challenging and enjoyable environment where students are able to undertake meaningful tasks and have their voices heard when developing long term changes for their community. 

Blacktown collaborated with Mount Druitt Ethnic Communities Agency (MECA) to provide community engagement and education. 
An interactive urban heat island model was used to demonstrate on the Urban Heat Island effect and how various surfaces impact localised temperatures. 

Blacktown Council collaborated on the program 'Powerhouse 50°C: Climate, Heat and Resilience' along with University of Sydney, Western Sydney University, and UNSW to deliver an education program involving 945 students from nine schools. The initiative advanced Recommendation 38 of the Heat Smart City Plan by promoting climate resilience through research participation, awareness-raising, and student engagement. The program addressed the Urban Heat Island Effect and supported adaptation through knowledge development and planning for heat-resilient infrastructure.

The Municipality of Bistrița actively collaborates with national government authorities to implement public policies and strategic projects aimed at green transition, energy efficiency, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions reduction, and sustainable urban development. This cooperation is structured around the following key areas:

1. Funding and Governmental Support
Bistrița has accessed funding through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP/PNRR), particularly for:

energy renovation of public and residential buildings

sustainable urban mobility (electric transport infrastructure, cycling paths)

digitalization of municipal services

The municipality also works with the Ministry of Environment and the Ministry of Development to obtain grants via:

the Environmental Fund Administration (AFM)

national programs such as “Public Lighting” and “Energy Efficiency Increase”

2. Emissions Reduction and Green Transition
Bistrița is a signatory of the Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy and has submitted a SECAP (Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan)

It aligns with Romania's Integrated National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) and the country's climate targets under the European Green Deal

The city participates in national programs to electrify the municipal fleet and expand EV charging infrastructure

3. Sustainable Economic Development
The municipality works with the Ministry of Economy and the North-West Regional Development Agency to attract investments in local industrial zones and support SMEs through state aid schemes and digitalization funds

Bistrița contributes to regional development strategies, promoting renewable energy and circular economy practices

4. Energy Renovation of Buildings
In partnership with the Government, the city is implementing projects to:

improve the thermal efficiency of residential blocks (co-financed through NRRP and the Regional Operational Programme)

modernize educational facilities and public administration buildings (schools, kindergartens, city hall)

The goal is to achieve nZEB (nearly zero energy building) standards for new and renovated structures

5. Other Forms of Cooperation
Bistrița takes part in inter-ministerial consultations and working groups on local climate adaptation

It collaborates with the General Inspectorate for Emergency Situations (ISU) and the Ministry of Environment on climate risk assessment and resilience planning

The city also engages in national pilot initiatives for smart local governance

column17: The City has collaborated with its county, St. Joseph County, Solid Waste Management District and Soil & Water Conservation District in community education and outreach. For example, the City collaborated with both districts in the hosting of an Arbor Day event in South Bend in 2022. The Office of Sustainability is also coordinating organizations such as the Soil & Water Conservation District to collaborate on climate adaptation efforts. The City does regular check-ins with local government within the state of Indiana. For example, the City regularly meets with the City of Bloomington to share best practices and advice for the EASSI program and waste management. The City's EASSI program is modeled after the City of Bloomington's SEEL program. The City also participated in the OKI Network (Ohio, Kentucky, Indiana Network). The Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact: https://southeastfloridaclimatecompact.org/

The Southeast Florida Regional Climate Change Compact (the Compact) is a partnership between Broward, Miami-Dade, Monroe, and Palm Beach Counties, to work collaboratively to reduce regional greenhouse gas emissions, implement adaptation strategies, and build climate resilience across the Southeast Florida region. The Compact emerged in late 2009 through the leadership of local government officials in Southeast Florida, who came together to discuss the climate change threats facing over six million residents in the region. Recognizing the shared challenge, but also significant opportunity to position Southeast Florida as an early leader, their call to action solidified a coordinated, regional response in the form of the Compact, which aims to ensure that the region continues to thrive in the face of shared climate change challenges. For over a decade, the Compact counties have successfully collaborated on mitigation and adaptation strategies, built bipartisan support for climate action, and forged partnerships with key stakeholders, including federal, state, and municipal governments and agencies; economic development entities; community-based organizations; and the academic community, enabling the development of a regional voice and vision for future prosperity in Southeast Florida.

 The Compact's efforts have three overarching objectives: 
• Share regional tools and knowledge. The Compact serves to create regional tools and standards, and transfer knowledge to build the local government capacity needed to implement regional climate solutions and avoid duplicative efforts.
• Increase public support and political will. Through a unified voice, the Compact provides the nonpartisan credibility, legitimacy, and continuity necessary for meaningful government action to address projected climate impacts.
• Coordinate action. The Compact catalyzes and supports the region's coordinated actions to accelerate the pace and impact of efforts that will increase the region's climate resilience.

The key question student researchers sought to address in their capstone project was, 'How can the City of La Crosse increase green space to mitigate urban heat island effects, considering those effects have been historically inequitably distributed?'

Highlights of the research include 
● Green space is inequitably allocated in La Crosse based on race and income.
● La Crosse can best improve the inequity of urban heat island effects by increasing urban
vegetation.
● They recommend that La Crosse increase tree canopy and create pocket parks in areas where
vulnerable populations reside.

City of La Crosse Green Space Expansion
Urban heat islands occur when air and surface temperatures in urban areas are warmer than in rural areas due to higher concentrations of non-reflective surfaces and less vegetation. Heat islands cause adverse health, physical, and economic effects, and they disproportionately impact vulnerable populations. Expanding green space within the City is a strategy that mitigates heat island effects. 

Problem Definition
Analysis found that the City's tree canopy and impervious surfaces are inequitably distributed. We identified three census tracts that La Crosse
should prioritize when considering our recommendations: Census Tracts 8, 10, and 11.01. These tracts were chosen because of their low percentage of tree canopy, high percentage of impervious surfaces, and high average summer temperatures.

Policy Options
● Tree Canopy: The expansion of trees on City-owned streets.
● Pocket Parks: The conversion of unused land into small, publicly accessible parks with various green spaces and urban structures.
● Green Roofs: The partial or complete covering of a building's roof with a layer of vegetation and soil, which can vary in intensity of vegetation quantity/size and soil/layer depth.

Recommendations
● Target green space expansion to areas with vulnerable populations and those lacking access to green space.
● Expand urban tree canopy and create pocket parks to lower the urban heat island effect experienced throughout the City.
● Identify buildings that can feasibly support green roofs and parties who can construct and maintain them.
● Strategize cooling centers for residents to escape high heat events.
Future studies of increasing green space in the City could include modeling the effect of policy options on heat mitigation and community attitudes and preferences in high-impact areas.
