In 2021, a Memorandum of Understanding entered into by and among the City Government of Ligao, Headquarters Maritime Group, BFAR 5, CFARMC, Barangay Maonon and Barangay Cabarian for the implementation of Adopt-a-Marine Protected Area (AMPA) Project.
The HMG thru HRMU5 support the implementation of the AMPA project in Ligao City particularly in barangays Maonon and Cabarian; conduct coastal clean-up, mangrove planting, underwater clean-up drive and otehr environmental protection programs in coordination and parthership with PNP, City Government of Ligao and CFARMC around the vicinity of the MPAs or at the 3 coastal barangays on a regular basis; assist and conduct information dissemination campaign on the proper management and protection of the adopted MPAs; conduct sustained maritime law enforcement operations in and around the adopted FSMR and in areas that impact said MPAs; coordinate with other law enforcement units to ensure maximum protection of the adopted MPAs; recognize Deputy Fish Warden of Ligao City who have undergone trainings as Maritime Group Force Multipliers; initiate a monitoring and evaluation scheme for measuring success of the AMPA Project and for developing a basis for the recognition awards related to the MPAs; and appoint a focal person who will be responsible for monitoring, reporting and decumenting the AMPA project in the City of Ligao, Albay.
The City of Ligao takes the lead role in the implementation of the AMPA Project and provide general supervision thru the City ENRO onthe identified MPAs in accordance with the appropriate regulations/ordinances and provision of the Local Government Code; implement Integrated Coastal Resource Management Plan; call on its concerned departments to assist the HMRU 5 in the conduct of activity in relation to AMPA; provide manpower, technical and financial support to the program whenever necessary; facilitate conduct of evaluation/field validation thru the assistance of appropriate agencies in the identified areas; provide provide necessary trainings/seminar on environmental laws and ordinances for Deputy Fish Wardens and partner agencies; provide trainings, workshops and conferences on marine sanctuaries management and protection; conduct IEC activities such as but not limited to workshops, dialogues and other campaigns regarding the AMPA Projects especially in areas where it operates; and support the capacity building efforts of HRMU 5 and other maritime stakeholders in relation to the implementation of the AMPA project.
BFAR V support the capacity building efforts of PNP-MG and Ligao City Deputy Fish Wardens in relation to the implementation of the AMPA Project; involve PNP-MG and Ligao City Deputy Fish Wardens in training workshop and conference on MPA's management and protection; assist the PNP-MG and Ligao City Depty Fish Wardens in enforcing rules and regulations of adopted MPAs; assist the PNP-MG and Ligao City Deputy Fish Wardens in the conduct of IEC activities such as but not limited to workshops, dialogues and other campaigns regarding the AMPA Project especially in areas where it operates; assist the PNP-MG and Ligao City Deputy Fish Wardens in crafting collaboration arrangement with other maritime stakeholders especially the LGUs located in its project sites; assist the PNP-MG and Ligao City fish Wardens in designing a monitoring and evaluation scheme that will be used for measuring the success of the AMPA Project and for providing a basis for recognition awards related to MPAs; and provide other technical assistance to the PNP-MG for the effective implementation of the AMPA Project.
The CFARMC assists in the preparation of Barangay/City Development Plan; recommend the enactment of City Fishery Ordinances to the SP thru its Committee on Fisheries; assist in the implementation and enforcement of fishery laws, rules and regulations in municipal waters; advise the SP in fishery matters thru its Committee on Fisheries; and assist the AMPA Project Management Committee (ManCom) in the formulation of appropriate fishing technology and recommend Fishery Law Enforment Ordinance Program and strategies towards more effective managment of MPA.
The Barangay Government of Maonon and Cabarian assist the City Government in the enforcement of existing environmental and/or fishery ordinances, rules and regulations; support the capability building efforts of HRMU in relation to the implementation of AMPA Project in its respective area of jurisdiction; cooperate with the other partices in the implementation of AMPA Project; and provide necessary manpower in the conduct of monitoring and enforcement activities for their MPAs.

In 2013, the MOA among the City Government of Ligao, DENR 5 and 3rd Albay District Representative was formalized regarding the establishment of Bambusetum located at Tuburan, Ligao City. 
The DENR V conduct selection and characterization of bambusetum size; source-out/propagate planting stocks for use of the project; prepare the field lay-out and spearhead the establishment of bambusetum; conduct proper labeling of all bamboo species and keep record of basic information (i.e. source of planting stock or provenance, date planted, type of planting material, etc.); conduct data collection and monitoring activitieson bamboo growth and development; coordinate maintenance activities with LGU Ligao City; prepare a bambusetum guide/brochure for information of bamboo enthusiasts, researchers, students and other visitors; conduct research study on propagation and cultivation for species in bambusetum that have no such information yet; and conduct training in bamboo technologies if needed by local communities.
The 3rd Albay District Representative Office provide support for the establishment and management of bambusetum as demo from in Kawa-Kawa, Tuburan, Ligao City, Albay; provide support for the establishment of road system/network leading to the bambusetum and otehr parts of the Kawa-Kawa; introduce legislation in pursuit of the welfare of farmers; and conduct inquiries, public hearings and investigations in aid of legislation on the matter of the bamboo industry development as a climate change mitigation and adaptation initiative.
The City of Ligao allocate a 1 hectare lot (expanded in 2018) for the establishment of bambusetum as a demo/model farm in Kawa-kawa, Tuburan, Ligao City, provide free access to DENR V personnel in the conduct of bamboo research activities such as data collection, dodumentation and gathering of bamboo planting materials and other activities necessary in project implementation;
provide support in developing the bambusetum areas as show-window for visitors and interested technology adopters; provide support in the protection and maintenance of the bambusetum project site; and ensure implementation of restrictions on the use and protection of the bambusetum i.e. protection from intruders, prohibition of litter and shoot collection, and felling of culms except for sanitation cutting and for research and propagation purposes.

Perth and Kinross Council welcomes applications for the Green Living Fund 2025/26.

The Green Living Fund is an opportunity for community groups to apply for a grant to support new initiatives that tackle climate-related priorities within the community, while also helping those in the community with the cost of living.

Proposals should be designed in to fit within at least one of the following criteria:

Energy - e.g. reducing consumption, promoting efficiency
Transport - e.g. encouraging active travel, decarbonising transport
Waste - e.g. reducing, reusing and recycling, repairing, sharing
Resilience - e.g. adapting to changing conditions - including flooding, drought
and heat
Nature - e.g. improving greenspace, increasing biodiversity, local food growing
Engagement - e.g. increasing public awareness and engaging communities.
The funding is available for all types of community organisations including, but not limited to community groups, community councils and charities. Groups are able to submit a joint application.
For the purpose of localising the decision making , the funds available will be divided across Council wards. The projects for each ward will be voted on by residents within each ward community.
Further details can be found at https://www.pkclimateaction.co.uk/blog/green-living-fund-2025-26

Nowon-gu operates the Nowon Environmental Foundation to foster collaborative governance and expand resident participation in carbon neutrality. Established as the first environmental foundation among basic local governments in Korea, it plays a leading role at the local level in responding to climate change and conserving the ecological environment. Currently, five affiliated centers are operated under the Foundation.

1. Carbon Neutrality Support Center: Provides feedback support for the implementation of carbon neutrality and conducts research on Nowon-specific policies.

2. Nowon Eco Center: Offers climate change response education and promotes citizen participation in carbon neutrality.

3. Jungnangcheon Environment Center: Supports the transition to carbon neutrality through aquatic ecosystem conservation and the creation of ecological culture.

4. EZ Center: Operates and promotes Korea's first Energy Zero House (EZ House).

5. Astronomy and Space Science Center: Serves as a venue for environmental education addressing climate change.

In addition, a Bicycle Culture Center and an Upcycling Center are scheduled for completion.

As a partner of Nowon-gu, the Nowon Environmental Foundation serves as a bridge between the administration and civil society to effectively promote local carbon neutrality and environmental policies.

The Council of Local Governments for Energy Transition in Response to the Climate Crisis serves as a collaborative platform for municipalities across Korea to jointly advance carbon neutrality and energy transition. Its key roles include:

1. Policy coordination and joint response: Facilitating cooperation among local governments to align policies on climate crisis response and energy transition, while collectively engaging with national policies and advocating for legal and institutional improvements.

2. Capacity building: Strengthening the expertise and administrative capacity of local governments through the sharing of best practices, training programs, and workshops.

3. Project cooperation: Promoting joint initiatives in renewable energy expansion, energy efficiency, and low-carbon projects in sectors such as transport and buildings, alongside public awareness campaigns and citizen engagement programs.

4. Networking and partnerships: Expanding collaboration not only among domestic local governments but also with international organizations such as ICLEI and the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM), as well as with overseas cities.

5. Representation of local voices: Advocating the perspectives of local governments to the national government, parliament, and international community, ensuring that policies reflect local contexts and needs.

Through these activities, the Council plays a pivotal role in strengthening multi-level governance and supporting a just and inclusive transition toward a carbon-neutral society.

In Nowon-gu, the building sector accounts for 73% of local GHG emissions, and given the district's large number of schools, reducing school emissions has been a significant challenge. Despite a steady decline in student numbers, energy use in schools continued to rise, underscoring the need for targeted interventions.

To address this, Nowon-gu, in partnership with the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education, implemented the “School GHG Reduction Project”, setting a goal of reducing electricity consumption by 10% compared to the previous year during the project period. A total of 10 schools were selected, and teachers, students, and parents were each assigned roles to ensure full participation of the entire school community in advancing carbon neutrality.

The project was carried out in six stages:

1. Building consensus among school members on the need to reduce emissions,

2. Assessing current energy use in schools,

3. Setting school-specific reduction goals,

4. Assigning roles and providing training,

5. Implementing practical actions such as switching off lights to reduce energy consumption,

6. Reviewing results, providing feedback, and sharing outcomes.

Monthly results were shared with all participants, followed by additional consulting to refine strategies. As a result, 9 out of 10 schools successfully reduced electricity consumption. Building on these outcomes, a reduction strategy report was produced and distributed across Seoul, contributing to the wider dissemination of carbon neutrality practices.

En abril de 2024 se realizó en la Región Metropolitana el taller “Hacia el desarrollo de Planes de Acción Comunales de Cambio Climático en Chile: Experiencias y próximos pasos”, organizado por el Gobierno de Santiago y WWF Chile, con apoyo del Ministerio del Medio Ambiente y la Asociación Chilena de Municipalidades (ACHM). La jornada permitió capacitar y acompañar a las y los asistentes en el proceso de planificación de los Planes de Acción Comunales de Cambio Climático (PACCC), en línea con las exigencias de la Ley Marco de Cambio Climático, priorizando a los municipios participantes del Desafío de Ciudades de WWF.

Durante la actividad se desarrollaron presentaciones a cargo del Gobierno de Santiago, WWF, el Ministerio del Medio Ambiente y la ACHM, abordando temáticas como la hoja de ruta regional para la gestión climática, los resultados de estudios de insumos para los PACCC en la RM, y experiencias locales de acción climática. Se enfatizó que la planificación debe responder a las realidades e impactos diferenciados de cada territorio, fortaleciendo las capacidades de los gobiernos locales y fomentando un trabajo colaborativo y horizontal entre municipios.

En la instancia participaron los municipios de Cerro Navia, Independencia, Lo Barnechea, Lo Espejo, Maipú, Peñalolén, Providencia, Quilicura, Renca, San Bernardo, Santiago y Vitacura.

The H&F Climate Alliance is a network led by the council to facilitate collaboration between local businesses and organisations in delivering climate action and achieving net zero emissions locally: https://www.lbhf.gov.uk/environment/climate-and-ecological-emergency/hf-climate-alliance. The Climate Alliance grew to 55 members and held 5 events in 2024. Support offered by the Climate Alliance focuses on three areas: 
1) Catalysing projects and partnerships: we facilitate new relationships and partnerships between H&F businesses and organisations, encouraging collaboration and delivery of impact. 
2) Advising on climate action: the H&F Climate Alliance draws on the climate, ecology and air quality expertise of H&F Council to support local organisations implement strategic climate action plans. 
3) Engaging businesses in delivering Net Zero: H&F Council has set an ambitious target to reach Net Zero emissions by 2030, to do this we need to work with stakeholders across the borough to deliver our strategy. 

In 2025 we launched H&F Green Innovators, a fund awarding up to £3,000 to businesses seeking to develop, test and pitch climate solutions within the borough: https://www.hfgreeninnovators.co.uk/. This collaboration between H&F's Climate Alliance, Imperial College London and the Startup Discovery School provides training, funding and ongoing support to businesses across the borough.

H&F businesses also benefit from a range of incentives that make taking climate action easier and more affordable, such as financial support to switch to e-cargo bikes. We delivered an SME Energy Efficiency Grant scheme over three years to support local small businesses to install energy efficiency measures and clean heating.

In 2025 we relaunched our Climate Champions programme, through which residents representing a wide range of businesses and civil society organisations completed 4 weeks of training, and now work in close collaboration with the H&F's climate team, furthering our respective climate goals. Involving local businesses in H&F Council's climate projects and drawing on their expertise and experience offers opportunities to scale impacts and ensure a just transition.

Further to our engagement with businesses and civil society groups, H&F's climate team is partnered with Imperial College London's Environmental Research Group and the NHS Trust in order to further our work tackling air pollution.

This project carried out by Community Development Halton (CDH), a non-profit organization with an office in Burlington. Their mission is to improve the quality of life for all residents of Halton through research, community development, planning, and promoting volunteerism.
In the summer of 2024, CDH team members on behalf of the City of Burlington, carried out a cooling centre study related to action 3-2 of the Climate Resilient Burlington plan (Identify gaps in public space cooling by assessing 
utilization of current cooling facilities and 
identifying the type of cooling supports and 
accessiblity needs of the community especially for vulnerable populations). The study was concerned with:
a) Which residents are most vulnerable to extreme heat events in Burlington
b) Who has access to cooling centres, and who does not have access
c) Exploring community-based participatory methods to place the voices of those who
might use cooling centres at the centre of planning cooling centres in Burlington 

The goal was to help ensure there are accessible cooling centres in Burlington for vulnerable residents, as we face growing numbers of extreme heat events. The team used Statistics Canada data to map heat vulnerable populations while cross referencing with outreach to individuals at community meal programs; cooperative and subsidized community housing communities, neighbourhoods impacted by poverty and inequality; community centres; Burlington libraries; and informal cooling sites such as outdoor spaces at parks and the waterfront. Relationships with those who facilitate community meal programs and who work directly in housing was very helpful. The work will help inform other actions in the Climate Resilient Burlington plan including an urban heat island assessment which together with this research will help inform future cooling sites, tree planting, and other infrastructure needs.

column17: Ormoc City has built a wide network of partnerships with climate-focused organizations, each contributing distinct support that strengthens local resilience and sustainability. The Climate Change Commission (CCC) provides policy guidance and technical support in aligning the city's local climate initiatives with the National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP) and assists in accessing national financing mechanisms such as the People's Survival Fund (PSF). WWF-Philippines works closely with the city on climate vulnerability assessments and sustainable energy, that includes renewable energy into local development strategies. The Smart Cities Network supports the adoption of digital innovations and smart technologies that enhance climate data management, disaster preparedness, and sustainable urban development. UNDP-Philippines provides technical assistance and capacity-building in resilience planning, governance strengthening, and inclusive development, while also supporting Ormoc in pilot-testing innovative climate solutions, particularly in advancing the circular economy through plastics reduction, sustainable consumption and production, and participation in programs such as the EU Green Economy Programme in the Philippines (EU-GEPP). The Global Covenant of Mayors for Climate and Energy (GCoM) guides the city in aligning with global standards for climate action planning, reporting, and emissions reduction, while CDP and ICLEI support Ormoc in climate data disclosure, greenhouse gas inventories, and monitoring of adaptation and mitigation measures to ensure transparency and accountability in climate governance. The National Resilience Council (NRC), through the Project Transform initiative and private sector partnership, plays a pivotal role in mainstreaming resilience into governance systems, strengthening collaboration between government, private sector, academe, and civil society, and building the adaptive capacity of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) through financial literacy and Business Continuity Planning (BCP). NRC also supports biodiversity assessments and promotes ecosystem-based solutions, providing the dual benefit of enhancing community preparedness while restoring and protecting the environment. In addition, the private sector partners with the city on projects related to circular economy, renewable energy, and disaster preparedness, contributing resources, innovation, and investment opportunities. The academe also provides critical support through research, capacity building, and scientific studies, including biodiversity assessments and climate risk analyses, which inform evidence-based planning and project development.\nThrough these partnerships, Ormoc City not only enhances the capacity of its technical personnel but also gains access to resources, tools, and global best practices that make local climate action more inclusive, data-driven, and transformative.\n

column17: Over the past months Westminster Council has been developing a Local Area Energy Plan for Westminster, in partnership with technical consultancy Buro Happold, and in collaboration with key local landowners and Business Improvement Districts. Local Area Energy Planning (LAEP) is the process of gathering extensive data on a local area's energy system, and then using this data to model how the current situation could evolve to create a fully zero-carbon energy system by a given date. In Westminster's case, the outcome of this work should tell us on a practical level what changes we need to make to Westminster's heating and power systems to achieve net zero energy emissions by 2040. The final LAEP report will be accompanied by an implementation plan which will identify key actions and priority projects for the council to support and/or implement in different parts of the city. Several local commercial landowners are contributing energy data on their estate/assets to support the creation of the LAEP, and neighbourhood forums are also being engaged in the creation to ensure that LAEP reflects neighbourhood plans. The plan was published in September 2024

column17: In late 2022 Westminster City Council launched a Sustainable City Charter for businesses and public bodies in Westminster, in partnership with the Westminster Property Association (WPA). The Charter is a public pledge open to any organisation which owns or occupies non-domestic buildings within Westminster's boundaries. By signing up to the Charter, organisations must agree to a series of seven key commitments related to their buildings, including: targeting net zero operational emissions for their buildings by 2040, implementing sustainable procurement policies for their buildings , actively engaging with their landlords and/or tenants to reduce building emissions, reducing waste and transport emissions and creating delivery consolidation schemes. To become a signatory, organisations must complete an application form setting out their specific aims for the year ahead and must report on energy use across their buildings in Westminster each year. In return, Charter signatories get access to exclusive knowledge-sharing events, are promoted in the media, and have first access to a range of council schemes. We are also developing additional benefits for Charter signatories including a digital toolkit for Charter signatories. The charter now has 63 organisations as full signatories, with another 70 in the process of signing up across Westminster, including a number of large landowners and developers such as Landsec, Derwent, Grosvenor Estate and other major institutions such as the Royal Opera House, LSE, University of Westminster and Imperial College NHS Trust. More information about the Charter can be found here: https://www.westminster.gov.uk/tackling-climate-change-westminster/business-climate-action/sustainable-city-charter

Nanaimo, was an early adopted of both the BC Energy Step Code and the Zero Code Step Code. The BC Energy Step Code and Zero Carbon Step Code are optional compliance paths in the BC Building Code that local governments may use. The Energy Step Code requires a minimum level of energy performance in new buildings; while the Zero Carbon Step Code regulates emissions in new buildings. column17: The City of Nanaimo has collaborated with the the Regional District of Nanaimo (RDN) on a number of projects related to reducing community greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and meets regularly with RDN Staff on this topic. Collaborative projects include: 1) a community team based volunteer project supported by ICLEI Canada (Agents of Change) called Acting for Climate Together (ACT), now in it's second year; 2) a sea level rise management strategy; 3) a woodstove exchange incentive program; 4) engagement related to energy efficiency and emissions standards for new residential- new educational sessions planed for 2025/26; 5) an energy concierge program for home owners (Home Energy Navigator); 6) a Manufactured Home Park Energy Efficiency and Emissions Reduction strategy- phase one completed in 2025 and 6) building efficiency rebates, outreach and education programs. In addition, solid waste management occurs at both the regional and municipal levels. In British Columbia, regional districts often manage transfer stations and landfills. The RDN owns and operates two solid waste management facilities in the region; the regional landfill and a transfer station. The City of Nanaimo provides collection services to residents and some businesses in the city. The City and RDN have been selected to jointly participate in the Circular Cities and Regions Initiative intended to build circular economy knowledge and capacity in the Canadian local government sector. The Circular Economy is a model of sustainable production and consumption designed to benefit society, its economy and the environment. In contrast to the 'take-make-waste' linear model, a circular economy is regenerative by design. It aims to design out waste and pollution, keep products and materials in circulation, and regenerate natural systems. In a circular economy, products are made to last longer, communities share resources, and businesses lease, reuse, repair, refurbish, repurpose, and remanufacture products and recycle materials for as long as possible. Circular economy principles and actions have been incorporated into the Nanaimo ReImagine City Plan and Action Plan.The City has partnered with the RDN and other RDN municipalities in developing and implementing a Regional Growth Strategy (RGS). The RGS is a strategic plan that provides a regional vision for sustainable growth and involves shared social, economic, and environmental goals between the region and the local governments within it. The Nanaimo Regional Transit System is provided in partnership by the RDN and BC Transit. Transportation planning is done in coordination with the City and other municipalities in the RDN.

Bentuk Kegiatan Kolaborasi Pemerintah Pusat dan Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam Aksi Iklim (2024-2025)
1. Program Rehabilitasi Mangrove - KLHK & BRGM dengan Pemkab Sumbawa (2024-2025)

Pemerintah pusat melalui BRGM (Badan Restorasi Gambut dan Mangrove) dan KLHK bekerja sama dengan Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam rehabilitasi kawasan pesisir.
Kegiatan meliputi:

Penanaman mangrove di wilayah pesisir Teluk Santong, Empang, Maronge, dan Labuhan Badas.

Pendampingan teknis untuk perawatan mangrove dan penguatan kelompok masyarakat pengelola pesisir.

Kegiatan edukasi ekosistem pesisir untuk desa-desa terdampak abrasi.

Dampak:
Mengurangi risiko abrasi, meningkatkan ketahanan pesisir, serta memperkuat ekonomi masyarakat melalui ekowisata dan budidaya kepiting.

2. Penguatan Sistem Mitigasi dan Kesiapsiagaan Bencana - BNPB & BPBD Sumbawa (2024-2025)

Pemerintah pusat melalui BNPB melakukan pendampingan kepada BPBD Kabupaten Sumbawa.
Kegiatan:

Penguatan Early Warning System (EWS) di daerah rawan banjir dan longsor (Alas Barat, Utan, Batu Lanteh).

Pelatihan Desa Tangguh Bencana (Destana).

Bantuan logistik peralatan kebencanaan dan peningkatan kapasitas relawan.

Dampak:
Meningkatkan kesiapan masyarakat menghadapi risiko iklim ekstrem.

3. Program Ketahanan Pangan dan Pertanian Adaptif Iklim - Kementan & Dinas Pertanian Sumbawa (2024-2025)

Kolaborasi dengan Kementerian Pertanian fokus pada adaptasi sektor pertanian.
Kegiatan:

Penyaluran benih tahan kekeringan untuk wilayah timur Sumbawa.

Pengembangan climate-smart agriculture dan penyuluhan budidaya adaptif.

Pompanisasi dan irigasi mikro untuk daerah rawan kekeringan.

Dampak:
Mengurangi kerentanan petani terhadap kekeringan dan menjaga stabilitas produksi pangan.

4. Pengembangan Infrastruktur Air dan Konservasi Sumber Daya Air - Kementerian PUPR (2024-2025)

Pemerintah pusat melalui PUPR mendukung adaptasi perubahan iklim dengan penyediaan infrastruktur air.
Kegiatan:

Pembangunan/rehabilitasi embung dan sumur bor di wilayah rawan kekeringan (Lunyuk, Moyo Hilir, Moyo Utara).

Normalisasi saluran dan pengendalian banjir di beberapa kawasan permukiman.

Penyediaan SPAM (air bersih) bagi desa yang kekurangan air saat musim kemarau.

Dampak:
Peningkatan akses air bersih dan ketahanan air menghadapi cuaca ekstrem.

5. Program Inventarisasi Gas Rumah Kaca dan SRN - KLHK & DLH Sumbawa (2024-2025)

Pemerintah pusat memberikan pendampingan teknis untuk pelaporan emisi GRK.
Kegiatan:

Pelatihan penggunaan Sistem Registri Nasional (SRN).

Penyusunan inventarisasi emisi sektoral (energi, limbah, pertanian, kehutanan).

Pendampingan dalam penyusunan aksi mitigasi berbasis data.

Dampak:
Sumbawa dapat menyusun target mitigasi yang sejalan dengan NDC nasional.

6. Percontohan Pengelolaan Sampah Berbasis Circular Economy - Kementerian LHK (2024-2025)

Program nasional yang diadaptasi ke daerah.
Kegiatan:

Pendampingan peningkatan kapasitas TPS3R.

Fasilitasi pelatihan bank sampah, komposting, dan pengurangan sampah plastik.

Pengembangan sistem pelaporan persampahan berbasis aplikasi.

Dampak:
Pengurangan emisi dari sektor limbah dan peningkatan keterlibatan masyarakat.

7. Program Energi Bersih & Peningkatan Akses Energi - Kementerian ESDM (2024-2025)

Fokus pada pengembangan energi bersih dan efisiensi energi.
Kegiatan:

Fasilitasi penerapan PLTS Atap untuk fasilitas publik (kantor desa, sekolah).

Pendampingan konversi energi untuk UMKM.

Penyediaan data potensi energi terbarukan (surya, angin, biomassa).

Dampak:
Peningkatan kontribusi Sumbawa dalam transisi energi bersih.

entuk Kegiatan Kolaborasi Pemerintah Provinsi NTB dan Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam Aksi Iklim (2024-2025)

Kolaborasi antara Pemerintah Provinsi Nusa Tenggara Barat (NTB) dan Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam aksi mitigasi dan adaptasi perubahan iklim difokuskan pada penguatan ketahanan lingkungan, pengurangan risiko bencana, transisi energi bersih, serta peningkatan kapasitas daerah. Adapun bentuk kolaborasi tersebut meliputi:

1. Pendampingan Penyusunan Dokumen Perubahan Iklim (RAD-PI, Kajian Kerentanan, dan Rencana Aksi Iklim)

Pemerintah Provinsi NTB melalui Dinas Lingkungan Hidup dan Dinas Kehutanan memberikan dukungan teknis kepada Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam:

Penyusunan dan pembaruan Kajian Risiko dan Kerentanan Iklim.

Integrasi aksi mitigasi dan adaptasi ke dalam dokumen perencanaan daerah.

Penyelarasan program kabupaten dengan arah kebijakan lingkungan hidup provinsi (Dokumen Hijau NTB dan RAD-GRK Provinsi).

Dampak:
Data kabupaten menjadi lebih terstandar, dan perencanaan iklim Sumbawa selaras dengan kebijakan provinsi.

2. Program Rehabilitasi Hutan dan Lahan Kritis pada DAS Prioritas

Kolaborasi antara Dinas Kehutanan Provinsi NTB dan Pemkab Sumbawa dilakukan melalui:

Penanaman kembali (reboisasi) kawasan hutan dan DAS kritis di wilayah Batulanteh, Ropang, dan Lantung.

Pembinaan Kelompok Tani Hutan (KTH) dan pemberdayaan masyarakat lokal dalam pengelolaan hutan.

Pembangunan persemaian tajar dan penyediaan bibit gratis untuk kegiatan rehabilitasi lahan.

Dampak:
Mengurangi risiko banjir, kekeringan, dan meningkatkan kapasitas serapan karbon.

3. Penguatan Ketahanan Bencana Daerah - BPBD Provinsi NTB & BPBD Kabupaten Sumbawa

Kolaborasi ini fokus pada pengurangan risiko bencana iklim.
Kegiatan meliputi:

Pelatihan dan pembentukan Desa Tangguh Bencana.

Sinkronisasi peta rawan bencana banjir, longsor, dan kekeringan.

Bantuan logistik kebencanaan untuk masa darurat cuaca ekstrem.

Pendampingan Early Warning System di kecamatan rawan.

Dampak:
Terbentuknya kesiapsiagaan yang lebih baik di tingkat masyarakat.

4. Program Pengembangan Energi Terbarukan

Dinas ESDM Provinsi NTB mendukung Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam:

Pengembangan PLTS atap untuk fasilitas publik (puskesmas, sekolah, kantor desa).

Pemetaan potensi energi surya, angin, dan biomassa tingkat kabupaten.

Sosialisasi efisiensi energi dan pelatihan energi bersih untuk UMKM.

Dampak:
Kontribusi kabupaten terhadap transisi energi bersih provinsi NTB semakin meningkat.

5. Program Pengendalian Sampah dan Plastik Sekali Pakai

Kolaborasi dengan DLHK Provinsi NTB termasuk:

Pembinaan bank sampah dan pusat daur ulang berbasis masyarakat.

Pelatihan pengurangan sampah plastik, komposting, dan manajemen sampah terpadu.

Integrasi target pengurangan sampah kabupaten ke dalam kebijakan provinsi NTB Zero Waste.

Dampak:
Peningkatan pengurangan sampah dan penurunan emisi dari sektor persampahan.

6. Pembangunan Infrastruktur Ketahanan Air dan Pesisir

Dinas PUPR Provinsi NTB mendukung Sumbawa dalam:

Normalisasi sungai dan saluran air di beberapa kecamatan.

Rehabilitasi embung desa dan fasilitas air bersih.

Penguatan struktur perlindungan pesisir dengan vegetasi pantai dan mangrove.

Dampak:
Meminimalkan risiko banjir, intrusi air laut, dan kekeringan berkepanjangan.

7. Program Pendidikan dan Literasi Perubahan Iklim

Dinas Pendidikan dan DLH Provinsi bekerja sama dengan sekolah-sekolah di Sumbawa melalui:

Program Adiwiyata tingkat provinsi.

Pelatihan guru tentang pendidikan lingkungan dan perubahan iklim.

Lomba lingkungan hidup untuk meningkatkan kesadaran pelajar.

Dampak:
Kesadaran iklim meningkat di kalangan generasi muda.

olaborasi NGO dan Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dalam Aksi Iklim (2024-2025)

Kolaborasi antara Pemerintah Kabupaten Sumbawa dan berbagai organisasi non-pemerintah (NGO) pada periode 2024-2025 berfokus pada penguatan kapasitas adaptasi, mitigasi, edukasi publik, serta konservasi lingkungan. Bentuk kegiatan kolaborasi tersebut meliputi:

1. Program Restorasi Ekosistem dan Rehabilitasi Mangrove

Beberapa NGO lingkungan bekerja sama dengan DLHK Kabupaten Sumbawa dan pemerintah desa pesisir untuk:

Penanaman mangrove di wilayah Teluk Santong, Labuhan Sumbawa, dan wilayah pesisir lainnya.

Pelatihan masyarakat pesisir tentang pemulihan ekosistem dan teknik penanaman mangrove yang sesuai lokasi.

Monitoring pertumbuhan mangrove berbasis komunitas.

Dampak:
Mengurangi abrasi, meningkatkan penyerapan karbon biru, serta memperkuat ekonomi desa pesisir melalui ekowisata mangrove.

2. Program Pengurangan Risiko Bencana Berbasis Komunitas

NGO kebencanaan dan kemanusiaan (misalnya Wahana Lingkungan Hidup daerah, Muhammadiyah Disaster Management Center/MDMC, atau lembaga lokal lainnya) bermitra dengan BPBD Kabupaten Sumbawa melalui:

Pelatihan kesiapsiagaan bencana untuk masyarakat desa.

Pemetaan risiko banjir, kekeringan, dan longsor berbasis komunitas.

Pembentukan relawan desa tangguh bencana dan pengajaran penggunaan early warning tools.

Dampak:
Memperkuat kapasitas adaptasi masyarakat terhadap risiko iklim ekstrem.

3. Advokasi dan Kampanye Pengurangan Sampah Plastik

NGO yang bergerak di isu persampahan berkolaborasi dengan DLHK, sekolah, dan pemerintah desa melalui:

Kampanye “kurangi plastik sekali pakai” di sekolah dan pasar tradisional.

Pembinaan bank sampah dan pelatihan daur ulang kreatif bagi perempuan dan kelompok UMKM.

Pendampingan penyusunan Perdes pengurangan sampah.

Dampak:
Terjadi peningkatan kesadaran masyarakat dan penurunan sampah plastik yang masuk ke sungai dan pesisir.

4. Program Ketahanan Pangan dan Pertanian Tanggap Iklim

Beberapa NGO pertanian berkolaborasi dengan Dinas Pertanian dan pemerintah kecamatan dalam:

Pendampingan petani untuk adaptasi cuaca ekstrem (pengelolaan air, varietas tahan kering, pertanian organik).

Demonstrasi plot pertanian berkelanjutan di desa-desa sentra produksi pangan.

Pelatihan manajemen hama ramah lingkungan.

Dampak:
Meningkatkan produktivitas pertanian meski terjadi perubahan pola hujan.

5. Penguatan Data dan Riset Perubahan Iklim

NGO berbasis riset bekerja sama dengan Pemda Sumbawa dan universitas lokal untuk:

Survei kondisi tutupan lahan dan potensi kawasan rawan kekeringan.

Pengumpulan data emisi sektor persampahan, energi, dan tata guna lahan.

Pembuatan laporan tematik perubahan iklim yang digunakan untuk penyusunan rencana aksi iklim kabupaten.

Dampak:
Data lebih akurat dan perencanaan kabupaten lebih berbasis bukti (evidence-based).

6. Pendidikan Lingkungan dan Gerakan Pemuda Peduli Iklim

Melibatkan NGO kepemudaan dan komunitas lokal dalam:

Pelatihan generasi muda tentang aksi iklim, konservasi, dan daur ulang.

Gerakan penanaman pohon di area publik—sekolah, fasum, dan bantaran sungai.

Lomba inovasi aksi iklim tingkat pelajar.

Dampak:
Terbentuknya relawan muda peduli iklim yang berkelanjutan.

7. Kemitraan dengan NGO Internasional

Beberapa NGO internasional yang sudah menjalankan proyek di NTB turut mendukung Sumbawa melalui:

Penguatan sistem adaptasi berbasis komunitas di daerah rawan kekeringan.

Program air bersih dan sanitasi berkelanjutan.

Dukungan teknis dalam pengembangan kebijakan aksi iklim tingkat kabupaten.

Dampak:
Transfer teknologi, peningkatan kapasitas lokal, serta pendanaan aksi iklim yang lebih kuat.

Also represented in our task force groups are private businesses in the construction, waste, energy, and agriculture sector as well as non profits in the conservation and climate sector and local school groups.

Durante el año 2024, la Municipalidad de Renca fortaleció su colaboración con el Gobierno Regional Metropolitano de Santiago (GORE RM), integrando acciones climáticas en diversas iniciativas financiadas o coordinadas a nivel regional. Esta colaboración ha sido clave para avanzar hacia un desarrollo urbano más resiliente y equitativo frente al cambio climático.

Uno de los hitos más relevantes fue la adjudicación del financiamiento regional para el diseño del Plan Maestro del Agua de los Cerros de Renca, proyecto estratégico que busca abordar simultáneamente los desafíos de escasez hídrica, riesgo de incendios forestales y restauración ecológica en un territorio altamente vulnerable y con presencia de asentamientos informales. El GORE RM financió el diseño de este plan a través de un fondo concursable, sentando las bases para futuras inversiones a gran escala con enfoque climático.

Además, se colaboró en la priorización y diseño de iniciativas de infraestructura verde, como el Parque Costanera, que será ejecutado con financiamiento conjunto del municipio y del GORE, incorporando criterios de justicia ambiental, acceso equitativo a espacios públicos y recuperación de servicios ecosistémicos del borde fluvial.

En materia de planificación territorial, Renca ha participado activamente en las instancias regionales vinculadas al Plan de Acción Regional de Cambio Climático (PARCC RM), así como en comités técnicos para la articulación del Plan Regulador Metropolitano de Santiago (PRMS). Esta participación busca alinear las metas comunales con los objetivos regionales de resiliencia, reducción de emisiones y adaptación, fortaleciendo la coherencia multiescalar de la política climática.

También se ha impulsado el trabajo conjunto en educación ambiental y participación ciudadana, especialmente en zonas periféricas, a través de campañas y actividades financiadas o apoyadas por el Gobierno Regional. Estas instancias buscan democratizar el acceso a la información y fortalecer las capacidades locales para enfrentar el cambio climático de forma justa e inclusiva.

Un caso emblemático fue la coordinación con Huechuraba para el diseño del Plan Maestro del Agua de los Cerros de Renca, proyecto que considera la recuperación ambiental de un ecosistema compartido. La colaboración incluyó intercambio técnico, visitas conjuntas al territorio y levantamiento de información hidrográfica y ecológica de la zona limítrofe.

Con Quinta Normal y Cerro Navia, se mantuvo una colaboración activa en torno a la recuperación del borde del río Mapocho, especialmente en lo relativo al diseño y ejecución del Parque Costanera, que se proyecta como un eje verde intercomunal con beneficios ecosistémicos y sociales compartidos. Este proyecto incorpora criterios de adaptación climática, conectividad ecológica y acceso equitativo al espacio público.

Con Recoleta e Independencia, se sostuvieron intercambios sobre estrategias de reciclaje domiciliario y eficiencia energética, especialmente en el marco del programa Comuna Energética y otras instancias del Ministerio de Energía.

Además, Renca ha participado junto a varias comunas vecinas en espacios regionales como el Plan de Acción Regional de Cambio Climático (PARCC RM) y la construcción del Plan Regulador Metropolitano de Santiago (PRMS), donde se ha promovido la integración de criterios de resiliencia climática en la planificación urbana a escala intercomunal.

Estas colaboraciones reflejan una visión compartida de los territorios como sistemas interdependientes, donde las soluciones a los desafíos del cambio climático requieren articulación más allá de los límites administrativos.

Municipios de Huechuraba, Recoleta, Quinta Normal, Cerro Navia, Independencia y Conchalí; Gobierno Regional Metropolitano; Ministerio del Medio Ambiente; Ministerio de Obras Públicas; Asociación de Municipios por la Acción Climática (AMUAC).

Renca concentra una importante base industrial y logística: cerca del 18% de los puestos de trabajo formales de la comuna corresponden a actividades manufactureras, transporte y almacenamiento. Esta configuración productiva plantea un desafío clave para avanzar en una transición justa y baja en carbono, que el municipio ha comenzado a abordar mediante colaboración con el sector privado.

Durante 2024 se ejecutaron múltiples acciones climáticas en conjunto con empresas del territorio:

Programa Empresas Verdes: En 2024, 12 empresas locales se incorporaron al programa voluntario de compromisos ambientales. Estas entidades implementaron medidas como separación en origen, instalación de luminarias LED en sus instalaciones, y reducción de residuos orgánicos mediante convenios con recicladores.

Campañas conjuntas de reciclaje y educación ambiental: Empresas como AGROSUPER y operadores logísticos del sector norte colaboraron en la logística y financiamiento de ferias ambientales comunitarias, beneficiando a más de 1.500 vecinos y vecinas a través de jornadas educativas y puntos verdes móviles.

Centro de Inteligencia Hídrica: Este centro, que comenzó a operar en 2024 con apoyo de empresas locales, permite monitorear y optimizar el consumo de agua en edificios públicos y próximamente en instalaciones privadas. Se instalaron sensores de monitoreo en 4 recintos piloto, y se espera escalar el modelo con apoyo del sector industrial.

Convenios con empresas de energía: A través de un convenio con ENEL, se ejecutaron diagnósticos de eficiencia energética en recintos municipales y se iniciaron gestiones para explorar opciones de electromovilidad corporativa en flotas privadas que operan en el Parque Industrial Lo Boza.

Iniciativas de economía circular: Se generaron vínculos con empresas para el uso de residuos orgánicos en compostaje local y con emprendedores circulares. En total, más de 40 toneladas de residuos fueron gestionadas con criterios de economía circular, muchas de ellas en alianza con industrias del territorio.

Estas colaboraciones reflejan un proceso progresivo de vinculación público-privada en torno a la acción climática, con foco en eficiencia, conciencia ambiental y preparación para escenarios regulatorios más exigentes. El municipio proyecta consolidar en 2025 una mesa público-privada climática, orientada a acompañar al sector en su descarbonización gradual.

column17: Recognizing momentum in the resilience work across the region, the East Central Florida Regional Planning Council adopted a resolution in 2018, recommitting to regionalism and supporting a program to convene stakeholders to develop a structure and framework for a united resilience effort. Committees were formed, and experts convened. Three pillars were identified under the resilience umbrella; (people) Health + Equity, (places) Built Infrastructure + Natural Environment, and (prosperity) Economic Resilience. Woven throughout each pillar is a reduction of risks, vulnerabilities, and the carbon footprint and an increase in sustainability goals region-wide. Resilience to any disaster rests on the premise that all aspects of a community- its places, people, and prosperity- are strong. With this resilience framework in mind, a Memorandum of Understanding was drafted to formalize partnership in the Collaborative throughout local governments and agencies in the 8-county and 78-city region. In May of 2019, the East Central Florida Regional Resilience Collaborative (ECFR2C) was formally established. The R2C has defined resilience as the ability to bounce forward in the face of short-term shocks like hurricanes or infrastructure failures and long-term stressors like affordable housing, aging infrastructure, and climate change. These shocks and stressors need to be approached holistically, striving for transformative change to address the drivers of these vulnerabilities and those that exacerbate them. The R2C is composed of a Volunteer Council Sub-Committee, a Steering Committee, and supporting technical advisory committees (TACs). Developed to expand the capabilities and capacities of local governments, address and focus discussions on specific regional concerns and establish partnerships and unique funding pathways and potential opportunities, these committees support R2C collective efforts and overall vision towards achieving a more resilient east central Florida community. 45 partners make up the R2C to date, encompassing not only local governments but business, academia, civil society, supporting foundations and organizations as well.

Fforest Fawr UNESCO Global Geopark is set within the Bannau Brycheiniog National Park comprising the western half of the National Park, stretching from Llandovery in the north to the edge of Merthyr Tydfil in the south, from Llandeilo in the west to Brecon in the east. A total area of 300 square miles. 

A major new pilot is looking to understand the growing and multiple impacts of climate change on cultural and natural heritage across the UK. Three UK UNESCO sites are set to receive funding and expert support to engage in the pilot over a 12-month period.

Teams at North Devon Biosphere Reserve, Fforest Fawr Global Geopark, Hadrian's Wall World Heritage Site, will test how new ways of collaborative working and improved sharing of data can help to better understand and address the impacts of climate change on the UK's cultural and natural heritage.

Funded by the HM Treasury Shared Outcomes Fund, the £1.8 million Climate Change & UNESCO Heritage project aims to explore, develop and test ways to overcome these barriers. With cultural and natural heritage being foundational to localising global challenges like climate change, the pilot will also capitalise on the huge potential UNESCO designated sites offer as testing grounds for developing new ways of working.

The project builds on research by the UK and Canadian National Commissions for UNESCO which found that UNESCO sites are not only ideal test beds for developing participatory approaches to global challenges, but are also well-placed to support genuine, on-the-ground collaborative action that can help to achieve outcomes aligned with the 2030 United Nations Sustainable Development Agenda. 

Work is already underway to bring together government departments and public agencies to explore these challenges at a national level. North Devon Biosphere Reserve, Fforest Fawr Global Geopark, and Hadrian's Wall World Heritage Site, have been selected as the three UNESCO sites that will join the project as local case study locations for a 12-month period ending July 2025. 

This will result in a climate risk assessment for this area of the National Park - and inform an resilience plan.

The York and North Yorkshire Local Area Energy Plans (LAEPs) facilitated by the York & North Yorkshire Combined Authority (YNYCA), via the Community Renewal Fund (CRF), enable the identification of technologies and approaches for each area within the county. These plans will aim to achieve net zero in the most efficient manner. Devolution for York & North Yorkshire alongside the creation of North Yorkshire Council provides an opportunity to initiate projects identified in the LAEPs. Areas for proposed action identified within the LAEPs consist of: 
•	domestic buildings
•	non-domestic buildings
•	transport and local generation
•	networks, storage and flexibility 
Additionally, YNYCA have been selected by the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to be one of three pilot places within the Local Net Zero Accelerator Programme. This programme looks to invest nearly £500 million into low carbon energy infrastructure, such as solar, wind, heat networks, heat pumps and energy efficiency measures over the next five years. Further benefits of the model include aggregating demand to build the green supply chain, creating 1,000 jobs, supporting decarbonisation of Council assets in support of our Net zero targets, and creating social value opportunities through schemes such as a Community Energy Fund. North Yorkshire Council are a key partner in this project.

Project: 'Establishing a Sustainable Water Supply System in Gradiška' 
Donor name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia through the Centre for International Cooperation and Development (CMSR).
The project is implemented by: The City of Gradiška.
Project duration: 17 months (June 2023 - November 2024).
Project value: The total investment value in this project is 1,564,847 euros, of which donor funds amount to 625,939 euros, while the remainder has been provided by the City of Gradiška.
General objective of the project: To improve the water supply system in Gradiška and ensure a continuous, long-term delivery of drinking water by utilising renewable solar energy sources.
The project aims to strengthen the public water supply service and implement sustainable energy sources. The project investment in an additional exploitation well, a photovoltaic power plant, and a transformer station at the water source in Žeravica is a significant strategic move that ensures all citizens have access to quality and continuous drinking water supply in the long term. The water supply network can currently operate without the planned investments, but the goal is to take preventive action to reduce natural water reserves, the drying up of extraction wells, and the increase in CO2 emissions (due to the expansion of the water supply network and the number of users). By using solar energy, the energy consumption at the water source will be fully covered. This would mean that on an annual basis, CO2 emissions would be reduced by 893 tCO2 (complementary to the electricity that would be consumed through the burning of fossil fuels). The establishment of a sustainable natural resource management system will be facilitated by the transfer of knowledge from municipal enterprises in Slovenia, in order to proactively address internal and external risks.

Project: “Reconstruction of Public Lighting with LED Lights in the City of Gradiška” 
Donor name: Government of the Republic of Slovenia through the Centre for International Cooperation and Development (CMSR).

The project is implemented by: The City of Gradiška.

Project duration: 17 months (May 2022 - October 2023).

Project value: The total investment value in this project is 2,055,308 million euros, of which donor funds amount to 822,123 euros, while the remainder has been provided by the City of Gradiška from savings on electricity consumption.

General objective of the project: The aim of this project is to reconstruct the public lighting system in the city of Gradiška by applying measures for LED energy-efficient and ecological public lighting through the implementation of optimal technical LED and SMART CITY solutions, which would demonstrate the effects of significant energy savings, consequently reducing CO2 emissions, improving and fully aligning with the EN 13201 standard for lighting parameters and traffic safety conditions, and reducing potential risks of environmental pollution due to the use of ecologically unacceptable lighting fixtures (e.g., sodium and/or mercury gas discharge lamps), preventing light pollution and the use of hazardous substances, and consequently the costs of disposal. The latest energy-efficient LED lights can achieve energy savings of between 50-70%. LED public lighting offers immediate savings in terms of energy, maintenance, and ongoing costs.

The most significant activities within the project involve the replacement of 6,126 old lamps with LED lights, as well as the installation of dimmers or light intensity adjusters throughout the entire territory of the city of Gradiška, where public lighting has already been installed.

Brief description of the project:

Completion of the construction of a multifunctional facility (education, centre for the aggregation of agricultural products) in the local community of Berek, along with equipping and external landscaping.

The Rural Resource Centre Berek (RRC Berek) will be a newly constructed facility in the local community of Berek, which will serve the business activities of the agricultural cooperative 'Lijevče polje MAŠIĆI.' The facility will function as a multifunctional centre for the transfer of knowledge and education for agricultural producers from the Lijevče field region, with the aim of improving the quality of vegetable cultivation. Through specialised training throughout the year, at least 200 producers will acquire new knowledge, and the facility will also serve as a 'hub' for the purchase and distribution of fresh vegetables. In addition, the centre will be beneficial for the local population and organisations engaged in rural development.

The Agricultural Cooperative 'Lijevče polje' in Mašići will increase the purchase of fresh vegetables from agricultural producers by 15% within a period of 12 months from the commissioning of the facility.

The level of activity in rural areas of at least 7 local communities in the Lijevča field will be intensified through the activation of the RRC Berek facility. It is expected that at least 10 meetings will be held annually by the local population.

Local communities that will benefit from the construction of the facility: Berek, Elezagići, Cerovljani, Jazovac, Mašići, Nova Topola, and Vilusi.

The AgriBOOST Project has been pivotal in advancing Butuan City's development goals by modernizing agriculture, enhancing food security, and promoting inclusive economic growth. Anchored on innovation and digitalization, AgriBOOST boosted local agricultural productivity through data-driven crop planning, efficient supply chain management, and direct market linkages. These innovations enabled farmers to align production with market demands, reduce post-harvest losses, and increase incomes, directly contributing to poverty reduction, economic development, and smart technology adoption. 

The project's contributions extend to the global Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). AgriBOOST addresses SDG 1 (No Poverty) and SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) by improving farmers' access to quality inputs, modern farming practices, and guaranteed markets, boosting yields and incomes. It advances SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by creating new opportunities across the agricultural value chain and reducing reliance on intermediaries. AgriBOOST's emphasis on sustainable practices like climate-smart farming and resource optimization supports SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production) and SDG 13 (Climate Action), building resilience against climate change, which integrates the DOST's SARAI Project into the digital tools. Contributing to SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure), through its digital agriculture platforms—including the AgriHub Web App, AgriBloom Mobile App, and AgriMart App, which support real-time monitoring, commodity forecasting, and database management, strengthening transparency, service delivery, and decision-making across the agricultural value chain, supporting Butuan City's vision of becoming a Smart Eco City. . Furthermore, gender-sensitive initiatives empower women farmers and entrepreneurs, promoting SDG 5 (Gender Equality). 

To ensure successful implementation and sustainability, AgriBOOST was built on five strategic pillars. First, institutionalization within LGU structures integrated the project into the Butuan City Food Security Framework, Annual Investment Plan (AIP), and local development plans, ensuring long-term support. Second, multi-stakeholder partnerships were formed with farmers and vendors' groups, academic institutions like Caraga State University and Father Saturnino Urios University, institutional buyers such as the hotel and restaurants, and national agencies (e.g., DA, DOST, DTI, and DICT), creating an ecosystem of shared responsibilities and resources. Third, capacity-building initiatives trained farmers and market players in agribusiness, digital agriculture, and climate resilience, empowering them to adapt and innovate independently. Fourth, a market-driven, value-chain focus connected farmers directly to institutional and commercial markets, sustaining incomes and encouraging continuous participation. Lastly, innovation and digitalization were prioritized through modern and tech-based solutions for farm production, digital marketplaces, and data-driven monitoring, ensuring transparency, accountability, and responsive program management.

column17: Çorlu Municipality has strengthened its strategic capacity not only at the local level but also through its collaborations with national and international climate networks in the areas of climate change mitigation and adaptation. The municipality has signed the European Union's “Covenant of Mayors” and committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions, improving climate adaptation, and increasing energy efficiency by 2030. and in this context, its Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) has been implemented based on internationally recognized methodology. Collaboration between Quang Binh and the National Government on Climate Action & Progress
Quang Binh has engaged in several formal collaborations with national government ministries and with national climate programs, to align provincial climate action with Vietnam's policies, international commitments (like the Paris Agreement / NDCs), and national strategies (e.g., national strategy on climate change, COP26, etc.). These collaborations include planning, implementation of projects, policy/rules development, and monitoring.
Here are key examples and progress:
1.	VN-SIPA / “Support to Vietnam for the Implementation of the Paris Agreement”
o	Quang Binh Province is a partner implementing VN-SIPA (Phase II) in coordination with the German Government's International Climate Initiative (IKI), GIZ, and the federal ministry (BMWK). The project supports the mainstreaming of nature-based adaptation (NbSA) in provincial planning, aligning local plans with national commitments under the Paris Agreement. 
o	As part of this, Quang Binh, in cooperation with relevant national ministries/agencies, has selected priority communes, built pilot NbSA models, and held consultative workshops to integrate NbSA into the provincial Climate Change Action Response Plan (2025-2030, vision to 2050). 
2.	Pilot Ecosystem-Based Adaptation Works in Urban Areas
o	Under VN-SIPA, three pilot projects in Đồng Hới City (urban ecosystem-based adaptation) were established, supported by national government frameworks and international cooperation. These include sustainable urban drainage systems, green infrastructure, and other nature-based urban solutions. Quang Binh and national partners (through GIZ/IKI) collaborated in technical design and deployment. 
o	These pilots also serve as models to inform national guidance/standards, so that future urban planning in other provinces can incorporate similar solutions. 
3.	Alignment with National Policy, Legal & Planning Instruments
o	Quang Binh has collaborated with national ministries/agencies (e.g. Ministry of Natural Resources & Environment (MONRE), the Ministry of Planning & Investment, others) to update its provincial Climate Change Action Plan (2025-2030, vision to 2050), making sure it aligns with national commitments (NDC, national strategy, COP26 outcomes, etc.).
o	The province has also participated in national processes to develop or review criteria for climate change/adaptation projects, vulnerability assessments, greenhouse gas emission reduction commitments, and integrating climate goals into sectoral and national planning. For example, a workshop was held jointly with WWF and IFC to assess vulnerability and update the provincial action plan. 
4.	Resilient Housing Cooperation
o	Quang Binh, via its provincial departments and in cooperation with national ministries (e.g., Ministry of Construction) and international organizations (UNDP, GCF), has developed and implemented resilient-housing programs for poor and near-poor households. These programs are designed to meet national design standards (storm/flood resistant), thus reflecting national guidance and ministry oversight. 
Progress & Outcomes
•	Adoption of Provincial Climate Action Response Plan: The plan for Quang Binh (2025-2030, vision to 2050) has been developed with national frameworks in mind, indicating that the province is aligning its medium-/long-term development with national climate goals (NDC, Paris Agreement). 
•	Implementation of Pilot Projects: Several pilot works (NbSA in agriculture, ecosystem-based adaptation in urban drainage, resilient housing) have been completed or are in progress. These provide proof of concept and build institutional capacity at the provincial level. 
•	Strengthened Institutional & Planning Integration: Quang Binh has increasingly integrated climate change and greenhouse gas emission reduction into its sectoral plans (agriculture, construction, transport, etc.), urban planning, legal/regulatory documents, and performed vulnerability/risk assessments in collaboration with national bodies and international partners. This helps in enabling coherent policy implementation.

Description of Collaboration between Quang Binh Province and NGOs/Associations on Climate-Related Issues
Quang Binh Province, a coastal region in central Vietnam highly vulnerable to climate impacts like flooding, erosion, and biodiversity loss, has actively partnered with non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and associations to address these challenges. These collaborations emphasize community-based adaptation, sustainable resource management, and policy integration, often aligning with national strategies like Vietnam's Climate Change Strategy to 2050. Key partnerships focus on ecosystem restoration, disaster resilience, and green economic transitions, involving both local and international entities. Below is an overview of notable collaborations and associated progress.
1. Partnership with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) on Urban Environment and Climate Change Adaptation

Description: Quang Binh collaborates with ADB through the Urban Environment and Climate Change Adaptation Project (approved in 2014, ongoing implementation), targeting Dong Hoi City and Bao Ninh Commune. The initiative involves NGOs and local associations in planning and execution, focusing on wastewater management, flood-resilient infrastructure, and resettlement for affected communities. Local women's unions and community groups participate in awareness campaigns and monitoring to ensure inclusive benefits.
Progress: By 2020, key components like the Bao Ninh Wastewater Treatment Plant were completed, serving over 50,000 residents and reducing pollution in coastal areas. Resettlement plans have relocated 200+ households with improved living conditions, and the project has enhanced early warning systems, cutting flood-related damages by an estimated 30% in pilot areas. This has positioned Quang Binh as a model for urban climate adaptation in central Vietnam.

2. Collaboration with the Center for Mariculture and Development (MCD) and Vietnam Association for Conservation of Nature and Environment (VACNE)

Description: MCD, a Vietnamese NGO specializing in coastal management, partners with Quang Binh's provincial authorities and VACNE (a national association) on projects like the Partnership for Equitable Resilience to Climate Change Impacts in Coastal Communities (2012-2014, with extended activities). Efforts include mangrove restoration in districts like Quang Trach and Bo Trach, involving local fishing associations and ethnic minority groups. VACNE's Resilient Community Chapter coordinates advocacy for policy integration, while MCD provides technical training on sustainable aquaculture.
Progress: Over 500 hectares of mangroves have been restored since 2012, boosting coastal protection against erosion and supporting livelihoods for 10,000+ fishers through eco-friendly practices. Community training programs have reached 5,000 participants, reducing vulnerability in 20 coastal communes. These efforts have attracted follow-on funding from AusAID and DFAT, contributing to a 15% increase in resilient agricultural yields in partnered areas.

3. Engagement with the Vietnam NGO Climate Change Working Group (VNGO-CC) and Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung (FES) Vietnam

Description: Through VNGO-CC (a network of 70+ NGOs) and FES Vietnam (a German foundation), Quang Binh works on capacity-building for youth and local associations in climate policy advocacy and green tourism. Projects include workshops on emission reductions in agriculture and tourism adaptation around Phong Nha-Ke Bang National Park, with involvement from the provincial Women's Union and youth environmental clubs.
Progress: Since 2015, over 2,000 youth and community members have been trained, leading to 50+ local initiatives like low-carbon farming models. FES-supported dialogues have influenced provincial plans, resulting in a 20% expansion of green tourism routes by 2023, generating 1,500 jobs and increasing eco-tourism revenue by 25%. This has also strengthened networks for ongoing monitoring of biodiversity hotspots.

4. Joint Initiatives with the Center for Ecological Community Development (ECODE) and Local Associations

Description: ECODE, under the Vietnam Union of Science and Technology Associations (VUSTA), collaborates with Quang Binh on interdisciplinary research and community-driven adaptation, such as flood-resilient agriculture in highland districts. Partnerships include the provincial Farmers' Association for pilot projects on sustainable livestock to cut methane emissions, aligned with national targets.
Progress: From 2018 onward, ECODE-led pilots have implemented methane reduction techniques across 1,000 farms, achieving a 10% emissions drop by 2024. Community feedback loops have improved project equity, with 60% of beneficiaries being women and ethnic minorities, enhancing food security for 15,000 households and reducing disaster recovery costs by 40% in tested areas.

Collaboration with Academia & Research Institutions in Quang Binh: Description & Progress

Quang Binh Province has developed multiple collaboration channels with universities, research centers, and think tanks to enhance evidence-based climate action. These partnerships help with identifying vulnerabilities, testing adaptation methods, informing planning, and building local capacity in climate science.

One key partner is the Center for Ethnic and Mountainous Area Resource Governance Research (CEGORN), which works with the provincial Department of Agriculture and Environment and academic specialists to design nature-based solutions for vulnerable smallholder agriculture. Under the VN-SIPA II framework, academic researchers support the selection of communes (based on ecological, social, and climatic vulnerability criteria), baseline surveys, participatory planning, and development of monitoring & evaluation systems. This ensures the interventions are grounded in scientific understanding of local ecosystems and risk exposure.

Another academic partnership is with the Central Vietnam Climate Change Research Center and other higher education institutions that conduct studies on ecosystem service functions, soil erosion, drought tolerance, forest regeneration, and risk mapping. These studies provide data inputs that inform provincial climate planning — for example, in determining where flood risk is highest, where coastline erosion is most severe, or which agricultural zones are likely to suffer from future climatic changes.

Progress includes:

Completion of workshops and surveys involving both academic experts and local communities to collect data on natural, social, and economic conditions, and on past extreme weather impacts. These feed into identifying priority villages/communes for adaptation action.

Development of research-informed criteria for selecting climate adaptation interventions (which balance ecological potential, cost-effectiveness, social equity, and scalability).

Integration of academic findings into the provincial Climate Change Action Response Plan (2025-2030, vision to 2050) so that master development plans, land‐use plans, and sectoral plans reflect scientific assessments of risk and adaptation potential.

Through these collaborations, Quang Binh is strengthening the scientific basis of its climate policies, making selection and prioritization of adaptation interventions more transparent and robust, and increasing local capacity to monitor and evaluate climate interventions.

Quang Binh has actively involved residents and community groups in the design, implementation, and monitoring of climate adaptation and resilience initiatives, ensuring that local knowledge, needs, and vulnerabilities shape climate action on the ground. A particularly strong example is the VN-SIPA II Project: through this program, local communities in selected communes—Tuyên Hóa, Bố Trạch, and Minh Hóa—are engaged in workshops to identify vulnerable villages and households based on criteria like exposure to climate hazards, ecological potential, social vulnerability, and community consensus. The community is involved in selecting beneficiaries in flood- or storm-prone areas; households share information on past flood or storm damage, which guides where and how resilient homes are built.

Progress from these collaborations includes increased capacity among community groups (better understanding of risk and adaptation options), improved uptake of NbSA practices among smallholder farmers, more resilient housing in vulnerable areas, and more effective targeting of vulnerable households (women-headed, ethnic minorities, PWDs). Local ownership has improved: when community members are part of planning and decision‐making, maintenance and sustainability of adaptation infrastructure improve.

Through these collaborative processes, Quang Binh is making sure climate action is not just delivered to communities, but co-designed with them—and that outcomes are more inclusive, responsive to local vulnerabilities, and more sustainable.

•	Guided implementation of Decree 06/2022/NĐ-CP on GHG reduction and the carbon market, including training for Hue's departments and enterprises on GHG inventory and MRV.
•	Progress: Training workshops completed; Hue has begun integrating local GHG data into the national system.
2. Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD)
•	Oversees the North Central Region Emission Reductions Program (ER-Program), where Hue is one of six participating cities/provinces.
•	Progress: In August 2024, the World Bank disbursed US$51.5 million under the FCPF ERPA; Hue is now implementing the Benefit-Sharing Plan for forest owners and communities, alongside strengthening coastal and watershed forest protection.
3. Ministry of Planning and Investment (MPI)
•	Worked with Hue to integrate green growth and climate resilience objectives into the city's Master Plan 2021-2030, vision 2050 (approved by the Prime Minister under Decision 1745/QĐ-TTg, 30 Dec 2023).
•	Progress: Green economy, circular economy, and climate resilience are now mandatory development targets guiding public investment allocation.
4. Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other central agencies
•	Supported Hue in international cooperation and climate finance mobilization (e.g., GCF, Luxembourg, JICA).
•	Progress: Enabled successful access to GCF/LuxDev CARe Hue (SAP040) and the VIE/301 and VIE/039 adaptation projects.

Collaboration between Hue City and Academia on Climate Issues

1. Hue University and its member institutions

Hue University, particularly the University of Agriculture and Forestry (HUAF) and the University of Sciences, has been a key partner of the city in research and training on climate change adaptation. Joint studies have focused on:

Flood and disaster risk modeling for the Huong River Basin,

Climate-smart agriculture and sustainable livelihoods in coastal and lagoon areas,

Forest carbon stock assessment and REDD+ monitoring.

Progress: Hue University researchers have contributed technical reports that informed the Provincial Climate Action Plan 2021-2030 and local community-based adaptation projects.

2. International Academic Partnerships

Hue University collaborates with foreign universities such as Kyoto University (Japan), University of Greifswald (Germany), and Wageningen University (Netherlands) on climate resilience, biodiversity, and ecosystem-based adaptation.

Example: joint projects on wetland ecosystem services in the Tam Giang-Cau Hai Lagoon and mangrove restoration for climate resilience.

Progress: These partnerships have produced peer-reviewed publications, pilot models of community-based adaptation, and training programs for local officials and students.

3. Data and Knowledge Co-production

Hue academic institutions (notably the Institute of Resources, Environment and Climate Change - IRECC under Hue University) have worked with the city government and international donors to conduct GHG inventories, vulnerability assessments, and circular economy metabolic analyses.

Progress: Results fed directly into Hue's Circular Economy Implementation Plan (2025) and informed adaptation measures under the Green Climate Fund (GCF)-supported projects.

4. Capacity Building and Education

Universities in Hue provide capacity-building programs for local officials, enterprises, and communities on climate change adaptation, disaster preparedness, and environmental management.

Progress: Hundreds of provincial and municipal officials have received training on climate policy integration, GHG monitoring, and community-based disaster risk reduction.
