Hue has engaged with NGOs and associations, and the progress made in climate-related and environmental initiatives:
1. WWF-Vietnam Collaboration
Hue has formalized a robust partnership with WWF-Vietnam, signing a cooperation agreement in October 2024 to support biodiversity conservation, sustainable development, and environmental protection 
Through WWF, the city has connected with major international partners such as the World Bank, ADB, IUCN, USAID, and Germany's environmental agencies—all aiding efforts in forest management, climate adaptation, and enhancing global visibility of Hue's environmental initiatives.
2. UNDP and HueIDS Engagement
Since at least 2020, the UNDP has been a strong collaborator, underpinned by a Memorandum of Understanding to support climate adaptation, biodiversity protection, low-carbon development, and the circular economy in Hue.
Projects and Outcomes:
•	Resilient Housing & Mangrove Restoration: UNDP aided in constructing hundreds of climate-resilient homes and rehabilitating up to 20 hectares of mangrove forests within the Tam Giang-Cau Hai Wetland Protected Area.
•	Low Carbon Urban Innovation: Piloted e-bike sharing systems (200 e-bikes, battery stations) and advanced digital tools like the Climate Business Index and the Disability Digital Map (D Map) in Hue City.
•	Plastic Waste Management: Supported community-based pilot models for managing plastic waste in a circular economy framework. 
Metabolic Analysis & Circular Economy Strategy (2023-2025):
•	Through partnerships between UNDP, Hue Institute of Development Studies (HueIDS), and Shifting Paradigms, Thừa Thiên Huế carried out Vietnam's first-ever metabolic analysis to assess material flows, resource use, and GHG emissions.
•	The analysis revealed the potential to reduce GHG emissions by 16%, cut waste by 89%, and conserve 14% of water—and even help grow local GDP by 4.5% and increase jobs by 2% by 2030.
•	Insights led to the city's Circular Economy Action Plan (Decision No. 284/KH UBND), officially adopted in mid-2025. Implementation involved over ten departments and was supported through stakeholder workshops organized with UNDP to ensure data consistency and robust collaboration.
3. Luxembourg & Green Climate Fund Projects (VIE/301 & VIE/039)
In partnership with the Luxembourg Development Cooperation Agency, Vietnam's government, and the Green Climate Fund, the City launched two significant adaptation projects in December 2024:
•	VIE/301 (2025-2029, USD 10 million): Focuses on enhancing early warning systems, integrating climate-resilience into planning, coastal forest restoration, and building climate-resilient value chains.
•	VIE/039 (2025-2026, over EUR 2 million): Targets climate-smart agriculture, improved financial access for smallholder farmers (especially women and vulnerable groups), market access, and strengthening public-private partnerships.
4. Local Community & Civil Society Engagement
•	The Center for Social Research and Development (CSRD), based in Hue, has long promoted environmental protection and resilience in vulnerable communities through grassroots engagement. It works across the region with partners like VRN, WARECOD, and international NGOs (e.g., Oxfam, NCA, RLS), emphasizing climate adaptation, environmental protection, and social justice
•	The Friends of Hue Foundation, a U.S.-based NGO operating in Hue since 2000, focuses on socioeconomic development, health, and sanitation. While its core mission isn't climate-related, it supports community resilience positively, particularly through mobile health clinics, peer education on sanitation, and shelters for vulnerable youth, which are critical components of climate-resilient social infrastructure.

Green Transport Strategies & Partnerships
1. Public Bike-Sharing (GIZ & Vietsoftpro)
•	A pioneering public bike sharing scheme was initiated through a public-private partnership involving Hue City, GIZ (Germany's development agency), and Vietsoftpro, supported by the DeveloPPP fund. This initiative was launched under the 2021-2026 mobility plan, enabling residents and tourists to access shared bicycles via app-driven systems, and contributing to emissions reduction in urban transport. 
2. E-Bicycle Mobility Rollout (GCOO)
•	The GCOO smart e-bike-sharing system began its service at the UNESCO-listed Imperial City, offering tourists and locals a modern, eco-conscious way to explore Hue. Since its pilot phase, GCOO has expanded to over 20 stations located in strategic city areas—cultural sites, hotels, pedestrian zones, and parks. 
•	GCOO - the smart electric-assist bike-sharing system launched from the Imperial Citadel and has quickly expanded across Hue City with over 200 e-bicycles, underscoring the city's effort to enhance green transportation infrastructure within heritage settings. 
3. Workshops & Advisory Support (UNDP) 
•	A landmark workshop on environmentally friendly public transportation brought together UNDP, local authorities, and experts to highlight and strategize interventions like:
o	Use of e-trucks for waste collection
o	Concessional loans to motivate uptake of electric vehicles
o	Bike and e-bike sharing models as viable, low-carbon transport options
•	The event underscored the link between green transport, improved air quality, public health, and the national mandate for transport electrification. 
4. National Workshop & Policy Alignment (UNDP & MoT)
•	In June 2023, UNDP and the Ministry of Transport co-hosted a national-level workshop in Hue to share global practices related to bicycle and e-bike sharing models. This gathering emphasized the need for enabling policies, proper urban planning, regulatory frameworks, and multi-sector coordination to scale green transport options. 
5. Green Transport within Urban Planning (ADB)
•	As part of the Hue Green City Action Plan, ADB is assisting with the development of integrated, sustainable urban transport systems—although specific green transport components weren't detailed in the source summary.

Here's an overview of how Hue City has engaged with vulnerable population groups around climate-related challenges, and the concrete progress achieved so far:
1. Resilient Housing for Coastal and Disaster-Prone Households
•	Starting as early as 2018, UNDP and the Green Climate Fund helped build climate-resilient homes for vulnerable coastal communities—especially targeting families facing storms, floods, the elderly, persons with disabilities, and ethnic minorities. Homes are elevated above historic flood levels and structurally designed to endure storms.
•	By late 2022, over 7,100 such homes had been completed, many serving as emergency shelters for neighbors during extreme weather events.
These efforts have significantly bolstered safety and recovery capacity for the most at-risk households.
2. Community-Based Adaptation (CBA) in Rural Areas
•	In Hương Phong Commune, a Community-Based Adaptation project was executed in partnership with UNDP, GEF, and CORENARM. A participatory process engaged the local community—mainly smallholder farmers with over 20% poverty rate—to develop climate-adapted livelihoods. Measures included mangrove restoration, salt-resilient rice-fish models, and eco-tourism.
This approach harnessed indigenous knowledge and local buy-in to protect natural resources while diversifying income.
3. Ecosystem-Based Adaptation (EbA) and Inclusive Approaches
•	A project under the ResilNam initiative involved CSRD, local government, Women's Union, and university partners to implement ecosystem-based adaptation—notably urban waterbody restoration and mangrove restoration at Tam Giang Lagoon.
o	Surveys revealed that women and low-income households place a higher value on ecosystem benefits (e.g., flood protection, seafood, recreation)—highlighting how EbA can be inherently inclusive and livelihood-enhancing.
Such measures deliver multi-fold outcomes: reducing disaster risk while directly benefiting the most vulnerable.
4. Large-Scale Climate Adaptation Projects with Vulnerability Focus
•	In July 2024, the Green Climate Fund approved the CARe Hue (VIE/301) project—a USD 10 million initiative extending to 2029—to improve resilience across 28 vulnerable communes. Focus areas include early warning systems, mainstreaming adaptation into local plans, ecosystem restoration (e.g., coastal forests), and climate-resilient value chains. It emphasizes gender inclusivity and tailored support for vulnerable groups.
•	Another linked project (VIE/039, 2025-2026, ~EUR 2 million) zeroes in on climate-smart agriculture, enhancing financial access for smallholder farmers—especially targeting women and vulnerable groups—as well as expanding market linkages and public-private partnerships.
Together, these initiatives are poised to deliver systemic, long-term resilience and inclusive development.

Here's a detailed overview of how Hue City's jurisdiction collaborates with the education sector around climate-related issues, along with the progress made:
1. Enhancing Disaster Resilience in Schools
•	A 2012 study introduced a methodology to assess disaster resilience in schools across Hue. It evaluated key dimensions—physical infrastructure, human resources, institutional readiness, community relationships, and environmental conditions—based on the Hyogo Framework for Action 2015-2030.
•	This tool helps school boards and policymakers identify vulnerabilities and set priorities to improve school safety and integrate disaster risk reduction (DRR) into education.
2. Integrating DRR and Climate Topics into Curriculum
•	A 2025 case study examined the current state of DRR and climate education in primary schools. It found that while DRR content is integrated into subjects like Vietnamese, Nature and Society, Geography, Science, Ethics, and Activities, climate change content remains largely absent from the curriculum.
•	Challenges include limited time, teaching materials, and drills or experiential exercises, although support from the government and committed teachers were cited as pivotal in promoting these topics.
3. Youth Engagement in Climate Awareness
•	The Learning Resource Center (LRC) of Hue University spearheaded a student-led network to deliver information on natural disasters and climate adaptation to vulnerable local communities. This represents a practical channel for students to contribute to resilience-building efforts in rural parts of the city.
4. Environmental Education & Behavior Change in Schools
•	Under the “Plastic Smart Schools” initiative (part of the broader “Hue - Plastic Smart City” project), WWF Vietnam partnered with local schools to foster environmental education. Since 2022, over 54,000 students across 180 schools participated in hands-on waste reduction activities—including sorting, collecting, and recycling.
•	In 83 pilot schools, “Green Houses” were installed to collect recyclables, yielding nearly 30 tons of waste, including more than 5.5 tons of plastic. This initiative significantly influenced household behaviors, as students inspired their families toward more sustainable practices.
Overall Assessment
•	Foundational progress: Hue has laid important groundwork in building educational resilience, embedding DRR education, and promoting environmental awareness through student engagement.
•	Areas for growth: The curriculum still lacks explicit climate change modules, and DRR efforts can be strengthened through resource investment and experiential learning.
•	Positive momentum: Programs like WWF's “Plastic Smart Schools” and youth networks demonstrate that hands-on, school-based initiatives can foster sustainable habits and contribute to community resilience.

Here's a refined overview of how Hue City has been collaborating with communication services to advance climate-related awareness, information dissemination, and resilience-building:
1. Improving Early Warning Systems and Community Communication
•	A key partnership between the Institute for Social and Environmental Transition (ISET) and Hue's Disaster Prevention & Control Office has enhanced the reliability and redundancy of the province's flood and storm Early Warning System (EWS).
o	This included installing backup river gauges to replace failing equipment and ensure timely alerts during extreme weather, particularly useful when main systems fail during power or internet outages.
o	ISET also helped establish a flood database, developed a “flood parking” map for community safety, and provided training on using EWS information.
•	These improvements significantly strengthen community communication capacity—especially to reach vulnerable groups—during climate emergencies.
2. Bridging Information Gaps for Farmers
•	A study on smallholder and ethnic-minority farmers in Hue highlighted a critical disconnect between access to climate data and its practical application in local livelihoods.
o	Many farmers expressed distrust or dissatisfaction with generalized climate information—it did not align with their lived experiences or decision-making needs.
o	The study recommended relying on locally trusted communication channels—such as successful farmers, agri-networks, and market contacts—to convey climate insights effectively.
•	Enhancing the quality and contextual relevance of climate information—rather than just increasing access—is essential for adaptation uptake in rural communities.
3. Student Networks Driving Local Climate Awareness
•	As early as 2013, the Learning Resource Center at Hue University established a student-led information network to deliver practical, climate and disaster adaptation guidance to vulnerable areas in the province.
o	This peer-based, digital-driven initiative helped connect at-risk communities with locally applicable knowledge.
4. Mainstreaming Climate Communication in Provincial Policy
•	Hue City's Climate Action Plan (2021-2031) includes initiatives aimed at strengthening cultural resilience and integrating climate awareness into public infrastructure and relics.
o	Decision No. 1720/QĐ UBND mandates upgrading heritage infrastructure—such as temples, museums, and cultural spaces—to be more resilient to climate impacts.
•	These actions not only preserve cultural heritage but also create public touchpoints for communicating about climate risk.
Overall, Hue's communication strategy for climate issues is multifaceted—spanning emergency infrastructure, localized farmer outreach, community education, and policy-based messaging.
•	Strengths include: integrating technology into EWS infrastructure, leveraging trusted local networks, and embedding communication into cultural assets.
•	Areas for continued growth: expanding climate messaging in rural media, strengthening mobile communication for remote communities, and scaling participatory communication platforms for sustainable awareness.

Below is a detailed overview of how Hue City's jurisdiction has collaborated with the healthcare sector in response to climate-related issues, including progress achieved:
1. Health System Response to Climate-Related Disasters
•	In Phú Vang District, healthcare providers rely on emergency support during extreme weather events—receiving limited in-kind assistance like medicines and supplies from the Hue City's Health Bureau. However, there is no dedicated funding from within the health system for prevention or treatment of climate- and disaster-related health risks. Requests for support go through local government channels and tend to be small and slow.
2. Raising Awareness: Heat Stress & Infectious Diseases
•	In June 2025, Hue hosted a national scientific workshop addressing the pressing health impacts of climate change: rising temperatures, floods, and extreme weather events are intensifying vector-borne and water-borne diseases (e.g., dengue, diarrhea), as well as non-communicable conditions like respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses. Experts emphasized that climate-related health risks necessitate an integrated One Health approach, bringing together the health, environmental, and agricultural sectors for sustainable solutions.
3. Capacity Building via International Support (USAID)
•	The city has also partnered with USAID on health and environment-related programs. While not explicitly focused solely on climate-health resilience, these collaborations include:
o	Support for medical and rehabilitation services for vulnerable populations (e.g., individuals affected by dioxin, war remnants, disabilities)
o	Projects linked to environmental health, disaster risk management, and climate adaptation based on community needs.
These efforts lay the groundwork for integrating climate resilience into community health.
4. Broader Climate Adaptation Framework (Indirect Health Co-benefits)
•	As part of the GCF-supported CARe Hue project (VIE/301), several climate adaptation strategies—including early warning systems, ecosystem restoration, and resilient value chains—could yield health co-benefits via improved environmental conditions, even though health is not a primary target.
Overall Assessment
•	Progress is emerging, especially in terms of intersectoral dialogue and early adaptation planning.
•	However, the health sector's formal integration into climate resilience planning remains limited, with gaps in funding, preparedness, and dedicated programming.
•	The increasing focus on One Health frameworks and international collaboration offers opportunities to strengthen this link going forward.

Here's an overview of how Hue City has collaborated with the financial sector to support climate-related initiatives—and the progress made to date:
1. Green Climate Fund (GCF) Support — CARe Hue Project (VIE/301)
•	The project “Climate Adaptation and Resilience in Hue City” (CARe Hue, code VIE/301) is a flagship initiative co-financed by the Green Climate Fund, the Government of Luxembourg, and Vietnam's government.
•	Approved in July 2024, it has a total budget of USD 10 million, with co-financing of around USD 1.35 million (USD 900,000 in grants and USD 450,000 in-kind).
•	As of mid-2025, approximately USD 1.12 million has already been disbursed. 
Key components facilitated by this finance include:
•	Enhancing early warning systems, ecosystem-based adaptation, and climate-resilient planning.
•	Integrating adaptation across local development strategies.
•	Establishing climate-resilient value chains and promoting gender-inclusive approaches.
•	Managing over 100,000 hectares of agricultural and forestry land for increased resilience and sustainability.
2. Complementary Project — VIE/039
•	Alongside CARe Hue, Hue City launched VIE/039 in December 2024: a EUR 2 million (approx. USD 2 million) initiative targeting climate-smart agriculture and inclusive finance, particularly for women and vulnerable smallholders.
It runs from 2025 to 2026 and is co-funded by Luxembourg and Vietnam, with collaboration from Vietnam Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development.
Primary aims include:
•	Expanding access to climate-smart agricultural financing.
•	Enhancing market access and supporting public-private partnerships.
•	Scaling sustainable and resilient livelihood solutions informed by interventions in CARe Hue.
3. Broader Finance Landscape & Strategic Synergies
•	Beyond specific projects, Hue's work feeds into the broader agenda of climate finance mobilization and private sector engagement, tied closely to Vietnam's NDC goals.
For example, UNDP's work across Vietnam on accelerating private sector engagement in climate-resilient and low-emission investments provides an enabling framework.
•	Additionally, results from Hue's metabolic analysis—a systems-level study of material flows and emissions—are being used to inform interventions and structural planning (e.g., circular economy strategies), which often require access to green/circular financing mechanisms.
Overall Assessment
•	Strong progress: Hue has successfully accessed and initiated major climate finance streams—including both multilateral and bilateral funding—for adaptation and resilience-building.
•	Inclusive impact design: Projects like VIE/039 are explicitly targeting marginalized groups, ensuring that climate finance reaches vulnerable populations.
•	Foundational strategy: The city is building out evidence-informed, strategic frameworks (e.g., circular economy) that position it well for further investment and private-sector engagement.

We are scaling-up to work across all 15 of our constituency local authorities, sector partners and community groups to support more joined-up delivery and collaborative working.

It will also work with local communities and Climate Action Networks to become more resilient to the impacts of climate change and support a just and fair transition to a low-carbon future.

To support Protected Landscapes in meeting their potential nature, climate, people and place DEFRA have established ambitious targets for National Parks. These targets will promote the actions that are most needed to achieve positive changes. They will set the ambition for how Protected Landscapes should achieve 3 outcomes from the Environmental Improvement Plan (EIP) 2023.
Goal 1: Thriving plants and wildlife
Goal 2: Mitigating and adapting to climate change
Goal 3: Enhancing beauty, heritage and engagement with the natural environment 
A range of indicators will be used to measure progress towards the targets and outcomes set out in the framework.

National Park Authorities should embed the targets into their statutory management plans. The national targets extend beyond the next five years and National Park Authorities are expected to develop bespoke interim targets and actions for the current 5 year plans period and a clear pathway for how the longer term targets will be achieved.

The Management Plan is the most 
important document that the National 
Park Authority produces. It sets out a 
long-term vision for the National Park (the entire area, not just the land that is owned by the Authority) and describes the objectives, policies and goals that the National Park Authority, other public bodies and stakeholders will pursue to achieve it. The Management Plan highlights the key priorities for action over the next twenty years to help address the challenges that the National Park will face. The current plan is adopted and is in operation from 2022-2027.

The plan is adopted by the Authority's Members and is available to the public on the Authority's website. The Authority reports on the progress made towards the plan's outcomes in the annual monitoring statement, which is subject to public scrutiny by Members and is published on the Authority's website once adopted. Park Authority produces. It sets out a

El Consorcio para la Gestión del Área Ecológica de Conservación Taita Imbabura, integrado por el Gobierno Autónomo Descentralizado Provincial de Imbabura y los Gobiernos Municipales de Otavalo, Antonio Ante e Ibarra, constituye un referente de articulación interinstitucional para la conservación de ecosistemas estratégicos y la acción climática territorial. Gracias a esta gestión conjunta, el Área Autónomo Descentralizada Taita Imbabura, ha sido incluida dentro de la tercera Contribución Determinada a Nivel Nacional (NDC) del Ecuador como una de las principales iniciativas priorizadas a escala nacional para la mitigación frente al cambio climático. Su incorporación se ubica específicamente en la categoría “Tierras forestales que siguen siendo tierras forestales: aumento anual de las reservas de carbono en la biomasa”, lo que implica un reconocimiento a los esfuerzos locales por vincular la conservación de la biodiversidad con los compromisos internacionales del país en el marco del Acuerdo de París.
El potencial de mitigación proyectado asciende a 12,47 Gg de CO₂ en un horizonte de diez años, tomando como referencia el contenido de carbono de dos ecosistemas claves: el bosque siempre verde andino de ceja andina y el bosque siempre verde andino montano, cuya superficie conjunta alcanza las 253 hectáreas dentro del área protegida. Estos ecosistemas, al mantenerse en pie y en regeneración natural, cumplen un rol fundamental como sumideros de carbono, acumulando en su biomasa aérea y subterránea grandes cantidades de CO₂ que, de no ser retenidas, contribuirían directamente al calentamiento global. Además, la riqueza florística y faunística de estos bosques andinos asegura que los procesos de captura de carbono sean sostenibles en el tiempo y refuercen la resiliencia ecológica frente a presiones como el cambio en el uso del suelo y la expansión agrícola.
Las cifras actuales aun no consideran la totalidad de la superficie del área protegida ni incluyen el aporte del ecosistema páramo, uno de los más representativos y estratégicos del Taita Imbabura. La futura incorporación de este ecosistema en los inventarios y estudios de carbono permitirá ampliar de manera significativa las cifras de mitigación, reforzando el aporte del Taita Imbabura no solo a la NDC nacional, sino también al fortalecimiento de mecanismos de transparencia climática, que constituye un logro técnico, sino también político y social: valida la capacidad de los GADs de impulsar acciones concretas desde lo local, conecta la conservación con la agenda climática global y proyecta oportunidades de financiamiento y cooperación internacional que resultan indispensables para garantizar la sostenibilidad de la gestión ambiental en el territorio.

The Provincial Ordinance No. 03, also known as the Local Coastal Greenbelt Zones in the province of Bataan, is a collaborative inter-local initiative designed to promote the sustainability, development, management, protection, and conservation of the community's environment, natural resources, and cultural heritage. This ordinance seeks to safeguard these valuable assets not only for the benefit of the present generation but also for future generations to come.

A key aspect of this ordinance is the designation of greenbelt zones along the coast, with a particular emphasis on the protection and preservation of mangrove areas. Scientific studies have shown that mangroves play a crucial role in addressing climate change by effectively sequestering greenhouse gases. By recognizing the importance of these coastal ecosystems, the ordinance highlights their vital function in mitigating the adverse effects of climate change.

Through this initiative, the province of Bataan aims to foster environmental stewardship and resilience, ensuring that its coastal ecosystems remain healthy and productive. The Local Coastal Greenbelt Zones serve as a foundation for sustainable development, balancing ecological preservation with the needs of the community.

Cà Mau Province's collaboration with the national government on climate-related issues is robust and multifaceted, primarily driven by the central government's strategic focus on the Mekong Delta, one of the most vulnerable regions to climate change. This partnership is crucial for Cà Mau, as the province's local budget is insufficient to address the scale of climate impacts.
Key Collaborations & Progress
1. National-Provincial Infrastructure and Livelihood Projects
Under the Mekong Delta Integrated Climate Resilience and Sustainable Livelihoods (MD ICRSL) initiative—the World Bank-financed program signed by the Government of Vietnam—Cà Mau received approval for Subproject 1: “Infrastructure to prevent coastal erosion, supply fresh water, and implement shrimp forest livelihood models” in the coastal areas. This subproject is managed locally by DARD (Department of Agriculture & Rural Development) and adheres to both national environmental regulations and the World Bank's safeguard frameworks.
2. Resilient Housing via Central Government and UNDP
In August 2024, a collaboration among the Government of Vietnam, UNDP, and the Green Climate Fund delivered 425 climate-resilient homes to vulnerable coastal households in Cà Mau. This project was implemented with input from national entities, including:
•	The Dike and Disaster Management Authority (Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development),
•	The Department of Housing Management and Real Estate (Ministry of Construction),
•	Together with the Cà Mau Provincial People's Committee and local agencies.
3. National Support for Coastal Erosion and Dike Upgrades
Cà Mau has consistently appealed to the central government for funding to address escalating coastal erosion and enhance dyke infrastructure on both western and eastern coasts. For example, in response to erosion and saline intrusion challenges, the province invested VND 700 billion (~USD 30 million) in adaptation measures. These included emergency embankments in key districts like Rạch Gốc and Vàm Xoáy, supported by national directives.
4. Technical Capacity-Building Initiatives
In July 2025, a GIS and Remote Sensing (RS) training workshop was held for both provincial and national stakeholders to bolster technical capacities for climate change monitoring across the Mekong Delta—illustrating ongoing knowledge-sharing collaborations.
5. Science-Based Monitoring and Net-Zero Planning
Can Tho University's DRAGON Mekong Institute is leading a “Monitoring and Adaptation Community” in Cà Mau, in close cooperation with national partners. This initiative supports climate risk management and connects the province to the broader Net-Zero Science and Technology Program, aiming for national net-zero-emission alignment by 2050.
6. Nature-Based Solutions Promotion via IUCN Partnership
Through support from the national government and international partners, the IUCN is implementing a mangrove restoration project (2023-2027) in Cà Mau. As of mid-2025, over 80,000 mangroves have been planted across 18 hectares, with a target of 160,000 trees by project end. The project also includes community training in sustainable aquaculture techniques tied to climate resilience.

Academic institutions, particularly Can Tho University's DRAGON-Mekong Institute, are actively collaborating with Cà Mau Province on a variety of climate-focused initiatives—from ground-level monitoring systems to strategic groundwater modeling and resilient livelihood strategies. These efforts are making tangible progress in empowering local communities, integrating scientific insights into policy frameworks, and fostering cross-sectoral capacity-building.Key Collaborative Initiatives
1. “Climate Change Adaptation in Cà Mau” — Can Tho University (DRAGON-Mekong)
•	Launch: On January 11, 2024, the Department of Agriculture & Rural Development of Cà Mau joined hands with the Climate Change Research Institute (DRAGON Mekong) at Can Tho University to kick off a project focused on climate adaptation in the province 
•	Goals and Components:
o	Enable farmers in the northern part of the province to access real-time environmental data like salinity, pH, or water levels.
o	Build an automated data processing and modeling tool that uploads simplified insights to a web platform.
o	Establish a local “monitoring community” to collect data from remote locations and train farmers on how to use the information to adapt their practices 
•	Current Status: The project is in progress with the aim to empower around 100 farmers using training materials and data insights 
2. Community Consultation for Climate Monitoring — DRAGON-Mekong & ADM
•	Date & Context: On April 16, 2024, DRAGON Mekong and ADM (Archer Daniels Midland Group) held a consultation in Thới Bình district to plan the “monitoring and adapting community.” This included defining information needs, training approaches, and equipment-sharing methods with local communities 
3. Groundwater Modeling Workshop — DRAGON-Mekong Institutes
•	Event: In June 2025, a scientific workshop presented research results on groundwater resources and their climate-change-induced fluctuations in Cà Mau.
•	Collaborators: Researchers from DRAGON-Mekong, Can Tho University (including Assoc. Prof. Dr. Văn Phạm Đăng Trí), along with local experts and governance stakeholders participated.
•	Content:
o	Status of groundwater use and management in the province.
o	Water quality trends analyzed using PCA methods based on data from 2015-2024.
o	Future groundwater scenarios for 2030, 2050, and 2070 modeled using MODFLOW and IPCC climate projections (SSP2 4.5, SSP5 8.5).
o	Proposed integrated solutions: automated monitoring, data sharing across sectors, community engagement, and policies aligned with climate realities.
•	Impact: This workshop fostered critical feedback from local authorities and technical experts, laying the foundation for integrated groundwater policy and scientific monitoring systems 
4. Community-Based Technical Support — Groundwater Monitoring Tools
•	Through the “Climate Adaptation in Cà Mau” initiative, DRAGON-Mekong engaged directly with communities in Trí Phải and Tân Lộc (Thới Bình district):
o	Distributed 20 portable water-quality monitoring devices to cooperatives, enabling measurements of salinity, pH, temperature, EC, and TDS.
o	Trained local farmers on using these devices and interpreting data to implement climate-smart rice-shrimp co-culture techniques.
o	Generated two functional “Observation & Adaptation Communities” composed of around 30 active members who share results and practices via social media 
5. Sustainable Livelihoods & Circular Economy Model
•	Project Completion: By early 2025, the Institute for Environment and Natural Resources, in collaboration with the provincial Department of Science & Technology, wrapped up a technical project on sustainable livelihood models suited to challenging natural conditions in Cà Mau.
•	Activities Conducted:
o	Demonstrated pilot models in Đầm Dơi, Trần Văn Thời, and U Minh districts.
o	Delivered training to over 70 farmer households and commune-level officials in December 2024.
o	Held a provincial-level closing workshop in January 2025 with multiple stakeholders to consolidate findings and uptake strategies 
6. Tourism & Climate Adaptation Workshop
•	Date & Purpose: On November 3, 2023, Can Tho University's Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities collaborated with the provincial Department of Culture, Sports & Tourism and the Union of Science and Technology Associations to host a workshop on integrating climate adaptation into eco-tourism development.
•	Focus: This forum evaluated current opportunities and risks for climate-resilient tourism in Cà Mau and emphasized the need for capacity building among tourism operators, legal frameworks, and environmental safeguards

Cà Mau Province's collaboration with non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and associations on climate-related issues is a vital component of its adaptation strategy. The province actively seeks and receives support from various international and local partners, leveraging their expertise, funding, and community-based approaches to address its unique vulnerabilities.
Key Aspects of Collaboration and Progress
1. Partnership with International NGOs: Cà Mau works with several prominent international NGOs, which provide both financial and technical support for specific projects.
•	UNDP and the Green Climate Fund (GCF): A significant collaboration has been on the project to build storm-resilient homes for poor and near-poor households. The province, in partnership with the UNDP and GCF, has successfully handed over hundreds of safe houses to vulnerable families, demonstrating a tangible outcome of this collaboration. This project not only provides secure shelter but also builds community resilience against extreme weather events.
•	World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF): WWF has a long-standing partnership with Cà Mau, focusing on mangrove forest conservation and sustainable livelihoods. A recent project, launched in December 2022, aims to enhance the climate resilience of mangrove ecosystems and communities. The project includes planting new forests, applying sustainable management guidelines for shrimp-forest models, and training local communities to improve their income from these eco-friendly practices. The goal is to benefit thousands of local farmers and children directly and indirectly.
•	International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN): Cà Mau collaborates with IUCN to restore coastal mangrove forests as a nature-based solution to coastal erosion and climate change. A project running from 2023 to 2027 aims to plant hundreds of thousands of new mangrove trees. The collaboration includes field surveys, community training on sustainable aquaculture, and promoting integrated farming models to enhance resilience and economic benefits for local communities.
•	Save the Children International: This organization, in collaboration with the Cà Mau Women's Union, has implemented projects to strengthen community capacity for climate change mitigation and disaster risk reduction. These projects focus on improving access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services and promoting the Safe School Model, benefiting thousands of people, including children.
•	World Vision International (WVI): WVI has implemented a project on community-based adaptation to climate change in Cà Mau. The project conducted studies and workshops to assess community vulnerabilities and needs, focusing on areas in Nam Can and Ngoc Hien districts. The project aims to improve education and awareness, strengthen community security, and support livelihoods to enhance resilience.
2. Collaboration with Associations and Local Organizations: The province also works closely with various local and national associations, often in partnership with international NGOs, to facilitate project implementation and community outreach.
•	Cà Mau Union of Friendship Organizations: This provincial union plays a central role as a bridge between the local government and foreign NGOs. It helps coordinate and manage projects, ensuring they align with provincial priorities.
•	Provincial Women's Union: The Women's Union is an active partner in many projects, particularly those focused on empowering women and children to cope with climate impacts. Their local networks are crucial for reaching vulnerable households and implementing community-level activities.
Progress and Outcomes
•	Increased Community Resilience: The partnerships have led to tangible progress in building the resilience of local communities through the provision of safe housing, improved WASH services, and the establishment of disaster preparedness plans.
•	Sustainable Livelihood Models: The collaboration has helped to scale up and certify sustainable economic models like 'shrimp-forest' farming. This not only benefits the environment but also provides a stable, high-value income for local residents, directly improving their livelihoods.
•	Financial and Technical Support: The collaborations have secured significant external funding and technical expertise, which Cà Mau would not have been able to access on its own. This support is crucial for implementing large-scale and complex climate adaptation projects.
•	Blue Carbon Initiatives: Projects with organizations like WWF and GIZ are helping Cà Mau lay the groundwork for participating in the international carbon credit market. By developing a mechanism to measure and verify carbon sequestration, the province can potentially generate a new and sustainable source of income from its mangrove forests.

Cà Mau Province's collaboration with industrial companies on climate-related issues is a strategic pillar of its development plan, focusing primarily on two key areas: the transition to a low-carbon energy economy and the creation of sustainable, climate-resilient value chains in agriculture and aquaculture. This partnership is crucial for Cà Mau, as the private sector provides the necessary capital, technology, and market connections to scale up climate action.

1. Renewable Energy Sector
Cà Mau has identified renewable energy as a key driver of its green economic transition. The province has vast potential for wind and solar power due to its long coastline and high number of sunny hours. Collaboration with the private sector has been instrumental in turning this potential into tangible progress.

Wind Power Investment: The province has actively attracted investment from domestic and foreign companies for wind power projects. As of late 2023, Cà Mau had 14 wind power projects with a total capacity of 694.2 MW already in commercial operation. Several other projects are either under construction or in the final stages of approval. The province's government has a policy of providing maximum support to investors, particularly in land clearance and grid infrastructure development, to ensure projects can be implemented smoothly.

Solar Energy Development: The private sector is also a key partner in solar power. The province has seen significant investment in both large-scale solar farms and decentralized rooftop solar systems. Over 2,800 rooftop solar systems have been installed across the province, with a total capacity of nearly 300 MWp. These systems are often installed on businesses and households, allowing for decentralized energy production and reduced reliance on the national grid.

Hydrogen Production: Several investors have expressed interest in researching and developing hydrogen production projects using wind and solar power in Cà Mau. The province has even included a total hydrogen production capacity of around 86,248 tonnes per year in its former energy development plan, indicating a strategic long-term collaboration with industries to develop a new, high-value clean energy source.

2. Sustainable Seafood and Agriculture Value Chains
Collaboration with the industrial and private sectors is critical for scaling up Cà Mau's climate-resilient aquaculture models.

Role of Processing and Export Companies: The private sector, especially seafood processing and export companies, plays a vital role in the success of the 'shrimp-forest' model. These companies act as a bridge between the farmers and the international market. They are the primary buyers of sustainably-produced shrimp, providing a stable and reliable market for local communities.

Certification and Value Chains: Industrial partners are essential for creating sustainable and branded value chains. By buying from farmers who adhere to 'shrimp-forest' and other certified production models, these companies help Cà Mau's products earn international certifications (e.g., ASC, BAP). These certifications not only enhance the value of the products but also guarantee their traceability, which is increasingly important for consumers and global markets. The private sector's investment in processing, cold storage, and logistics is a crucial part of this value chain, ensuring that the benefits of sustainable farming reach the end consumer.

Progress and Outcomes

Economic Diversification and Growth: The collaboration has helped Cà Mau move from a resource-dependent economy to one that is increasingly driven by clean energy and high-value sustainable agriculture. The revenue from these sectors contributes to the province's economic growth while reducing its carbon footprint.

Increased Investment: By streamlining administrative procedures and providing support, the provincial government has successfully attracted billions of dollars in private sector investment for green projects, which are essential for both climate adaptation and mitigation.

Branding and Market Access: The partnership with seafood processing companies has allowed Cà Mau to establish itself as a source of premium, climate-friendly seafood on the international stage. This branding provides a competitive advantage and a sustainable source of income for local communities.

Below is a refined overview of how Cà Mau Province collaborates with residents and community groups on climate-related issues, highlighting key initiatives, achievements, and community-driven progress:
Community-Led Climate Adaptation in Cà Mau
1. “Monitoring & Adapting Community” in Trí Phải & Tân Lộc
•	Project Overview: As part of the “Climate Change Adaptation in Cà Mau” initiative led by DRAGON Mekong (Can Tho University), 20 water-quality monitoring devices were distributed to two farmer cooperatives in Trí Phải and Tân Lộc communes. These devices measure salinity, pH, temperature, electrical conductivity (EC), and total dissolved solids (TDS), aiding informed decision-making in rice-shrimp farming.
•	Community Impact: These efforts established two active “Monitoring & Adaptation Communities”, each comprising around 30 engaged members. They share insights and data results via social media platforms. Moreover, monitoring information from these communities—covering 10 sites per commune—is integrated with data from the provincial Department of Agriculture & Rural Development.
2. Consultative Engagement & Participatory Planning
•	A community consultation was conducted in April 2024 involving DRAGON Mekong, ADM, and residents of Trí Phải and Tân Lộc. The session identified local challenges—especially salinity intrusion and lack of early-warning data—and co-designed support strategies, including handheld salinity and pH meters.
3. Community-Based Adaptation with World Vision
•	Earlier, World Vision International (WVI) collaborated with local communities on a Community-based Adaptation to Climate Change (CBAC) pilot in Nam Càn and Ngọc Hiển districts.
•	The project comprised Participatory Rapid Appraisal (PRA) sessions in 6 villages (15-20 participants per group), capturing insights on vulnerabilities, disaster histories, and climate impacts. Outcomes informed tailored action plans targeting education, training, infrastructure, and adaptive livelihoods.
4. Nature-Based Community Engagement: Mangrove Restoration
•	In a collaborative mangrove restoration initiative (2023-2027), communities are actively introduced to integrated livelihoods—shrimp-mangrove, shrimp-crab, and multi-species farming under a mangrove canopy.
•	The project includes training on sustainable aquaculture, environmental best practices, and community awareness-building, aligning with national climate strategy and leveraging natural carbon sequestration mechanisms.
5. Community Resilience via Resilient Housing
•	Through a national partnership involving the central government, UNDP, and the Green Climate Fund, 425 climate-resilient houses were delivered to vulnerable coastal households in Cà Mau. Although largely implemented via governmental channels, the project directly benefitted local families, bolstering community resilience to floods and storms.
6. Tourism Communities and Climate Awareness
•	Many of Cà Mau's eco- and community-based tourism sites operate closely with local residents who depend on natural and cultural assets. Climate impacts—such as salt intrusion, extreme weather, and erosion—threaten infrastructures, livelihoods, and heritage.
•	In response, local authorities and community members are encouraged to develop resilient tourism strategies, such as diversifying activities, strengthening environmental safeguards, and raising awareness through cooperative engagement.

•	Wind Power Expansion: As of mid-2025, Cà Mau has 14 commercially operating wind power projects totaling 694.2 MW, with more under development.

•	Electricity Export Strategy: Provincial authorities are crafting plans to export electricity—possibly to Singapore. Discussions with Singaporean officials and developers like VSIP suggest interest in cross-border grid linkage and industrial collaboration.

Ca Mau is actively collaborating with the transport sector to bolster its resilience against rising sea levels, coastal erosion, and extreme weather events. This partnership manifests through integrated development planning, large-scale infrastructure projects, and a strategic focus on building a sustainable and adaptive transport network for the future.

The core of this collaboration is the integration of climate change adaptation and mitigation measures into the province's socio-economic development plans, including specific strategies for the transport sector. The provincial 'Action Plan to Respond to Climate Change for the period 2021 - 2030, with a vision to 2050' serves as a foundational framework, guiding the transport sector's development to align with climate resilience goals.

Infrastructure Fortification and Adaptation
A significant aspect of the collaboration is the implementation of large-scale infrastructure projects that serve dual purposes: enhancing transport connectivity and protecting the coastline. A prime example is the ongoing construction of the Western Sea Dike. This project not only aims to prevent coastal erosion and safeguard livelihoods but also incorporates a crucial coastal transport route. This integrated approach ensures that investments in transport infrastructure simultaneously contribute to climate adaptation.


Similarly, numerous projects are underway to reinforce riverbank and coastal erosion protection systems, which often include the construction or upgrading of adjacent road networks. These initiatives are critical in a province where a dense network of rivers and canals is integral to both transportation and daily life. By building climate-resilient transport infrastructure, Ca Mau aims to ensure the continued movement of goods and people, even in the face of climate-related disruptions.

Progress and Future Outlook
The collaboration between Ca Mau Province and the transport sector has yielded tangible progress in enhancing the region's climate resilience. Key achievements include:

Integrated Planning: Climate change considerations are now a mandatory component of transport infrastructure planning and development in the province.

Dual-Purpose Infrastructure: The construction of multi-functional projects, such as the Western Sea Dike with its integrated coastal road, demonstrates a strategic approach to maximizing the benefits of public investment.

Enhanced Connectivity: Upgraded and newly constructed transport routes are improving connectivity between different parts of the province, which is vital for emergency response and economic development in the face of climate challenges.

Looking ahead, the collaboration will continue to focus on developing a modern, synchronous, and climate-resilient transport system. This includes further investments in upgrading road and waterway networks, with a particular emphasis on ensuring their durability against the impacts of climate change. The overarching goal is to transform the transport sector into a key enabler of Ca Mau's sustainable and climate-resilient development, ensuring the province can withstand the challenges of a changing climate while continuing to foster economic growth and improve the lives of its residents.

Phu Yen Province's collaboration with the national government on climate-related issues is primarily executed through the implementation of major National Target Programs and ADB-funded projects, focusing heavily on resilient infrastructure and poverty reduction.
Key Collaboration Mechanisms and Progress
1. The CRIEM Project (Climate Resilient Infrastructure)
This is the most significant, high-profile collaboration focused directly on climate adaptation and social equity.
•	Project Name: Construction of Climate-Resilient Infrastructure for Ethnic Minorities (CRIEM) - Phu Yen Sub-project.
•	National Government Role: The project is part of a larger national initiative, with the national government (specifically the Ministry of Finance) negotiating the official ADB (Asian Development Bank) loan agreement on behalf of the country. The project agreement was formally witnessed by the Prime Minister and other high-ranking government officials, underscoring its national importance.
•	Phu Yen's Role: The Provincial People's Council approved the investment plan (approximately 911.47 billion VND, including ADB loan capital and provincial counterpart funds). The province's Project Management Unit is the main investor, responsible for implementation.
•	Progress: The project has passed the necessary legal and financial approval stages at both the central and provincial levels. The province is currently focused on the critical stage of site clearance, land price appraisal, and infrastructure relocation to ensure the project—slated for construction start—can proceed on schedule.
2. National Target Programs
Phu Yen integrates climate adaptation into broader national socioeconomic development plans, which are centrally directed and funded.
•	National Target Program on Sustainable Poverty Reduction (2021-2025):
o	Collaboration: The provincial government receives central budget capital allocated under this program (specifically for projects like diverse livelihood development and job creation for the poor). This funding, in part, supports models that enhance livelihoods and increase income stability, which is essential for low-income households to cope with climate-related shocks.
o	Focus: Provincial plans prioritize projects that reduce the poverty rate, especially among ethnic minorities and in remote areas, by strengthening their capacity to cope with climate-related risks and ensuring they have access to basic social services.
•	National Target Program on Socio-Economic Development in Ethnic Minority and Mountainous Areas:
o	Collaboration: This program provides a major source of central government funding (over 323 billion VND for the 2021-2025 period in Phu Yen) specifically directed at improving infrastructure and production capacity in vulnerable minority communities.
o	Goal: To build resilient infrastructure (e.g., water supply systems, roads) and support production methods that are better suited to environmental changes.
3. Training and Awareness
The central government actively collaborates on capacity building.
•	Training and Communication: Agencies like the Central Propaganda and Training Commission and the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE) organize training conferences in Phu Yen. These events are aimed at provincial and district-level officials, mass organizations, and the media to enhance their knowledge and skills in communicating, adapting to, and resolving issues related to environmental protection and climate change.
In summary, the collaboration ensures that Phu Yen's local actions—from building roads and water systems to promoting poverty reduction models—are financially backed by the national budget and international ODA (mediated by the central government) and align with Vietnam's overarching national strategies on climate change and sustainable development.

Phu Yen Province's collaboration with public authorities, primarily Central Government Ministries and neighboring provinces, focuses on integrating national strategies, receiving technical and financial support, and inter-regional cooperation for climate resilience and green development.
Key Areas of Collaboration and Progress
1. Integration of National Strategies and Policy Guidance
Phu Yen's efforts are guided by national programs, requiring close coordination with central agencies, especially the Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment (MONRE).
•	National Programs Implementation: The province actively implements national frameworks like the National Target Program to Respond to Climate Change and the National Strategy on Green Growth.
•	Capacity Building and Awareness: There's ongoing cooperation to enhance knowledge for local officials and the community.
o	Progress: The Central Propaganda Department and experts from MONRE regularly organize training conferences in Phu Yen to disseminate knowledge and skills for effective communication on environmental protection and climate change response.
•	Planning Integration: Provincial planning (Socio-Economic Development Plan, construction, irrigation, agriculture) is continuously revised to integrate climate change scenarios (such as sea level rise and extreme weather) based on data and guidance from MONRE's specialized agencies.
2. Major Infrastructure Projects and Investment
Phu Yen partners with the Central Government to secure funding for critical, climate-adaptive infrastructure.
•	ODA Projects: The province acts as the implementing authority for large-scale, climate-related projects funded through Official Development Assistance (ODA), which are typically brokered and supervised by central Ministries.
o	Example: The CRIEM Project (Climate-Resilient Infrastructure for Ethnic Minorities) focuses on investing in combined infrastructure, such as clean water supply systems, to enhance the livelihood development and climate adaptation capabilities of vulnerable communities.
•	Green Energy Development: In line with national energy transition goals, the province promotes and licenses clean energy projects.
o	Progress: Phu Yen has successfully attracted investment for solar and wind power projects (e.g., 6 completed solar power projects), contributing to national efforts to reduce carbon emissions and increase the use of renewable energy.
3. Inter-Provincial and Regional Cooperation
Collaboration with neighboring provinces is essential for managing shared resources and regional climate impacts.
•	Regional Cooperation Agreements: Phu Yen, along with Khanh Hoa and Ninh Thuan provinces, signed a comprehensive agreement to cooperate on various socio-economic issues, including:
o	Environmental Protection, Disaster Prevention, and Climate Change Adaptation.
o	Goal: This cooperation aims to leverage regional strengths and coordinate efforts to tackle common climate-related challenges like drought, saltwater intrusion, and coastal erosion across the South Central Coast region.
•	Agricultural Adaptation: The provincial Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (DARD) coordinates with the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) to promote sustainable practices.
o	Progress: This includes implementing measures to adjust water regulation, convert crop structures in drought-prone or saltwater-affected areas, and invest in upgrading irrigation systems to cope with prolonged and severe drought conditions.

Phu Yen Province's collaboration with academia on climate-related issues is primarily focused on research, strategic planning, and capacity building, leveraging expertise from provincial and national institutions.
Key Areas of Collaboration and Progress
1. Research and Scientific Consulting
The Province works with scientific institutions to develop data-driven adaptation strategies.
•	Risk Assessment and Planning: The provincial Department of Natural Resources and Environment (DONRE) has cooperated with research bodies like the Southern Sub-Institute of Meteorology, Hydrology, and Environment to prepare a draft action plan for climate change response. This collaboration focuses on:
o	Data Collection: Gathering and analyzing data on temperature, rainfall, and humidity trends in the province.
o	Impact Assessment: Evaluating the specific impacts of climate change, such as sea level rise, coastal erosion, and changes in weather patterns (typhoons, floods), particularly on key sectors like coastal tourism and infrastructure.
•	Progress: This collaboration is an ongoing process to establish the scientific basis for the province's future climate adaptation policies and investments.
2. Infrastructure Technology and Monitoring
Academic expertise is directly integrated into major climate-resilient projects.
•	CRIEM Project (Climate-Resilient Infrastructure for Ethnic Minorities): The province's multi-component, ADB-funded CRIEM project specifically includes a component for 'Upgrading Technology and the Disaster Risk Analysis System.'
o	Academic/Technical Input: This component relies on technical expertise to implement monitoring infrastructure, such as building a fixed hydrographic station, upgrading meteorological stations, installing water level and rainfall measurement stations, and deploying advanced equipment like remote-controlled hydrographic meters.
o	Goal: The installation and operation of this high-tech network require cooperation with relevant technical academies and institutes to ensure data is collected and analyzed effectively for sustainable, climate-resilient infrastructure development.
3. Policy Forums and Green Growth Strategy
Academia contributes to high-level strategic discussions.
•	Policy Dialogue: The provincial government, led by its senior leadership, actively participates in and hosts scientific seminars and workshops on topics like 'Phu Yen - Sustainable Green Development.'
o	Collaborators: These events involve scientists, university professors, research institute representatives, and professionals (often members of the Phu Yen Alumni Association in Hanoi).
o	Goal: The aim is to gather expert consultation and intellectual resources to help the province integrate green growth and climate-resilience principles into its long-term development plans, such as the provincial master plan for 2021-2030, with a vision to 2050.
4. Local University Engagement (Phu Yen University)
The local university is positioned to become a regional center for research and technology transfer.
•	Focus: While specific climate research projects are not always publicly detailed, Phu Yen University (PYU) is a key partner in the province's goal to develop high-quality human resources and serve as a research and technology transfer center for the South Central Coast and Central Highlands region. This strategic focus is essential for training the personnel needed for climate adaptation and green economic transition.
•	Progress: PYU actively signs cooperation agreements with other regional universities, which includes joint research and sharing of results, indirectly enhancing the capacity of its faculty and students to tackle local environmental and climate issues.

Phu Yen Province actively collaborates with Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs), particularly in disaster relief, environmental protection, and strategic planning for climate change adaptation.
Key Areas of Collaboration and Progress
1. Disaster Relief and Emergency Aid
NGOs and international organizations are crucial partners for immediate response to climate-related disasters.
•	Post-Disaster Support: After major events like Typhoon Damrey (2017), Phu Yen received significant emergency aid and relief funds (over $1 million in one period) mobilized by international NGOs and organizations.
•	NGO Partners: Organizations such as Loreto (Australia), MCNV (Netherlands), and various international humanitarian programs have provided support for timely recovery, helping the province mitigate the damage caused by natural disasters.
2. Community-Based Climate Adaptation Projects
Collaboration focuses on local-level action, environmental protection, and building community resilience.
•	Mangrove Restoration: The province has engaged in projects to restore coastal mangrove forests—a critical natural defense mechanism against sea level rise and coastal erosion—often with technical assistance from partners.
o	Example: Collaboration on a project for 'Afforestation on coastal sand dunes in Central Vietnam,' involving entities like the Institute of Resources and Environment at Hue University and a German partner company, aims to strengthen coastal protection.
•	Environmental Protection Models: The Vietnam Fatherland Front (VFF) Committee of Phu Yen Province, a key association/social organization, implements model projects at the residential level to raise awareness and promote community action.
o	Progress: These models involve forming core groups and self-governance groups in residential areas to disseminate knowledge, commit to environmental protection, and develop solutions for adapting to unusual natural disasters.
•	ODA Projects with NGO-like Scope: Large-scale projects, such as the CRIEM Project (Climate-Resilient Infrastructure for Ethnic Minorities), although officially financed by international financial institutions and managed by the provincial government, function with the core development goals often emphasized by NGOs: reducing poverty and inequality through climate-resilient infrastructure (e.g., clean water systems) in vulnerable ethnic minority communities.
3. Strategic Consultation and Green Growth
Local associations and expatriate Vietnamese groups play a role in high-level policy advice.
•	Phu Yen Fellow-Countrymen Association in Hanoi: This association, composed of successful professionals, experts, and scientists from Phu Yen, actively collaborates with the provincial government.
o	Progress: They co-organized the scientific workshop 'Phu Yen - Sustainable Green Development,' offering specialized expertise, ideas, and strategies to integrate green growth, science-technology, and innovation into the province's key planning documents and political resolutions. This input is crucial for shaping Phu Yen's long-term, climate-conscious development trajectory.

Phu Yen Province actively collaborates with residents and community groups to address climate-related issues primarily through awareness campaigns, adapting agricultural production, and integrating environmental protection into rural development programs. This collaboration is often facilitated by mass organizations like the Fatherland Front and the Farmers' Union.
Key Areas of Collaboration and Progress
1. Public Awareness and Capacity Building
The provincial authorities rely on collaboration with the community and mass organizations to spread knowledge and change behaviors related to climate change.
•	Training and Communication: Local government agencies, especially the Department of Natural Resources and Environment (DONRE), coordinate with the Fatherland Front, Farmers' Union, and other local organizations to organize training sessions and communication campaigns.
o	Progress: These activities aim to raise awareness of climate change impacts (like drought, floods, and sea level rise) and promote practical solutions. Training workshops have been organized for community leaders and residents to enhance their capacity for proactively responding to climate change.
•	Community Competitions: Local authorities encourage community-level initiatives and creativity.
o	Progress: Competitions like 'Farmers adapting to Climate Change,' often held by the District Farmers' Union, encourage residents to develop and share creative, low-cost solutions, such as reusing materials for household items.
2. Climate-Adaptive Production Models
Collaboration focuses on restructuring local production to be more resilient to the impacts of extreme weather.
•	Agricultural Restructuring: The province works with farmers, guided by the local Department of Agriculture, to shift production patterns due to increasing drought and saltwater intrusion.
o	Progress: Farmers have actively converted from water-intensive rice to drought-resistant crops like peanuts (groundnuts) and other annual plants in water-scarce areas. The local government supports this by providing guidance on water regulation and new farming techniques.
•	Coastal Protection: In coastal areas facing severe erosion, the collaboration involves community monitoring and implementation of solutions.
o	Progress: Local communities are engaged in efforts to protect and restore marine resources and coastal ecosystems, contributing to local resilience against rising sea levels and storm surges.
3. Community-Driven Environmental Protection
Community participation is central to improving environmental quality, which is intrinsically linked to climate resilience.
•	New Rural Development (Nông Thôn Mới - NTM): Community groups, mobilized by the Fatherland Front and other political-social organizations, are crucial to achieving the environmental criteria of the NTM program.
o	Progress: This includes establishing and maintaining community-managed models for environmental protection, focusing on issues like waste segregation at the source, preventing pollution, and general sanitation in rural areas. The collective effort contributes to a greener, cleaner environment, a key element of long-term sustainable development and climate mitigation.
•	Tree Planting: Phu Yen has an ambitious tree-planting project that relies heavily on community involvement.
o	Progress: The project aims to plant 15 million trees from 2021-2025, with local communities, organizations, and businesses participating to increase forest cover, which helps absorb CO2 and protects against natural disasters like landslides and floods.

La Municipalidad de San Borja ha desarrollado diversas colaboraciones estratégicas con entidades gubernamentales, empresas privadas y organizaciones de la sociedad civil para impulsar acciones climáticas sostenibles e inclusivas.

Uno de los ejemplos más relevantes es su participación en el Programa Municipal EDUCCA, del Ministerio del Ambiente (MINAM), a través del cual se desarrollan campañas educativas, como “Ecocanje” y jornadas de arborización, que involucran activamente a vecinos, colegios, juntas vecinales y recicladores.

También ha establecido alianzas con empresas privadas en actividades de responsabilidad social y ambiental. Por ejemplo, en campañas de recolección de residuos electrónicos o reciclaje de plástico, donde empresas locales aportan logística y premios sostenibles para incentivar la participación ciudadana.

Asimismo, San Borja colabora con universidades y centros de investigación, como la PUCP, en estudios sobre eficiencia energética, gestión de áreas verdes y uso responsable del agua, lo que permite diseñar políticas basadas en evidencia científica.

Además, el distrito participa en redes internacionales como el Pacto de Alcaldes por el Clima y la Energía, que fomenta la cooperación intermunicipal y el acceso a financiamiento climático internacional

column17: En 2013, el Ayuntamiento de Zapopan firmó un convenio de colaboración con la agencia de Naciones Unidas para los asentamientos humanos ONU-Hábitat. El convenio serviría para elaborar el índice de Prosperidad urbana de Zapopan y formar parte de la red global de Ciudades Prósperas, pero adicionalmente, esta iniciativa permitió desarrollar la Estrategia Territorial Zapopan 2030 (ETZ2030). Dicha estrategia territorial fue desarrollada por un equipo interdisciplinario de expertos locales e internacionales, que trabajaban en conjunto con el equipo de la Oficina de Proyectos Estratégicos del Gobierno de Zapopan, para estudiar el territorio y elaborar estrategias de planeación y gestión urbana con un importante componente de participación ciudadana. Cabe mencionar que se trató de un ejercicio innovador, ya que dentro del proyecto de ciudades prósperas que ONU-Habitat impulsa a escala global, Zapopan es el primer municipio que se ha enfocado en la implementación de una visión territorial a partir de estos conceptos y donde ésta se vincula con los objetivos de la agenda urbana de Hábitat III., lo anterior, bajo l premisa de que la implementación de las mejores prácticas modernas de evaluación socioambiental de impactos (evaluación ambiental estratégica, evaluación de efectos acumulativos, evaluación de impacto social y a la salud en contexto de cambio climático, entre otras) resulta indispensable ante su poca eficacia para las actuales manifestaciones de impacto ambiental o impacto urbano. No se adjunta el archivo de la ETZ2030 completo, solo una síntesis, debido a que excede las dimensiones permitidas. El documento completo se puede consultar en: https://portal.zapopan.gob.mx/Zapopan2030/EstrategiaTerritorialZapopan2030_DOCUMENTO2.pdf
